A Probabilistic Deep Ensemble Framework for the Objective Assessment of Friedreich Ataxia
Maneesha Randeniya , Kanishka Ranaweera , Student Member, IEEE, Thang Ngo , Louise A. Corben , Senior Member, IEEE, Malcolm Horne , Member, IEEE, Pubudu N. Pathirana 
Abstract ? Objective: Friedreich Ataxia (FRDA) is a rare neurodegenerative disease in which reliable clinical as- sessment is often limited by inter-rater variability and the sensitivity of conventional rating scales. This study aims to develop an objective, data-driven framework that predicts FRDA severity with greater accuracy while also quanti- fying prediction uncertainty. Methods: Inertial data were collected from the Ataxia Instrumented Measurement Cup (AIM-C) while standardized motor tasks were performed. A probabilistic deep ensemble framework was implemented by combining InceptionTimePlus and RNN-FCNPlus archi- tectures, each augmented with bounded probabilistic out- put heads. Models were trained on raw IMU signals using a negative log-likelihood loss function with regularization strategies, and their performance was evaluated on an independent test set. Ensemble predictions were gener- ated by aggregating mean and variance estimates across models. Results: There was strong agreement between the proposed ensemble and clinical mFARS scores, reflected in a Pearson correlation of 0.81, Spearman?s correlation of 0.76, R� of 0.46, RMSE of 10.30, and MAE of 8.79 on the unseen test set. Uncertainty was systematically evaluated using Uncertainty Characteristics Curves (UCC), where the ensemble achieved an Area Under UCC (AUUCC) of 8.83. Conclusion: The probabilistic deep ensemble framework enables more accurate prediction of FRDA severity while providing uncertainty estimates that indicate the reliability of each prediction. Significance: This study demonstrates that wearable sensing with deep learning enhances ob- jective and reliable severity evaluation in FRDA while im- proving robustness in small and heterogeneous biomedical datasets.
Index Terms? CNN, Deep Ensemble, Friedreich Ataxia, FCN, InceptionTime, RNN, Time Series, Uncertainty Quan- tification

I.	INTRODUCTION
RIEDREICH Ataxia (FRDA) is a progressive autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder, usually beginning in adolescence, with significant involvement of the central and peripheral nervous systems, and the heart. The predominant neurological features are peripheral neuropathy and ataxia, most apparent in movements of the upper limbs and during speech, walking, and eye movements. Progression leads to loss of independence in activities of daily living (ADL) and eventually being unable to walk. Convention- ally, the severity of neurological impairment is assessed using clinical examination, which is quantified using standardised rating scales such as the modified Friedreich Ataxia Rating Scale (mFARS). Clinical rating scales are inherently sub- jective and susceptible to inter-rater variability.
These limitations have motivated the search for objective, repeatable, and clinically relevant assessments to better quantify disease progression and serve as endpoints in clinical trials. The Ataxia Instrumented Measurement Cup (AIM- C), which measures movements used to drink from a cup, was developed to address these concerns. This device captures high-resolution kinetic and kinematic data using inertial measurement units (IMUs) and pressure sensors. Features including movement smoothness, trajectory variability, and grip force modulation are strongly correlated with the mFARS. This assessment provides a more ecologically valid and objective assessment of upper limb ataxia than conventional clinical scales,.
Earlier studies?used these features in models of the mFARS assessment built using traditional Machine Learning (ML) techniques such as Extra Tree Regressor, Support Vector Regression, and Gaussian Process Regression. However, better modelling of clinical scales might be achieved by applying recent advances in analytical techniques to these high- dimensional time series signals from IMUs. In this regard, Deep Learning (DL) models are powerful tools for analyzing complex biomedical data with distinct advantages over traditional ML methods. Unlike ML approaches, which often depend on manually crafted features and extensive domain expertise, DL architectures autonomously learn hierarchical patterns directly from raw input data. This may provide advantages in the case of signals recorded by the AIM- C, which may contain intricate temporal dependencies and subtle patient-specific variations. The predictive accuracy and generalizability of diverse clinical tasks have improved when models such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Recurrent architectures have been used.
Despite their advantages, the deployment of DL models is hindered by limited availability of labeled data in rare diseases such as FRDA,. Recruitment constraints, ethical considerations, and resource limitations are all impede the size of data sets, and the clinical context often limits the use of conventional data augmentation methods, such as random sampling or synthetic signal generation. Furthermore, new models should not only perform well with small datasets but should also quantify uncertainty in predictions. This aspect has been largely overlooked in prior FRDA research using ML models,. Clinical decisions that are contingent on progression require confidence in the model, and uncertainty estimation provides this. Confidence in the model is largely overlooked by ML models that measure the severity of ataxia in FRDA.
To address these challenges, we present a probabilistic deep ensemble framework using sensor-derived time series data designed specifically to assess the severity of ataxia in FRDA. The proposed approach integrates two complementary DL architectures and employs a custom probabilistic output head that constrains predictions within the valid clinical score range while simultaneously estimating the associated uncertainty. Despite being trained on a limited dataset, our ensemble model outperformed both traditional ML baselines and individual DL models in terms of predictive accuracy and robustness. Moreover, generating prediction-specific confidence intervals introduces a critical layer of transparency and reliability, positioning our framework as a clinically meaningful enhancement to current assessment practices.
II.	RELATED WORK
A.	Objective Assessment in FRDA and the Role of AIM-C
The severity of ataxia in FRDA is conventionally quantified by the mFARS, a quantified rating of the clinical assessment,. As these scales are inherently subjective and prone to inter-rater variability, sensor-based devices, such as the AIM-C, were developed to provide objective assessments of motor dysfunction.
The AIM-C quantifies upper limb ataxia from sensor data of movements that simulate drinking from a cup. Detailed motion and grip dynamics are captured by a triaxial accelerometer, gyroscope, and pressure sensor embedded within the device. Data from these sensors provides high-resolution measurement of features such as movement smoothness, trajectory stability, and grip control.
Previous studies demonstrated that AIM-C features corre- lated strongly with clinical scales, and mapped to mFARS scores. These earlier analyses were hampered by sensor artifacts that arose when the AIM-C was used in the real- world clinic. This was addressed by adding a robust anomaly detection framework, which filtered out anomalous segments by leveraging Isolation Forests and adaptive median filtering. This improved AIM-C reliability in predictions over repeated trials of the drinking task.
This prior work confirmed that the AIM-C was an eco- logically and clinically valid assessment of ataxia in FRDA that used multimodal sensing capability. These characteristics make it particularly well-suited for integration with DL models that learn directly from sensor signals.
 
B.	ML and DL for Biomedical Time Series
The application of ML and DL techniques to biomedical time series data captured from IMUs has grown rapidly in parallel with the proliferation of wearable sensors in health- care. For example, established ML algorithms, such as Support Vector Machines, Random Forests, and Gradient Boosting, use manually extracted features from IMU signals to classify motor impairments and estimate gait-related metrics,. However, feature engineering requires domain-specific knowledge for these methods, which limits scalability and generalization into the broader patient population.
Recently, attention has shifted to end-to-end DL architec- tures that directly learn hierarchical temporal representations from raw IMU sequences. Models such as Convolutional Neu- ral Networks (CNNs), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), and their hybrids have shown improved performance in clinical applications,. A systematic review of AI and wear- able sensorsfound that while ML is still used in 76% of IMU-based healthcare studies, the field is shifting towards DL, especially in neurological assessment, where complex data requires more expressive models. They also reported that a small median dataset size of around 50 participants or less makes robust generalization difficult, and underscores the need for models that perform well despite few participants, such as occurs in rare diseases.
DL models are improving data efficiency and robustness by increasing the use of self-supervised learning, contrastive representation learning, and temporal attention mecha- nisms. In particular, significant gains can be achieved when labeled data are limited, using self-supervised pretrain- ing on IMU data. These advances highlight the value of DL architectures in enhancing prediction accuracy when data is limited.

C.	Uncertainty Estimation in Clinical Prediction Models
Although DL models accurately predict the reference stan- dard that they model, their reliability needs to be quantified, especially in a clinical setting. This becomes important when data is limited and factors influencing patient variability are not well understood.
Uncertainty estimates communicate the confidence of model predictions. Recent studies have introduced principled uncertainty-aware frameworks across various domains. For instance, Lu et al.proposed a rater confusion estimation approach to model inter-rater disagreement in video-based Parkinson?s disease severity scoring, effectively handling label uncertainty in noisy clinical datasets. Similarly, sampling- based methods such as Monte Carlo Dropout and deep en- sembles are widely applied in medical image classification to capture both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. Sarawgi et al.further demonstrated the utility of multimodal uncertainty-aware ensembling in Alzheimer?s disease severity estimation, where prediction confidence informed the weight- ing of model components.
Despite these advances, systematic integration of uncertainty quantification into clinical prediction pipelines remains limited. The failure to report uncertainty in many clinical

D.	Motivations and Contributions
While previous studies using ML models using sensor- derived features from AIM-C have demonstrated their validity for assessing the severity of upper limb ataxia in FRDA, limitations remain:
?	No prior work incorporates estimates of the uncertainty of prediction of the severity of ataxia.
?	Models mostly rely on handcrafted features, reducing generalizability to new patient cohorts or unseen vari- ations in sensor data.
?	DL architectures have not been used to model raw IMU signals directly from the AIM-C, limiting the ability to capture complex temporal patterns.
?	Ensemble-based DL frameworks have not been studied to establish whether they improve estimates of ataxia severity using AIM-C data.
Our work addresses these gaps by introducing a probabilistic deep ensemble framework that (1) learns directly from raw AIM-C signals, (2) jointly predicts both disease severity and associated uncertainty, and (3) maintains robustness in small sample scenarios typical of rare disease datasets like those from individuals with FRDA.
 
III.	METHODS
A.	Participants and Data Collection
Clinical and AIM-C data were collected from 10 age/sex matched controls and 53 adults whose diagnosis of FRDA was confirmed by genetic testing. Ethical approval for the study was granted by the Monash Health Human Research Ethics Committee (HREC 02114A) and the Royal Children?s Hospital Research and Ethics Committee (HREC 74035). All participants provided written informed consent in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
Participants were adults with FRDA who, at the time of study, were capable of performing upper limb motor tasks using sensor-based assessment. Participant demographics for each cohort are summarized in Table I. The mFARS was used to assess overall clinical severity. The mFARS was used to clinically assess severity and comprises standardized measurements of upper and lower limb function, bulbar function, and upright stability. It is scored out of 93, with a greater score indicating greater clinical severity.
In a standardized task, each participant used the AIM-C device to simulate drinking from a cup. The participant was required to lift the cup from a table, bring it to their mouth to simulate drinking, and then return it to the starting position. A single instance of the drinking task was defined as a trial, and a single test was the performance of five consecutive trials.
TABLE I
PARTICIPANT CHARACTERISTICS ACROSS TRAINING AND TEST COHORTS
To establish test-retest reliability, 22 individuals completed multiple tests within a single session, referred to here as retests. One or two follow-up tests were performed by a subset of participants (n = 26), with a minimum interval of one year (ranging from 1 to 2 years), allowing for a longitudinal analysis
B.	Preprocessing and Signal Segmentation
Raw multivariate time-series data were acquired from the AIM-C device during each standardized drinking task. Each test recording consisted of five consecutive trials, with the device capturing synchronized signals at a sampling rate of 100 Hz from a triaxial accelerometer, triaxial gyroscope, and a pressure sensor, yielding seven channels in total. The recorded data were stored in structured files, each representing one test session.
To enhance signal quality, a denoising process was applied to all channels before further analysis. This included median filteringwith a kernel size of five to suppress high- frequency noise, followed by mean subtraction to eliminate low-frequency drift. All signals were subsequently aligned to zero at the first time step to correct for initialization offsets.
Trials were segmented into the component tests using denoised signals and an automated segmentation strategy that identified temporal boundaries corresponding to distinct instances of the drinking motion. From each test recording, five non-overlapping trials were extracted based on these boundaries, ensuring high-quality temporal alignment with the performed motor task.
Since individual trials varied in length across participants, all segments were zero-paddedto match the maximum se-
 
quence length observed in the dataset. This allowed consistent temporal dimensions across samples, facilitating DL model compatibility. Each segment was subsequently normalized using z-score normalization, computed across the training set to ensure distributional consistency. Channel-wise mean and standard deviation values were calculated and applied uniformly to the training and test sets.
Following preprocessing, the final dataset consisted of 560 trials derived from 112 AIM-C test recordings from both individuals with FRDA and control participants. These were then partitioned into fixed training and test cohorts, as detailed in Table I. All trials were formatted as three-dimensional tensors of shape (N, C, T ), where N is the number of trials, C = 7 is the number of sensor channels, and T is the padded temporal length. This structured dataset served as the input for all DL experiments and was consistently used across model training and evaluation.
C.	Deep Ensemble Architecture
For accurate and interpretable prediction of ataxia severity from AIM-C sensor signals, we propose a deep ensemble learning framework that integrates two time-series models adapted for probabilistic regression. The base models, Incep tionTimePlus and RNN FCNPlus, are standard architectures from the tsai python library, which were independently trained and combined at the prediction level to leverage their complementary strengths. Although these architectures are not inherently probabilistic, we equipped each with a custom regression head designed to produce bounded severity pre- dictions along with associated uncertainty estimates, thereby enabling interpretable interval outputs.
The InceptionTimePlus model is adapted from the InceptionTime architecture by Fawaz et al., designed for time-series classification. It employs multiple convolutional filters with varied kernel sizes and dilation rates in parallel, allowing it to extract features at multiple temporal scales. Each inception module incorporates optional bottleneck layers, max- pooling branches, and Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) blocks to improve discriminative capacity. As the InceptionTimePlus model?s architectural properties capture both short-term and long-term temporal patterns, subtle variations in upper-limb motor activity typical of sensor-based assessments can be recognised.
The RNN FCNPlus model is a hybrid architecture that combines a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) with a Fully Convolutional Network (FCN). The RNN branch models long-term temporal dependencies using stacked vanilla RNN layers applied to the transposed input sequence. In parallel, the FCN branch extracts localized features through a cascade of 1D convolutional layers followed by global average pooling. The outputs from both branches are concatenated to form a joint feature representation. This hybrid design leverages the temporal modeling capacity of RNNs to capture long-range dependencies. At the same time, the convolutional branch im- proves robustness by extracting local patterns and suppressing noise through hierarchical filtering and pooling.
To ensure predictions adhere to the clinical bounds of the mFARS scale (), both models use a bounded probabilistic head. This head transforms learned features into a predictive mean (�) and variance (�2) using a two-layer feedforward network. The output mean is passed through a sigmoid activation (denoted as sigmoid) and scaled by 93 to constrain it within the clinically valid range (maximum mFARS score), while the variance is activated using the softplus function to ensure positivity: each model?s variance captures aleatoric uncertainty, that is, the irreducible noise inherent in the data (e.g., natural variability in individual performance). When multiple models are ensembled, the variability among their predictions further captures epistemic uncertainty, which arises due to model uncertainty stemming from limited training data. D.	Incorporating Uncertainty via Predictive Variance
The use of ensemble aggregation not only enhances pre- dictive robustness but also the quantification of principled uncertainty. Since each model produces both a predictive mean and variance, aggregating these across multiple models yields a combined estimate of total uncertainty. This is particularly valuable in clinical contexts where confidence in automated
 
This score provides an intuitive, percentage-based measure of prediction certainty, facilitating real-world applicability of the proposed model in clinical settings.

incorporate several inductive biases that contribute to robust generalization. InceptionTimePlus leverages residual connections, stochastic depth, and squeeze-and-excitation blocks, all of which help preserve expressive capacity while reducing the risk of overfitting. Meanwhile, RNN FCNPlus combines temporal summarization via gated recurrent units (GRUs) with convolutional feature extraction, enabling it to suppress local signal noise and avoid over-specialization to individual timesteps. Furthermore, the use of global average pooling layers in both models (as opposed to flattening operations) sig- nificantly reduces the number of trainable parameters, which further improves stability in small-sample training regimes.
Input signals were standardized based on training set statis- tics and reshaped to the channel-first format required by the architectures. A 90/10 training-validation split was used within the training cohort for hyperparameter tuning and early stopping, while the final performance was reported on the separate test cohort described in Section III-F. This consistent partitioning scheme ensured robust and unbiased evaluation of model generalizability.
F.	Evaluation Setup
1)	Model Performance Evaluation: Model performance was evaluated on a completely held-out test set consisting of seg- mented AIM-C trials from individuals unseen during training. Each test sample consisted of five consecutive trials, consistent with the structure of the training dataset. For each sample, severity predictions were generated for all five trials, and the median-of-5 value was used as the final prediction. This aggregation strategy mitigates intra-subject variability and enhances robustness to transient anomalies in sensor signals. The predicted mFARS scores were compared against ground-truth clinical scores using four standard regression metrics: Pearson correlation coefficient (r), Spearman rank correlation coefficient (?), Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), and Mean Absolute Error (MAE). These metrics provide a comprehensive assessment of both linear and monotonic
relationships, as well as absolute prediction accuracy.
2)	Uncertainty Quantification: To assess the reliability of predictive uncertainty, we adopted the Uncertainty Charac- teristic Curve (UCC) framework, as proposed by Navra?til et al.. For each test sample, the ensemble model produces a predictive mean � and standard deviation � derived from the aggregated posterior. Using these values, a prediction interval was constructed:
Lower = � ? k�,	Upper = � + k�
where k is a scaling factor controlling the confidence level of the interval. For evaluation, prediction intervals were com- puted over a continuous range of k values, and the correspond- ing miss rate (proportion of ground truth values falling outside the interval) and normalized bandwidth (interval width relative to the full mFARS range of 93) were recorded.
where c ?balances the trade-off between interval compactness and coverage. In this study, c = 0.7 was used to prioritize tighter intervals. The scaling factor k? that minimizes this cost defines the OOP.

A lower AUUCC indicates better calibration: narrow intervals that cover most true values. This framework offers a holistic and interpretable measure of uncertainty quality in regression tasks with bounded outputs.

IV.	RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
A.	Performance Comparison of Machine Learning and Deep Learning Models
This section compares the predictive performance of tra- ditional ML algorithms and modern DL architectures for mFARS score estimation. The evaluation was conducted using consistent train?test splits across both ML and DL pipelines.
1)	Machine Learning Models: ML models were trained on handcrafted features derived from raw sensor signals, using a feature extraction framework developed in our prior work. These features encapsulated clinically relevant temporal and frequency-domain characteristics of motor function and served as inputs to a diverse set of regression models. All models were implemented and evaluated using the PyCaret Python library, which provided a unified pipeline for preprocess- ing, model training, hyperparameter tuning, and performance evaluation.
As shown in Table II, the Extra Trees Regressoroutperformed all other ML models, achieving a Pearson cor- relation of r = 0.7287, Spearman correlation ? = 0.6963, R2 = 0.4372, RMSE = 10.54, and MAE = 8.34. These results highlight its effectiveness in modeling complex non-linear relationships and reducing variance through random feature selection and split generation.
Other tree-based models, such as Decision Trees and Ran- dom Forests, demonstrated moderate performance, with r values between 0.66 and 0.69 and RMSE values between 11.45 and 11.88. While the Decision Tree Regressor achieved the highest ? = 0.7162, it lagged in overall accuracy. Boost- ing methods (Gradient Boosting, AdaBoost) performed less favorably, and the LightGBM Regressor yielded the weakest results, with R2 = 0.03 and RMSE = 13.82, indicating poor generalization.
2)	Deep Learning Models: To exploit temporal patterns in raw IMU sequences, we employed a set of DL architectures provided by the tsai python library, which offers state- of-the-art time series regression models. These models were

Among the DL models, RNN FCNPlus achieved the high- est predictive performance, with a Pearson correlation of r = 0.753, Spearman correlation of ? = 0.690, RMSE of 10.74, and MAE of 9.02, as shown in Table II. This indicates a strong linear relationship between predicted and actual scores (r > 0.75), suggesting the model?s robustness in modeling the underlying disease severity.
Other high-performing models included InceptionTimePlus (r = 0.718, RMSE = 11.78) and RNN FCN (r = 0.751,
RMSE = 11.17), both of which leveraged architectural in- novations to effectively model long-range temporal depen- dencies. The performance of Fully Convolutional Network (FCN) variants was weaker (e.g., FCN with r = 0.634 and RMSE = 13.97), consistent with prior observations that purely convolutional models may underperform on tasks requiring sequential context modeling.
3)	Comparative Analysis: Overall, DL models consistently outperformed classical ML models across most of the evalu- ation metrics. The best DL model (RNN FCNPlus) achieved a 3.3% improvement in Pearson correlation and a 0.20-point reduction in RMSE compared to the best ML model (Extra Trees). This confirms the advantage of directly modeling raw temporal dynamics rather than relying solely on derived features.
Nonetheless, the Extra Trees Regressor performed surpris- ingly well given the simplicity and reduced data requirements of ML pipelines, which may be advantageous in settings with limited computational resources. These findings empha- size the trade-offs between interpretability, performance, and infrastructure demands when selecting predictive modeling approaches for clinical use in rare diseases such as FRDA.

B.	Ensemble Model Performance
Given the inherent challenges posed by small-sample biomedical datasets, ensemble learning offers a powerful strat- egy to enhance model robustness and mitigate variance. In this study, we constructed multiple deep ensemble models by com- bining complementary architectures from the tsai library. To ensure robust and fair evaluation, all individual and ensemble models were trained and evaluated five times using different training?validation splits, and the final performance metrics were reported as the average across these runs. Performance metrics reported in Table II represent the mean across these repetitions.
1)	Performance Across Ensemble Architectures: Among all evaluated ensembles, the model E1: InceptionTimePlus + RNN FCNPlus yielded the best predictive performance, with a Pearson correlation of r = 0.8109, Spearman correlation of ? = 0.7565, RMSE of 10.30, and MAE of 8.79. This model benefited from the complementary strengths of the Incep- tionTimePlus architecture, which is known for its multiscale temporal filters, and RNN FCNPlus, which captures sequential dynamics via recurrent units. The high correlation scores (both r and ? > 0.75) underscore the ensemble?s ability to capture complex, nonlinear progression patterns that typify mFARS scores. These results are summarized in Fig. 2, highlighting the comparative advantage of E1.
The next best-performing ensemble, E5: RNN FCNPlus + ResNet, achieved r = 0.773 and RMSE of 11.91, demon-

Interestingly, ensemble E4: RNN FCNPlus + ResNetPlus + InceptionTimePlus showed slightly weaker performance (r = 0.711), despite incorporating three strong models. This may reflect over-smoothing due to excessive averaging or possible architectural redundancy, where the combined models offer overlapping rather than complementary representations.
2)	Comparison with Individual DL Models: Among all evaluated models, the ensemble E1 (InceptionTimePlus + RNN FCNPlus) achieved the best overall performance, out- performing both its individual counterparts and other ensemble variants across all key evaluation metrics. Specifically, E1 im- proved the Pearson correlation from 0.7528 (RNN FCNPlus) to 0.8109 and the Spearman correlation from 0.6897 to 0.7565, indicating stronger alignment with clinical severity rankings. Furthermore, E1 reduced the RMSE from 10.74 to 10.30 and MAE from 9.02 to 8.79, demonstrating improvements in both error magnitude and consistency. While not all ensem- ble models yielded performance gains across every metric, E1 distinguished itself by combining architectural diversity with probabilistic modeling to deliver robust, monotonic, and clinically meaningful predictions.
 
Other ensemble models also surpassed the perfor- mance of their constituent base models. For example, E5: RNN FCNPlus + ResNet achieved r = 0.773, higher than both RNN FCNPlus (0.753) and ResNet (0.681). Similarly, E4, composed of RNN FCNPlus, ResNetPlus, and Inception- TimePlus, reached r = 0.711 and ? = 0.704, offering balanced improvements over its base models across both linear and rank-based correlations. Although E4 exhibited a slightly higher RMSE (11.87), its stronger correlation metrics suggest improved generalization and reduced bias in capturing disease- specific trends.
By averaging predictions from independently trained mod- els, the ensembles helped mitigate overfitting and smoothed fluctuations due to random initializations or data partitioning. This strategy was especially valuable in the current study, where the dataset is limited in size and exhibits inherent vari- ability in participant signal profiles. The ensemble approach captured a broader and more stable mapping from time series features to clinical severity, offering a reliable foundation for objective assessment in FRDA.
3)	Cross-Validation Performance Consistency: To assess the generalization ability of the proposed ensemble (E1), we conducted a 5-fold cross-validation. Fig. 3 illustrates predicted versus actual mFARS scores for each fold, with the red dashed line indicating ideal predictions.
The ensemble achieved an average Pearson?s r of 0.825 and Spearman?s ? of 0.700 across folds, confirming strong agreement between predicted and true scores. The consistent performance highlights the model?s robustness under varying data splits and supports its reliability in clinical settings.

C.	Uncertainty Quantification Analysis
In addition to point prediction accuracy, evaluating the reliability of model-generated uncertainty intervals is essential in clinical contexts. Table III summarizes the uncertainty quantification results for all DL models. Two key metrics, which are Miss Rate and Bandwidth, were measured at each model?s OOP on the UCC, while AUUCC serves as an overall indicator of uncertainty quality.
Among individual models, RNN FCNPlus achieved the best overall performance, with the lowest AUUCC score of 9.11, and the lowest Miss Rate (0.333), indicating its ability to produce compact and reliable prediction intervals. In compar- ison, models such as FCN and FCNPlus exhibited high miss rates (0.722 and 0.667, respectively) despite having narrow bandwidths, reflecting poorly calibrated uncertainty estimates. Ensemble models demonstrated further improvements in uncertainty estimation. The top-performing ensemble, E1: In- ceptionTimePlus + RNN FCNPlus, maintained a low AUUCC (8.83) with a balanced Miss Rate of 0.417 and Bandwidth of
8.66. Other ensembles, such as E4 and E5, also performed competitively, with AUUCC values of 10.07 and 10.31, re- spectively. While their AUUCC scores were marginally higher,Normalized Bandwidth
Fig. 4. UCC curves for the top three individual and ensem- ble models. The plot highlights the best-performing individual model (RNN FCNPlus) and ensemble model (E1: InceptionTimePlus + RNN FCNPlus). Miss Rate and Bandwidth are computed at each model?s OOP on the UCC. these models still surpassed most individual architectures in overall calibration. The UCC curves in Fig. 4 further illustrate these findings. In particular, RNN FCNPlus and E1 exhibited favorable trade- offs between coverage and interval width across operating points. This reinforces the effectiveness of uncertainty quan- tification, especially in scenarios involving limited and hetero- geneous data, as apparent in FRDA.

V.	CONCLUSION
This study presents a probabilistic deep ensemble frame- work for objectively predicting neurological disease severity in FRDA using time series data from a single instrumented task. By integrating bounded probabilistic output heads with ensemble learning, the proposed approach delivers accurate mFARS predictions alongside uncertainty intervals that indi- cate the reliability of each prediction. Among the evaluated models, the InceptionTimePlus + RNN FCNPlus ensemble achieved the highest overall performance in both predictive accuracy and uncertainty calibration. These results support the clinical feasibility of AI-driven severity assessment in rare neurological diseases. Future directions include incorpo- rating pretrained time series models, extending applicability to pediatric populations, and modeling longitudinal disease progression to strengthen robustness and translational impact.


Alpha-lipoic acid supplementation improves pathological alterations in cellular models of Friedreich ataxia

Abstract

Background
Friedreich ataxia (FRDA), the most common autosomal recessive ataxia, is characterized by degeneration of the large sensory neurons and spinocerebellar tracts, cardiomyopathy, and an increased incidence of diabetes. The underlying pathophysiological mechanism of FRDA, driven by a significantly decreased expression of frataxin (FXN), involves increased oxidative stress, reduced activity of enzymes containing iron?sulfur clusters, defective energy production, calcium dyshomeostasis, and impaired mitochondrial biogenesis, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction.

Methods
This study is aimed at evaluating the role of alpha-lipoic acid (ALA) in reversing the pathological alterations in fibroblasts and induced neurons derived from FRDA patients. Iron accumulation, lipid peroxidation, transcript and protein expression levels of frataxin, mitochondrial proteins, as well as mitochondrial bioenergetics were examined.

Results
Treatment with ALA was able to correct partially the pathological alterations in mutant fibroblasts. The optimal ALA concentration was dependent on the number of expanded GAA triplet repeats in the FXN gene. The positive effect of ALA was also confirmed in induced neurons derived from FRDA mutant fibroblasts. Our results also suggest that the positive effect of ALA was mediated by Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptor Gamma activation.

Conclusions
Our results suggest that ALA treatment can increase the expression levels of frataxin and reverse the mutant phenotype in cellular models of FRDA.

Background

Friedreich ataxia (FRDA; OMIM #229,300) is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disease with a prevalence of approximately 1 in 50,000 individuals, characterized by progressive gait and limb ataxia, sensory loss, muscle weakness, dysarthria, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The disease is caused by pathogenic variants in the frataxin (FXN) gene that commonly consist of expanded GAA triplet repeats in its first intron resulting in transcriptional silencing and subsequent reduction in frataxin protein expression. While healthy individuals carry fewer than 33 repeats, 96% of FRDA patients are homozygous for a hyperexpansion of GAA codon that can exceed 1000 GAA copies. The remaining 4% of patients are compound heterozygous, possessing a point mutation in one FXN allele and an expanded GAA repeat in the other. The length of the GAA expansion is negatively correlated with the expression of the encoded protein, frataxin.

Frataxin is a ubiquitously expressed mitochondrial protein essential for iron homeostasis, biosynthesis of iron-sulfur clusters (ISCs), and cellular energy production. Reduction in frataxin expression impairs the activity of ISC-dependent enzymes and the mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes, disrupts calcium homeostasis, promotes mitochondrial iron accumulation, increases oxidative stress, and results in cell death. These functions affect to the activity of key enzymes such as aconitase and mitochondrial complex I, as well as DNA synthesis and repair mechanisms. The primary affected areas include large sensory neurons of the dorsal root ganglia (DRG), the dentate nucleus of the cerebellum, and a variety of other central nervous system (CNS) cells. However, cardiomyopathy is the most prominent cause of death for FRDA patients.

Depending on the frataxin expression levels, FRDA patients exhibit two different phenotypes: the classical phenotype, characterized by early onset and rapid progression, and the atypical phenotype with late onset and slower progression. This disease is commonly associated with progressive ataxia and muscle dystrophy. In addition, FRDA often leads to severe symptoms, including cardiomyopathy, scoliosis, diabetes, sensorineural hearing loss, and optic neuropathy.

Several experimental models of FRDA have been developed to better understand the disease's underlying mechanisms, such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae yhf?, Droshophila melanogaster UAS-DfhIR, and FXN knock-in mouse models. All these models showed iron accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and high levels of oxidative stress. Nevertheless, the sequence of pathophysiological events underlying FRDA remains poorly understood.

Nowadays, two main strategies are being explored to develop potential treatments for FRDA. The first focuses on increasing frataxin expression levels using genetic therapies, while the second aims to reduce oxidative stress using iron chelators or antioxidants.

Due to its antioxidant power and neuroprotective properties, ALA is a promising compound for reducing pathophysiological alterations in cellular models of FRDA. Its effects are attributed to its ability to scavenge reactive oxygen species (ROS), induce the expression of antioxidant systems, and reduce cellular damage. Furthermore, ALA is able to regenerate endogenous antioxidants such as glutathione and vitamin E. Additionally, ALA activates transcription factors, including PPAR?, Nrf2 or PGC1�, promoting mitochondrial biogenesis. Moreover, it has been demonstrated that PPAR? agonists rescued phenotypic features in cellular and animal models of FRDA.

The protective effect of ALA has been suggested in several neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's, Huntington's, and multiple sclerosis. However, further studies are needed to fully elucidate the therapeutic potential and effectiveness of ALA.

This study evaluates the effects of ALA on the pathophysiological features of FRDA in patient-derived cellular models, aiming to determine its therapeutic potential in alleviating oxidative stress and restoring frataxin expression and mitochondrial function.

Methods

Reagents
Sudan Black (199664), (?�) �-LA (62320), Luperox(r) DI (tert-Butyl peroxide) (168521), Prussian blue (03899), paraformaldehyde (PFA) (158127), dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) (17093) and trypsin were purchased from Sigma Chemical Co. (St. Louis, MO). Phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) (102309) was obtained from iNtRON Biotechnology (Seongnam, Republic of Korea).

(ab178860), anti VDAC (ab14734), anti-SDHB (ab14714),Goat Anti-Rabbit IgG H&L (ab6721), Rabbit Anti-Mouse IgG H&L (ab6728), Rabbit Anti-Goat IgG H&L (ab6741), and Aconitase kit were purchased from Abcam (Cambridge, UK). Anti-iron response protein 1 (IRP1) (sc-166022), anti-ferritin light chain (sc-74513), anti-SOD1, anti-catalase (sc-2711803) and deferiprone (sc-211220) were purchased from Santa Cruz Biotechnology (Dallas, TX, USA). Anti-PhosphoPGC1� (S571) was purchased from R&D Systems (Minneapolis, MN, USA). Anti-actin was acquired from MyBiosource (San Diego, California, USA). Anti-lipoic acid antibodies (437695) were purchased from Merck (Rahway, NJ, USA). Anti-TOMM20 antibodies (H00009804-M01) and a cocktail of protease inhibitors (complete cocktail) were purchased from ThermoFisher Scientific (Waltham, MA, USA). The Immun Star HRP substrate kit was from Bio-Rad Laboratories Inc. (Hercules, CA, USA). The information about the reagents is included in Table 1 in Supplementary Material.

Ethical statements
Approval of the ethical committee of the Hospital Universitario Virgen Macarena y Virgen de Roc�o de Sevilla (Spain) was obtained, according to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and all the International Conferences on Harmonization and Good Clinical Practice Guidelines.

Cell cultures
Two cell lines of fibroblasts derived from patient skin biopsies (P1 and P2) and two age- and sex-matched controls fibroblast cell lines from healthy volunteers (C1 and C2) were grown in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM) (Gibco(tm), ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) supplemented with 10% FBS (Gibco(tm), ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), 100 mg/ml penicillin/streptomycin. Fibroblasts were cultured at 37�C and 5% CO2. Patient 1 (P1) harbours 350/350 GAA repeats and patient 2 (P2) carries 450/560 GAA repeats in the first intron of FXN. All experiments were performed using cells with a passage number below 12. Patients and control fibroblasts were treated with ALA for seven days.

Generation of induced neurons (iNs) from control and FRDA (P1 and P2) fibroblasts by direct reprogramming
Neurons were generated from FRDA and control fibroblasts by direct reprogramming as previously described by Drouin-Ouellet et al.. Controls and patients-derived fibroblasts were seeded in �-Slide 4-Well plates (Ibidi Inc., Martinsried, Germany). The day after, dermal fibroblasts were infected with one-single lentiviral vector containing neural transcription factors (Acsl1 and Brn2) and two shRNA against the REST complex, generated as previously described. Cells were infected with a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 30. The plasmids were a gift from Dr. Malin Parmar (Developmental and Regenerative Neurobiology, Lund University, Sweden). After 24 h, medium was replaced with fresh fibroblast medium. Fibroblasts medium was replaced with neural differentiation medium after 48 h (NDiff227; Takara-Clontech) as described. Neural differentiation medium was refreshed every 48-72 h. On day 21, neural differentiation medium was also supplemented with ALA. Twenty-seven days post-infection neuronal cells were identified by the expression of Tau. DAPI?+?and Tau?+?cells were considered induced neurons. Images were taken at DeltaVision system with an Olympus IX-71 fluorescence microscope with 60???oil objective and analysed by Fiji-ImageJ software, version 2.9.0.

Iron metabolism
Prussian blue staining
Iron accumulation was assessed by Perls' Prussian blue staining in fibroblasts and neurons. Images were taken by light microscopy AE2000 (Motic, Spain) and an integrated camera Axioxam ERc) with a 20X objective and analyzed by FIJI-ImageJ software, version 2.9.0. Iron content was also measured in cell culture extracts using mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) (Tarohda et al., 2005). ICP-MS was performed with an Agilent 7800 mass spectrometer (Agilent Technologies, Sana Clara, CA, USA). Extracts were obtained by acid digestion with HNO3.

LIP determination
We determined labile iron levels by a Calcein-AM (calcein-acetoxymethyl ester, Invitrogen) assay. Cells were incubated with Calcein-AM, which crosses the membrane and reacts with esterases located in the cytosol, resulting in the formation of calcein. Calcein is a fluorochrome that is not able to permeate through membranes, so it remains trapped in the cytosol. Calcein loses its fluorescence when bound to iron and recovers it upon the release of iron, allowing the estimation of intracellular labile iron levels.

First, cells were seeded in 12-well plates. 6???104 cells were seeded in each well and incubated at 37 �C for 24 h. At the start of the assay, the cells were washed twice with 1X PBS, then cells were incubated with calcein-AM at 0.25 ?M for 30 min at 37�C in loading medium (HBSS supplemented with 20 mM HEPES pH 7.4). After the incubation with Calcein-AM, two washes with 1X PBS were performed, and measurement medium was added (HBSS supplemented with 20 mM HEPES, 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM glucose, pH 7.4). After adding the measurement medium, the first fluorescence reading (F1) was taken using a POLARstar Omega plate reader spectrophotometer (BMG Labtech, Ortenberg, Germany) (excitation: 485 nm; emission: 535 nm). Finally, an iron chelator, deferiprone, was added to the measurement medium at a final concentration of 500 ?M, and a second fluorescence measurement (F2) was taken after 1 h. The ratio F2/F1 normalized to the protein amount was used as a relative indicator of the labile iron content.

Sudan black staining
Lipofuscin accumulation was determined by Sudan Black B (SBB) stainingas previously described. SSB staining quantification was assessed by light microscopy. Autofluorescence was assessed by confocal microscopy using an SP5MP-AOBS (Leica, Mannheim, Germany) with a 20X objective. Images were analysed by Fiji-ImageJ software, version 2.9.0.

Determination of aconitase activity
Both cytosolic and mitochondrial aconitase activity were assessed following the manufacturer's instructions from Aconitase Assay kit (Biovision, Abcam).

Evaluation of susceptibility to ferroptosis
Cellular death by ferroptosis was induced by the supplementation of 5 ?M of erastin, a ferroptosis activator. A density of 8000 cells/well were plated on 96-multiwells plates. After 24 h, nuclei were stained with Hoechst 3342 (Invitrogen) for 15 min at 37 �C. Cells were rinsed with PBS1X and incubated with 1 ?M propidium iodide (PI) and 5 ?M erastin. Images were taken every hour using an automatized microscope CellDiscovererer7 (Zeiss,Oberkochen, Germany) at 5X. Nuclei stained with Hoechst and PI were quantified using Stardist from Fiji-ImageJ and cellular death rate was determined.

Lipid peroxidation
Measurements of membrane lipid peroxidation
Lipid peroxidation was evaluated using 4,4-difluoro-5-(4-phenyl- 1,3-butadienyl)-4-bora-3a,4a-diaza-s-indacene-3-undecanoic acid (BODIPY(r) 581/591 C11), a lipophilic fluorescent dye (Alcocer-G�mez et al., 2015; Pap et al., 1999). Cells were incubated with 5 ?M BODIPY(r) 581/591 C11 for 30 min at 37 �C. 500 ?M Luperox(r) for 15 min were used as positive control of lipid peroxidation. Lipid peroxidation in fibroblasts was evaluated by an Axio Vert A1 fluorescence microscope with a 20X objective. Images were analysed with Fiji-ImageJ software, version 2.9.0.

Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis
Cells were seeded in 8-well Permanox chamber slides (177,380, ThermoFisher Scien-tific, Waltham, MA, USA) in DMEM glucose medium for three days. Cells were fixed with 3.5% glutaraldehyde in 0.1 M phosphate buffer for 10 min at 37 �C. After fixation, cells were post-fixed in 2% OsO4, rinsed, dried, and embedded in Durcupan Resin (44,610-1EA, Sigma-Aldrich (Saint Louis, MO, USA)). Using a diamond knife, ultrathin pieces of 70 nm were cut and examined using a transmission electron microscope (FEI Tecnai G2 Spirit BioTwin) equipped with a Xarosa digital camera (20 Megapixel resolution) and Radius image acquisition software version 2.1 (EMSIS GmbH, M�nster, Germany).

Protein expression levels
Immunoblotting
Western blotting was performed using standard Methods. After transferring protein to a nitrocellulose membrane, the membrane was incubated with primary antibodies diluted 1:1000, and then with the corresponding secondary antibody coupled to horseradish peroxidase at a 1:2500 dilution. Specific proteins were identified by ChemiDoc(tm) MP Imaging System (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA) using the Immun Star HRP substrate kit (Biorad Laboratories Inc., Hercules, CA, USA). ImageLab(tm) version 10.0 software (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA) was used to analyze protein expression levels.

Immunofluorescence microscopy
iNs were plated on ?-Slide 4-well plates (Ibidi Inc., Martinsried, Germany). Cells were rinsed once with PBS, fixed in 3.8% paraformaldehyde for 10 min at room temperature. Then, cells were permeabilized with 0,1% Triton X-100 for 10 min. Next, cells were incubated with a blocking solution containing 5% donkey serum for 1 h. Primary antibodies, diluted 1:200-1:500 in blocking solution, were incubated overnight at 4 �C. Unbound antibodies were removed by washing twice with PBS. Cells were incubated with secondary antibodies, diluted 1:300 in blocking solution, for 2 h at room temperature. Finally, cells were stained with 1 ?g/mL DAPI for 15-20 min. Images were taken with a DeltaVision system with an Olympus IX-71 fluorescence microscope with a 60???oil objective and analysed by Fiji-ImageJ software, version 2.9.0.

Frataxin transcript expression levels
Real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR)
FXN gene expression in fibroblasts was analysed by qPCR using mRNA extracts. mRNA was isolated with Trizol(tm) (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA), following manufacturer's instructions. RNA was retrotranscribed using Iscript cDNA synthesis Kit (Bio-Rad,Hercules, CA, United States) to obtain complementary DNA (cDNA). qPCR was performed using TB Green(tm) Premix Ex Taq(tm) (Takara Bio Europe S.A.S., Saint-Germain-en-Laye, France). CFX Connect Real-Time PCR Detection System (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA) was used to detect accurate quantification of gene expression. Frataxin primers were 5'-CCTTGCAGACAAGCCATACA-3' (Forward primer) and 3'-CCACTGGATGGAGAAGATAG- 5' (Reverse primer), amplifying a sequence of 149 nucleotides. Actin was used as a housekeeping control gene and the primers were 5'- AGAGCTACGAGCTGCCTGAC -3' (Forward primer) and 3'- AGCACTGTGTTGGCGTACAG -5' (reverse primer).

Mitochondrial function
Assessment of mitochondrial respiratory function using Seahorse extracellular flux analyzer
Mitochondrial respiratory function and oxygen consumption rate (OCR) of control and FRDA fibroblasts were measured using Mito-stress test assay in a XFe24 extracellular flux analyzer (Seahorse Bioscience, Billerica, MA, USA). Cells were seeded in XF24 cell culture plates with a density of 10,000 cells/well and placed in a 37 �C incubator with 5% CO2.

The day after, cells were washed twice with 500??L of pre-warmed assay medium (XF base medium supplemented with 10 mM glucose, 1 mM glutamine and 1 mM sodium pyruvate; pH?7.4 Cells were placed in a 37 �C incubator without CO2 for 1 h to allow equilibrating with the assay medium. Pre-warmed oligomycin, FCCP and rotenone & antimycin A were loaded into the ports A, B and C of sensor cartridge, respectively. The final concentrations of injections were as follows: 1.5 ?M oligomycin, 2 ?M FCCP, 1 and 2.5 ?M rotenone & antimycin A, respectively.

The cartridge was calibrated by the XFe24 analyzer, and the assay was carried out using Mito-stress test assay protocol. OCR was measured followed by the sequential addition of oligomycin, FCCP and rotenone & antimycin A. This approach allows us to determine different parameters of mitochondrial function such as basal respiration, maximal respiration, spare respiratory capacity and ATP production. When the experiment was finished, cell number of each well was calculated by performing a staining with DAPI using the BioTek(tm) Cytation(tm) 1 Cell Imaging Multi-Mode Reader (Biotek, Winooski, VT, USA).

Statistical analysis
Statistical analysis was performed as formerly described by our research group. We used non-parametric statistics that do not have any distributional assumption in cases when the number of events was small (n?<?30). In these cases, multiple groups were compared using a Kruskal-Wallis test. In cases when number of events was higher (n?>?30), we applied parametric tests. In these cases, multiple groups were compared using a one-way ANOVA. Statistical analyses were conducted using the GraphPad Prism 9.0 (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA). The data are reported as the mean?�?SD values or as representative of at least three independent experiments. P-values of less than 0.05 were considered significant.

Results

Pathophysiological characterization of FRDA fibroblasts
FRDA fibroblasts show low frataxin protein and transcript expression levels
First, we assessed the expression of the FXN gene at the transcriptional and protein level. RT-qPCR assays confirmed a decrease in FXN gene expression in patient-derived fibroblasts (Fig. 1A). Specifically, P1-derived fibroblasts, which contain 350 GAA repeats in each allele, exhibited a 60% reduction in gene expression, while P2-derived fibroblasts, with 450 and 560 GAA repeats in each allele, showed an 80% reduction in comparison to control fibroblasts. Frataxin protein levels, determined by Western blot analysis, were also significantly reduced in both patient-derived fibroblast lines. Notably, we observed a greater reduction of FXN protein expression levels in P2 fibroblasts (Fig. 1B and C).

B Immunoblotting analysis of cellular extracts from controls (C1 and C2) and FRDA patient cell lines (P1 and P2). Protein extracts (15 ?g) were separated on a SDS polyacrylamide gel and immunostained with antibodies against FXN. Actin was used as a loading control. C Densitometry of FXN. E Measurement of aconitase activity. Mitochondrial and cytosolic extracts were separated and quantified to determine cytosolic and mitochondrial aconitase activity by colorimetric assay. FRDA fibroblasts manifest impaired ISC protein expression levels
Since frataxin has an important role in Fe-S cluster assembly, we decided to evaluate the expression levels of proteins also involved in this process such as ISCU, NFS1, LYRM4 and mtACP. Western blot assays showed that these proteins were downregulated in patient-derived fibroblasts, with a more pronounced reduction in P2 fibroblasts (Fig. 1D).

Fe-S clusters are essential for the enzymatic activity of aconitase. Aconitase catalyzes the conversion of citrate into isocitrate and is also related to iron metabolism. Therefore, we assessed mitochondrial and cytosolic aconitase activity in both patient-derived and control fibroblasts. We observed reduced cytosolic aconitase activity in both lines in comparison to control and a reduced mitochondrial aconitase activity in P2 fibroblasts (Fig. 1E).

Mitochondrial dysfunction in FRDA fibroblasts: mitochondrial protein expression levels
Fe-S clusters also play a crucial role in the mitochondrial electron transport chain, since these clusters are contained in certain mitochondrial subunits and are essential for mitochondrial electron transport. We assessed the expression levels of mitochondrial complexes subunits such as NDUFS1, a complex I subunit, SDHB, a complex II subunit, and the mitochondrial mass marker VDAC by Western blot analysis. Our results showed that their levels were significantly reduced in FRDA fibroblasts compared to controls (Fig. 2A and B).

Protein extracts (15 ?g) were separated on an SDS polyacrylamide gel and immunostained with antibodies against NDUFS1, SDHB and VDAC. Actin was used as a loading control. B Densitometry of the Western blot. Data represent the mean?�?SD of three separate experiments. Data represent the mean?�?SD of three separate experiments. Altered expression levels of proteins related with iron metabolism
Considering that frataxin deficiency also contributes to the dysregulation of iron metabolism, we analyzed the expression levels of proteins involved in regulating cellular iron intake, export, and storage. Proteins such as IRP1 and TfR were overexpressed in FRDA fibroblasts, suggesting an increased iron influx into the cells. Conversely, cytosolic and mitochondrial ferritin were downregulated in FRDA fibroblasts, indicating insufficient iron availability for storage. (Fig. 3A and B).

A.U., arbitrary units

Iron accumulation in FRDA fibroblasts
Iron metabolism dysregulation in FRDA promotes cellular iron accumulation, which is a hallmark of the disease. We conducted two different techniques to determine cellular iron levels. Prussian blue staining showed that iron accumulation was more evident in FRDA fibroblasts compared to control fibroblasts (Fig. 3C and D). These results were further confirmed by ICP-MS, which revealed increased iron levels in P1 and P2 fibroblasts compared to control fibroblasts. Interestingly, iron levels were higher in P2 fibroblasts which show lower levels of FXN expression (Fig. 3E). Furthermore, to evaluate free iron availability, we performed a calcein assay to measure the labile iron pool (LIP). We observed that LIP was reduced in FRDA fibroblasts (Fig. 3F).

Lipofuscin accumulation and lipid peroxidation in FRDA fibroblasts: Bodipy C-11, Sudan black staining and autofluorescence
Since iron is a reactive element, cellular iron accumulation may trigger the formation of reactive oxygen species and cause oxidative stress, which leads to lipid peroxidation and the accumulation of lipofuscin granules. These granules contain oxidized proteins, lipids, and metals. To determine lipid peroxidation levels, we used Bodipy C-11 labeling. We observed higher levels of fluorescence in FRDA fibroblasts compared to control fibroblasts (Fig. 4A and B), indicating increased lipid peroxidation.

Figure 4: Determination of lipid peroxidation and lipofuscin accumulation in control and FRDA fibroblasts. A Representative images of lipid peroxidation in control and FRDA cells using BODIPY(r) 581/591 C11 staining. Scale bar?=?20?m. B Fluorescence quantification of the oxidized form of BODIPY(r) C11. C Representative images of Sudan Black staining and autofluorescence obtained by confocal microscopy of control and FRDA fibroblasts (P1 and P2). Scale?=?50?m. D Quantification of Sudan Black staining. E Quantification of autofluorescence. Data represent the mean?�?SD of three separate experiments (30 cell images for each condition). Statistical significance between control and FRDA fibroblasts is expressed as *p?<?0.05, **p?<?0.01, ***p?<?0.001 and ****p?<?0.0001. A.U., arbitrary units

Next, we used Sudan Black staining to determine lipofuscin accumulation. FRDA fibroblasts exhibited higher levels of lipofuscin compared to controls (Fig. 4C and D). Given that lipofuscin is an autofluorescent pigment, we confirmed these findings by measuring autofluorescence. FRDA fibroblasts displayed greater autofluorescence than control fibroblasts (Fig. 4C and E). Both results suggest that fibroblasts with FXN mutations show increased lipofuscin accumulation.

Effect of ALA supplementation on pathophysiological alterations in FRDA fibroblasts and iNs.
Effect of ALA on frataxin protein and transcripts expression levels in FRDA fibroblasts
Next, we evaluated the effect of ALA, a well-known antioxidant, on cell pathological alterations. First, we determined the most effective dose for each FRDA fibroblast cell line. For that purpose, we performed dose-response curves and measured frataxin expression levels by Western blot. After these screenings with different concentrations, we observed that 10 ?M of ALA was the lowest concentration able to increase frataxin expression levels in P1 fibroblasts (Fig. 5A and C), while 50 ?M was the most effective in P2 fibroblasts (Fig. 5B and C). These doses (10 ?M for P1 and 50 ?M for P2) were used in all subsequent experiments. Once these doses were established, we evaluated the effect of ALA on frataxin transcript expression levels by RT-qPCR. As shown in Fig. 5D, ALA treatment significantly increased transcript levels of frataxin in both FRDA fibroblast cell lines.

Effect of ALA on susceptibility to erastin-induced ferroptosis in FRDA fibroblasts
To investigate whether ALA could prevent cell death, we induced ferroptosis by treating cell culture with erastin for 24 h under different conditions: without previous treatment and previously supplemented with ALA (negative controls were also analyzed). Images were taken every hour, and we observed that after 15 h of incubation, erastin induced cell death in FRDA fibroblasts but not in control fibroblasts (Fig. 6A and B). We also calculated the cellular death rate after 24 h of erastin exposure (Fig. 6C). However, the sensitivity of FRDA fibroblasts pre-treated with ALA to erastin was significantly reduced, suggesting that ALA supplementation may protect FRDA fibroblasts against ferroptosis.

Effect of ALA on proteins related to ISC biosynthesis in FRDA fibroblasts.
Given that ALA was able to reduce the cellular death rate induced by erastin, we next analyzed the effect of ALA at the molecular level. We assessed expression levels of proteins involved in ISC biosynthesis, such as FXN, LYRM4, ISCU, NFS1 and mtACP before and after ALA supplementation. Western blot assays showed that ALA supplementation significantly increased FXN, ISCU and mtACP expression levels in FRDA fibroblasts and improved, but not significantly, LYRM4 and NFS1 expression levels (Fig. 7A and B). As mtACP is involved in lipoic acid biosynthesis, the positive effect of ALA was also corroborated by assessing the lipoylation levels of mitochondrial proteins by Western blotting and immunofluorescence (Fig. S1A, S1B, S1C and S1D). As anticipated, the decreased levels of protein lipoylation in FRDA fibroblasts improved significantly following ALA supplementation.

Statistical significance between untreated and treated fibroblasts is expressed as #p?<?0.05, ##p?<?0.01, ###p?<?0.001, ns: not significant

To go further, we hypothesized that these positive results were related to an improvement in ISC biosynthesis efficiency. To confirm this hypothesis, we determined aconitase activity. We observed that cytosolic aconitase activity significantly improved after supplementation of ALA in P1 and P2 fibroblasts. ALA also increased mitochondrial aconitase activity in P1 and P2 fibroblasts, although it was statistically significant only in P2 (Fig. 7C).

Effect of ALA on mitochondrial dysfunction in FRDA fibroblasts
Next, we examined the effect of ALA on mitochondrial protein expression levels and mitochondrial function. As is shown in Fig. 8A and B, ALA treatment increased expression levels of NDUFS1, SDHB and VDAC in P2, and NDUFS1 in P1 fibroblasts. Furthermore, although the expression levels of SDHB and VDAC in P1 fibroblasts also increased with treatment, this increase was not statistically significant. Altogether, those findings imply that ALA treatment has a positive impact on mitochondrial metabolism in FRDA fibroblasts.

Since we found an increase in VDAC expression, a marker for mitochondrial mass, after ALA treatment, we wondered if this supplementation could also induce mitochondrial biogenesis. To address this question, we studied the effect of ALA on key proteins involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, such as PGC1-�, P-PGC1-�, SIRT1, PPAR? and P-PPAR?. We found that expression levels of these proteins increased after ALA treatment in both P1 and P2 FRDA fibroblasts (Fig. S2A and B).

Effect of ALA on mitochondrial function in FRDA fibroblasts
To study the effect of ALA on mitochondrial function, we determined oxygen consumption rate using a Seahorse XFe24 analyzer. After treating FRDA fibroblasts with ALA, OCR was increased in FRDA fibroblasts (Fig. 9A and B). These improvements could be a consequence of increased mitochondrial protein expression and enhanced ISC biosynthesis. Figure 9A and B show the respiratory profile of control and P1 and P2 fibroblasts untreated and treated with ALA. Supplementation with ALA improved mitochondrial parameters such as maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity in P1 fibroblasts (Fig. 9C) and basal respiration, maximal respiration and ATP production-coupled respiration in P2 fibroblasts (Fig. 9D).

Effect of ALA on lipid peroxidation, and iron and lipofuscin accumulation in FRDA fibroblasts
Lipid peroxidation and iron accumulation have been described as the main hallmarks of the disease. Therefore, we decided to study the effect of ALA on these pathophysiological features. Bodipy assay showed that ALA supplementation significantly reduced lipid peroxidation on FRDA fibroblasts (Fig. 10A and B). Additionally, methods such as Prussian blue staining and ICP-MS assays revealed that ALA supplementation reduced iron accumulation in both cell lines (Fig. 10C, D and E).

As we observed in Sudan Black staining and autofluorescence assay, the reduction in lipid peroxidation and iron accumulation led to a decrease in lipofuscin accumulation determined by Sudan Black staining (Fig. 11A and B) and autofluorescence (Fig. 11C and D). We also observed a high number of lipofuscin-like aggregates per cell in P2 fibroblasts using transmission electron microscopy that were significantly reduced after ALA treatment (Fig. 12A and B). Interestingly, TEM analysis also revealed that mitochondrial morphology in FRDA cells showed mitochondrial vacuolization and condensation of mitochondrial compounds forming dense lipofuscin-like granules (Fig. S3, S4 and S5).

Effect of ALA on cellular antioxidant system
One of the main factors leading to ferroptosis in FRDA fibroblasts is the deficiency of the antioxidant system, which leads to high levels of oxidative stress. To assess the enzymatic antioxidant system and the impact of ALA on them, we performed Western blot assays to measure the expression levels of antioxidant enzymes such as GPX4, SOD1 and catalase. We also determined the expression levels of NRF2 transcription factor which regulates the expression of antioxidant enzymes. As is shown in Fig. S6A and B, antioxidant enzymes and NRF2 expression were downregulated in FRDA fibroblasts with respect to control. After ALA supplementation, these antioxidant protein expression levels were significantly increased.

ALA induces frataxin expression through PPARy activation in FRDA fibroblasts
To further investigate if mitochondrial biogenesis was a key mechanism for inducing frataxin expression, we used a selective PPARy inhibitor, T000070907. We used 2?M and 6?M in P1 and P2 fibroblasts, respectively, in order to inhibit PPARy activation. The addition of T000070907 prevented the ALA-induced increase in frataxin expression levels. (Fig. 13A and B). We also observed that supplementation with T000070907 prevented the ALA-induced increase of PPAR?, P-PPAR?, PGC1� and P-PGC1� expression levels. These results suggested that ALA plays an important role in the PPAR? activation and, consequently, inducing mitochondrial biogenesis in FRDA fibroblasts.

Effect of ALA on FRDA iNs
To further study FRDA in neuronal cell models, we transdifferentiated FRDA and control fibroblasts into iNs by direct reprogramming. This technique allowed us to study the disease in one of the most affected cell types. Control and FRDA fibroblasts were infected with lentiviral vectors containing proneural genes and the REST complex. After 27 days, fibroblasts were converted into iNs showing a typical neuron-like morphology and positive immunoreactivity against Tau, a neuron-specific protein.

We evaluated two parameters related to this technique, conversion efficiency and purity. We found different values of these parameters for each fibroblast line. While control cells showed a conversion efficiency of 25%, P1 and P2 showed efficiencies of 40% and 10%, respectively. The purity of the control iNs culture was 50%, compared to 60% for P1 iNs and 80% for P2 iNs.

Next, we studied this cellular model by examining the main pathophysiological features observed in FRDA fibroblasts, specifically frataxin expression and iron accumulation, and the effect of ALA on these iNs. Figures 14A and 15A show that frataxin protein expression was reduced in P1 and P2 iNs, which was restored after 10 ?M and 50 ?M of ALA treatment, respectively. Regarding iron accumulation, Prussian blue staining revealed an increase in P1 and P2 iNs, which was reduced following ALA supplementation (Figs. 14B and 15B).
