Figure 2.Long-term changes in glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels during therapy in FA Longitudinal changes in HbA1c levels depicting the progression of glycemic control during therapy in patient with FA.
Neurological function, measured by the International Cooperative Ataxia Rating Scale (ICARS), also showed improvement over 3 years: scores improved from 85 to 71 points. Enhanced kinetic function was evident, as illustrated by more accurate Archimedes spiral drawing (Fig. 3A and 3B). The simultaneous improvement in glycemic variability and neurological scores underscores a shared mitochondrial pathophysiology in both metabolic and neurological manifestations.
Figure 3.Drawings of the Archimedes spiral to assess kinetic function in FA. (A). Baseline drawing of Archimedes spiral, illustrating impaired kinetic function prior to therapy initiation. (B). Follow-up drawing of the Archimedes spiral, showing improved accuracy and enhanced kinetic function after 3 years of treatment.
Discussion
Mitochondrial dysfunction in FA necessitates therapeutic strategies targeting mitochondrial protection. Mitochondriotropic agents improve metabolic control by enhancing mitochondrial function, reducing oxidative damage, and slowing apoptosis, as demonstrated in MIDD [11, 12]. However, certain antihyperglycemic agents (eg, metformin, thiazolidinediones) may worsen mitochondrial impairment by inhibiting complex I. While sulfonylureas were historically used, their risks (hypoglycemia, ?-cell stress) favor safer alternatives like glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) analogs or DPP-4 inhibitors, which lack direct mitochondrial toxicity.

In FA, mitochondrial dysfunction disrupts pancreatic ?- and �-cell ATP production, impairing insulin secretion and causing dysregulated glucagon release [15]. This leads to paradoxical hyperglucagonemia during hyperglycemia and inadequate glucagon response to hypoglycemia, exacerbating glycemic variability. Our patient's initial presentation demonstrated this dual pathophysiology, with both insulin resistance and deficiency. Mitochondriotropic therapy produced 3 key metabolic improvements, such as enhanced peripheral insulin sensitivity, preserved and potentially enhanced glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, and HbA1c reduction without escalating insulin therapy. These therapeutic effects likely represent both the reversal of chronic glucotoxicity and direct mitochondrial protection, with the dissociation between fasting and postprandial C-peptide responses indicating reduced basal ?-cell workload due to normalized fasting glucose levels, and restored glucose-responsive insulin secretion capacity. Future studies involving glucagon dynamics and insulin clamp techniques could further characterize these dynamic endocrine effects.

Imeglimin, a novel antihyperglycemic agent, uniquely targets mitochondrial dysfunction by improving respiratory chain activity, reducing oxidative stress, and boosting ATP/NAD+ synthesis [16]. Its dual action, enhancing insulin secretion and sensitivity, makes it particularly relevant for FA-related DM, where mitochondrial failure drives both ?-cell loss and insulin resistance.

There is evidence supporting the role of antioxidants in FA therapy, as oxidative stress has been identified as a consequence of reduced FXN levels [17]. Jauslin et al demonstrated that CoQ10 and its analogues could prevent cell death in fibroblasts from FA patients [18]. In a clinical trial published in 2008, CoQ10 was combined with vitamin E which demonstrated significant improvements in the ICARS scores after 2 years of treatment [19]. These results suggest that the combination of CoQ10 and vitamin E can help improve motor coordination and reduce the progression of FA-related symptoms, likely by enhancing mitochondrial function and reducing oxidative stress. L-carnitine plays a vital role in transporting long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria for ATP generation via ?-oxidation [20]. In recent years, there has been increasing interest in the therapeutic potential of L-carnitine and acetyl L-carnitine for conditions associated with nervous system injury and degeneration [21]. Schols et al reported a significant improvement in mitochondrial ATP production in patients with FA who received L-carnitine [22].

Gene therapy offers a promising approach for definitive treatment of FA by correcting faulty genes using techniques like adeno-associated viral (AAV) vectors and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing [23]. These methods have shown success in preclinical models by delivering functional FXN to affected tissues, particularly the heart and nervous system. Several AAV-based therapies, such as AAVrh.10hFXN are currently in clinical trials, showing early promise in improving FXN expression and disease markers [24]. However, these therapies are still in the trial phase, with challenges like immune responses and safe delivery to be addressed before approval for widespread patient use. Until such gene therapies become widely available, agents that enhance mitochondrial function may play a crucial role in delaying disease progression and stabilizing symptoms in patients with FA.

Natural history studies indicate FA typically progresses at 0.77 points annually on the Scale for Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA) (SE 0.06) [25], with ICARS scores showing strong correlation to SARA measurements across disease stages [26]. For our patient, this would predict a 2.31-point worsening (ICARS 87.31) over 3 years. Remarkably, we observed a 14-point ICARS improvement (final score 71), representing a 16-point positive deviation from expected progression.

This case represents the first reported instance of concurrent long-term glycemic stabilization and ataxia improvement in FA, achieved through combined mitochondriotropic therapy. While previous studies have demonstrated neuroprotective benefits of these agents, our findings uniquely highlight their dual metabolic and neurological efficacy, particularly through the synergistic use of these agents. The observed outcomes-a 14-point ICARS improvement (in contrast to expected disease progression) and sustained glycemic control with reduced variability-suggest these agents may collectively, though partially, address FA's mitochondrial pathophysiology. The temporal association of clinical improvements with therapeutic interventions, despite progressive ?-cell failure, supports the hypothesis that targeting multiple modes of mitochondrial dysfunction may be more effective than isolated therapies, highlighting the synergy of these agents. However, the individual contributions of each component remain unclear due to their complementary mechanisms and warrant future comparative studies to delineate agent-specific effects. This case reinforces mitochondriotropic therapy as a promising interim strategy for FA management, bridging the gap until gene therapies become clinically viable.
Learning Points
Mitochondriotropic agents stabilize glycemic control and improve ataxic symptoms in FA.
The stable glycemic control achieved is likely due to improved insulin sensitivity & preserved ?-cell function.
Mitochondriotropic agents reduced ICARS for ataxic symptoms by 14 points in 3 years.
Ours is the first report to demonstrate improvement in both glycemia and ataxia in FA.


Impact of age on neurofilament light chain in Friedreich ataxia: a 1-year longitudinal study

Abstract
Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA) is a recessive inherited ataxia caused by intronic GAA repeat expansions in FXN gene. The repeat length is the major determinant of age at onset, usually occurring in adolescence. Clinical manifestations include progressive gait and limb ataxia, sensory loss, cardiomyopathy, and scoliosis. Neurofilament light chain protein (NfL) has been recently studied as a potential plasma biomarker for the disease. We performed a longitudinal study in 62 patients with FRDA, including 12 children (age 12-17 years) and 50 adult patients (age 18-45). The characteristics of our patient cohort largely matched those of a population mostly recruited in therapeutical clinical trials, with a mean age of 25.1 � 8.5 years, age at onset 13.1 � 4.8 years, and disease duration 12 � 7 years. We found higher NfL levels in children in comparison with adult patients. Plasma concentrations remained stable at 1-year follow-up. We observed a significantly inverse correlation between plasma NfL levels and patient ages, while no correlations were found with other clinical or genetic variables. Our study confirms the typical NfL profile in FRDA patients. Our data further support the role of NfL as early indicator of axonal damage and as potential pharmacodynamic biomarker of therapeutical response especially valuable in pediatric populations.
Introduction

Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA) is an autosomal recessive multi-systemic disorder presenting with progressive gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, sensory loss, areflexia, cardiomyopathy, diabetes mellitus, and scoliosis.1 The onset of symptoms most commonly occurs during childhood or adolescence, and patients become wheelchair-bound on average 15 years after disease onset. The causative genetic defect is a homozygous GAA (guanine-adenine-adenine) trinucleotide repeat expansion in the first intron of the FXN gene.2 Only few patients (3-4%) are compound heterozygotes for the GAA expansion on one allele and a point mutation on the other allele of FXN gene. The presence of GAA expansion leads to reduced amount of both mRNA and encoded protein, frataxin, which is involved in mitochondrial iron metabolism, iron-sulfur cluster biosynthesis, and in the mitochondrial oxidative-phosphorylation system.3 Larger expansions correspond to smaller residual amount of frataxin, which in turn determines increased mitochondrial oxidative stress and cellular damage, particularly relevant in the nervous system and the heart. In patients, larger expansions are associated with younger age at onset, more severe phenotype and a more rapid disease progression. In natural history studies and interventional clinical trials FRDA disease progression and response to therapeutical interventions have been commonly tracked by clinical and neuroimaging measures.

In recent years, measurement of neurofilament light chain protein (NfL) has increasingly been considered in the contest of clinical trials and safety monitoring.4

NfL is a protein mostly concentrate in neuronal axons, where it plays a crucial role in maintaining stability, shape and regulation of the axon's diameter, while in case of axonal damage, it is released into cerebrospinal fluid and in blood.5 NfL levels have been measured in various types of genetic ataxia,6 including autosomal dominant spinocerebellar ataxias (SCAs),7-9 and FRDA.10-13 In patients with SCAs, NfL concentrations are elevated in comparison to healthy controls, and blood levels progressively increase during the course of the diseases. Vice versa, in FRDA patients the NfL concentration is high in the early stage and then it decreases with advancing age. A clear correlation between plasma levels and measures of disease progression has been demonstrated in few studies, though not consistently across all investigations.10-14 Here we conducted a 1-year prospective study in a large cohort of FRDA patients, with the aim of comparing NfL level and its profile of change in children and young adults.

Materials and methods

Participants and clinical evaluations

We enrolled children (age 12-17 years) and adult patients (age 18 to 45 years) with FRDA. Inclusion criteria were (i) confirmed genetic diagnosis of FRDA, and (ii) age at onset before age 25. Exclusion criteria were the presence of severe concomitant medical/cognitive conditions unrelated to FRDA or clinical conditions preventing the completion of clinical assessments established by the protocol. Healthy control subjects were recruited from the community or from unrelated family members. Study participants were evaluated at baseline and after a 12 � 2 months interval. Demographical data, clinical and genetic characteristics, and concomitant medical conditions were collected. Neurological examination included administration of SARA scale,15 modified FARS scale,16 and activity of daily living (ADL) as part of the FARS.17

Blood samples were obtained from not fasted participants. The study was evaluated and approved by the Local Ethics Committee on 13 January 2021 (Protocol N. 80). All subjects or legal guardians gave written informed consent for the participation in the study, and all procedures were carried out in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

NfL and frataxin mRNA analyses

Anonymize blood samples were collected into 5 mL EDTA Vacutainer Tubes (Becton Dickinson, Rutherford, NY) and immediately sent to the laboratory at room temperature. Upon arrival, 3 mL were centrifuged at 2,500?g for 3 min, and the plasma aliquots stored at ?80�C until NfL assays. NfL concentrations were measured by the Human Simple Plex assay kit (ProteinSimple, CA, USA) on Ella device (ProteinSimple, CA, USA), according to the manufacturers' instructions. Calibration of Ella was performed using the in-cartridge factory standard curve, and plasma samples were measured with a 1:2 dilution in Sample Diluent provided by the kit. Triplicates were automatically performed in Simple Plex assay microfluidic platform, and data were expressed as pmol/mL. Plasma obtained from healthy subjects was used as controls to monitor assay performance. Longitudinal samples were tested in the same analytical run.

At baseline, an additional blood sample collection in TempusTM Blood RNA (5 mL) was used for analysis of frataxin mRNA expression. Total RNA was extracted from 3 mL whole blood using Tempus Spin RNA Isolation Reagent kit (ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), according to manufacturer's protocol. One ?g RNA samples was reverse transcribed with the LunaScript RT Super mix kit (New England BioLabs, MA, USA). The FXN mRNA was measured by qRT-PCR in an ABI PRISM7500 Sequence Detection System (Life Technologies, Carlsbad, CA, United States) using Power SYBR Green I dye chemistry. Data were analyzed using the 2???Ct method with TATA box binding protein (TBP) as a housekeeping gene and expressed as fold change relative to the controls.

Statistical analyses

Inter-group differences between two or more groups were assessed using Wilcoxon or Kruskal-Wallis tests. Spearman correlation test was used to correlate NfL levels with clinical and demographical variables. A two-tailed Wilcoxon-Rank test was applied to analyze paired data from longitudinal measurements. Correlation was assessed by computing Spearman ?. Data are presented as mean � standard deviation (SD). The level of significance was set at P < 0.05. Statistical analyses were conducted using JMP(r), version 11 (SAS Institute Inc., USA).

Results

Between October 2021 and July 2022, we enrolled 62 subjects with FRDA: 12 children (mean age 15.2 � 1.7 years) and 50 adults (mean age 27.5 � 7.7). Healthy controls were 12 minors (aged 15.2 � 1.9 years), and 18 adults (age 26.4 � 4 years) (Table 1).

Table 1: Baseline data of FRDA patients and healthy controls 
Seventeen adult control subjects, 46 adult FRDA patients, and 11 FRDA children performed follow-up evaluations at 1 year interval (11.6 � 1.6 months). Children had a mean age at onset of 9.5 � 2.9 years and disease duration of 5.9 � 1.9 years. In adult patients age at onset was 14.0 � 4.9, and disease duration was 13.5 � 7.1 years.

Concomitant medical conditions observed in adult patients were arterial hypertension (n.4); hypercholesterolemia (n.4); hypo- or hyperthyroidism (n.2); psoriatic arthritis (n.1) and Crohn disease (n.1). A 14 year-old FRDA patient had diabetes mellitus. All patients, except one, were homozygous for the presence of GAA expansion on both FXN alleles: mean length of shorter allele (GAA1) was 787 � 186 triplets in children and 653 � 203 triplets in adult patients. One adult patient was compound heterozygous for GAA expansion (830 triplets) and c.157delC variant on the other FXN allele (p.R53AfsX75). FXN mRNA was significantly reduced in FRDA patients, being ?25% of controls (P = 0.0001) (Table 1).

NfL plasma concentrations were higher in children with FRDA (28.5 � 7.7 pg/mL) in comparison with both age-matched control (5.3 � 2.7 pg/mL; P < 0.001) and adult FRDA patients (21.6 � 8.1; P < 0.04) (Table 1; Fig. 1A). Adult patients had also higher NfL levels in comparison with controls. No difference was found in NfL level between children and adult controls (Fig. 1A).

No significant difference between baseline and 1-year follow-up were observed (paired Wilcoxon test for repeated measures).
At 1-year follow-up, NfL levels showed no significant changes in the groups of adult FRDA patients (?0.15 pg/mL; ?0.7%) and in controls. In children with FRDA we observed a trend toward NfL reduction, with a mean change at 1-year follow-up of ?3.5 pg/mL (?11.9%; P = 0.265) (Figure 1B).

SARA and ADL scores significantly increased in both adult patients and in children. In adults, SARA increased 1.30 point (P < 0.0001) and ADL of 0.83 point (P = 0.006). In children, SARA increased 1.25 point (P = 0.05) and ADL 2.7 points (P = 0.006). mFARS score did not significantly change between baseline and follow-up.

Correlations between clinical, biochemical and genetic measures

We confirmed in our cohort the well-established inverse correlations between GAA1 repeat size and age of onset (AOO) (? = ?0.38; P = 0.002). Disease duration significantly correlated with clinical measures of disease severity: ADL (? = 0.71), SARA score (? = 0.67), and mFARS score (? = 0.63) (P < 0.0001 for all). FXN expression directly correlated with age (? = 0.39; P = 0.01) and AOO (? = 0.53; P = 0.0001), and inversely correlated with GAA1 (? = ?0.41; P = 0.004) (Fig. 2A-C).

Discussion

NfL is an indicator of axonal damage,18,19 and it has been extensively studied as a potential biomarker for disease progression, therapeutic response, and safety.5,20,21

In Huntington disease, for example, elevated NfL levels might allow accurate distinction between premanifest and juvenile-onset Huntington disease and between people with premanifest Huntington disease and healthy individuals. Moreover, NfL increases with disease progression and correlates with striatal atrophy.22,23 In genetic ataxias as Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3), NfL concentrations increase with disease severity and positively correlate with SARA score, while in other type of SCAs, such as SCA1, SCA2 and SCA7, correlation between NfL and disease status was not observed.6

Increased NfL has consistently been demonstrated in FRDA patients,10-14 and we confirmed this finding in our population. In terms of raw concentration, our values are in line with those previously reported, though obtained with a different analytical technology. In fact, we assessed plasma NfL concentrations by the use of the Simple PlexTM Ella (EllaTM) microfluidic platform, while the majority of previous studies assessed either plasma or serum NfL using the Single Molecular Array (SimoaTM, Quanterix).10-13 In a single study the ELISA technique was used14 (Table 2).
The comparison between SimoaTM and EllaTM immunoassays demonstrated that the results obtained with the two technologies are strongly correlated (? = 0.86, P < 0.0001), and that both platforms offer excellent sensitivity for the use in clinical practice.24 However, it should be mentioned that the absolute values of NFL measured by SimoaTM are globally lower that the values measured by EllaTM and therefore the assay methodology should be considered when interpreting absolute NfL values in cross-study comparisons.24

We showed that NfL plasma concentrations are higher in children with FRDA both compared with age-matched healthy controls and compared with adult FRDA patients (�18 years) (Fig. 1A).

In physiological conditions, children have elevated NfL level after birth, then the concentration decreases by ?6.8% per year until the age of 10.25 In young and adult individuals NfL remains stable for several decades, and it increases in elderly people �60 years.6 The high NfL concentration in the first decade of life has been associated to the growth and maturation of central nervous system.26

In our study, we avoid the bias of physiological NfL changes, by the selection a cohort of patients aged between 12 and 45 years, when NfL levels are stable. The trend of NfL observed in FRDA differs from that described in adult-onset disorders, as concentrations do not increase with disease progression, but are high in proximity of disease onset and decrease in more advanced disease stages.

A similar pattern of neurofilament dynamics has been observed in other pediatric neurodegenerative diseases. In spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), for example, both NfL and phosphorylated neurofilament heavy subunit (pNfH) are elevated at disease onset and show an age-related decrease.27

Significant inverse correlations between NfL and AOO, disease duration and the clinical measures of disease severity were observed in both SMA27 and in FRDA.10

We found that age but not disease severity was the major determinant for NfL blood concentrations.

Our results are in line with other studies in FRDA, in which NfL and age were consistently proven to be related, while no correlations with disease progression or clinical scores were observed.10,14 In particular, correlation with age was found in cohorts including both pediatric and adult patient populations, while in cohorts mainly composed of adult FRDA patients, NfL values are higher than in controls, but do not correlate with age.11,12 Interestingly, Johnsson et al.13 describe NfL concentration similar to healthy controls in two severely affected FRDA patients, aged 55 and 57, with a disease duration of 40 and 42 years.13

To explain this finding, it has been hypothesized that NfL is high when important damage of central and peripheral nerve axons occurs and both degenerative and regenerative processes might coexist.28 In later FRDA disease phases, NFL is maintained stable matching a constant neuronal degeneration, and then it declines in the very late stage when neuronal loss prevails.28

Our study defines the distinctive NfL profile over time of FRDA disease and confirms that neurofilament represents one of the most informative and early indicators of axonal damage.

NfL may also play a potential role as pharmacodynamic biomarker in response to therapeutic interventions, as demonstrated in SMA following treatment with nusinersen (Spinraza).29 This may be particularly relevant in pediatric populations where functional measures are less sensitive or disease evolution occurs more slowly.30


Leriglitazone improves iron homeostasis and ferroptotic markers in frataxin-deficient dorsal root ganglia neurons

Abstract
Friedreich ataxia (FA) is a neurodegenerative disease characterized by degeneration of the large sensory neurons and spinocerebellar tracts, muscle weakness, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. It is caused by a deficiency of the mitochondrial protein frataxin, leading to iron dyshomeostasis, defective energy production, and oxidative stress. Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPAR?) and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) signaling pathways play crucial roles in regulating mitochondrial function and protecting against oxidative stress, and their dysregulation contributes to neuronal degeneration in FA. In this study, we used frataxin-deficient primary cultures of dorsal root ganglia neurons to better understand the mechanism of action of leriglitazone, a novel brain-penetrant, full, and selective PPAR? agonist, by assessing the rescue of several cellular markers altered under frataxin deficiency. Leriglitazone improved most of the analyzed parameters, including cell survival, mitochondrial respiratory activity, iron homeostasis, and oxidative stress. Moreover, increased lipid peroxidation, a key marker of ferroptosis, was almost completely rescued by leriglitazone. NRF2 and PPAR? coactivator 1 alpha (PGC1�) levels that were decreased in frataxin-deficient neurons were normalized by leriglitazone. Interestingly, the combination of leriglitazone and the NRF2 activator omaveloxolone, a drug that has been approved to treat FA, was able to rescue both survival and mitochondrial function. In summary, our findings in this neuronal model suggest that targeting the PPAR? pathway with leriglitazone may be a promising therapeutic strategy for FA by improving mitochondrial function, bioenergetic cell alterations, and iron homeostasis. Likewise, a combination therapy with omaveloxolone may be an alternative for FA patients.
1. Introduction
Friedreich ataxia (FA) is an inherited recessive disease characterized by progressive gait and limb ataxia with associated limb muscle weakness, scoliosis, diabetes, absent lower limb reflexes, dysarthria, and decreased vibratory sense and proprioception. Most patients also present hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, with cardiac dysfunction being the leading cause of death. In 96?% of affected individuals, the disease is caused by homozygous GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions in the first intron of FXN, which encodes frataxin, a small mitochondrial protein. The remaining 4?% of individuals are compound heterozygous for a GAA expansion and an FXN point/insertion/deletion mutation. The primary consequence is a 70?%-90?% decrease in the basal frataxin level, a change that primarily affects the dorsal root ganglia (DRG), cerebellum, and heart. Frataxin has been related to the biosynthesis of iron-sulfur (Fe-S) clusters, heme maturation, iron storage or detoxification, and modulation of iron regulatory protein-1 activation (reviewed by Monfort et al.). Frataxin deficiency alters cellular iron homeostasis and causes oxidative stress. Indeed, increased iron levels have been reported in the brains of patients with FA,and in the DRG of FA mouse models,. Other metabolic alterations-including impairment of mitochondrial biogenesis and decreased content and/or function of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) components-have been observed in many biological models of frataxin deficiency and in samples from patients with FA,,,,.
In recent years, ferroptosis has been described as an important mechanism involved in FA cellular degeneration,. Ferroptosis is a regulated form of cell death triggered by the accumulation of lipid peroxidation products in membranes and determined by an iron-dependent reactive oxygen species (ROS) overload. To induce this type of cell death, redox-active iron and reduction of antioxidant defenses are required. Among them, glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) plays a key role in reducing lipid peroxides in a glutathione-dependent manner. GPX4 is regulated via nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2), a transcription factor involved in adapting to oxidative stress conditions. Although oxidative stress induced by frataxin deficiency should activate NRF2, in most of the FA models, NRF2 activity is impaired,,,, leading to decreased levels of GPX4 and increased lipid peroxidation. Thus, the combination of mitochondrial iron accumulation, increased oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and NRF2 impairment leads to ferroptosis in FA.
The NRF2 stabilizer called omaveloxolone prevents mitochondrial alterationsand is the first medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) to treat FA patients (marketed under the brand name Skyclarys),. Omaveloxolone preserves NRF2 from degradation, enhancing the antioxidant response, which in turn improves mitochondrial function, prevents lipid peroxidation, and ameliorates some clinical features of the disease. However, omaveloxolone treatment is not curative, and some adverse effects have been described,,.
Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor ? (PPAR?) is a nuclear receptor that is involved in the regulation of fundamental cellular processes, such as di?erentiation, development, and metabolism, and it is a key regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and function. Dysregulation of the PPAR? and PPAR? coactivator 1� (PGC1�) pathway has been reported in FA,,,,. PPAR? agonists induce a neuroprotective and restorative effect in various preclinical models of neurodegenerative diseases,,Leriglitazone is one of the active metabolites of pioglitazone. It is a well-tolerated brain-penetrant, full, and selective PPAR? agonist with high oral bioavailability, reaching central nervous system concentrations signi?cantly above the level safely achieved with pioglitazone and other glitazones,,,. PPAR? agonists act through nuclear receptors that bind to DNA sequences in the promoter sites of key genes that counteract oxidative stress, stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis, and decrease inflammation, thus preventing axonal degeneration and neuroinflammation. Leriglitazone was previously shown to improve impairments due to frataxin loss in FA cellular and animal models, and it was tested in a phase 2 clinical study in patients with FA.
In this study, we analyzed the effect of leriglitazone treatment in primary cultures of frataxin-deficient DRG sensory neurons. We analyzed cell survival and parameters related to mitochondrial function and oxidative stress, including mitochondrial respiration, iron dyshomeostasis, markers of ferroptosis, NRF2 levels and activation, and PGC1� levels. Finally, we evaluated the effect of the combinatorial treatment with leriglitazone and omaveloxolone and compared its effects to those that leriglitazone and omaveloxolone exert separately. The results strongly suggest that leriglitazone should be considered a potential candidate to treat FA, either alone or in combination with omaveloxolone.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Animals
Male and female Sprague Dawley rats (RRID:RGD_70508) were maintained in standard conditions with a 12-h photoperiod, a constant temperature of 20 �C, and food and water available ad libitum. Only neonatal rats were used in this work and all experiments were performed according to the National Guidelines for the regulation of the use of experimental laboratory animals issued by the Generalitat de Catalunya and the Government of Spain (article 33.a 214/1997), which comply with the ARRIVE guidelines. The experimental protocols were evaluated and approved by the Experimental Animal Ethical Committee of the University of Lleida (CEEA 02-01/24).
2.2. Culture and treatment of primary neonatal rat DRG neurons
Primary DRG neuronal cultures were established from P3-P4 neonatal Sprague Dawley rats following the purification protocol described by Sanz-Alc�zar et al.. Lentiviral transduction with scrambled sequence control (Scr) and short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) targeting frataxin messenger RNA (FXN1 and FXN2) was performed 1-2 days after plating the neurons. Six hours after viral infection, the medium was removed and new medium containing dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, vehicle) or 600?nM leriglitazonewas added. Omaveloxolone alone was used at 50?nM, as published. In the combinatorial treatments, leriglitazone and omaveloxolone were used at the indicated concentrations. All experiments were conducted 5 days after lentivirus transduction.
2.3. Human skin fibroblast cultures and treatments
Human skin fibroblasts (Table 1) were obtained from Dr. Marek Napierala (Department of Neurology, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center), and cultured in a 5?% CO2 atmosphere at 37�C, with Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) (GIBCO, ref. 11965-092) supplemented with 10?% fetal bovine serum (GIBCO, ref. A5256701), 1?% penicillin/streptomycin (GIBCO, ref. P4458), and 1?% non-essential amino acids (GIBCO, ref. 11140-050). Cells were treated with either dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, vehicle) (Sigma, ref. D2650) or 600?nM leriglitazone for 48?h, or 50?nM omaveloxolone for 24?h. For the Seahore experiments and OXPHOS analyses, fibroblast cultures were treated for 5 days.
2.4. Neuronal viability
Neuronal survival was measured with a?16???objective lens and cross-marked wells as described previouslyand expressed as the percentage of neurons counted after 5 days with respect to the initial value (100?%). Cellular viability was also measured by the 3-(4, 5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2, 5-diphenyltetrazoliumbromide (MTT) assay (ref. M5655, Sigma-Aldrich,). MTT is a colorimetric assay used to assess cell viability as a function of cell number based on metabolic activity. DRG neurons (12,000-14,000 cells/well) were seeded into 96-well plates (ref. 655090, Greiner,) with collagen and treated for 5 days with vehicle (DMSO) and varying concentrations of leriglitazone, and/or omaveloxolone as indicated in the figure legend. After treatment, MTT was dissolved in PBS and added to each well at a final concentration of 1.09?mM. Cells were incubated for 4?h at 37�C and 5?% CO2 to allow the formation of formazan crystals. The resulting formazan was solubilized in DMSO, and absorbance was measured at 540?nm using a microplate reader (BioTek Epoch EPOCH-SN, Agilent).
2.5. Mitochondrial respiration
The oxygen consumption rate (OCR) of rat DRG neurons and human-derived fibroblasts and was measured using the Seahorse XFp Cell Mito Stress Test Kit (ref. 103010-100, Agilent) on the Seahorse XFp Analyzer (Agilent) following the manufacturer's protocol, with some modifications. DRG neurons were plated at 14,000 cells/well, while fibroblasts were plated at 40,000 cells/well. The next day, vehicle, leriglitazone, omaveloxolone, or both drugs were added, and the OCR measured after 5 days. One hour before the assay, the culture medium was changed to Dulbecco's Modified Eagle's Medium (DMEM, pH 7.4) with 2?mM glutamine, 1?mM pyruvate, and 10?mM glucose. The plates were placed in a 37�C non-CO2 incubator, and the OCR was measured according to the manufacturer's instructions. Mitochondrial function was assessed using a sequential injection of oligomycin (1.5 ?M), FCCP (3.0 ?M), and rotenone-antimycin A (0.5 ?M).
2.6. Western blotting
Five days after drug treatment, primary cultures of DRG neurons were lysed with 2?% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), 125?mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, a protease inhibitor cocktail (ref. 04 693 159 001, Roche), and a phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (ref. 04 906 837 011, Roche). Then, the samples were treated with ultrasounds generated by an ultrasonic bath and incubated at 95�C for 5?min. The protein concentration was quantified by MicroBCA kit (ref. 23235, Thermo Scientific). The samples (7-10 ?g of protein) were subjected to SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, then transferred to polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes and incubated with I-Block (ref. T2015, Thermo Scientific) to block nonspecific protein binding. Nitrocellulose membranes were used to detect frataxin. The following primary antibodies were used: frataxin (1:500; ref. Ab219414, Abcam), OXPHOS (1:20,000 to detect complexes III, IV, and V, and 1:4000 to detect complexes I and II; ref. 458,099, Invitrogen), GPX4 (1:1000; ref. sc-166570, Santa Cruz), NRF2 (1:1000; ref. ab62352, Abcam), and PGC1� (1:500; ref. ab72230, Abcam). After blotting, the membranes were stained with Coomassie brilliant blue (CBB). The total protein stained was quantified with the Image Lab software (Bio-Rad) and used as loading control for normalization of the target proteins.
2.7. Oxidative stress analysis: mitochondrial superoxide, mitochondrial iron, and lipid peroxidation
The mitochondrial superoxide and ferrous iron (Fe2?+) contents were determined with the fluorescent probes MitoSOX Red (M36008, Thermo Scientific) and Mito-FerroGreen (M489-10, Dojindo), respectively. BODIPY(tm) 581/591 C11 (D3861, Thermo Scientific) was used to quantify lipid peroxidation. All probes were used according to the manufacturers' instructions. Rat DRG neurons were plated in ibiTreat 4-well m-slides (ref. 80426, Ibidi) pre-treated with 0.1?mg/mL of collagen. Five days after lentiviral transduction, DRG neurons were washed once with Hank's balanced salt solution (HBSS) with 10?mM HEPES, incubated at 37�C either with 2.5 ?M Mito-Ferro Green (30?min), 5 ?M MitoSOX Red (15?min), or 10 �M BODIPY(tm) 581/591 C11 (30?min). Following incubation, the neurons were washed, and images were captured with a confocal microscope (FV1000, Olympus) with a 60???objective and using the Z stack configuration. For each probe, all images were acquired with the same laser intensity (with respect to the Scr DMSO neurons). The images were analyzed with the Image J analysis software. Lipid peroxidation in fibroblasts was analyzed by measuring malondialdehyde (MDA), a compound derived from the peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids. To do that, the MDA Assay Kit (Assay Genie, ref. MAES0041) was used. Cells were seeded onto M6 plate, and the manufacturer's protocol was followed. The results were obtained using a microplate reader.
2.8. Immunofluorescence, image acquisition, and analysis
DRG neurons and fibroblasts were first plated on glass coverslips (ref. CB00120RA020MNZ0, Epredia) coated with collagen and seeded in a 4-well-plate with the corresponding medium. After 5 days of drug treatment, the cells were fixed with a 4?% paraformaldehyde (PFA) and cold methanol. Cells were permeabilized using a 0.5?% Triton X-100 solution in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and then were incubated with a blocking buffer containing 5?% bovine serum albumin (BSA) and 0.5?% Triton X-100 in PBS. The neurons were incubated with the primary antibodies-NRF2 (1:100; ref. ab62352, Abcam) and transferrin receptor 1 (TFR1, 1:100; ref. 13-6800, Invitrogen)-overnight at 4�C. Then, the cells were incubated with the secondary antibody-goat anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 594 (1:400; ref. A11012, Invitrogen) or goat anti-mouse Alexa Fluor 488 (1:400; ref. A11017, Invitrogen) for 1?h at room temperature in the dark. Nuclear localization of NRF2 in neurons was visualized using Hoechst stain (1:400). Images were captured with a FV1000 laser-scanning confocal microscope was used with a 60???objective (Olympus) for DRG neurons and with a 20x objective for fibroblasts, using the Z stack configuration. Fluorescence intensity was quantified using the Image J software.
2.9. Determination of reduced glutathione (GSH) and oxidized glutathione (GSSG)
The GSH/GSSG-Glo(tm) Assay (ref. V6612, Promega) was used to quantify GSH, GSSG, and the GSH/GSSG ratio. The cells were seeded in a 96-well white plate (ref. 33696, SPL) pre-treated with 0.1?mg/mL of collagen, and the assay was performed following the manufacturer's instructions. For each experimental condition, two wells were used: one for total GSH and another for GSSG. A standard curve was constructed to determine the GSH concentration in each sample. The plate was read using the ChemiDoc instrument to detect chemiluminescence. The data were normalized based on the protein concentration.
2.10. Statistical analysis
All data are presented as the mean � the standard error of the mean (SEM). The normality of the data was assessed with the Shapiro-Wilk test. For data with a normal distribution, Student's t test was used to compare two groups, whereas one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to compare multiple groups. Data that were not normally distributed were compared with the Kruskal-Wallis test followed by Dunn's test for multiple comparisons. The representative images shown in the figures were chosen to closely match the average values of the respective groups. A p-value of <?0.05 was considered significant. GraphPad Prism 9.0 (GraphPad Software, Inc., La Jolla, CA, USA) was used for statistical analysis and to prepare graphs.
3. Results
3.1. Leriglitazone increased frataxin levels and decreased cell death induced by frataxin depletion
Given that DRG sensory neurons are one of the earliest targets in FA, we compared the effects of leriglitazone on neonatal rat DRG neurons transduced with lentiviral vectors carrying frataxin-interfering shRNA (FXN1 or FXN2) or a non-interfering shRNA (Scr) as a control for 5 days. We used leriglitazone at 600?nM which is within the range of concentrations reported to be effective in cellular models,. In this model, as previously published,,, frataxin levels began to decline at 24?h after transduction and, at the end of the experiment, the mean frataxin levels were 50?% and 20?% for FXN1 and FXN2 neurons, respectively (Fig. 1A and B). We explored whether leriglitazone could increase frataxin levels by using western blotting to analyze cellular extracts after 5 days of drug treatment (Fig. 1A). Consistent with previous findings, leriglitazone totally prevented the reduction seen in frataxin levels in FXN1 neurons, and there was a tendency to increase the levels in FXN2 neurons Fig. 1B). Moreover, we analyzed cell survival by cross-marked wells in Scr and frataxin-deficient FXN1 and FXN2 cells, as well as the effect of the treatment (Fig. 1C). As shown inFig. 1D, frataxin-de?cient neurons showed, as previously published,, a signi?cant decrease in cell survival compared with control neurons (48?% and 39?% cell survival in FXN1 and FXN2 cells, respectively). Leriglitazone significantly increased the survival in both FXN1 and FXN2 neurons (to 82?% and 71?%, respectively). Cell viability was also assessed by the MTT assay. In agreement with the cross-marked well methodology, FXN1 neurons showed decreased viability which was rescued by leriglitazone treatment (Fig. 1E).

Significant differences between conditions are indicated (p values < 0.05(*), 0.01(**), or 0.001(***)).
3.2. Leriglitazone rescued decreased mitochondrial respiration in frataxin-deficient neurons
Many reports have demonstrated that mitochondrial respiration is impaired in different cellular and animal models of FA, as well as in tissues from patients with FA,,,,. We studied how efficiently leriglitazone could recover several mitochondrial alterations that we previously identified in frataxin-deficient DRG neurons. Specifically, we described a reduction in ATP-linked respiration, maximal respiration, and spare capacity following transduction with shRNAs FXN1 and FXN2 compared with non-interfering shRNA (Scr). Here, Oxygen Consumption Rate (OCR) was analyzed in FXN1 and FXN2 neurons after leriglitazone treatment and compared it with the OCR in Scr neurons (Fig. 2A and B). In frataxin-deficient FXN1 and FXN2 neurons, leriglitazone increased the maximal and spare capacity to the levels found in Scr cells treated with vehicle (Fig. 2?C, D and E). A similar result was obtained when OCR was analyzed in fibroblast from FA patients and compared to control cells. The decrease in maximal respiration observed in patients' fibroblast was partially reverted by leriglitazone treatment (Supplementary Fig. S1).
Fig. 2. Leriglitazone rescues decreased mitochondrial respiration in frataxin-deficient DRG neurons. Scr, FXN1, and FXN2 cells were treated with DMSO (vehicle) or 600?nM leriglitazone (LERI, L). (A) Mitochondrial respiration analysis of Scr versus FXN1 neurons. Significant differences are indicated: Scr vehicle versus FXN1 vehicle (*) and FXN1 LERI versus FXN1 vehicle (#). (B) Mitochondrial respiration analysis of Scr versus FXN2 neurons. Significant differences are indicated: Scr vehicle versus FXN2 vehicle (*), Scr LERI versus Scr vehicle (#) and FXN1 LERI versus FXN1 vehicle ($). (C-E) Basal respiration, ATP-linked respiration production, maximal respiration, and spare capacity were obtained from A and B for Scr (C), FXN1 (D), and FXN2 (E) cells. The data are presented as the mean � SEM from n?=?4-5 independent cultures. (F) Indicated proteins of the mitochondrial OXPHOS system were analyzed by western blot. Representative western blot images are shown. (G and H) Histograms represent the mean �?SEM from n?=?3-4 independent experiments from NDUFB8 (G) and SDHB (H). CBB protein stain was used as a loading control. Significant differences between conditions are indicated (p values < 0.05(*), 0.01(**), or 0.001(***)).
Because several proteins in the OXPHOS system contain Fe-S clusters, it is possible that deficiencies in their activities can be attributed to decreased protein levels, as we described in a cellular model and the FXNI151F mouse model of FA,. Moreover, leriglitazone already showed its ability to increase the levels of some OXPHOS complexes in a model of Rett Syndrome. Thus, we used western blotting to analyze selected proteins from each mitochondrial complex in untreated versus treated DRG neurons (Fig. 1?F). NDUFB8 (complex I) was decreased in FXN1 and FXN2 cells (Fig. 1?G), while SDHB (complex II) was reduced only in FXN2 neurons compared with their controls. Leriglitazone treatment showed a tendency to increase NDUFB8 (complex I) or SDHB (complex II) levels (Fig. 2?G and H). No differences between Scr and frataxin-deficient neurons were observed in UQCR2 (complex III), MTCO1 (complex IV), and ATP5A (complex V) (Supplementary Fig. S2), consistent with our previous findings. These results indicate that leriglitazone contributes to the improvement in the mitochondrial respiration function by improving activity and efficiency of the existing complexes, more than increasing its protein amount.
3.3. Leriglitazone ameliorated iron dysregulation and oxidative stress in frataxin-deficient neurons
Because it is well known that iron metabolism is dysregulated in FA, and leriglitazone was shown to reduce iron accumulation in the dentate nucleus of FA patients as measured by quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) in the FRAMES clinical trial in patients with FA, we explored whether leriglitazone could ameliorate these alterations. We analyzed whether iron accumulates in mitochondria of frataxin-deficient DRG neurons by quantifying intramitochondrial Fe2+ with confocal microscopy after labelling neurons with Mito-Ferro Green. Frataxin-deficient DRG neurons presented increased mitochondrial Fe2+ compared with Scr neurons (Fig. 3A). Quantification of green fluorescence showed a 2.2- and 2.4-fold increase in Fe2+ accumulation in FXN1 and FXN2 cells, respectively, compared with Scr cells (Fig. 3B), in agreement with our previously published results. Treatment with leriglitazone fully restored mitochondrial Fe2+ to the normal levels found in vehicle-treated Scr neurons (Fig. 3B). Excess Fe2+ can promote oxidative stress inside the mitochondria. Using the fluorescent probe MitoSox, increased mitochondrial superoxide levels were also observed in frataxin-deficient cells (Fig. 3?C). Quantification of red fluorescence showed a 2.3- and 2.4-fold increase in mitochondrial superoxide accumulation in FXN1 and FXN2 cells compared with Scr cells (Fig. 3D). In these frataxin-deficient neurons, leriglitazone treatment fully prevented superoxide levels accumulation (Fig. 3D).
Fig. 3. Leriglitazone reduces oxidative stress and iron alterations in frataxin-deficient DRG neurons. Scr, FXN1, and FXN2 cells were treated with DMSO (vehicle) or 600?nM leriglitazone (LERI). Representative Z-stack images obtained with confocal microscopy are shown. The scale bar represents 10 �m. (A and B) Mitochondrial Fe2?+?staining with MitoFerro Green probe. The data are presented as the mean � SEM from n?=?3 independent isolations. Between 90 and 180 cells were analyzed in each condition. (C and D) Mitochondrial superoxide levels were analyzed using MitoSox Red. The data are presented as the mean � SEM from n?=?3 independent isolations. Between 90 and 180 cells were analyzed in each condition. (E and F) TFR1 was analyzed by immunofluorescence staining. The data are presented as the mean � SEM from n?=?3 independent isolations. Between 50 and 120 cells were analyzed in each condition. In B, D, and F, each biological replicate is color coded (day to day variability), small symbols represent experimental replicates, and the big symbols are the mean of each culture. Significant differences between conditions are indicated (p values < 0.05(*), 0.01(**), or 0.001(***)).
This increase in iron can be attributed to several factors, especially upregulation of the TFR1, the main protein involved in cellular iron uptake. Such an increase has been described in cellular and animal models of FAas well as in human FA fibroblasts. To evaluate this possibility, TFR1 was analyzed by immunohistochemistry in Scr, FXN1, and FXN2 neurons (Fig. 3E). Based on quantification, TFR1 was increased in FXN1 (2.2-fold) and FXN2 (2.6-fold) neurons compared with Scr neurons (Fig. 3?F), which can contribute to iron accumulation. Again, leriglitazone reverted the TFR1 increase in FXN1 and FXN2 neurons to the normal levels found in vehicle-treated Scr neurons (Fig. 3?F). These results show that iron metabolism alterations in DRG neurons are pronounced and represent one of the possible factors that accounts for the vulnerability of frataxin-deficient neurons. In this context, leriglitazone is able to restore all these alterations by exerting a protective role.
To additionally validate some of these results in human cells, mitochondrial iron and TRF1 were quantified by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence staining respectively, in fibroblast from FA patients and controls (Supplementary Fig. S3). As shown, mitochondrial ferrous iron and TRF1 protein levels were both increased in patients' fibroblast and leriglitazone treatment was able to revert such alteration.
3.4. Leriglitazone rescued ferroptotic markers in frataxin-deficient neurons
Ferroptosis has recently been proposed to be involved in several models of FA,,,,,. Lipid peroxidation plays a central role in driving ferroptotic cell death; it can be caused by iron-induced oxidative stress and impairment of the GSH-GPX4 antioxidant system. GSH is required for GPX4 activity, which reduces lipid peroxides into lipid alcohols.
We have recently characterized ferroptosis in DRG neurons, both in the in vitro cellular model of frataxin-deficient DRG neurons as well as in DRG isolated from the FXNI151F mouse. Here, we assessed to what extent leriglitazone could rescue the changes caused by frataxin deficiency in our primary cultures of DRG neurons. GPX4 levels were analyzed by western blotting (Fig. 4A); the quantification showed, as expected, decreased GPX4 levels in frataxin-deficient neurons. Treatment with leriglitazone fully prevented this reduction (Fig. 4B). The analysis of the redox state showed decreased levels of reduced GSH in FXN1 and FXN2 cells compared with Scr cells; however, leriglitazone could not reverse such decrease (Fig. 4?C). When GSSG was analyzed, leriglitazone was able to reduce GSSG levels in FXN1 and FXN2 neurons (Fig. 4D). The GSH/GSSG ratio decreased by approximately 40?% and 55?% in FXN1 and FXN2 cells, respectively, compared with Scr cells. Treatment with leriglitazone fully restored the GSH/GSSG ratio to the control levels (Fig. 4E). Total glutathione (GSH+GSSG) was decreased in FXN1 and FXN2 neurons compared with Scr neurons. Leriglitazone did not affect the levels of total glutathione (Supplementary Fig. S4), indicating that the positive effect of the treatment on the GSH/GSSG ratio is probably due to the decrease in oxidative stress, which would reduce GSSG levels. In this regard, we assessed cellular lipid oxidation in sensory DRG neurons by using BODIPY C11 581/591 (Fig. 4?F). Frataxin-deficient cells showed increased green fluorescence indicative of lipid peroxidation. Based on quantification, the ratio of oxidized to reduced Bodipy C11 was increased by 2.2- and 3.4-fold in FXN1 and FXN2 cells, respectively, compared with Scr cells (Fig. 4?G). Treatment with leriglitazone reduced lipid peroxidation, with a decrease of 40?% and 60?% in FXN1 and FXN2 neurons respectively, compared with their respective controls (Fig. 4?F and G). Taken together, these data clearly indicate that, in our model, leriglitazone rescued the ferroptosis markers analyzed.

(A and B) GPX4 levels were analyzed by western blotting. Representative images are shown; CBB protein staining was used as a loading control. The histogram presents the mean � SEM of n?=?5-6 independent cultures. (C, D and E) Reduced GSH, GSSG, and the GSH/GSSG ratio were measured. Each biological replicate is color coded (day to day variability), small symbols represent individual neurons that were analyzed, and big symbols are the mean of the same culture. Significant differences between conditions are indicated (p values < 0.05(*), 0.01(**), or 0.001(***)).
Similar results were obtained when GPX4 levels, the GSH/GSSG ratio and lipid peroxidation was analyzed in fibroblast cultures from FA patients and compared to control cells (Supplementary Fig. S5). The decrease in GPX4 and the GSH/GSSG ratio observed in FA fibroblasts was almost fully reverted by leriglitazone treatment. Moreover, lipid peroxidation analyzed as MDA content was almost 2-fold higher in FA fibroblast compared to control fibroblasts and leriglitazone fully rescue such phenotype.
3.5. Leriglitazone fully prevented NRF2 impairment and prevented PGC1� downregulation in frataxin-deficient DRG neurons
NRF2 is the main transcription factor that regulates cytoprotective responses to ferroptotic damage as well as oxidative stress, but its response is impaired in several models of FA,,,. We analyzed the levels of NRF2 by western blotting and, as expected, there was a 50?% and 80?% reduction in FXN1 and FXN2 cells, respectively (Fig. 5A and B). Leriglitazone was able to fully prevent the decay of NRF2 in FXN1 and partially in FXN2 neurons. Because NRF2 exerts its effects in the nucleus, to determine whether such alterations affected their location, we also analyzed NRF2 with confocal microscopy (Fig. 5?C). Consistent with the western blotting results, we found a decrease in total NRF2 in FXN1 and FXN2 cells (Fig. 5D). These results are in agreement with our previous findingsand those from DRG isolated from the YG8sR mouse model. Thus, we were especially interested to see whether leriglitazone could rescue this alteration. The treatment significantly increased total NRF2 levels in Scr, FXN1, and FXN2 neurons (Fig. 5D). There were similar results regarding cytosolic NRF2 (Fig. 5E). Active nuclear NRF2 decreased by 50?% and 55?% in FXN1 and FXN2 cells, respectively, compared with Scr cells. Again, leriglitazone increased nuclear NRF2 to levels above the vehicle-treated Scr (Fig. 5?F). Because both nuclear and cytosolic NRF2 showed similar patterns, there were no differences in the nuclear-to-cytosolic ratio (Supplementary Fig. S6).

(G and H) PGC1? levels were analyzed by Western blotting. A representative image is shown; CBB protein staining was used as a loading control. Dysregulation of the PPAR? pathway has been reported in tissues from a mouse model of FA and in frataxin-de?cient cellular models,,,,. One of the important targets of PPAR? is PGC1�, so we analyzed its levels in DRG neurons showing a reduction of 44?% and 53?% in FXN1 and FXN2 cells, respectively, compared with Scr cells (Fig. 5?G and H). Leriglitazone could fully prevent the decrease in PGC1� levels in FXN1 cells, compared with vehicle-treated FXN1 cells.
3.6. Leriglitazone in combination with omaveloxolone rescued decreased viability and mitochondrial respiration in frataxin-deficient DRG neurons
Up to date, omaveloxolone is the only FDA and EMA-approved drug to treat FA patients. However, patients treated with omaveloxolone have experienced side effects, including transaminases elevation,leading to dose reduction in some patients. Likewise, a phase 2 clinical study with leriglitazone on FA (study MT-2-03; FRAMES) showed promising results, but some side effects were also reported, with peripheral edema being the most frequent.
Combining omaveloxolone and leriglitazone could be considered as a potential treatment with less side effects. To explore possible synergism between these two drugs, several experiments were performed in frataxin-deficient DRG neurons. Concentrations of leriglitazoneand omaveloxolone,,were selected based on those reported to be effective in in vitro models of FA. Cell viability was analyzed by the MTT assay in Scr and FXN1 cells after treatment with leriglitazone alone, omaveloxolone alone or in combination (Fig. 6A). As shown, in frataxin-deficient FXN1 neurons, either alone or together resulted, at the doses analyzed, in a significant increase in cell viability compared to vehicle-treated FXN1 cells. The combination that displayed the highest survival in FXN1 cells was 300?nM leriglitazone plus 25?nM omaveloxolone and the lowest was the combination of 600?nM leriglitazone plus 50?nM omaveloxolone. Interestingly, in Scr cells, the same combination (600?nM leriglitazone and 50?nM omaveloxolone) showed a minor but significant decrease in cell viability compared to vehicle-treated Scr cells, indicative of some toxicity.
Fig. 6. The combination of leriglitazone and omaveloxolone at lower doses recovers cell viability and mitochondrial respiration impairment in frataxin-deficient DRG neurons. Scr and FXN1 cells were treated with DMSO (vehicle), leriglitazone (LERI) and/or omaveloxolone (OMAV) at different concentrations. (A) MTT assay was used to determine cellular viability. The data are presented as the mean � SEM from n?=?4-10 independent isolations. Significant differences are indicated: Scr or FXN1 cells treated with LERI and/or OMAV versus Scr vehicle (#) and FXN1 treated cells with LERI and/or OMAV versus FXN1 vehicle (*). (B) Mitochondrial respiration analysis of Scr versus FXN1 neurons. Significant differences are indicated: FXN1 vehicle versus Scr vehicle (*); FXN1 600?nM LERI versus FXN1 vehicle (+); FXN1 300?nM LERI versus FXN1 vehicle (#); FXN1 50?nM OMAV versus FXN1 vehicle ($); FXN1 300?nM LERI and 50?nM OMAV versus FXN1 vehicle (&). (C) Basal respiration, ATP-linked respiration production, maximal respiration, and spare capacity were obtained from B. The data are presented as the mean � SEM from n?=?5 independent cultures. (D) Mitochondrial respiration analysis of Scr versus FXN1 neurons. Significant differences are indicated: FXN1 vehicle versus Scr vehicle (*); FXN1 600?nM LERI versus FXN1 vehicle (+); FXN1 50?nM OMAV versus FXN1 vehicle (#); FXN1 300?nM LERI and 25?nM OMAV versus FXN1 vehicle ($).
