Directional-approach task
In the Directional-approach Task (Fig. 4), SCA participants performed worse than HC (p?<?0.001), with results remaining significant after controlling for global cognition (data in the Supplementary Table 2). Performance across all participants was worse during trials requiring a 180� perspective shift compared to a 90� shift (p?=?0.008). However, the interaction between group status and perspective angle was not significant (p?=?0.135). The SCA participants used a specific strategy with unique houses less frequently than HC (70% vs. 94%, p?=?0.011), and not using this strategy was associated with worse task performance (rpb?=?0.38, p?=?0.002).

Figure 4: Directional-approach task-mean number of correct responses. Group comparisons are adjusted for age, sex, education, and BDI. SCA, Spinocerebellar ataxias; HC, Healthy controls, *p?<?.05; **p?<?.01; ***p?<?.001.

For the Directional-approach Task, global cognition was significantly associated with performance in SCA participants (??=?0.05, p?=?0.013), whereas no associations were found with SARA or FA-ADL scores. Directional-approach Task performance in SCA participants was also associated with visuospatial functions (??=?0.16, p?<?0.001), executive functions (??=?0.21, p?<?0.001), and attention and working memory (??=?0.18, p?=?0.001), but not with verbal memory or language. These associations remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons.
In SCA participants, self-reported spatial navigation abilities, as measured by the SBSOD, showed no significant associations with MMSE, SARA, FA-ADL scores, PTSOT angular deviations and correct quadrants identified, Directional-approach Task scores, or cognitive domains except for language (??=?0.58, p?=?0.030). After correction for multiple comparisons, the association with language was no longer significant.
Discussion
In this study, we focused on spatial perspective taking, an important aspect of spatial navigation, in patients with degenerative ataxias and its relation to cognitive functions, motor impairment, and self-reported spatial navigation abilities.
We found that SCA patients performed significantly worse than HC on both perspective taking tests. In contrast, FRDA patients demonstrated only partial deficits relative to HC. The pronounced disruption in spatial perspective taking in SCA was associated with global cognitive performance and several specific cognitive domains, but not with cerebellar motor impairment or FA-ADL.
These findings support the growing evidence that the cerebellum plays a crucial role in navigation, including spatial perspective taking. Our study is the first to demonstrate deficits in this ability in SCA patients. These results align with research in animal models of cerebellar damage, which have shown impaired spatial navigation in mice with cerebellar lesions, including the mouse model of SCA155,56,57. Our results are also in line with previous findings in several patients with cerebellar tumors or stroke, who exhibited impairment in mental rotation, an ability distinct from perspective taking, yet closely related to it27,35. It should be noted that worse performance on the more challenging trials with the 180� perspective shift than with the 90� shift indicates that the impairment in the Directional-approach Task is indeed determined by impaired perspective taking ability rather than other factors (e.g., severity of cognitive impairment, lack of attention, etc.). Interestingly, SCA patients were more likely to rely on non-specific or suboptimal strategies during the Directional-approach task compared to healthy controls, and the use of such strategies was significantly associated with poorer task performance. This pattern may reflect executive dysfunction, which is supported by the observed associations between task performance and executive functions scores in our cohort.
The observed impairment in perspective taking may not exclusively reflect a deficit in spatial transformation per se, but could be part of a broader disruption in cerebellar-supported cognitive functions. The cerebellum is increasingly recognized as a structure involved in building internal forward models that enable the prediction of sensory consequences of actions and the coordination of temporally structured sequences, both in the motor and cognitive domains. These internal models are thought to support mental simulation and flexible manipulation of internal representations, the functions potentially relevant for imagining spatial perspectives and anticipating spatial configurations from different orientations58,59,60.
Perspective taking is a crucial component of spatial navigation, a fundamental skill in daily life. Impairments in spatial navigation are associated with increased dependency, reduced autonomy, and a heightened risk of getting lost, all of which can significantly diminish the quality of life29,61. The mean score of 10.43 out of 18 on the Directional-Approach task in our SCA patients is only marginally better than chance, indicating a substantial impairment.
The severity of the perspective taking impairment in SCA patients in our results, as measured by the Directional-approach Task (mean percentage of correct answers 58%), was similar in magnitude to that of patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment (aMCI) due to a non-Alzheimer pathology (54% correct) and was only slightly milder than that of aMCI patients due to Alzheimer disease (44.6% correct) in a study using a shorter version of the same test62. This comparison with a neurodegenerative disorder known for its marked impairment of spatial navigation puts our results in context and suggests a possible clinical significance of our findings in ataxia patients.
In contrast to SCA patients, the FRDA group showed less severe impairment despite the more pronounced motor disability. This is analogous to the less severe cognitive, neuropsychiatric, and also social cognitive impairment in FRDA patients compared to SCA found in previous studies6,63. The difference may stem from the less severe cerebellar grey matter atrophy in FRDA64. However, the potential involvement of extra-cerebellar structures, such as the basal ganglia, on these non-motor manifestations in SCA cannot be ruled out65.
In accordance with our hypotheses, we found that the perspective taking impairment in SCA patients was associated with general cognition and specific cognitive domains, namely visuospatial functions, executive functions, and attention and working memory. These domains are related to spatial navigation and form the core of the cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome2,26.
In addition, the perspective taking ability in SCA patients did not correlate with cerebellar motor impairment as measured by the SARA or with motor functional impairment as measured by the FA-ADL scale. This dissociation reflects previous findings in cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome, such as neuropsychiatric symptoms and deficits in social cognition, which likewise show no direct relationship with motor impairment10,66. While this dissociation is not always consistently observed in neuropsychological tests, the overall evidence confirms that distinct cerebellar regions regulate motor and cognitive functions9,67,68,69. Neuroimaging studies further support this distinction, identifying separate motor and cognitive-affective areas within the cerebellum3,70. Notably, functional neuroimaging studies in healthy individuals have shown that spatial navigation, including perspective taking, primarily activates the posterior cerebellar lobe-a region associated with cognitive processing14. Our results from the perspective taking tests fit well into this picture.
Interestingly, despite the objectively identified deficits in spatial perspective taking, SCA patients reported only slightly worse spatial navigation abilities compared to HC on the self-reported questionnaire. Their self-reported navigation abilities were not associated with performance on the Directional-approach Task or with performance on the PTSOT, as measured by angular deviations and correct quadrants identified. Previous studies in healthy individuals have shown that self-reported navigation ability is linked to spatial task performance71,72,73, including perspective taking tests, particularly the PTSOT51,74. However, in clinical population, self-reported, unlike informant-reported measures fail to reliably distinguish cognitively impaired individuals from HC, possibly due to reduced awareness of cognitive deficits or difficulties in accurately assessing one's own abilities75,76. In SCA patients, this partial lack of awareness may be further influenced by "dysmetria of thought" a phenomenon observed in cerebellar disorders2. Moreover, given that motor impairment in ataxia is the primary perceived and functionally limiting difficulty in patients with ataxia, it may dominate the patients' perception of their overall disability. Consequently, cognitive difficulties-such as impairments in spatial perspective taking-may be perceived as less relevant or may go unnoticed. Another possible contributing factor is that patients with significant motor impairment tend to travel less frequently, and while travelling, they are often accompanied and even physically supported by their caregivers, who may take on the responsibility for spatial navigation and the patients may thus have fewer opportunities to evaluate their navigation skills in real-world settings. As a result, self-reported spatial navigation questionnaires may not be reliable indicators of cognitive performance in individuals with cerebellar disorders and restricted mobility.
The main strength of this study is its novelty, as it is the first study to investigate spatial perspective taking, a key component of spatial navigation, in patients with degenerative ataxias, or indeed any cerebellar disorder. By employing well-established and ecologically valid tests, alongside a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment, the study provides valuable insights into the cognitive deficits associated with ataxias. Additionally, the comparison of SCA and FRDA patients highlights distinct patterns of cognitive and perspective taking impairments in these conditions.
However, several limitations must be acknowledged. The relatively small sample size, a challenge inherent to studies on rare diseases, limits the generalizability of our findings. The heterogeneity within the SCA group, which included various genetic subtypes, further complicates the interpretation and limits the possibility to assess differences between various SCA subtypes. Moreover, the FRDA group underwent a less comprehensive testing protocol, which may have influenced the comparability of results. Finally, the absence of neuroimaging data prevents direct correlations between cognitive deficits and cerebellar or extra-cerebellar structural changes. Future studies should aim to address these limitations by including larger, more genetically homogenous cohorts, taking also age of onset and disease duration into account, and, importantly, incorporating advanced neuroimaging techniques such as voxel-based morphometry or functional connectivity studies to explore the structural-functional correlates of perspective taking abilities. Additionally, future studies might explore the discrepancy between spatial navigation deficits and patients' self-awareness of these deficits in greater detail, employing informant-rated measures as well. Studies aimed at evaluating spatial navigation across a broader spectrum, with a focus on aspects beyond perspective taking, are currently underway.
Conclusion
This study is the first to demonstrate impairments in spatial perspective taking, an important subcomponent of spatial navigation, in SCA patients with deficits of similar magnitude to those observed in dementing conditions. Impaired perspective taking was associated with cognitive deficits but not with motor impairment. The milder deficits observed in FRDA patients align with the less pronounced cerebellar atrophy compared to SCA. Our findings expand the understanding of the cognitive impairments in SCA, highlighting the functional dissociation between motor and non-motor cerebellum. Furthermore, our findings support the presence of clinically significant spatial navigation deficits in SCA, adding to the existing knowledge of complex cognitive dysfunction in these disorders.
For the Directional-approach Task, global cognition was significantly associated with performance in SCA participants (??=?0.05, p?=?0.013), whereas no associations were found with SARA or FA-ADL scores. Directional-approach Task performance in SCA participants was also associated with visuospatial functions (??=?0.16, p?<?0.001), executive functions (??=?0.21, p?<?0.001), and attention and working memory (??=?0.18, p?=?0.001), but not with verbal memory or language. These associations remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons.

In SCA participants, self-reported spatial navigation abilities, as measured by the SBSOD, showed no significant associations with MMSE, SARA, FA-ADL scores, PTSOT angular deviations and correct quadrants identified, Directional-approach Task scores, or cognitive domains except for language (??=?0.58, p?=?0.030). After correction for multiple comparisons, the association with language was no longer significant.

Discussion
In this study, we focused on spatial perspective taking, an important aspect of spatial navigation, in patients with degenerative ataxias and its relation to cognitive functions, motor impairment, and self-reported spatial navigation abilities.

We found that SCA patients performed significantly worse than HC on both perspective taking tests. In contrast, FRDA patients demonstrated only partial deficits relative to HC. The pronounced disruption in spatial perspective taking in SCA was associated with global cognitive performance and several specific cognitive domains, but not with cerebellar motor impairment or FA-ADL.

These findings support the growing evidence that the cerebellum plays a crucial role in navigation, including spatial perspective taking. Our study is the first to demonstrate deficits in this ability in SCA patients. These results align with research in animal models of cerebellar damage, which have shown impaired spatial navigation in mice with cerebellar lesions, including the mouse model of SCA155,56,57. Our results are also in line with previous findings in several patients with cerebellar tumors or stroke, who exhibited impairment in mental rotation, an ability distinct from perspective taking, yet closely related to it27,35. It should be noted that worse performance on the more challenging trials with the 180� perspective shift than with the 90� shift indicates that the impairment in the Directional-approach Task is indeed determined by impaired perspective taking ability rather than other factors (e.g., severity of cognitive impairment, lack of attention, etc.). Interestingly, SCA patients were more likely to rely on non-specific or suboptimal strategies during the Directional-approach task compared to healthy controls, and the use of such strategies was significantly associated with poorer task performance. This pattern may reflect executive dysfunction, which is supported by the observed associations between task performance and executive functions scores in our cohort.

The observed impairment in perspective taking may not exclusively reflect a deficit in spatial transformation per se, but could be part of a broader disruption in cerebellar-supported cognitive functions. The cerebellum is increasingly recognized as a structure involved in building internal forward models that enable the prediction of sensory consequences of actions and the coordination of temporally structured sequences, both in the motor and cognitive domains. These internal models are thought to support mental simulation and flexible manipulation of internal representations, the functions potentially relevant for imagining spatial perspectives and anticipating spatial configurations from different orientations58,59,60.

Perspective taking is a crucial component of spatial navigation, a fundamental skill in daily life. Impairments in spatial navigation are associated with increased dependency, reduced autonomy, and a heightened risk of getting lost, all of which can significantly diminish the quality of life29,61. The mean score of 10.43 out of 18 on the Directional-Approach task in our SCA patients is only marginally better than chance, indicating a substantial impairment.

The severity of the perspective taking impairment in SCA patients in our results, as measured by the Directional-approach Task (mean percentage of correct answers 58%), was similar in magnitude to that of patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment (aMCI) due to a non-Alzheimer pathology (54% correct) and was only slightly milder than that of aMCI patients due to Alzheimer disease (44.6% correct) in a study using a shorter version of the same test62. This comparison with a neurodegenerative disorder known for its marked impairment of spatial navigation puts our results in context and suggests a possible clinical significance of our findings in ataxia patients.

In contrast to SCA patients, the FRDA group showed less severe impairment despite the more pronounced motor disability. This is analogous to the less severe cognitive, neuropsychiatric, and also social cognitive impairment in FRDA patients compared to SCA found in previous studies6,63. The difference may stem from the less severe cerebellar grey matter atrophy in FRDA64. However, the potential involvement of extra-cerebellar structures, such as the basal ganglia, on these non-motor manifestations in SCA cannot be ruled out65.

In accordance with our hypotheses, we found that the perspective taking impairment in SCA patients was associated with general cognition and specific cognitive domains, namely visuospatial functions, executive functions, and attention and working memory. These domains are related to spatial navigation and form the core of the cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome2,26.

In addition, the perspective taking ability in SCA patients did not correlate with cerebellar motor impairment as measured by the SARA or with motor functional impairment as measured by the FA-ADL scale. This dissociation reflects previous findings in cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome, such as neuropsychiatric symptoms and deficits in social cognition, which likewise show no direct relationship with motor impairment10,66. While this dissociation is not always consistently observed in neuropsychological tests, the overall evidence confirms that distinct cerebellar regions regulate motor and cognitive functions9,67,68,69. Neuroimaging studies further support this distinction, identifying separate motor and cognitive-affective areas within the cerebellum3,70. Notably, functional neuroimaging studies in healthy individuals have shown that spatial navigation, including perspective taking, primarily activates the posterior cerebellar lobe-a region associated with cognitive processing14. Our results from the perspective taking tests fit well into this picture.

Interestingly, despite the objectively identified deficits in spatial perspective taking, SCA patients reported only slightly worse spatial navigation abilities compared to HC on the self-reported questionnaire. Their self-reported navigation abilities were not associated with performance on the Directional-approach Task or with performance on the PTSOT, as measured by angular deviations and correct quadrants identified. Previous studies in healthy individuals have shown that self-reported navigation ability is linked to spatial task performance71,72,73, including perspective taking tests, particularly the PTSOT51,74. However, in clinical population, self-reported, unlike informant-reported measures fail to reliably distinguish cognitively impaired individuals from HC, possibly due to reduced awareness of cognitive deficits or difficulties in accurately assessing one's own abilities75,76. In SCA patients, this partial lack of awareness may be further influenced by "dysmetria of thought" a phenomenon observed in cerebellar disorders2. Moreover, given that motor impairment in ataxia is the primary perceived and functionally limiting difficulty in patients with ataxia, it may dominate the patients' perception of their overall disability. Consequently, cognitive difficulties-such as impairments in spatial perspective taking-may be perceived as less relevant or may go unnoticed. Another possible contributing factor is that patients with significant motor impairment tend to travel less frequently, and while travelling, they are often accompanied and even physically supported by their caregivers, who may take on the responsibility for spatial navigation and the patients may thus have fewer opportunities to evaluate their navigation skills in real-world settings. As a result, self-reported spatial navigation questionnaires may not be reliable indicators of cognitive performance in individuals with cerebellar disorders and restricted mobility.

The main strength of this study is its novelty, as it is the first study to investigate spatial perspective taking, a key component of spatial navigation, in patients with degenerative ataxias, or indeed any cerebellar disorder. By employing well-established and ecologically valid tests, alongside a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment, the study provides valuable insights into the cognitive deficits associated with ataxias. Additionally, the comparison of SCA and FRDA patients highlights distinct patterns of cognitive and perspective taking impairments in these conditions.

However, several limitations must be acknowledged. The relatively small sample size, a challenge inherent to studies on rare diseases, limits the generalizability of our findings. The heterogeneity within the SCA group, which included various genetic subtypes, further complicates the interpretation and limits the possibility to assess differences between various SCA subtypes. Moreover, the FRDA group underwent a less comprehensive testing protocol, which may have influenced the comparability of results. Finally, the absence of neuroimaging data prevents direct correlations between cognitive deficits and cerebellar or extra-cerebellar structural changes. Future studies should aim to address these limitations by including larger, more genetically homogenous cohorts, taking also age of onset and disease duration into account, and, importantly, incorporating advanced neuroimaging techniques such as voxel-based morphometry or functional connectivity studies to explore the structural-functional correlates of perspective taking abilities. Additionally, future studies might explore the discrepancy between spatial navigation deficits and patients' self-awareness of these deficits in greater detail, employing informant-rated measures as well. Studies aimed at evaluating spatial navigation across a broader spectrum, with a focus on aspects beyond perspective taking, are currently underway.

Conclusion
This study is the first to demonstrate impairments in spatial perspective taking, an important subcomponent of spatial navigation, in SCA patients with deficits of similar magnitude to those observed in dementing conditions. Impaired perspective taking was associated with cognitive deficits but not with motor impairment. The milder deficits observed in FRDA patients align with the less pronounced cerebellar atrophy compared to SCA. Our findings expand the understanding of the cognitive impairments in SCA, highlighting the functional dissociation between motor and non-motor cerebellum. Furthermore, our findings support the presence of clinically significant spatial navigation deficits in SCA, adding to the existing knowledge of complex cognitive dysfunction in these disorders.








The clinical burden of Friedreich ataxia in the United States: A retrospective claims database analysis

Highlights
?
Matched-cohort study to evaluate the real-world burden of Friedreich ataxia (FRDA)
?
FRDA is associated with higher risks of poor clinical outcomes than controls.
?
Results show that patients with FRDA also have a significantly higher risk of death.
?
Findings underscore a high clinical burden and unmet need for advances in treatment.

Abstract
Background
Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is a terminal, rare, autosomal recessive genetic disorder associated with debilitating comorbidities. However, limited real-world data on clinical outcomes associated with FRDA have been presented.
Methods
The Komodo Research Data (01/2016-03/2023) was used to identify patients with FRDA who had �2 independent non-diagnostic early-onset cerebellar ataxia codes, 1 non-diagnostic FRDA specific code, and �12 months of continuous enrollment before and after the index date (defined as a random date with FRDA diagnosis). Individuals without early-onset cerebellar ataxia were eligible for controls. The controls were matched at a 5:1 ratio on age, sex, insurance type, US region, and continuous enrollment and assigned the same index date as the matched patients.
Results
After matching, the study included 652 patients with FRDA and 3260 matched controls (mean age 33.2 years; 51.4 % females). During the follow-up period (median 26.2 months for cases and 28.3 months for controls), the incremental clinical burden in FRDA cases vs. matched controls was high: patients with FRDA had significantly higher odds of loss of ambulation (odds ratio: 158.0), cardiomyopathy (59.2), scoliosis (49.0), falls (7.4), diabetes (2.5), head injury (2.4), and fracture (3.3) compared to controls (all p < 0.001). Patients with FRDA also experienced a higher risk of mortality than controls (hazard ratio: 3.9).
Conclusions
Real-world data suggested patients with FRDA were associated with substantial and incremental clinical burden compared to matched controls and will benefit in advances in treatment for FRDA.

1. Introduction
Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is an inherited, autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic mutations of the FXN gene, leading to deficiency of the protein frataxin. Frataxin has roles in mitochondrial function, ATP production, and counteracting oxidative stress in cells. Frataxin deficiency in FRDA leads to progressive neuropathology, primarily involving the dorsal root ganglia, dentate nuclei of the cerebellum, regions of the spinal cord, and the spinal and peripheral nerves. As a result, people with FRDA develop worsening ataxia of the limbs, dysarthria, and muscle weakness, resulting in problems with movement, gait, coordination, and balance. FRDA is the most common inherited ataxia but remains rare, and primarily presents in people of Eurasian and North African descent,,]. The estimated prevalence of FRDA ranges from 1 in 29,000 to 100,000 White Europeans and varies across geographic regions. However, recent epidemiological data on FRDA is limited, further complicated by low disease awareness, delayed diagnosis, and inconsistent availability of FRDA-specific coding.
FRDA onset is typically during childhood or adolescence, although the clinical course is heterogenous and depends on the severity and type of FXN mutation, timing of symptom onset, and organ involvement. A large natural history study of 1115 patients with FRDA in the North America and Australia-the Friedreich Ataxia Clinical Outcome Measures study (FACOMS)-reported that 29 %, 39 %, 21 %, and 11 % of patients had symptom onset during the age of 0-7 years, 8-14 years, 15-24 years, and >24 years, respectively. Patients with FRDA have increased risk of cardiomyopathy (66 % of cases), bladder dysfunction (41 %), visual (25 %) or hearing (13-39 %) impairment, and diabetes mellitus (30 %),,,]. Other variable symptoms include muscle spasms, scoliosis, difficulty eating or drinking, abnormal auditory function, and depression. Notably, earlier symptom onset is associated with faster disease progression and higher frequency of cardiomyopathy, scoliosis, visual loss, and diabetes. Despite the variable phenotype, patients typically experience progressive limb ataxia and loss of lower-limb reflexes and eventually lose ambulation. For example, 70 % of patients in FACOMS were ambulatory at enrollment, which decreased to 49 % by end of follow-up (median of 5 years). The lifespan of patients with FRDA is shortened, with a mean age of 37.5 years at death; cardiac involvement is the major determinant of mortality risk.
There is no cure for FRDA and, until recently, the management of the disorder focused only on supportive care to manage symptoms. However, the first therapy for FRDA, omaveloxolone, an Nrf2 activator that improves mitochondrial function, redox balance, as well as reduces inflammation in models of FRDA, was approved by the United States (US) Food and Drug Administration in 2023 for patients aged 16 years and olderon the basis of the results from the randomized, placebo-controlled, and double-blind MOXIe Part 2 trial (Clinicaltrials.gov ID: NCT02255435).
Given the recent introduction of omaveloxolone for the treatment of FRDA, it is important to establish the clinical burden of the disorder in the real world, prior to omaveloxolone introduction, to form a basis for subsequent comparison in the new treatment landscape. A study by Powell et al. (2023), using the US Merative MarketScan Commercial database (August 2010 to September 2020), recently examined clinical burden of FRDA in the US. However, due to the lack of a specific International Classification of Diseases, 10th edition (ICD-10) code for FRDA between 2015 and 2020, the results from that study were limited to a cohort of patients identified in or before 2015. Before 2015, there was a FRDA specific ICD-9 (G334.0), which was later replaced by an unspecific ICD-10 code encompassing early onset cerebellar ataxia not limited to FRDA. Eventually, an ICD-10-specific FRDA code of G11.11 was created on October 1, 2020, presenting the opportunity for a more comprehensive claims database analysis of patients with FRDA. Accordingly, this study aimed to address these gaps in the literature and illustrate the underlying unmet medical need in patients with FRDA after this timepoint (i.e., 2016-2023) by comparing their clinical burden with that of matched controls without FRDA.
2. Methods
2.1. Data source
This retrospective, matched case-control study used Komodo Research Data (KRD) between January 2016 and March 2023. The KRD contains closed claims data directly from 150+ payers representing over 185 million patient lives covered by different healthcare plans, including Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial plans. The covered patient population has a good US census-level representation of all ages, incomes, races, and ethnicities. Because the data were de-identified and previously collected, no ethical review was required.
2.2. Population and study design
Patients who met the following criteria were selected into the study as cases: (1) at least two independent non-diagnostic early-onset cerebellar ataxia codes (ICD-10: G11.1 or G11.11), and one non-diagnostic FRDA-specific code (ICD-10: G11.11); and (2) at least 12 months of continuous enrollment before and after the index date, defined as a random date with FRDA diagnosis (Fig. 1). Non-diagnostic diagnosis codes refer to FRDA codes that appear on claims for therapeutic or routine medical services, such as office visits or procedures, rather than on claims whose primary purpose is diagnostic evaluation, such as laboratory tests or imaging. Requiring at least one non-diagnostic code ensured that individuals whose FRDA code appeared only during an initial work-up were excluded since such patients frequently present with similar symptoms but are ultimately determined not to have FRDA. A randomly selected FRDA diagnosis date was used to define index date to capture patients at different stages of disease progression and to reflect the overall FRDA population in the real world. Patients without early-onset cerebellar ataxia (controls) (i.e., without a diagnosis code of G11.1? during the entire data period) were selected by matching to cases at a 5:1 ratio on age, sex, insurance type, US region, and continuous enrollment. The same index date as matched patients with FRDA was assigned to matched controls.

Fig. 1. Sample selection of patients with FRDA, prior to matching.
Abbreviation: FRDA, Friedreich ataxia.
The study design is described in Fig. 2. The baseline period was defined as the 12 months before the index date. The study period was defined as the period from the index date to the end of continuous enrollment, end of data availability, or death, whichever the earlier, with a minimum of 12 months.
Fig. 2. Study design.
Abbreviation: FRDA, Friedreich ataxia.

2.3. Study endpoints
Patient characteristics, including demographics, clinical characteristics, and comorbidities and symptoms of FRDA, were described during the baseline period. Demographic information included patients' age category, sex, race/ethnicity, US region, and insurance type. Clinical characteristics included the observed duration of disease, year of the index date, ambulatory status, and the Elixhauser Comorbidity Index (ECI) which measures and categorizes comorbidities that impact health outcomes based on ICD diagnosis codes. Comorbidities associated with FRDA included cardiomyopathy, scoliosis, depression, visual impairment, anxiety, diabetes, and sensorineural hearing loss. Symptoms of FRDA included cardiac arrythmia, falls, dysphagia, dyspnea, muscle cramps, dysarthria, and cognitive impairment.
Additionally, the following clinical complications/outcomes were assessed during the study follow-up period: loss of ambulation, cardiac arrythmia, cardiomyopathy, visual impairment, scoliosis, falls, dyspnea, diabetes, head injury, fracture, dysarthria, bladder dysfunction, pneumonia, sensory hearing loss, dysphasia, and death.
2.4. Statistical analyses
Patient baseline characteristics were summarized descriptively for cases and controls, using counts and proportions for categorical variables, and mean with standard deviations (SD) and/or median with interquartile range (IQR) for continuous variables. During the study period, the proportions of patients with an event were summarized and compared between cases and matched controls using generalized equation estimation (GEE) models. Odds ratios (OR) with 95 % confidence intervals (CI) were reported in risk of event analyses. The incidence of loss of ambulation (defined as at least one diagnosis of paraplegia, quadriplegia, confined to bed, or wheelchair use), diabetes, and death, and the time to loss of ambulation, the development of diabetes, and death, were described for cases and matched controls using Kaplan-Meier (KM) analysis. For loss of ambulation and diabetes, separate analyses were performed for the overall population and the subset of population without the respective complication at baseline. For all analyses, statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Analyses were conducted in SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC, US) and Snowflake.
3. Results
3.1. Sample selection and characteristics of FRDA cases before matching
A total of 823 patients with FRDA who met all study criteria were selected from the database (Fig. 1). The baseline and clinical characteristics of FRDA cases prior to matching are described in Table S1. The mean age of FRDA cases at the index date was 35.5 (SD: 17.7) years and 52.2 % were female. Of the 79.7 % of patients with race/ethnicity group information, 75.5 % were White. The mean observed duration of FRDA (i.e., the duration from the first observed FRDA diagnosis in the data to the index date) was 30.1 (SD: 20.5) months and approximately half (47.9 %) of patients were non-ambulatory at baseline. The top three comorbidities associated with FRDA were cardiomyopathy (31.8 %), scoliosis (29.2 %), and depression (25.8 %), and the top three symptoms associated with FRDA were cardiac arrythmia (26.6 %), neuropathic pain (24.1 %), and falls (21.6 %).
3.2. Characteristics of FRDA cases and controls after matching
After matching, 652 FRDA cases and 3260 matched controls were included for analysis (Table 1). In the matched cohorts, the mean age was 33.2 (SD: 17.9) years and 51.4 % were female. Among patients with race/ethnicity group data, 73.9 % of cases and 50.4 % of controls were White.

FRDA cases after matching were slightly younger than those before matching but had comparable comorbidity burden at baseline. In addition, compared with matched controls, FRDA cases after matching had significantly higher comorbidity burden at baseline, with a mean (SD) weighted ECI score of 6.6 (8.0) vs. 0.6 (4.4). A total of 45 % of cases were non-ambulatory (i.e. having at least one diagnosis of paraplegia, quadriplegia, confined to bed, or wheelchair use) at baseline, compared to just 0.6 % of controls. Additionally, more patients with FRDA had all examined comorbidities than matched controls, including cardiomyopathy (33.4 % vs. 0.9 %), scoliosis (31.7 % vs. 0.9 %), vision impairment (24.2 % vs. 13.7 %), depression (24.1 % vs. 10.5 %), anxiety (19.8 % vs. 13.0 %), and diabetes (14.3 % vs. 7.4 %). Further, more patients with FRDA experienced cardiac arrythmia (26.8 % vs. 5.2 %), neuropathic pain (23.0 % vs. 6.3 %), falls (20.1 % vs. 2.8 %), dysphagia (16.1 % vs. 1.3 %) head injury (9.0 % vs. 3.6 %), and fracture (7.7 % vs. 3.4 %) than matched controls at baseline.
Baseline characteristics of the 171 unmatched FRDA cases were presented in Table S2. These cases were excluded because they could not be matched to controls based on aforementioned matching factors (i.e., age, sex, insurance type, US region, and continuous enrollment).
3.3. Clinical events during the follow-up period
3.3.1. Risk of complications
During the follow-up period (median: 26.2 months for cases and 28.3 months for controls), the odds of experiencing all examined clinical complications were significantly higher among the FRDA cases than the matched controls (Table 2). Notably, FRDA cases had significantly higher odds of loss of ambulation (62.6 % vs. 1.3 %; OR: 158.0), cardiomyopathy (41.9 % vs. 1.4 %; 59.2), visual impairment (41.1 % vs. 24.5 %, 2.3), diabetes (21.3 % vs. 10.3 %; 2.5), falls (31.4 % vs. 6.4 %; 7.4), head injury (17.8 % vs. 8.9 %; 2.4), and fracture (17.6 % vs. 6.5 %; 3.3, all p < 0.001) during follow-up compared to controls.

3.3.2. Incidence and time to loss of ambulation
Among all FRDA cases and matched controls, the proportions with loss of ambulation by 1, 3, and 5-years post-index were 60.1 % vs. 1.0 %, 72.2 % vs. 1.7 %, and 77.4 % vs. 2.7 %, respectively (log-rank p < 0.001) (Fig. 3a). The estimated hazard ratio (HR) was 74.3 (95 % CI: 55.6, 99.3). Among FRDA cases and controls with ambulation at baseline, the proportions that lost ambulation by post-index were 27.4 % vs. 0.3 % at 1 year, 49.4 % vs. 0.9 % at 3 years, and 58.9 % vs. 1.8 % at 5 years, respectively (log-rank p < 0.001) (Fig. 3b). The estimated HR was 63.4 (95 % CI: 37.8, 106.3).

Fig. 3. Kaplan-Meier analysis of time to loss of ambulation during follow-up among (A) all matched FRDA cases and controls and (B) matched FRDA cases and controls with ambulation at baseline.
Abbreviation: FRDA, Friedreich ataxia.

3.3.3. Incidence and time to development of diabetes
Among all FRDA cases and matched controls, the proportions with diabetes by 1, 3, and 5-years post-index were 18.1 % vs. 9.1 %, 25.0 % vs. 11.9 %, and 30.2 % vs. 13.8 %, respectively (log-rank p < 0.001) (Fig. 4a). The estimated HR was 2.2 (95 % CI: 1.9, 2.7). Among FRDA cases and controls without diabetes at baseline, the proportions that developed diabetes post-index were 4.5 % vs. 1.6 % at 1 year, 12.6 % vs. 4.4 % at 3 years, and 18.7 % vs. 6.7 % at 5 years, respectively (log-rank p < 0.001) (Fig. 4b). The estimated HR was 2.9 (95 % CI: 2.1, 4.1).

Fig. 4. Kaplan-Meier analysis of time to diabetes during follow-up among (a) all matched FRDA cases and controls and (b) matched FRDA cases and controls without diabetes at baseline.
Abbreviation: FRDA, Friedreich ataxia.
3.3.4. Mortality
Patients with FRDA experienced higher rates of mortality than matched controls beginning at 3-years after the index date. Among all FRDA cases and matched controls, the mortality rate was 0.0 % vs. 0.1 % at 1-year post-index, 2.3 % vs. 1.0 % at 3 years, and 7.7 % vs. 1.9 % at 5 years, respectively (Fig. 5) (log-rank p < 0.001). The estimated HR was 3.9 (95 % CI: 2.4, 6.4).

Fig. 5. Kaplan-Meier analysis of overall survival.
Abbreviation: FRDA, Friedreich ataxia.
4. Discussion
This study used a large, representative, real-world, US dataset and performed analyses to compare clinical outcomes between patients with FRDA and matched controls who had similar demographic characteristics. The results indicated that patients with FRDA had a substantially higher clinical burden, including more comorbidities at baseline, higher rates of multiple clinical manifestations during the study period, and elevated mortality. Loss of ambulation, cardiomyopathy, scoliosis, visual impairment, and dysarthria were particularly prevalent among patients with FRDA compared to controls, which are expected to negatively impact physical functioning, quality of life, and lifespan.
During the baseline period, the proportion of patients without ambulation was much higher among FRDA cases than matched controls (45.1 % vs. 0.6 %). In addition, among those with ambulation at baseline, significantly more patients with FRDA experienced loss of ambulation, estimated at 59 %, by the end of year 5, compared with people without FRDA (2 %), during the study period. In the analysis of loss of ambulation in the FACOMS study, the median time to loss of ambulation, defined by dependency on a wheelchair, ranged between 11.5 years (for early-onset patients) to 23.5 years (for late-onset patients). The current study focuses on a cross-sectional cohort of FRDA patients from a claims database to capture the clinical burden of the general FRDA population, whereas the FACOMS study assessed the natural history of FRDA using registry data and measured time to loss of ambulation from symptom onset. In addition, unlike FACOMS, this study relied on diagnosis codes of paraplegia, quadriplegia, confined to bed, or wheelchair use to define loss of ambulation. These could explain the differences in the observed results.
Patients with FRDA in this study had nearly three times the risk of developing diabetes compared to matched controls, and 19 % of the FRDA cohort newly developed diabetes during the entire study follow-up. The reported prevalence of diabetes across studies of FRDA cases has varied widely from 5 to 40 % depending on the population and setting,,,]. Among the entire FACOMS cohort with FRDA (n = 1104), 9 % had diabetes; similarly, a post-hoc analysis of the impact of diabetes among 811 patients in FACOMS reported that approximately 9 % of adults and 3 % of children had diabetes. The comparatively higher prevalence of diabetes in the current cohort with FRDA (14.3 % at baseline) may be due to the older age of this cohort (33.2 vs. 30.1 years in FACOMS), as well differences in monitoring, patient motivation, and disease management between patients under the oversight of a natural history study compared with real-world patients with FRDA. Regardless, the post-hoc analysis of FACOMS observed that diabetes was independently associated with greater FRDA symptom burden even when controlling for age and FXN mutation type, underscoring the importance of the prevention of the disorder in patients with FRDA.
Declining mobility and increased risk of clinical complications can have substantial negative impacts on patients' quality of life, physical safety, and potentially mortality. For example, compared to matched controls, the current study observed a high rate of falls (31.4 % vs. 6.4 % during the study period), head injury (17.8 % vs. 8.9 %), and fracture (17.6 % vs. 6.5 %) among FRDA cases, reflecting impaired coordination and limitations to mobility. Eventually, over three-quarters of patients with FRDA lost ambulation by the end of study follow up compared to just 3 % of matched controls. A recent (2023) study of patients with FRDA and their caregivers identified impaired coordination, limitations to mobility, inability to engage in daily activities, fatigue, and lower limb weakness as the most impactful symptoms of FRDA. Thus, the high rates of mobility-related complications observed in this study are expected to be highly impactful to these patients. Cardiomyopathy, a primary determinant of mortality among patients with FRDA, was present in 41.9 % of the FRDA cohort during the study period, similar to the rate in the MOXIe Part 2 trial (39.0 %). Arrythmia was present in 43.1 % of FRDA cases, which can contribute to worsening systolic function and eventual heart failure in this population. The FACOMS study did not report the proportion of patients with cardiomyopathy and arrythmia, respectively, but noted that 68 % had FRDA-related cardiac disease, including cardiomyopathy and arrythmia. Furthermore, the impact of the physical symptoms of FRDA may also impact patients' mental health. Over one-quarter (26 %) of patients with FRDA in this study had depression at baseline, which is notable given prior reports that depression is one of the most impactful variables for predicting quality of life in this patient population.
Powell et al. (2023) is another study that has estimated clinical complications in patients with FRDA using real-world claims data from Merative MarketScan Commercial database. The study included 447 FRDA cases (index date cutoff September 20, 2015) and 2309 matched controls without FRDA and assessed their clinical outcomes in the 1-year post-index period. 41 % of the FRDA cohort in Powell et al. lost ambulation, 30 % had cardiomyopathy, 21 % had scoliosis, and 17 % had diabetes, which are lower than the rates reported in the current study. The different clinical complication rates between these two studies are likely driven by different follow-up duration: the follow-up duration is 1-year in Powell et al. and the median follow-up duration is >2 years in the current study. In addition, while not reported by the authors, the definition of loss of ambulation in Powell et al. (2023) likely differs from that in the current study.
Lastly, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first study assessed and compared the risk of death between patients with FRDA and matched controls using real-world data. Our analyses demonstrated that the risk of death in FRDA cases was four times as that in matched controls.
The present findings contribute valuable and up-to-date information about the clinical burden of FRDA, a historically understudied disease with limited literature on long-term patient outcomes. Strengths of the study include the relatively large cohort given the rarity of FRDA, the representativeness of the study population (including patients covered by different insurance schemes and patients at different disease stages of disease progression), the timeliness of the data, use of a database covering >90 % of the US population, and the matching process with controls without FRDA. An additional strength is the robustness of the analytic approach ensuring a pre- and post-index period of 12 months, which can better capture patients' disease trajectory. Building upon the current findings, future studies could include analyses of the clinical burden among patients with early or late onset of FRDA symptoms, as well as investigations of the impact of FRDA on the quality of life and social wellbeing of caregivers.
This study is subject to several limitations, some of which are inherent to retrospective claims databases studies (i.e., miscoding, incomplete records, etc.). First, medical claims data only capture diagnostic and procedure codes that providers recorded for reimbursement purposes. Misclassification bias attributable to coding errors or data omissions may exist. Second, as a FRDA-specific diagnosis code was not available between January 2016 and September 2020, the study required all included FRDA cases to have a FRDA-specific code (i.e., G11.11) that was introduced in October 2020. This criterion might result in exclusion of patients who either did not receive a FRDA-specific code or were lost to follow up before October 2020. Taken together, these two limitations may partially explain differences in some of the patient characteristics observed in this study versus those reported in natural history studies with richer individual patient data. For example, in the current study, 74 % of patients with FRDA with available race/ethnicity data were White, while over 93 % of patients in a prior FRDA natural history study by Issacs et al. were White. However, 23.6 % of the current cohort with FRDA did not have race/ethnicity data available. In addition, race was self-reported in the database and did not contain information about the genetic background of the individual and a classification of multiple races. All these may have led to an underestimation of the White racial group in this study. Although the patient population included in the current study could be different from that from Issacs et al., due to different data sources. Third, while this study used matching methods to reduce the effects of confounding, causal inferences should be made cautiously as there may be uncontrolled confounding factors. Finally, the mean age of the current FRDA cohort was approximately 33 years at index (a random FRDA diagnosis). Thus, this study captured a relatively older population with a disease that typically appears in late childhood among early-onset patients and >25 years of age in late-onset patients, and the outcomes of the cohort with FRDA may reflect those with more advanced disease. Future studies using data with genetic and/or richer clinical data are recommended to analyze the impact of racial background and onset timing on patients' outcomes. Additional analyses are also warranted to evaluate the economic burden of FRDA, compare the clinical burden between patients with FDRA and patients with other chronic neurological disease affecting younger people, and assess the real-world effectiveness of current and upcoming treatment options for FRDA.
5. Conclusions
This US retrospective study using recent real-world data illustrates that patients with FRDA experience a substantial clinical burden which is more severe compared to age- and sex-matched controls without FRDA. These findings describing the high rates of clinical complications and progression of disability among patients with FRDA underscore the unmet needs for effective treatments to improve overall outcomes in this population.






Type and position of repeat interruptions as determinants of disease severity and expansion size in Friedreich ataxia
Purpose
In Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) the size of the smaller GAA expansion is a major determinant of disease severity; interruption motifs were identified after the discovery of the pathogenic expansions; however, their impact is only recently investigated.
Methods
164 patients with FRDA with biallelic expansions and 15 patients without FRDA were analyzed for interruption(s) number, position, and motif. Expansion size and age at onset of ataxia (AAO) were determined for patients with FRDA.
Results
Three groups of patients with FRDA were identified by the simultaneous analysis of the precise distance ("depth") between the interruptions (mostly nontriplet) and the 3? end of the expansion (P < .001), the smaller expansion size (P < .001), and AAO (P < .001). Classical FRDA corresponds to absence of interruption or interruption depth < 8 repeats, with AAO often <15 years (area under the curve [AUC] = 0.90; 95% CI, 0.84-0.96); LOFA to interruption depth of 8 to 18 repeats (AUC = 0.97; 95% CI, 0.94-1), with AAO 15 to 34 years (AUC = 1; 95% CI, 1-1); and vLOFA to interruption depth > 18 (AUC = 0.97; 95% CI, 0.92-1), with AAO > 34 years. Multiple (>5) triplet interruptions hamper further expansion.
Conclusion
This study provides the molecular basis for a novel classification of FRDA that should be recommended for correct diagnosis.
Introduction

Friedreich ataxia (FRDA, OMIM 229300) is one of the most common inherited ataxias with an estimated incidence of 1 in 40,000 in Europe. It is caused by the homozygous expansion of a GAA trinucleotide repeat in intron 1 of the FXN gene (HGNC:3951) or, less frequently, by compound heterozygosity of one GAA expansion and 1 loss-of-function variant on the other allele.1 Pathogenic variants in FXN gene (the intronic expansion or loss-of-function variants) lead to a reduced expression of the correspondent protein, called Frataxin, thus causing the disease. FRDA is characterized by neurological signs, such as loss of coordination and balance, dysarthria, and deep sensory loss, and by nonneurological signs, such as osteoarticular involvements (kyphoscoliosis and foot deformities), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, diabetes mellitus, and optic atrophy.
Since the discovery of the FRDA gene, the spectrum of disease onset has been greatly extended to include 3 classes according to disease severity: classical FRDA with onset ranging from 2 to 25 years, late-onset FRDA (LOFA) with onset ranging from 25 to 40 years, and very-late-onset FRDA (vLOFA) with onset occurring after 40 years.2,3 As with most expansion diseases, the most important determinant of disease onset and severity is expansion size; because FRDA is a recessive disease, the most important determinant is the size of the smaller of the 2 expansions (referred to as GAA1, as opposed to GAA2 for the larger expansion), considered as the determinant of the residual levels of the Frataxin protein.4,5
However, expansion size accounts for only 36% to 63 % of the variation in age of onset, with very important deviations on both sides of the correlation curve.3,4,6 Although interruptions in sequence repeat were discovered shortly after FRDA gene discovery in 1996, the first report of their role in disease severity was only published in 2021, pointing the prominent role for interruptions located at the 3? end of the expansions.7
In this study, we used data from 8.5 years of routine FRDA diagnostic testing to investigate both the sequence motif of the interruptions and their precise position with respect to the 3? end of the expansion as determinants of disease onset. We also compared interruption motifs between expansions in patients with FRDA and normal/intermediate alleles identified in patients without FRDA and in the general population. We found that both precise position and motif of the interruptions play an important role in expansion size determination and pathogenicity.
Materials and Methods
Participants
Participants with progressive ataxia were recruited over an 8.5 year period (August 2013-January 2022) from more than 15 French university hospital centers, as well from 1 Algerian and 1 Lebanese center. FXN expansion testing was performed for diagnostic purposes with written informed consent for genetic analyses and agreement for further use of genetic and clinical data for research. The Interruption Characterization in Repeat Expansion Causing Friedreich Ataxia project was approved by the Montpellier University Hospital Institutional Review Board (approval number IRB-MPT_2020_03_202000372); it was proposed to 15 participants with symptomatic ataxia but negative for FRDA (named as controls) and to all participants with genetically confirmed FRDA, according to the following inclusion criteria: (1) biallelic GAA expansions in the intron 1 of FXN (pathogenic expansion, defined as > 75 GAA or premutations defined as 33 to 75 GAA.8,9 (2) Symptomatic ataxia, defined by Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA) score � 4. When available, unaffected family members (parents or siblings) were also included in this study for segregation analyses. Two participants with FRDA harboring a single-nucleotide pathogenic variant, and one patient harboring a large deletion, in trans of the GAA expansion, and identified over the same recruitment period, were excluded from the study. Because no further sample or testing was required, the referring physicians who requested genetic testing were contacted and a letter of information related to the study was sent to all potential participants to ensure their agreement. In case of nonopposition, clinical data were collected by the corresponding physician based on clinical records. Age at onset of the disease was determined as being the onset of ataxic symptoms leading to gait impairment for the participants. Nonataxic signs (scoliosis, cardiomyopathy, diabetes, etc) occurring before the onset of ataxia were not considered for determination of the age at onset.
Molecular studies
3?Triplet primer polymerase chain reaction
Two distinct triplet primer polymerase chain reaction (TP-PCR) were performed using a forward GAA7 primer, which included a GC clamp sequence and the fluorescein amidite label (CCGCCGCGAAGAAGAAGAAGAAGAAGAA) and 2 distinct reverse primers (GCTGGGATTACAGGCGCGCGA and AGGACCATCATGGCCACACTT, respectively) at annealing temperature of 60 �C and 62 �C, respectively, and 33 and 30 cycles, respectively, with elongation time of 30 seconds (adapted from Ciotti et colleagues).10 Fragments were analyzed on ABI3500 sequencers (Applied Biosystems 3500 Dx or 3500 XL Genetic Analyzers).
Long-range PCR
Long-range PCR were performed for expansion size determination using the Expand Long Template PCR system kit (Roche/Merk/Sigma Aldrich ref.11681834001) with the forward primer (GGCTTAAACTTCCCACACGTGTT) and the TP-PCR reverse primer 2 (AGGACCATCATGGCCACACTT), at annealing temperature of 62 �C and 10 cycles with elongation time of 3 minutes followed by 25 cycles with 15 seconds of increment for each additional cycle, and with 2 different concentrations of genomic DNA (5 and 10 nanograms, respectively, adapted from Poirier et al11). Long-range PCR products were run on a 1.5% agarose gel, alongside appropriate fragment size markers.
Sanger sequencing
Long-range PCR products were purified on columns (QIAquick PCR Purification Kit [250] Cat. No./ID: 28106) and sequenced with the ABI bigdye terminator kit (BigDye Terminator v3.1 Cycle Sequencing Kit). Sequencing was performed using the ABI3500 sequencers and analyzed with the Sequencing Analysis V.7.0 (Applied Biosystems) and 4Peaks (Nucleobytes BV) softwares. For Sanger sequencing of control individuals (having at least 1 normal allele which may mask part of the repeat sequence), TP-PCR was performed with a GAA7 forward primer without the GC clamp and without the fluorescent label. After the TP-PCR reaction, primers were removed by digestion with ExoI and rSAP (New England Biolabs), and a 2 ?L aliquot was used for Sanger sequencing.
Statistical analyses
Baseline characteristics were analyzed as frequencies and percentages for categorical variables, and as means, standard deviations, medians, interquartile ranges, and ranges for continuous variables. We used Fisher's exact test for categorical variables and analysis of variance or the Kruskal-Wallis test, depending on the normality of the distribution, which was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test.
The K-means approach was used to identify 3 homogeneous clusters (according to the elbow method). For each cluster, we identified outliers using Euclidean distances between each participant and its cluster's barycenter in the principal component analysis space.
The discriminative ability of the threshold (sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, and positive and negative likelihood ratio) was estimated, and a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve was generated to estimate the area under the curve (AUC) with its 95% confidence intervals (95% CI).
All analyses were conducted using R software (version 4.4.0).
Results
Interruptions in patients with FRDA
Over a period of 8.5 years, we established a FRDA molecular diagnosis for 164 patients from 158 families, through identification of biallelic expansions by reverse triplet-primed PCR followed by long-range PCR for expansion size determination. The reverse triplet-primed PCR method allowed to identify profiles with uninterrupted repeat motifs over the last �130 repeats of both expansions in 73 participants, and abnormal profiles in the remaining 91 participants. Long-range PCR products of these 91 participants were sequenced by Sanger sequencing with the reverse primer to determine the nature of the abnormal profiles.
In 5 participants, the abnormal profile was explained by insertion, duplication, or deletion involving the GAAGAAAATAAAGAAAA sequence at the 3? end of the expansion. These 5 participants were considered has having biallelic uninterrupted expansions, such as the 73 participants with uninterrupted TP-PCR profile (Supplemental Table 1). The remaining 86 participants appeared to have repeat interruptions on 1 or both alleles, and sometimes also in cis or trans with an insertion, duplication or deletion of the 3? nonrepeated sequence. Most of the interruptions were nontriplet interruptions (found in 83 participants), with interrupted motifs of 2, 4, 5, or 6 nucleotides (GA, GAAA, GAAAA, GAAAAA, GAAG, and TAAA motifs) and combinations thereof (Figure 1, Supplemental Table 1). We refer to these interruptions as "nontriplet" interruptions. Only 3 interruptions were triplet interruptions that did not affect repeat length, 2 consisting of GAG motifs and one of CAA motifs (Table 1, Supplemental Table 1) and will subsequently be referred to as "triplet" interruptions.

The GAAA interruption causes a 1-nucleotide shift between the 2 expansions for the larger TP-PCR fragments. C. Absence of TP-PCR amplification peaks occurs over a large segment, due to the numerous interruptions. E. TP-PCR profile of a participant homozygous for 2 uninterrupted expansions. Corresponding reverse Sanger sequences (obtained with a 3? prime primer) are shown on top of interrupted profiles. One letter sequence shown at the top are reverse complement sequences and should be read from right to left (5? to 3?). Positions of the GAA7 primer for which interruptions prevent proper annealing during the PCR reaction are indicated by horizontal overlapping lines between the Sanger sequence and the TP-PCR profile. Note that in both the A and B examples, the interrupted Sanger sequence has a higher intensity (higher sequencing peak of the G nucleotide(s), arrows) when compared with the uninterrupted sequence (dotted arrows), indicating that the interruption lies in the smaller expansion fragment, which amplifies more efficiently during the PCR reaction. This observation was consistently verified for patients for whom relatives were available for phasing between interruption(s) and size and was used for phasing of the remaining patients.

Motif, depth, and number of interruptions identified in patients with FRDA Sixty patients had interruption(s) on only 1 allele, and 26 patients had interruption(s) on both alleles (total of 112 interrupted alleles).
