Interruptions were relatively short in sequence, often affecting a single repeat or 2 repeats with or without short intervening GAAn tracks. Only 6 cases had 3 interrupted repeats, and 2 had 5 interrupted repeats (Table 1). They cluster at the 3? end of the expansions, with only 3 interruptions being located 32, 35, and 37 repeats away from the 3? end, respectively. For this reason and because the 5? end of the small expansions appeared to be free of interruption, we made no attempt to investigate 5? interruptions.
Interruptions in individuals without FRDA ("controls")
We also sought to investigate the distribution of interruption sequence in normal/premutation alleles by searching for interruptions in approximately 2410 individuals without FRDA analyzed over the same period range (August 2013-January 2022). FRDA diagnosis was excluded in these individuals by absence of biallelic expansion or premutation or by absence of FXN single-nucleotide pathogenic variant or duplication/deletion in trans of the expansion/premutation allele. In most cases, these individuals presented with ataxia distinct from typical FRDA presentation, and FXN expansion testing was performed for exclusion purposes. Most individuals without FRDA carry pure GAA alleles, but 15 individuals with interruptions, subsequently referred to as "controls," were identified, including 1 with interruption on both alleles (Table 2). Eleven controls had interruptions in normal/"premutation" allele range (9 to 73 repeats in length). Ten had "triplet" (GAG/GGA) interruptions (8 GAG and 2 GGA), and only 1 individual had a nontriplet interruption (GAAA). Fisher test calculation indicates that distribution of triplet versus nontriplet interruptions are markedly different between the normal/"premutation" allele group and the expansion group (P < 10?10), with nontriplet interruptions being vastly overrepresented in expansions (109/112) and triplet interruptions being overrepresented in normal/"premutation" alleles (10/11).
Table 2. Motif, depth, and number of interruptions identified in controls (patients without FRDA)
Fourteen controls had interruption(s) on only 1 allele, 1 control had interruption(s) on both alleles (GGA110GAA10 and GAAmGAAAGAA2, respectively) and was counted as "triplet" control, see text). Variations at the 3? end of the repeats: del, deletion; ins, insertion; nt, nucleotides. Nontriplet interruptions (GAAA and GAAG) are in bold. Note that 1 "premutation" has 12 triplet (GAG) interruptions and only 1 nontriplet (GAAA) interruption and was therefore counted as triplet interruption. Size of alleles is indicated in triplet equivalent. Interruptions are classified according to increasing depth. The GAA51[(GAA)0-5GAG)]21(GAA)14 interruption indicates that there are 21 GAG interruptions variably interspersed with 0 (1 case) to 5 GAA repeats.
The remaining 4 control participants had interruptions in an expansion allele. This is not unexpected given the approximate 1 in 100 frequency of heterozygous FXN expansions in the European population. One participant had an almost pure GAAGGA hexanucleotide repeat expansion (GAAGGA)72(GAA)4 (NC_000009.12:g.69037287_69037304GAAGGA[72]GAA[4]), and another participant had a complex GAAnGAG repeat motif (GAA51[(GAA)0-5GAG)]21(GAA)14) (NC_000009.12:g.69037287_69037304GAA[51](GAA[0-5]GAG)[21]GAA[14]), amounting to 140 triplet repeats in length. The third participant was biallelic for an almost pure GGA expansion (GGA)110(GAA)10 and a very large expansion with a GAAA interruption (GAA)mGAAA(GAA)2 in trans (NC_000009.12:g.69037287_69037304[GGA[110]GAA[10]];[GAA[1000]GAAA[1]GAA[2]). FRDA diagnosis was nevertheless excluded for him because of inconsistent, early-onset, clinical presentation and mostly because her 50 years old unaffected sister carried the same set of expanded alleles. The fourth participant had a GAAG interruption ((GAA)150GAAG(GAA)15, amounting to �170 triplet repeats in length (NC_000009.12:g.69037287_69037304GAA[150]GAAG[1]GAA[15]), similar to those seen in patients with FRDA. Despite the small number of patients in this group, Fisher test calculation indicates that triplet interruptions (3/5, GGA or GAG) are also overrepresented in the group of "non-FRDA" expansions compared with the FRDA group (3/112, P = .0007). The number of interruptions also differed between controls (normal/premutation/expansion range combined) and participants with FRDA. Only 5 controls had a single interruption, and 10 had interruption number ranging from 7 to almost pure GGA/(GAAGGA) expansions (10/15, Table 2), whereas none of the participants with FRDA had more than 5 interruptions on 1 allele (0/112, P < 10?10).
Correlation between position of the interruptions and both disease onset and expansion size in participants with FRDA
We next investigated the impact of expansion interruptions on disease onset and expansion size in our 164 participants with FRDA (Supplemental Table 1). When available, parental DNA were used to determine the correspondence between the sequencing profile and the size of the expansion (expansion size variations remained limited, see below). Also, smaller expansions have a higher rate of PCR amplification, which robustly translates into proportional higher sequencing peaks on Sanger electropherograms (Figure 1). We took advantage of this observation for inferring the phase between interruptions and GAA1 and GAA2 alleles of patients for whom parental DNA was not available (Supplemental Table 1).
It appeared that the precise position of the interruptions with respect to the 3? end was a much better predictor of earlier onset (ie, severity) and expansion size, than just the presence or absence of an interruption. This was particularly striking for the vLOFA, in whom the interruptions were located 20 or more repeats away from the 3? end of the expansion, in contrast to participants with earlier onset. We therefore set to use the K-means algorithm for defining statistically different clusters of participants, based on the position of interruption, age at onset, and size of the smallest of the 2 expansions (classically called GAA1). Because of the high variability in interruption patterns and lengths, we based our statistical analysis on the position of the interruption that has the greatest distance to the 3? end of the expansion and named this distance the "depth" of the interruption. For example, the GAAnGAAAGAAAAGAA21 interruption (Figure 1, Table 1) has a depth of 23. Likewise, depth of (GAAGAAA) repeats refers to the GAAA interruption that has the greatest distance to the 3? end of the expansion. For example, in row 5 of Table 1, the GAAn(GAAGAAA)2GAA2 interruption corresponds to the GAAnGAAGAAAGAAGAAAGAA2 sequence, and the GAAA interruption with the greatest distance (underlined) has a depth of 5. Also, because the K-means algorithm does not accommodate values of 0, uninterrupted expansions were scored with a depth value of 1 (interruptions at depth of 1 or 2 were considered as insertion, duplication or deletion of the 3? end sequence and were labeled "uninterrupted," see first paragraph of Results section). First, the "Elbow method" was used to define the optimal number of clusters, K (accounting for most of the differences between clusters) to be used in K-means calculations. This method, based on minimization of the Sum of Square of distances within clusters (SSwithin) yielded a K number of 3. Subsequent K-means analysis indicated that clusters 1, 2, and 3 only partially corresponded to the clinically known classical FRDA, LOFA, and vLOFA groups, respectively (Figure 2). Two participants in cluster 2 were identified as "outliers" with a high level of certainty (85%) when compared with the barycenter of the cluster (Figure 2) and corresponded to 2 independently identified atypical cases (Figure 2). The first participant carried on the smaller allele a pathogenic uninterrupted ("pure") premutation of 51 (�1) GAA repeats. The combination of abnormally small expansion size, absence of interruption and age at onset (27 years) was at departure from any of the 3 clusters. This participant had a typical LOFA presentation and a single-nucleotide or insertion/deletion pathogenic variant in trans of the larger expansion was excluded in this case. The second participant with late-onset ataxia (25 years) had a GAAA interruption at a depth of 20 on a 670 repeat expansion, whereas her sister belonged to cluster 1 with no interruption on a 770 repeat expansion and a significantly earlier onset (12 years). The presumed de novo occurrence of the GAAA interruption in an already expanded allele probably accounts for the observed discrepancies of the second outlier.
Figure 2. Clustering of participants with FRDA by K-means analysis. All 3 parameters are considered: interruption depth, age at onset (AO), and size of the smaller of the 2 expansions (GAA1 number of repeats). Horizontal and vertical lines represent thresholds that best separate the 3 clusters. Red squares, classical patients with FRDA; cyan diamonds, LOFA patients; yellow triangles, vLOFA patients; boxed x, outlier patients. A. Distribution of AO in patients with FRDA (years) according to size of the expansion (number of triplets). B. Distribution of interruption depth according to expansion size, demonstrating that interruption depth is a major determinant of final expansion size. C. Distribution of interruption depth according to AO (years).
K-means analysis was reinitiated after exclusion of the 2 outliers with molecular peculiarities (Figure 2). The robust grouping of patients into 3 clusters allowed us to define optimal "depth" thresholds that discriminate best between clusters 1 and 2 and between clusters 2 and 3, respectively, by using ROC curve statistical analyses (see Materials and Methods section). The results indicate that cluster 3 most often corresponds to interruption depth equal to or above 19 (sensitivity = 1, specificity = 0.90, AUC = 0.97; 95% CI, 0.92 to 1), cluster 2 to interruption depth equal to or above 8 (sensitivity = 0.98, specificity = 0.93, AUC = 0.97; 95% CI, 0.94 to 1), and cluster 1 to absence of interruption or interruption depth ranging from 2 to 8 (Figure 2). The depth difference between the 3 groups is highly significant (P value < .001, Table 3). This approach also allowed to redefine significant thresholds for groups based on age of onset (P value < .001, Table 3) and GAA1 expansion size (P value < .001, Table 3). ROC curve statistical analyses indicate that classical FRDA corresponds most often to onset before age 15 years (sensitivity = 0.81, specificity = 0.88, AUC = 0.90; 95% CI, 0.84 to 0.96)(cluster 3), whereas LOFA significantly clusters with ages of onset ranging from 15 to 34 years (sensitivity = 0.98, specificity = 1, AUC = 1; 95% CI, 1 to 1)(cluster 2), and vLOFA with ages of onset above 34 years (cluster 1, Figure 2). Likewise, GAA1 thresholds between the 3 groups appear to lie around 215 (sensitivity = 0.93, specificity = 0.93, AUC = 0.99; 95% CI, 0.97 to 1) and 550 (sensitivity = 0.94, specificity = 0.91, AUC = 0.98; 95% CI, 0.97 to 1) GAA repeats, respectively (Figure 2). Parental studies performed when samples were available (not shown) and sibling analyses (Supplemental Table 1) indicated that in all cases expansion size remained within 1 of the 3 group limits over 1 generation, suggesting that interruptions drive the size clustering.
Table 3. Description of patient population with FRDA by clusters, based on age at onset, depth of interruption, and size of the GAA1 expansion
Discussion
Shortly after identification of the FRDA gene expansion, (GAAGAAA)2 interruptions in patients and (GAAGAG)n interruptions in controls were identified,8,12 but the contribution of interruptions as a modulator of severity was only reported in 2021 by Nethisinghe et al,7 who identified a prominent role for the interruptions that are located at the 3? end of the expansions. We explored the role of these interruptions since more than 20 years and collected data from a single diagnostic center over an 8.5-year period.
A striking difference in interruption motifs was detected between participants with FRDA and controls. Nontriplet interruptions (such as GAAA) were vastly overrepresented in participants with FRDA, whereas triplet interruptions (such as GAG) being more frequent in controls. Additionally, the number of interruptions also differed between the 2 groups. Although most of participants with FRDA had only 1 or 2 nontriplet interruptions, 10 out of 15 controls exhibited between 7 interruption and nearly a pure GGA/GAAGGA expansion. These results suggest that 7 or more GAG/GGA interruptions (usually in the form of GAAGAG/GAAGGA hexamer repeats) are sufficient to prevent either pathogenicity or further expansion.
Our identification of a healthy individual (sister of a patient without FRDA) with a bona-fide expansion in trans of a (GGA)110(GAA)10 expansion suggests that the pure GGA motif is not pathogenic, unlike the GAA motif. This observation corroborates the findings that the pure (GAAGGA)67 hexamer repeats are not pathogenic either.13,14 These results indicate that sequencing of small expansions and premutation with interruption or non-GAA repeats is mandatory for accurate pathogenicity evaluation. On the other hand, we identified a GAA51 premutation in a participant with FRDA, therefore lowering the threshold of pathogenic pure GAA expansion previously set at about 70 GAA.9
Among participants with FRDA, the majority have 1 or a few nontriplet interruptions located within the last 40 repeats of the expansion (3? interruptions). We found that the precise position of the "deepest" interruption (the furthest from the 3? end) correlates remarkably well with age of onset of ataxia and size of expansion. This position called the "depth" of the interruption(s) has a trimodal distribution centered at "depth" of 1 (no interruption), 9, and 24 repeats, respectively, and defines 3 groups of patients who differ by age of onset and size of the smallest of the 2 expansions (GAA1). We propose to use this molecularly based clustering for a novel definition of the LOFA, vLOFA, and classical FRDA classes. According to our study, vLOFA patients would correspond to age of onset after 34 years, whereas LOFA patients would correspond to age of onset between 15 and 34 years. Significant overlap between the 2 most severe groups exists, however, and age of onset alone may not reflect the exact severity of the disease. Disease progression, age in wheelchair, and nonneurological signs, as well as biochemical parameters, such as blood frataxin concentrations,15,16 should also be considered for possible correlation with the presence of interruptions. In addition, peculiar events may also explain the discrepancies between interruptions, size and onset, 2 of which were identified in the course of this study: 1 case of a de novo interruption occurring on an already full-size expansion and having modest effect on size lowering and onset delay, and 1 case of premutation for which expansion size in blood may not reflect actual size in affected tissues.8 The same mechanism could apply for LOFA participant P35 who has a pure 300-repeat GAA1 that may derive from a premutation (parental DNA was not available for study), whereas all other pure expansions have 430 or more GAA repeats. When available, family studies indicated that expansion size remained stable within 1 of the 3 group limits. These results corroborate our previous observation of a GAA�90(GAAGAAA)2GAA21 expansion that was stably transmitted over 3 generations and 4 patients with FRDA12 (expansions ranging from 112 to 135 repeats) in a large La R�union island family, from which many of our vLOFA patients originate. The role of interruptions in the stability and pathogenicity of expansions is well documented in the field of expansion diseases.17, 18, 19 Therefore, it is not unexpected that it also plays an important role for FRDA.
Our results indicate that interruptions determine to some extent a certain ceiling level for repeat expansions. The fact that the ceiling level inversely correlates with the depth of interruption indicates that the interruption themselves, not flanking polymorphisms in linkage disequilibrium with the interruptions, are the molecular determinants. The role of DNA repair mechanisms, particularly of mismatch repair mechanisms, for the generation of repeat instability is well documented.20,21 How repeat interruptions intervene precisely with these DNA repair mechanisms requires further studies.
An important limitation of our work resides in the fact that only interruptions located at the 3? end of the expansions were explored. Nethisinghe et al7 explored both 5? and 3? interruptions by respective 5? and 3? RT-PCR methods, and found that 5? interruptions are both less common and do not significantly correlate with age of onset of the disease.7 For these reasons, and because we found no evidence of 5? interruption in the small expansions (up to 130 repeats, which explained most of our vLOFA participants, we made no attempt to investigate 5? interruptions. Possible interruptions in the middle of the large FRDA expansions were never explored and the development of long-read high-throughput sequencing technologies will certainly be of help to this end. These technologies, based on single molecule sequencing (as opposed to the "wash and scan" approach of the short-read sequencing) have already demonstrated their benefits in characterizing complex structures for diseases with large pathogenic expansions, such as the FGF14 GAA repeat region of Spinocerebellar Ataxia type 27b (SCA27b).22,23 Long-read high-throughput sequencing should allow to precisely determine the size the expansions, as well as to identify all interruptions along the entire length of the expansions and to determine the phase between size, interruptions, and possibly contributing flanking polymorphisms at the molecular level, therefore also opening the possibility to explore the contribution of somatic instability.22,23
In summary, we suggest that multiple interruptions (7 or more triplet interruptions in the FXN expansions) hamper further expansion of large normal and premutation alleles, and even pathogenicity at least in the small expansion size range, whereas few interruptions (1 to 5, usually nontriplet interruptions) stabilize expansion size in a 3? "depth"-dependent manner. In contrast, absence of interruption in the premutation size range is potentially pathogenic, presumably by a somatic instability mechanism. We therefore recommend analyzing the presence of interruption in expansions and premutations for an accurate diagnosis of FRDA. In particular, the sequencing of interruptions in small expansions and premutations is mandatory for correct assessment of pathogenicity.


A new c.681dup RUNX1 variant in familial leukemia

Abstract
Constitutional RUNX1 gene variants are associated with Familial Platelet Disorder (FPD) and predispose to a variety of hematological malignancies, included Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) and, albeit less frequently, Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL). In this study, we report on a proband with primary diagnosis of AML, followed by T-ALL after transplant, and a positive familial history for leukemia over three generations. A new heterozygous germline pathogenic RUNX1 (c.681dup, p.(Leu228ThrfsTer33)) variant was found in the proband and his affected mother.

Introduction
RUNX1, encoded by the RUNX1 gene at 21q22.12 is the human homolog of the Drosophila runt, sharing the runt-homology domain (RHD) with both RUNX2 and RUNX3 related genes. RUNX1 is constitutively expressed in the hematopoietic cells, and it is frequently mutated in leukemia. It is responsible for the DNA binding by the RUNX1-CBFβ complexwhich regulates differentiation steps of hematopoiesis and stem cell generation during development. Constitutional RUNX1 mutations are associated with a Familial Platelet Disorder (FPD) predisposing to a variety of hematological malignancies, mostly Myelodysplastic Syndromes (MDS) and Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML), and, less frequently, T- and B- Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL)and Lymphomas. Inherited heterozygous RUNX1 variants, however, are not sufficient for the development of the leukemic phenotype. Additional somatic hits, such as mutation or deletion of the RUNX1 wild-type allele, pathogenic variants affecting other genes, or acquired chromosome rearrangements, have been identified at time of leukemia development. Here, we describe a novel pathogenic RUNX1 variant in a Family with autosomal dominant leukemia and coexistence of the autosomal recessive Friedreich Ataxia (FRDA).

Proband
A 43 years-old male was admitted at the Città della Salute e della Scienza in Turin in November 2022 because of leucocytosis and thrombocytopenia. Laboratory findings were as follows: Hb 11.2 gr/dl, WBC 36.160 × 109/l with 79% blasts, PLTs 11.00 × 109/l, AST 414 UI/l (ULN 50), ALT 277 UI/l (ULN 50), LDH 3185 U/l (ULN 280). Bone Marrow (BM) aspirate showed 74% of blasts. Immunophenotype identified a predominant cell population positive for myeloid and immature antigens (CD13, CD33, weak MPO, CD34, weak CD38, HLA-DR, weak CD45), and also 8% of hypogranulated blasts, expressing CD7 and cyCD79a but negative for MPO, cyCD3, CD10, CD1a, CD2, CD5, CD3 and CD19. The BM biopsy showed 90% of cellularity and diffuse infiltration from hypogranulated blasts and expression of CD33, CD34, CD7, CD79a and MPO, supporting the diagnosis of AML without maturation. Additionally, histological analysis on a voluminous anterior mediastinal mass, documented at CT scan, showed extramedullary disease localization. The final diagnosis was AML. Chemotherapy was administered using a FLAI-Venetoclax (V-FLAI) scheme.

The family history disclosed hematological malignancies in close relatives (Fig. 1). In particular, the proband’s mother, aged 72, was under treatment in another Centre because of refractory AML, and the grandfather from the maternal side had died at the age of 70 because of undefined leukemia. Germline and somatic analysis in both the proband and his mother identified the same germline c.681dup, p.(Leu228ThrfsTer33), RUNX1 variant (Chromosome (Chr) 21, position 34834534, reference genome Hg38–Table 1 and Fig. 2). The c.681dup classification resulted as pathogenic, based on the ClinGen criteria (https://clinicalgenome.org/docs/clingen-myeloid-malignancy-expert-panel-specifications-to-the-acmg-amp-variant-interpretation-guidelines-version-2/, https://cspec.genome.network/cspec/ui/svi/doc/GN008). Applied classification criteria are shown in the Table 1 of the Online Resource 1. In addition, the diagnosis of FRDA emerged in the mother and her three siblings, the patient and his brother being obligate carriers. Accordingly, the genetic test confirmed the heterozygous trinucleotide-GAA repeat expansion (1000±50) in the FXN gene, in the proband’s brother. Genetic counselling did not reveal any other clinical condition.

Mutational status is shown as + (wild-type allele) and − (mutant allele) for FXN trinucleotide repeat expansion, RUNX1 c.681dupA and MPO c.2031–2 A > C. Black: relatives with positive history for hematological malignancies. Blue: relatives with FRDA (blue circlet for the carriers). White: no information or healthy individuals. The numbers in brackets in Members investigated represent the age at diagnosis for the proband and his mother and the age at time of sampling for the healthy brother. Fig. 2 Schematic representation of the RUNX1 c.681dup variant localization at the different RUNX1 isoforms and site of thymine duplication within the genomic sequence. Created in BioRender.

Five months after diagnosis, in May 2023, the proband underwent BM transplant from a 9/10 Matched Unrelated Donor (MUD). However, after three months, the BM was massively infiltrated by 97% of blasts positive for immature and T cell lineage antigens (CD34, TdT, weak CD38, CD7, cyCD3, CD2, weak CD5, CD4, CD1 and CD10). Around 25% of these blasts co-expressed weak CD13, and HLA-DR antigens. This pattern was compatible with ALL of T-lineage (T-ALL). Histological examination reported a massive infiltration by hypo-a-granular blasts (90%). Immunohistochemistry showed TdT, cyCD3, CD2, CD7, CD5, cyCD79a, partial CD1a and CD4 positivity; supporting the diagnosis of T-ALL. Notably, the host origin of this leukemia was supported by the identification of the familial RUNX1 mutation in BM cells. Salvage therapy was started according to the GIMEMA ALL 1913 protocol. At early evaluation, 20 days after chemotherapy, 98% of blasts persisted. The patient died at the end of August 2023.

Genotypic studies
The genomic characterization of the proband, his mother, and his healthy brother was carried out by Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) and Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms array (SNPa -Affymetrix). Results from proband and his mother are shown in detail in Table 1; Fig. 3; and in Table 1 of Online Resource 2, respectively (See material and methods in Online Resource 3). In addition to the RUNX1 variant, the proband and his mother shared an intronic MPO (c.2031–2A>C, p.(?)) variant, currently classified as Variant of Uncertain Significance (VUS) by the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics, ACMG, Varsome database (v.13.14.3, https://varsome.com). The classification criteria are also reported in Table 2 of the Online Resource 1. Both RUNX1 and MPO variants were absent in the healthy brother. Notably, the proband showed also a pathogenic variant at the NF1 gene (c.1019_1020insAAAATAGG, p.(Val341LysfsTer2)) that was maintained at the time of the post-transplant T-ALL (Table 1). However, we excluded its germline origin because absent in both the mother and the healthy brother, as well as in DNA obtained from proband nails. Moreover, no signs of Neurofibromatosis, associated with NF1 gene mutations, were observed in the patient (Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man, OMIM®. Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD. MIM Number: #162200: 06/26/2024: World Wide Web URL: https://omim.org/). As expected in T-ALL, additional somatic variants affecting NOTCH1 (c.4754T>C, p.(Leu1585Pro)) and FBXW7 (c.1040G>A, p.(Arg465His)) (Table 1) were found in the proband’s post-transplant leukemia. Somatic variants with a low allelic frequency at TET2, DNMT3A, and FAT1 genes were identified in the only available maternal sample in remission after chemotherapy (Table 1). The low allelic frequency of these genes suggested clonal myeloid hematopoiesis that is frequently associated with RUNX1 mutations.

Fig. 3 Schematic representation of the genetic characterization of the proband leukemias through SNP array. The losses are reported in red and the gains in blue. Anomalies specifically associated with AML (A) or T-ALL (B). C Anomalies common to both AML and T-ALL; the arrow indicates the unique germline anomaly found also in the proband mother and his healthy brother. AML: Acute Myeloid Leukemia, T-ALL: T Lymphocytes-Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia, CT: Chromotripsis, Chr: Chromosome. Created in BioRender. Lema, A. (2025)

Interestingly, SNPa provided further insights on both germline and somatic changes (Fig. 3 and raw data in the Online Resource 4). First, one gain at 1p31.1 was present in the proband, his mother and in the healthy brother, indicating that at least this genomic event was of germline origin and unlikely related to the leukemia phenotype (Fig. 3). Expected further somatic variants at RUNX1, in particular mutations or deletions involving the second allele, were not identified in the genotypic characterization of the proband via NGS and SNPa. Additionally, SNPa clarified that homozygosity of both the NF1 and the FBXW7 variants (VAF ≥90%) was due to the concomitant somatic deletions at 17q11 and 4q31 (Fig. 3), respectively. Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization (FISH) confirmed these deletions and revealed also a small clone (around 8%) with a rearranged BCL11B gene (Materials and methods in the Online Resource 3 and Figure in the Online Resource 5).

Discussion
In the present Family, the dominantly inherited leukemia segregated with a pathogenic germline c.681dup RUNX1 gene variant. Notably, typical FDP features, such as thrombocytopenia, bleeding, and/or bruising, did not emerge from our patient medical history. Both the mother and the maternal grandfather were old leukemic patients (≥70 years), while the proband developed the leukemia at 43 years of age. In our proband the myeloid leukemia found at diagnosis was followed by a T-lymphoid leukemic phenotype after transplantation (Table 1). Remarkably, heterozygous germline RUNX1 mutations are involved in predisposition to both AML and T-ALL. The presence of shared genetic markers at SNPa and of the same NF1 gene mutation, in both AML at diagnosis and T-ALL after transplant is a noteworthy observation (Table 1; Fig. 3), suggesting a common origin from an immature leukemic cell able to activate both the myeloid or the T lymphoid differentiation program, respectively at diagnosis and post-transplantation. Interestingly, we previously observed these pathobiological features in acute leukemia with activated BCL11B gene. Thus, our hypothesis is that the genetic markers shared by both AML and T-ALL cells identify the leukemic stem cell, while the different additional aberrations seen at diagnosis and after transplant are the biomarkers of the clonal evolution underpinning the different phenotypes.

As far as we know the c.681dup RUNX1 gene variant has never been described. It is generated by a single duplication of a thymine responsible for frameshift and an anticipated stop-codon and it is located between the RUNT and TAD domains, a region rarely affected by pathogenic variants. The consequent frameshift involves all the RUNX1 isoforms, maintaining only the RUNT domain in all three cases, with the TAD and Inhibitory domain going lost (Fig. 2). It is well established that variants introducing premature termination codons (PTCs) can trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD). For NMD to occur, however, the PTC must meet specific criteria, particularly it should not be located in the last exon or in a site less than 50–55 nucleotides upstream of the final exon–exon junction. Moreover it should be located > 200 bp downstream of the start codon. Thus, in our RUNX1 variant NMD is predicted to affect the two longest isoforms (B and C), whereas NMD is not expected in the shortest isoform (A), with the PTC lying within 50 nucleotides from the last exon–exon junction. Consequently, haploinsufficiency is likely affecting the isoform B and the isoform C which is mostly expressed in the whole blood (from the GTEx Portal on 02/17/2026.).

This rare RUNX1 event in our family coexisted with FRDA, a rare recessive genetic condition. In particular, the mother was affected by FRDA, while both the proband and his brother were healthy carriers. This disease in almost all cases arises from a homozygous expansion of a nucleotide triplet (GAA) within the first intron of the FXN gene, encoding for a protein that is involved in the formation of iron-sulphur proteins at mitochondrial level. Its reduced expression has been correlated to telomere dysfunction in FRDA cells. Moreover, alterations at DNA repair pathways have also been described in FRDA. As far as we know, however, the leukemia risk, if any, in Families with FXN gene mutations is unknown. Indeed, in our Family, the leukemia is attributable to the RUNX1 germline variant rather than to the FXN repeat expansion.

Lastly, a third germline variant, i.e., the intronic c.2031–2A>C MPO variant, was found only in patients bearing the RUNX1 variant and the leukemia phenotype. MPO germline variants were suggested to behave as predisposing factors to myeloid neoplasias, and decreased MPO transcription in cells bearing the c.2031–2A>C has been observed in the hematological malignancies. However, the classification of the c.2031–2A>C is still challenging. It is “conflicting” from ClinVar, while, by adopting ACMG criteria, the Varsome database (v.13.14.3, https://varsome.com), defines the variant of uncertain significance (Table 2 of the Online Resource 1). Its role in leukemia predisposition, if any, remains to be clarified.

In conclusion, we have described a unique Family with autosomal dominant leukemia segregating with a new rare germline pathogenic RUNX1 variant (c.681dup, p.(Leu228ThrfsTer33)). Genomic investigations provided us with in depth characterization of the AML and the T-ALL phenotypes characterizing the proband leukemias respectively at diagnosis and after transplantation.
Association of Crus I With Cerebellar Cognitive Affective Syndrome in Individuals With Friedreich Ataxia
An fMRI Study

Abstract
Background and Objectives
Friedreich ataxia (FA) is an inherited neurodegenerative disease characterized by progressive cerebellar and systemic dysfunction. In addition to motor impairment, individuals with FA frequently display cognitive and affective disturbances, referred to as cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome (CCAS). The CCAS scale (CCAS-S) is a validated tool to assess these symptoms in clinical and research settings. Previous studies suggest that Crus I, a posterior cerebellar region involved in executive and salience networks, may play a role in the pathophysiology of CCAS. However, the structural and functional basis of CCAS in FA remains incompletely understood. The aim of this study was to assess whether structural atrophy and functional connectivity changes in Crus I are associated with CCAS in individuals with FA.
Methods
This cross-sectional case-control study was conducted at the Hôpital Universitaire de Bruxelles. Structural MRI data were acquired to quantify volumes of Crus I and the prefrontal cortex (PFC) using CERES and Vol2Brain segmentation pipelines. Resting-state functional MRI was analyzed with the CONN toolbox to assess functional connectivity (rsFC) of Crus I. The CCAS-S was administered to assess cognitive function. Linear regression models evaluated the association between brain volumes and CCAS-S scores while seed-to-voxel analyses tested differences in Crus I connectivity patterns between groups.
Results
Fifty-six participants were included: 28 individuals with genetically confirmed FA (mean age 32 ± 14 years, 57% female) and 28 age-matched and sex-matched healthy controls (mean age 33 ± 7 years, 57% female). Individuals with FA exhibited significant atrophy of Crus I (mean normalized volume 1.5 ± 0.2 vs 1.9 ± 0.3; p < 0.001). Crus I volume significantly predicted CCAS-S scores (standardized β = 0.45; 95% CI 0.09–0.81). rsFC analyses revealed loss of Crus I–PFC connectivity in individuals with definite CCAS, whereas those without definite CCAS showed preserved partial connectivity. Increased rsFC between Crus I and left insular/opercular cortices was associated with CCAS severity.
Discussion
Our findings indicate that structural atrophy and altered rsFC of Crus I are associated with the performance on the CCAS-S in individuals with FA. These results support a cerebello-cortical disconnection model and may inform future neuromodulation interventions. Limitations include sample size and lack of structural connectivity measures.
Introduction
Friedreich ataxia (FA) is a recessive genetic disorder that impairs mitochondria energy metabolism and leads to oxidative stress and cell death. FA is a systemic disease that predominantly involves the heart and the CNS, which are, respectively, responsible for the lower life expectancy and the disability associated with the disease.1 On CNS pathology, FA is characterized by atrophy of the dorsal root ganglia and spinal cord posterior column and a progressive cerebellar dentate nuclei degeneration.2 Clinically, individuals typically become overtly symptomatic with the onset of cerebellar signs, after which progressive involvement of cerebellar, pyramidal, visual, and auditory pathways contributes to the worsening of neurologic impairment over time. The amounting cerebellar ataxic motor symptoms drive the patient disability and have the greatest impact on their daily life activities.3 However, motor coordination is only part of the cerebellum function. The posterior lobes, which constitute the largest part of the cerebellum, are involved in the regulation of cognitive processes through dense cerebello-cortical loops.4
Initially less studied than motor symptoms, the cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome (CCAS), described by Schmahmann in 1998,5 outlines deficits in executive, visuospatial, memory, language, and affective domains resulting from cerebellar dysfunction. Now considered a cornerstone of cerebellar ataxiology, CCAS is interpreted as a form of thought dysmetria and is pragmatically assessed using the validated CCAS-scale (CCAS-S).6 In FA, cognitive symptoms, assessed using the CCAS-S, strongly correlate with cerebellar motor ataxic symptoms, suggesting a common core cerebellar pathophysiology for both coordination and cognitive impairments in FA.7 However, the impact of the CCAS on instrumental activities of daily living, its progression, and the underlying mechanisms in individuals with FA are still incompletely understood. Furthermore, CCAS in FA lacks a definite structural and functional model that explains the patients' cognitive pattern. In a 2022 meta-analysis of neuropsychological studies realized with individuals with FA, the domains most commonly affected, and with the largest effect sizes, were the executive and attentional domains.8 Strikingly, the tests that discriminated between individuals with FA and healthy individuals (e.g., verbal fluency, digital span, and inhibition tasks) orient to prefrontal cortex (PFC) structural or functional integrity.9,10 Of interest, the CCAS-S built to screen and assess CCAS also relies heavily on tests involving PFC functions: the CCAS-S is based on 10-item tests among which 7 are based on tests that rely on PFC.6 This suggests that the common denominators of cognitive impairment in FA are cerebellar and PFC dysfunctions, both the number of neurons and cortical surface of the PFC and the cerebellum size have dramatically increased,11 and, in the cerebellum particularly the Crus I and II lobules of the posterior cerebellum.12 Crus I displays high structural volume covariance with the PFC.13,14 Functionally, Crus I is robustly activated for executive tasks in the multidomain task battery and functional cerebellar atlas.15,16 Crus I also shows high fMRI resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) with the executive control and saliency networks4,17 as well as with the PFC.18 A dependency of the CCAS on Crus I and PFC integrity is described in cerebellar stroke studies that mapped CCAS with lesions involving Crus I,19 and PFC atrophy is described after cerebellar strokes due to disconnection.20 Similarly, in an electroencephalographic investigation on patients with spinocerebellar ataxia type 2, a positive correlation between cerebellum posterior lobes and PFC connectivity with CCAS-S scores was described.21 Together, these facts suggest that the CCAS in FA could be related to an altered relationship between Crus I, the saliency network that gates the activation of the executive control network, and the PFC.22
The core hypothesis of this study is that individuals with FA and CCAS have altered Crus I structural and functional dysfunction. The aim of this study was, therefore, to assess the integrity of the Crus I structure and connectivity in individuals with FA in comparison with healthy individuals using MRI volumetry and fMRI rsFC investigations.
Methods
Participants
Genetically confirmed adult individuals with FA recruited at HUB-Hôpital Erasme, Brussels, were included in the study and matched for age and sex with healthy controls who had no history of neurologic diseases or psychoactive substance use.
Clinical Outcomes
Clinical evaluations were performed on the same day as the imaging sessions. Age at symptom onset (ASO) was defined as the age at which the first motor symptoms of Friedreich ataxia were reported by the patient or caregiver. Disease duration (DD) was calculated as the time interval between ASO and the date of the MRI scan. Cerebellar motor deficits were measured using the Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA). This 8-item scale assesses gait, stance, sitting balance, speech, finger chase, nose-to-finger coordination, rapid alternating pronation/supination of the upper limbs, and heel-to-shin movements, with a maximum score of 40 reflecting the most severe impairment.23 Cerebellar nonmotor symptoms were evaluated using the CCAS-S. The CCAS-S consists of 10 tasks: semantic and phonemic fluency, verbal category switching, forward and backward digit span, cube copying, verbal recall, verbal similarities, a go/no-go task, and an affect evaluation. Each item on the CCAS-S yields a raw score, contributing to a total score ranging from 82 (the sum of minimum passing scores across items) to 120 (the maximum possible score). Althoughthe total score is not diagnostic on its own, it provides a quantitative measure that can support longitudinal follow-up. The diagnosis of CCAS is based on the number of failed items: failure on one item suggests possible CCAS, failure on 2 items indicates probable CCAS, and failure on 3 or more items defines definite CCAS. Based on the CCAS-S scoring thresholds, it is possible for individuals to obtain a relatively high total score, above 90, while still meeting the criteria for definite CCAS, because failure on 3 subtests does not necessarily imply a low overall score, given the additive nature of the scale.6
MRI Acquisition and Analysis
Structural MRI data were acquired using a hybrid 3-T SIGNA PET-MRI scanner (GE Healthcare, Milwaukee, WI) equipped with a 24-channel head and neck coil. The imaging protocol included 3D T1-weighted MRI sequences with at least 150 slices for detailed brain and cerebellar morphological analysis.24 Brain volumetric analyses were performed using specialized tools for automated segmentation: CERES25 for cerebellar structures, enabling quantification of subregional atrophy in Crus I, and Vol2brain26 for the PFC, from which medial and dorsolateral PFC volumes were extracted and summed.26 All volumes were normalized to intracranial volume to adjust for individual variability.24
Statistical Analysis
Independent-sample t tests were performed to compare normalized volumes between individuals with FA and controls. The significance threshold was set at p < 0.05. To investigate the relationship between cerebellar and PFC atrophy and cognitive impairment, we used a stepwise linear regression model with the CCAS-S total raw score as the dependent variable and normalized volumes of Crus I and the PFC as predictors. Model selection followed a stepwise approach, where predictors were iteratively added or removed based on their contribution to model fit, evaluated using ANOVA F-tests to compare nested models. Model performance was assessed using R2, adjusted R2, and root mean square error (RMSE). The significance of individual predictors was evaluated using standardized beta coefficients (β) and associated p values, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. Spearman rank correlations were computed between normalized structural brain metrics (Crus I, PFC, total cerebellum, and total brain volumes) and disease severity (SARA score, ASO, and DD) to explore associations between normalized volumetric parameters and clinical scores.
fMRI Analysis
Analyses of fMRI data were performed using CONN release 22.a and SPM12.
All MRI scans were acquired on a 3T SIGNA PET-MRI scanner (GE Healthcare) with a 24-channel head and neck coil. Functional images were obtained using T2*-weighted GE-EPI covering the whole brain (TR/TE: 3,000/34 ms; 40 slices; voxel size: 2.9 × 2.9 × 3 mm). Four dummy scans preceded each run. A high-resolution 3D T1-weighted image (1-mm isotropic) was acquired for co-registration.27
Cerebellum Crus I seed definition: cerebellar lobules were segmented automatically using the Automatic Cerebellum Anatomical Parcellation tool, which applies a U-Net architecture combined with Locally Constrained Optimization (ACAPULCO; version 0.2.1). A bilateral cerebellar cortical Crus I, generated from the SUIT atlas by selecting voxels corresponding to the left (label 9) and right (label 10) Crus I regions,28 regions-of-interest (ROI) was defined for each participant.
Preprocessing and First-Level Analysis
Functional and anatomical data were preprocessed using the CONN toolbox's standard pipeline. Functional images underwent realignment (SPM realign and unwarp), slice timing correction, outlier detection (ART: framewise displacement >0.9 mm or global BOLD signal change >5 SD), normalization to MNI space, segmentation, and smoothing (8-mm FWHM Gaussian kernel). Realignment accounted for susceptibility-motion interactions, and normalization was performed using unified segmentation with IXI-549 tissue probability maps. Denoising included regression of 5 CompCor components each from white matter and CSF, motion parameters and their derivatives, outlier scans, task/session effects, and linear trends, followed by band-pass filtering (0.01–0.1 Hz). The effective post-denoising degrees of freedom ranged from 6.5 to 50.8 (mean 46.8). At the first level, seed-to-voxel connectivity (SBC) maps were computed for the Crus I seed. Fisher-transformed bivariate correlation coefficients were estimated using a weighted general linear model (GLM), representing functional connectivity strength across the brain.29
Group-Level Analyses
At the second level, three models were tested: (1) a between-group comparison of Crus I connectivity between patients with Friedreich ataxia (FA) and healthy controls using a 2-sample t test; (2) a voxel-wise regression model within the full FA group examining the relationship between Crus I connectivity and CCAS-S raw scores; and (3) within-group analyses to examine Crus I connectivity patterns separately in healthy controls, individuals with FA without definite CCAS, and individuals with FA with definite CCAS. For each group, first-level Fisher-transformed bivariate correlation maps were entered into a second-level GLM. Statistical inference was based on Gaussian Random Field theory,30 with a cluster-forming voxel-level threshold of p < 0.001 (uncorrected) and significance assessed at the cluster level using a family-wise error (FWE)–corrected threshold of p < 0.05. Sample-specific T-thresholds were applied based on degrees of freedom (T(27) for healthy controls; T(13) for each FA subgroup).
Standard Protocol Approvals, Registrations, and Patient Consents
All participants provided written informed consent before participation in the study. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the CUB Hôpital Erasme, Brussels, Belgium (Reference CCB: B4062021000183). All procedures involving human participants were conducted in accordance with the ethical standards of the institutional and national research committee and with the 1964 Helsinki Declaration and its later amendments. No experiments involving animals were conducted. No individual person's identifiable data (e.g., photographs or videos) are included in this article. The study was not a registered clinical trial.
Results
Participants
Twenty-eight individuals with FA and their respective controls participated in the study, including 27 individuals homozygous for a GAA1 triplet expansion and one compound heterozygous individual carrying a GAA1 expansion on one allele and a point mutation in the FXN gene on the other. Of the 28 individuals with Friedreich ataxia, 14 met the criteria for definite CCAS (i.e., failed 3 or more CCAS-S items) while the remaining 14 did not. Main characteristics of the participants are summarized in Table 1.
Table 1 Clinical Characteristics

Volumetry
Individuals with FA had similar intracranial cavity volumes as healthy participants and similar normalized brain volumes and PFC. Individuals with FA displayed significantly smaller normalized Crus I volumes (Table 2).
Table 2 Volumetric Analysis
Stepwise linear regression analysis identified normalized Crus I volume, but not normalized PFC volume, as a significant predictor of the CCAS-S score (F(1,26) = 6.67, p = 0.016, R2 = 0.20, adjusted R2 = 0.17, RMSE = 13.9). Higher normalized Crus I volume was a significant predictor of higher CCAS-S scores. No significant correlation was found between normalized Crus I volume and SARA score (ρ = −0.065, p = 0.743), ASO (ρ = −0.276, p = 0.154), or disease duration (ρ = −0.246, p = 0.208). Normalized total cerebellar volume showed no association with SARA score (ρ = −0.271, p = 0.163), ASO (ρ = −0.329, p = 0.088), and DD (ρ = −0.351, p = 0.067). Normalized total brain volume correlated with DD (ρ = −0.507, p = 0.006) but not with ASO (ρ = −0.348, p = 0.070) or SARA score (ρ = −0.328, p = 0.088). Normalized PFC volume correlated with ASO (ρ = −0.405, p = 0.032) and DD (ρ = −0.441, p = 0.002), but not with SARA score (ρ = −0.250, p = 0.199). All correlation results between clinical and volumetric measures are given in eTable 1.
Crus I–Functional Connectivity
In the between-group comparison, individuals with FA exhibited 2 clusters of increased functional connectivity with Crus I compared with healthy controls (Figure 1, Table 3). A large cluster of 2,501 voxels (peak MNI: +20, −62, −18; p-FWE <0.000001) encompassed bilateral posterior cerebellar regions, including lobule VI, lobule VIII, and Crus I/II, as well as portions of the vermis and occipital cortex. A smaller second cluster of 386 voxels (peak MNI: −48, −6, −2; p-FWE = 0.008) was located in the left insular and opercular cortex. In individuals with FA, Crus I–whole brain connectivity, using voxel-wise regression analyses with CCAS-S raw scores as a continuous regressor in the second-level model, revealed a significant negative correlation in a cluster encompassing the left anterior insula and putamen (peak MNI: −20, +14, −08; 363 voxels; p-FWE = 0.0108).

Crus I–Functional Connectivity According to CCAS Status
In healthy controls and in individuals with FAs with or without CCAS, a large cluster encompassing the posterior cerebellum and occipital/parietal cortex was consistently observed (e.g., x = −34, y = −74, z = −26; >23,000 voxels; p-FWE <0.000001) (Figure 2, Table 4). Crus I–PFC connectivity showed a different pattern in each group: widespread and bilaterally distributed in healthy controls, limited to small and fragmented clusters in individuals with FA without definite CCAS, and entirely absent in those with definite CCAS. In healthy controls, a large cluster centered in the right dorsolateral and medial PFC (x = +40, y = +60, z = 0; 11,171 voxels; T(27) > 3.69, p < 0.05 FWE), spanning extensive bilateral medial and lateral prefrontal areas. In FA without CCAS, Crus I–PFC connectivity was reduced to 3 smaller clusters: left medial PFC (x = −42, y = +58, z = +4; 170 voxels; p-FWE = 0.031), right superior PFC (x = +24, y = +68, z = +12; 157 voxels; p-FWE = 0.043), and dorsal PFC (x = +16, y = −38, z = +58; 161 voxels; p-FWE = 0.039). In individuals with FAs with definite CCAS, no significant PFC clusters remained. Table 5 lists all significant Crus I connectivity clusters for each group.

Discussion
The main findings from this study are that, in individuals with FA compared with healthy controls, (1) Crus I is significantly atrophied (2), Crus I displays higher intracerebellar rsFC and higher rsFC with the left insular and opercular cortices that correlate with performance on the CCAS-S, and (3) definite CCAS, assessed using the CCAS-S, is associated with loss of rsFC between Crus I and the PFC.
Although the sample size in our study is somewhat limited, our FA cohort shares key demographic and clinical characteristics including age, genotype, ASO, DD, and symptom severity with the European Friedreich's Ataxia Consortium for Translational Studies, which includes over 600 individuals in a multicenter, international natural history study.1 Similarly, the individuals with FA in our cohort showed results consistent with the CCAS-S performances in previous studies as well as those obtained in a large cohort of Australian individuals with FA.7,31 In addition, the Crus I volume atrophy we observed in individuals with FA is consistent with the Crus I atrophy observed in the MRI volumetrics from the ENIGMA-Ataxia Working Group study on 248 individuals with FA,32 and in smaller national cohorts.33,34 Together, these considerations suggest that our findings could be generalizable to the whole FA population.
In individuals with FRDA, we observed structural and functional alterations in cerebello-cortical circuits linked to cognitive performance. Specifically, Crus I showed significant atrophy compared with healthy controls, alongside increased rsFC within the cerebellum and with left insular and opercular cortices, changes that correlated with performance on the CCAS-S. Notably, the presence of a definite CCAS was associated with a loss of rsFC between Crus I and the prefrontal cortex. These findings may support a model of functional compensation, in which functional dysfunction prompts the recruitment of additional or alternative neural resources to preserve cognitive function. In this study, increased rsFC with non-prefrontal cortical areas may reflect compensatory engagement (neural compensation) while the disruption of cerebello-prefrontal connectivity may mark the breakdown of neural reserve.35 In healthy individuals, Crus I displayed widespread rsFC with the medial PFC (mPFC) and dorsolateral PFC (dlPFC) in agreement with previous rsFC MRI studies.18 Individuals with FA without definite CCAS also displayed significant rsFC between Crus I and the mPFC and dlPFC but with smaller and fewer clusters. This observation mirrors results from a fMRI study investigating the rsFC of the superior posterior cerebellar lobes (a mask that included cerebellum lobule VI, Crus I, Crus II, and lobule VIIb) with the PFC in individuals with FA, which also highlighted more restricted rsFC between superior posterior cerebellar lobes and PFC,36 as well as findings from another fMRI rsFC investigation in individuals with FA, showing reduced rsFC in the cerebellum and the PFC.37
In our study, individuals with FA and definite CCAS failed to show significant rsFC between Crus I and PFC. This suggests that loss of Crus I–PFC connectivity may contribute to the cognitive phenotype in Friedreich ataxia. Several arguments support this claim. First, the cognitive tasks in neuropsychological test batteries, such as fluency, Stroop, and Trail Making tests, which tap into prefrontal cortex functions, show the largest effect sizes among cognitive measures in individuals with FA.8,10 Similarly, in previous studies that assessed the CCAS-S in individuals with FA, fluency and digit span tasks were also the most frequently impaired.7,31 Second, an fMRI study using a verbal n-back working memory task, a task that also relies strongly on PFC, found similar performance in individuals with FA but cerebellar-PFC rsFC dysconnectivity compared with healthy individuals.38 Strikingly, this study also reported reduced activation and connectivity in the left anterior insula and rostrolateral prefrontal cortex in individuals with FRDA, with deficits more in relation to impaired task-set maintenance and salience processing than to executive control per se.38 By contrast, we observed increased resting-state functional connectivity between Crus I and the left insular and opercular cortices, alongside a loss of Crus I–PFC connectivity in patients with definite CCAS. These patterns could suggest that, in the presence of measurable cognitive impairment, salience-related regions may become overengaged to compensate for declining executive resources and point to a compensatory shift toward alternative networks when executive dysfunction emerges. Third, the cerebello-cortical canonical circuitry suggests that the interaction between Crus I and PFC occurs through cerebello-cortical loops.18 Thus, impairment of one partner in this reciprocal loop could lead to impairment of its counterpart through diaschisis. Diaschisis (διάσχισις, “shocked throughout”) refers to the structural or functional disconnection of interacting cortical areas, leading to remote dysfunction between affected brain areas and their connected counterparts and, potential subsequent atrophy.20 This mechanism has been identified in relation to cognitive performances in human diseases that involve Crus I and impaired executive functions such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder39 as well as in a cohort of individuals with SCA2.21 All these investigations highlighted disconnections between Crus I and PFC. Reciprocally, strokes in the anterior cerebral circulation are associated with cerebellar diaschisis,40 and patients with frontotemporal dementia (FTD) associated with the CR9ORF72 mutation (the most common mutation in FTD) exhibit significant Crus I atrophy.41 Finally, stimulating the cerebellum with cerebellar transcranial direct current stimulation (ctDCS) improves the CCAS in mixed cerebellar ataxia cohorts as well as in individuals with FA,42 likely by increasing connectivity between cerebellum posterior lobes and PFC.43 In our study, Crus I volume was a significant predictor of CCAS-S performances but not of motor severity, age at symptom onset, or disease duration, highlighting a dissociation between cognitive and motor cerebellar substrates. This support the selective involvement of Crus I in nonmotor cerebellar functions, particularly its role in higher-order cognition through a prefrontal cortical loop. Altogether, these findings and our results support a role of Crus I and PFC interplay in cognitive performances and a framework for understanding CCAS in individuals with FA.
Our study has several limitations. First, we did not correct CCAS-S performances according to speech impairments, and items that pertain to executive functions, such as phonemic, semantic, and category switching fluencies, are timed and negatively influenced by dysarthria, which could be a potential driver of false positives in the CCAS-S in our study.31 However, this bias is likely limited because the validated formula to correct verbal fluencies in individuals with FA, based on the PATA rate, only marginally improves fluency scores by less than 5%.44 Furthermore, in comprehensive neuropsychological test batteries, even after correcting for speech and motor impairments, tests assessing executive functions remain the most frequently altered.44 Similarly, we focused on Crus I connectivity for its implication in executive function, executive control, and saliency network, whereas speech production is associated with anterior cerebellum activations.45 Based on that, speech disturbances probably only had a minor effect on our findings. Second, our study is also limited by the lack of standardized cognitive screening or adjustment for years of education. Because educational attainment may influence CCAS-S performance,46 this raises the possibility of false-positive results among individuals with FA. Furthermore, although the overall sample size aligns with that of previous neuroimaging studies in rare diseases such as FA, subgroup analyses were exploratory and not formally powered to detect small effect sizes, warranting cautious interpretation. Technical limitations may also warrant cautious interpretation of our data. Crus I atrophy in FA may bias seed-based connectivity results because smaller seed volumes can reduce signal quality and underestimate functional coupling. Although spatial normalization and standard anatomical parcellation help standardize seed placement, they do not fully correct for partial volume effects or local signal loss. Finally, our study is limited by the lack of structural connectivity measures such as MRI tractography or diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) sequences. In individuals with FA, structural connectivity studies found that several distant cortical, notably the PFC, and subcortical regions were aberrantly connected with the cerebellum.47 Similarly, microstructural anomalies in the dentato-thalamo-cortical cerebellar efferent tracts and, to a lesser extent, throughout the brain have been identified in FA48 and correlate with clinical metrics, including an attentional cognitive task. Further fMRI studies using volume-matched seeds and DTI sequences that will assess the potential links between performance on the CCAS-S and integrity of the cerebello-cortical track would bring further support to the Crus I involvement in FA with definite CCAS. Still, future structural connectivity studies are likely to harvest similar results because structural and functional MRI studies show highly congruent results when performed together.
In conclusion, despite the study's limitations and the fact that a clear relationship between definite CCAS, based on the CCAS-S, and meaningful cognitive impairment affecting activities of daily living in individuals with FA remains uncertain, our findings provide converging evidence for the involvement of Crus I connectivity in individuals with FA presenting with definite CCAS. These results help delineate a functional neuroanatomical framework for cognitive impairment in FA, centered on the cerebello-cortical circuitry. Recognizing this network-level dysfunction reinforces the clinical relevance of CCAS in FA and opens avenues for targeted therapeutic strategies, such as noninvasive brain stimulation approaches (e.g., ctDCS targeting Crus I), aimed at restoring disrupted connectivity and mitigating cognitive symptoms.

Coexistence of Friedreich's Ataxia and Esophageal Cancer: A Case Report

ABSTRACT
Friedreich's ataxia (FA) is a rare autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder. Although FA is frequently associated with cardiomyopathy and diabetes mellitus, its coexistence with solid malignancies is exceptionally rare. To date, only a limited number of gastrointestinal cancers have been reported in patients with FA. This case report presents the first documented occurrence of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) in a genetically confirmed FA patient, highlighting the diagnostic challenges and therapeutic considerations encountered in this unique clinical setting. A 48-year-old Iranian man with a 29-year history of Friedreich's ataxia presented with an 8-month history of progressive dysphagia, recurrent hematemesis, and recent onset of complete aphagia. On examination, he was cachectic and exhibited severe alopecia, kyphoscoliosis, dysarthria, and a non-ambulatory status. Laboratory evaluation demonstrated profound anemia and elevated alkaline phosphatase levels. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a circumferential, obstructing mass in the mid-esophagus, and histopathological analysis confirmed moderately differentiated ESCC. Given the patient's advanced frailty, underlying cardiomyopathy, and severe malnutrition, curative chemoradiotherapy was deemed contraindicated. Palliative management included blood transfusion, nasogastric decompression, and placement of an esophageal stent. Despite these supportive interventions, the patient experienced hemodynamic instability and progressive neurological deterioration, ultimately succumbing to disease progression.

Abbreviations
ESCC
Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma
FA
Friedreich's ataxia
Key Clinical Message
This case underscores that although ESCC is an exceptionally rare comorbidity in Friedreich's ataxia, clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion when patients develop progressive or worsening dysphagia, particularly in the presence of alarm features such as gastrointestinal bleeding. FA-related genomic instability may increase susceptibility to malignancy, highlighting the need for prompt endoscopic evaluation rather than attributing symptoms solely to neurodegenerative progression. Optimal care relies on early recognition, multidisciplinary management, and careful consideration of FA-specific comorbidities and socioeconomic factors to deliver comprehensive and effective patient-centered care.
1 Introduction
Friedreich's ataxia (FA) is a rare, autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder caused by pathogenic GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions in the FXN gene [1]. Clinically, FA is characterized by progressive gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, sensory neuropathy, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy [1, 2]. Although primarily considered a neurological disease, non-neurological complications have also been documented. Onset typically occurs in childhood or adolescence, and the disease markedly reduces both life expectancy and quality of life. Common comorbidities and complications include scoliosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, pes cavus, diabetes, bone fractures, depression, visual loss, arrhythmias, and psychosis [3]. In contrast, associations with solid tumors are exceedingly uncommon, with only rare reports of gastrointestinal malignancies in patients with FA observed to date [4, 5]. Among these, no previously documented cases of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) coexisting with FA have been described in the literature.

Esophageal cancer represents an aggressive malignancy with a generally unfavorable prognosis. Its development has predominantly been attributed to environmental and lifestyle risk factors, including tobacco exposure, alcohol consumption, and chronic gastroesophageal reflux [6]. To date, the coexistence of FA and esophageal cancer has not been extensively characterized, and no definitive pathophysiological relationship has been established. The rarity of this association poses significant challenges in early recognition, diagnostic evaluation, and formulation of optimal therapeutic strategies.

In this report, a novel presentation of ESCC complicating the course of FA is described. Particular emphasis is placed on the diagnostic pitfalls and management complexities encountered, which were further exacerbated by factors including parental consanguinity, socioeconomic barriers to care, and frailty related to longstanding FA. This case aims to contribute to the limited body of evidence on malignancy in FA and to highlight the need for heightened clinical vigilance and multidisciplinary care strategies in such rare clinical scenarios.

2 Case Presentation
A 48-year-old unemployed Iranian male with a known diagnosis of FA presented with an 8-month history of progressively worsening dysphagia, initially to solids and subsequently to liquids. Episodes of retrosternal food impaction requiring liquids for clearance were reported, along with recurrent hematemesis. In the 2 weeks preceding admission, the patient developed complete aphagia accompanied by melena, dizziness, and marked functional decline. FA was diagnosed at age 19 based on clinical findings and confirmed by genetic testing. The patient's parents were consanguineous, and four of his five siblings were similarly affected by FA. A notable family history of malignancies was present, including breast, colorectal, and brain cancers in maternal and paternal relatives, as well as a paternal fatal stroke. Socioeconomic limitations had contributed to restricted access to healthcare and delayed diagnostic evaluation.

On examination, the patient appeared cachectic with a body mass index of 16 kg/m2, marked pallor, severe scalp alopecia, and kyphoscoliosis. The oropharynx was dry, with partial edentulism evident. Neurological evaluation demonstrated dysarthria, delayed speech, and complete inability to ambulate. Abdominal examination was unremarkable, whereas rectal examination confirmed the presence of melena. The constellation of findings suggested advanced nutritional compromise and progressive neurodegenerative disability in the setting of longstanding FA.

3 Diagnostic Assessment
3.1 Laboratory Findings
Initial laboratory investigations revealed severe microcytic anemia, with a hemoglobin level of 8.6 g/dL. Urinalysis revealed ketonuria (2+) and microscopic hematuria (RBC 1+). Inflammatory markers were elevated, with a markedly increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Alkaline phosphatase levels were significantly elevated (884 IU/L), suggestive of possible hepatic or osseous involvement.

3.2 Upper Gastrointestinal Endoscopy
Following written informed consent, esophagogastroduodenoscopy was performed. The endoscope was introduced orally and advanced to the second portion of the duodenum. In the middle third of the esophagus, an ulcerated, circumferential mass causing near-total luminal obstruction was visualized (Figure 1). Due to a large amount of retained food material within the esophageal lumen and the risk of aspiration, the procedure was expedited. Multiple biopsies were obtained from the lesion and submitted for histopathological analysis. The endoscopic diagnosis was a malignant-appearing tumoral lesion resulting in severe esophageal narrowing.

FIGURE 1
Endoscopic image demonstrating an ulcerated esophageal mass (arrow) located 28 cm from the incisors.

3.3 Histopathological Examination
Histopathological and macroscopic evaluation of the biopsy specimens revealed four small, gray, soft-tissue fragments, collectively measuring 0.6 cm in greatest dimension. Microscopic examination demonstrated features consistent with a moderately differentiated ESCC, arising from the esophageal mucosa.

3.4 Diagnostic Medical Imaging
Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the chest and abdomen confirmed a mid-esophageal mass with evidence of local invasion, staged as T3N1. No overt distant metastases were detected; however, hepatic sonography revealed an isoechoic lesion in the left lobe of the liver measuring 18 × 17 mm and one to two hyperechoic nodules measuring 8 mm in the right lobe, raising suspicion of early hepatic involvement.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain demonstrated cerebellar atrophy consistent with the patient's known FA diagnosis. No intracranial metastatic lesions were identified.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed severe FA-related dilated cardiomyopathy with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 20%, indicating significant impairment of systolic function.

4 Therapeutic Intervention
4.1 Urgent Supportive Measures
Upon admission, the patient was noted to have severe anemia with hemodynamic instability. An urgent transfusion of two units of packed red blood cells (PRBCs) was administered. Due to persistent dysphagia and complete inability to tolerate oral intake, a nasogastric tube was placed to facilitate nutritional and medical management.

4.2 Palliative Intervention
Given the near-total esophageal obstruction and advanced dysphagia, an esophageal self-expanding metallic stent was placed endoscopically for palliation of obstructive symptoms. The procedure was performed with precautionary measures due to the patient's frailty and high risk of aspiration. Symptomatic relief of dysphagia was temporarily achieved.

4.3 Oncology Treatment Considerations
Multidisciplinary evaluation determined that definitive chemoradiotherapy or surgical intervention posed an unacceptably high risk. This decision was based on poor functional status (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group [ECOG] performance score of 4), refractory anemia, and severe FA-related cardiomyopathy with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 20%. Consequently, curative oncologic therapies were deferred, and management was focused on supportive and palliative care.

5 Outcome
Following transfusion, the patient experienced recurrent hemoglobin decline and developed progressive hypotension, necessitating continuous norepinephrine infusion. Diastolic blood pressure could be maintained at 9–10 mmHg with vasopressor support and dropped to 5–6 mmHg when norepinephrine was withheld. The patient's condition further deteriorated, characterized by a decline in Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score, hypoxemia, gasping respirations, and bradycardia. Despite supportive measures, the clinical course culminated in asystolic cardiac arrest, and death was pronounced.

6 Discussion
This case report provides valuable insights into the rare coexistence of FA and ESCC, thereby contributing to the limited literature on malignancies in patients with FA. Among the report's strengths is its thorough documentation of the clinical presentation, genetic background, diagnostic workup, and management challenges in a socioeconomically disadvantaged context. The detailed family history and genetic confirmation of FA enhance the study's scientific rigor. However, limitations include the inherent limitations of single-case reports, which limit broad applicability, and the absence of molecular tumor profiling, which could have further elucidated mechanistic links between FA and carcinogenesis. Additionally, the rapid clinical decline precluded long-term follow-up and assessment of therapeutic efficacy.

The pathophysiological underpinnings of increased cancer risk in FA are increasingly recognized. FA results from GAA trinucleotide expansions in the FXN gene, leading to frataxin deficiency and disrupting mitochondrial iron metabolism, thereby elevating oxidative stress. This biochemical milieu induces DNA damage and genomic instability, potentially facilitating tumorigenesis [7-9]. While hematologic malignancies, particularly leukemia, have been reported in FA, solid tumors such as ESCC are exceedingly rare, with few cases documented. The strong family history of diverse cancers in this patient suggests a possible synergistic effect of genetic predisposition and frataxin deficiency in carcinogenesis.

This case also highlights significant diagnostic challenges. Progressive dysphagia is a common symptom in FA due to neuromuscular dysfunction [10] and was initially misattributed, resulting in an 8-month delay before endoscopic evaluation. Such delays can be detrimental, especially when symptom progression includes bleeding and complete aphagia, which are red flags for malignancy [10]. This underscores the necessity for heightened clinical vigilance and prompt diagnostic endoscopy in FA patients presenting with atypical or worsening dysphagia.

Multidisciplinary complexity further complicates management. FA-associated kyphoscoliosis restricts surgical options [11], while cardiomyopathy heightened anesthesia risk [12], consistent with known disease complications. Moreover, socioeconomic factors, including low income and limited access to healthcare, contributed to delayed presentation and hindered continuous care. Consequently, palliation with esophageal stenting was prioritized to improve quality of life, reflecting pragmatic clinical decision-making in a frail patient with advanced malignancy.

6.1 Recommendations
Annual endoscopic screening should be considered for FA patients presenting with dysphagia to facilitate early tumor detection. Early integration of neurology, oncology, and palliative care teams is essential to address the multifaceted needs of FA patients with malignancies. Families with consanguinity and multiple FA-affected members should be screened for hereditary cancer risk to enable proactive monitoring.

7 Conclusion
This case emphasizes that esophageal cancer, although rare, should be considered in patients with FA who present with progressive or worsening dysphagia, especially when accompanied by alarming symptoms. Early and proactive diagnostic evaluation, multidisciplinary collaboration, and consideration of socioeconomic factors are crucial for optimizing care and enhancing patient outcomes in this complex clinical context.

8 Key Learning Points
Rare Malignancy Association: ESCC can rarely coexist with FA, requiring increased clinical suspicion.
Diagnostic Pitfalls: Progressive dysphagia with bleeding should prompt early endoscopic evaluation, not solely attributed to neurodegeneration.
Multidisciplinary Challenges: FA-related cardiomyopathy, frailty, and socioeconomic barriers can severely limit cancer treatment options.
Clinical Recommendations: Early surveillance, coordinated multidisciplinary care, and genetic counseling may improve outcomes in this high-risk population.
