2. Materials and methods
2.1. Compound collection, ADMET analysis and target identification
Identification of the PREO and TLEO compounds was conducted using GC-MS analysis, as previously reported by our laboratory [22,27]. Subsequently, SMILES representations and 2D structural data files (SDF) for all components were obtained from PubChem. Compounds whose structures were not catalogued within PubChem underwent structural prediction using DataWarrior software (v6.1) [28]. The ADMET properties of the complete compound set were then predicted employing the SwissADME and pkCSM web tools [29,30].
To predict compound-associated biological targets, the Swiss Target Prediction tool was utilized with Homo sapiens specified as the target organism [31]. Each compound's canonical SMILES notation was queried individually, and all identified targets corresponding to protein-coding genes were retained.
2.2. Disease selection and target procurement
Common subtypes of neurodegenerative disorders (Alzheimer's disease, Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Friedreich ataxia, Huntington's disease, Lewy body disease, Parkinson's disease, Spinal muscular atrophy) and psychiatric conditions (autism spectrum disorder, attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, schizophrenia) were curated from authoritative clinical reports, prioritizing those with substantial epidemiological evidence. Individual queries for each selected disorder were performed using the GeneCards and Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) resources to generate lists of candidate gene targets [32,33]. Given the focus on druggable targets and core molecular pathways, predictions were filtered to retain exclusively protein-coding genes. The definitive association between these genes and their functional protein products was established by cross-referencing the gene symbols against the UniProt Knowledgebase (UniProtKB), thereby obtaining standardized protein nomenclature and functional descriptors [34].
2.3. Venn diagram and gene enrichment analysis
The comprehensive lists of protein targets identified for the essential oils (PREO and TLEO) and for the curated panel of neurodegenerative and psychiatric disorders were computationally integrated using the Venny 2.0 online tool (https://bioinfogp.cnb.csic.es/tools/venny/). This integration, visualized via Venn diagram construction, allowed for the precise identification of protein targets common to both the essential oils and the disease states. Following this intersection analysis, the resulting common protein targets were subjected to functional enrichment analyses. Specifically, Gene Ontology (GO) term enrichment was conducted using the WebGestalt platform, while KEGG pathway enrichment analysis was executed via the KOBAS server, aiming to annotate the biological significance and pathway involvement of the shared target space [35,36].
2.4. Protein-protein interaction network
Protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks were computationally generated for the compiled target proteins using the STRING (v11) platform [37]. To maximize the biological relevance and reliability of the predicted interactions, the analysis parameters were configured to enforce a stringent minimum confidence score of 0.900. This high threshold selectively filters interactions supported by strong evidence, minimizing inclusion of speculative links. Proteins failing to establish any connections above this confidence level (isolated nodes) were deliberately omitted to focus the analysis on interconnected functional modules. In the resultant network visualization and subsequent analyses, each protein entity was treated as an individual node, with edges quantitatively representing the confidence level of their predicted association.
2.5. Construction of compound-target-pathway networks
Following PPI network generation, the identified protein targets were partitioned into two principal categories based on molecular function: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) and non-GPCR targets. The classification protocol involved cross-referencing multiple authoritative resources: biomedical literature for established receptor functions, NCBI Gene entries for molecular characteristics, and UniProtKB classifications for definitive protein family assignments, thereby minimizing misclassification. Each categorized target set (GPCRs, non-GPCRs) was then contextualized with its interacting essential oil compounds (TLEO, PREO) and mapped to relevant KEGG pathways; pathway inclusion was contingent upon documented involvement of the target proteins in the pathway biology. These integrated compound–target–pathway relationships were visualized using Cytoscape software (version 3.10.2). Network topology analysis was performed using the CytoHubba and CytoNCA plugins within the Cytoscape environment, which were employed to calculate node centrality parameters and identify key hub targets [[38], [39], [40]].
2.6. Protein and ligand selection
Based on the topological analysis of the GPCR-centric and non-GPCR-centric Compound-Target-Pathway networks, a subset of key entities was extracted for molecular docking validation. Target prioritization involved selecting the 15 highest-scoring nodes within each category (GPCR targets and non-GPCR targets), ranked exclusively by their degree centrality metric calculated using CytoHubba and CytoNCA. Compound prioritization followed an analogous approach: the 5 compounds from PREO and the 5 compounds from TLEO possessing the highest degree values (reflecting the number of predicted target associations) were identified. These high-degree targets and compounds, representing the most interconnected elements within their respective network modules, were then advanced to molecular docking analysis to probe binding site complementarity and interaction energies.
2.7. Ligand preparation
The molecular structures of the eleven investigated compounds, initially provided in SDF format, underwent a sequential preparation protocol. First, hydrogen atoms were added to each structure using the Avogadro software (v 1.2.0), explicitly configured to model physiological conditions at pH 7.4 [41]. Subsequently, the hydrogen-added structures were subjected to energy minimization utilizing the Merck Molecular Force Field 94 (MMFF94) to optimize their geometry and reduce steric clashes. Finally, the minimized structures were converted into the PDBQT file format, suitable for molecular docking studies, employing the Open Babel cheminformatics toolkit [42].
2.8. Homology modeling and protein preparation
A systematic computational protocol was implemented for the preparation of the molecular structures corresponding to the thirty protein targets (comprising two distinct sets of fifteen targets each). The acquisition and initial modeling of these structures followed a dual-track strategy. The first set of structures was sourced directly from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, representing high-confidence computational predictions [43]. The second set required de novo modeling due to the absence of experimentally resolved structures; consequently, homology modeling was performed utilizing two complementary computational platforms: Swiss-Model (leveraging comparative protein structure modeling based on identified templates) and trRosetta (employing deep learning-based ab initio folding principles) [44,45]. All generated structural models (both AlphaFold predictions and homology models) were subsequently subjected to rigorous structural validation to assess their geometric and stereochemical quality. This evaluation was conducted using the SAVES 6.0 web server (https://saves.mbi.ucla.edu/), which provides integrated analyses including the ERRAT score for non-bonded atomic interactions, Verify3D for residue environment compatibility, and Ramachandran plot assessment for backbone dihedral angle plausibility. For each individual protein target, the specific structural model (whether AlphaFold-derived or originating from Swiss-Model or trRosetta) demonstrating the most favorable convergence of these validation metrics was selected for subsequent refinement.
The selected, validated structures for all thirty targets then underwent a comprehensive preprocessing pipeline. Initial steps involved the inspection and rectification of structural deficiencies, specifically the identification and addition of any missing atoms. Subsequently, non-relevant molecular components, such as crystallographic water molecules and any non-amino acid heteroatoms or ligands not pertinent to the study's focus, were meticulously removed. Following this cleanup, hydrogen atoms were added, explicitly assigning protonation states appropriate for physiological conditions (pH ∼7.4). The resulting hydrogenated structures were then subjected to energy minimization using the Swiss-PDB Viewer software. This minimization step employed an appropriate molecular mechanics force field to relax the structures, alleviate potential steric clashes introduced during modeling or hydrogen addition, and optimize local geometry towards a lower energy conformation. Finally, to render the structures compatible with downstream molecular docking simulations, Kollman united atom partial charges were calculated and assigned. The fully preprocessed and minimized structures were ultimately converted into the PDBQT file format using the AutoDockTools package (MGLTools 1.5.7) [46].
2.9. Molecular docking analysis
Computational identification of allosteric binding sites across the protein targets was performed using the Passer 2.0 algorithm, which employs a hybrid approach combining pocket geometry analysis with evolutionary sequence conservation metrics to detect putative regulatory cavities distal from orthostatic sites [47]. Following comprehensive scanning of each protein's surface, the single most probable allosteric pocket was selected for each target based on the convergence of highest prediction confidence scores, spatial distinctiveness from active sites, and favorable physicochemical properties indicative of ligand binding potential. Subsequently, molecular docking was executed using AutoDock Vina 1.2.3 to quantitatively evaluate binding interactions between the curated ligand library and identified allosteric pockets [48]. The docking protocol implemented a Lamarckian genetic algorithm with exhaustive search parameters (exhaustiveness = 8), confining the search space to a 25 Å3 grid box centered on the predicted allosteric site coordinates. Each docking experiment generated multiple binding poses, with the dominant conformation selected according to both lowest binding energy (ΔG, kcal/mol) and cluster analysis consistency. Binding affinity values were systematically extracted from the highest-scoring pose for comparative analysis across all protein-ligand complexes.
2.10. Dynamic simulation analysis
The top-ranked ligands for both GPCR and non-GPCR targets underwent molecular dynamics simulations to evaluate complex stability, executed in GROMACS 2024.4 [49]. Protein structures utilized AMBER positional restraints throughout the simulation protocol, while ligand parameters were derived using the General AMBER Force Field (GAFF) with atomic partial charges calculated via the RESP2.5 method at the HF/6-31G level of theory. Systems were solvated in a triclinic TIP3P water box extending 1.2 nm beyond the solute, neutralized with counterions, and maintained at 0.15 M NaCl ionic strength. After energy minimization (steepest descent, 10,000 steps), stepwise equilibration was performed: initial NVT phase (100 ps, V-rescale thermostat @ 310 K) with protein heavy-atom position restraints (1000 kJ/mol·nm2), followed by NPT equilibration (100 ps, Berendsen barostat @ 1 atm) with backbone restraints (400 kJ/mol·nm2). Production simulations proceeded unrestrained for 120 ns under NPT conditions (Parrinello-Rahman barostat) with a 2-fs integration time step.
Trajectory analysis employed three stability metrics: 1) Backbone Cα RMSD relative to minimized structure (convergence threshold <0.25 nm), 2) Per-residue α-carbon RMSF identifying flexibility hotspots, and 3) Ligand-specific SASA monitoring hydrophobic burial. The AMBER positional framework combined with RESP2.5 charges enabled precise electrostatic representation, while GAFF parameters ensured accurate ligand torsion potentials. Stability was confirmed through RMSD plateaus within 50-100 ns, ligand RMSF below 0.15 nm in binding pockets, and SASA reductions exceeding 40% versus unbound states, collectively validating sustained binding under physiological sampling conditions.
2.11. Binding free energy calculations and per-residue decomposition
To quantitatively evaluate binding strength and identify critical residue-level contributions, Molecular Mechanics/Poisson-Boltzmann Surface Area (MM/PBSA) calculations were performed on the final 20 ns of stable molecular dynamics trajectories for each protein-ligand complex using the gmx_mmpbsa tool. A total of 200 equally spaced snapshots were extracted from the equilibrated portion of each trajectory to ensure statistical robustness.
The binding free energy (ΔGbind) for each complex was calculated as
where each free energy term comprises molecular mechanics energy (E-mm) and solvation free energy (G-solvation). Using the single trajectory approach, bonded interactions cancel, leaving non-bonded contributions: E-mm = E-vdw + E-ele. Solvation free energy was calculated as the sum of polar (G-polar) and non-polar (G-nonpolar) contributions. Polar solvation energy was determined by solving the Poisson-Boltzmann equation with solute and solvent dielectric constants of 2 and 80, respectively, at 310 K. Non-polar solvation energy was estimated from solvent-accessible surface area using G-nonpolar = γ × SASA + β, where γ = 0.02267 kJ/mol/Å2 and β = 3.849 kJ/mol. Entropic contributions were omitted; therefore, reported values represent relative binding enthalpies.Per-residue decomposition analysis identified energetic hotspots by summing van der Waals, electrostatic, and solvation energy components for each amino acid. Residues with absolute energy contributions exceeding 2.0 kJ/mol were considered significant interaction hotspots.
3. Results
3.1. ADMET analysis of the compounds
Phytochemical analysis identified 57 compounds in PREO, with citronellol, geraniol, and eugenol representing prominent constituents. Pharmacokinetic (PK) profiling suggested that the majority of PREO compounds exhibited favorable drug-like properties: 72% demonstrated high gastrointestinal (GI) absorption, 87% were blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeant, and 85% conformed to Lipinski's rule of five (≤1 violation). Aqueous solubility was observed for 81% of constituents. Eugenol emerged as the lead compound within PREO according to ADMET analysis, exhibiting optimal PK metrics (zero Lipinski violations, high predicted bioavailability).
TLEO contained 53 characterized compounds, notably linalool, eucalyptol (1,8-cineole), and linalyl acetate. PK assessment indicated that 94% of TLEO constituents displayed high GI absorption, 96% were BBB permeant, and 89% adhered to Lipinski guidelines. Favorable solubility was demonstrated by 92% of compounds. Linalool was identified as the prime therapeutic candidate in TLEO due to its robust PK profile and absence of Lipinski violations. Collectively, both essential oils demonstrate considerable promise for central nervous system (CNS)-targeted applications. Comparative analysis indicates TLEO possesses marginally superior GI absorption and BBB permeation characteristics relative to PREO (Table S1).
3.2. Identification of common targets
A four-way Venn diagram of 7190 elements indicated 252 shared targets (3.5%) common to all four sets (Fig. 2A). This core overlap highlights potential convergent therapeutic targets. Uniquely, neurodegenerative disorders (ND) accounted for 2427 targets (33.7%), psychiatric conditions (PC) for 2207 targets (30.6%), TLEO for 34 targets (0.5%), and PREO for 39 targets (0.5%). Significant two-way overlaps included 1789 targets (24.8%) shared between neurodegenerative disorders (ND) and psychiatric conditions (PC), and 107 targets (1.5%) communal between TLEO and PREO, while neurodegenerative disorders (ND) and TLEO shared 19 targets (0.3%), and psychiatric conditions (PC) and PREO joint 17 targets (0.2%).

3.3. Protein-protein interaction network analysis
STRING analysis of the 252 shared targets in Fig. 2, filtered for high-confidence interactions (interaction score >0.9), highlighted a highly interconnected protein–protein interaction (PPI) network comprising 240 nodes and 1812 edges, with significant PPI enrichment (p < 1.0 × 10−6). Target classification delineated 44 GPCRs, with CHRM2 emerging as a central hub associated with cholinergic signaling. The remaining 208 non-GPCR targets included key nodes such as NR1H3 (a nuclear receptor involved in lipid homeostasis), COMT (regulating catecholamine metabolism), AHR (a mediator of xenobiotic response), and NLRP2 (implicated in neuroinflammatory processes). These hub proteins collectively mapped onto pathways related to neuroinflammation and dysregulation of lipid and neurotransmitter metabolism, thereby providing mechanistic insight into the potential of TLEO and PREO to exert neuroprotective and psychotropic effects via multi-target pathway modulation.
3.4. Gene Ontology and KEGG pathway analysis
Gene Ontology enrichment analysis prognosticated significant associations across biological processes, cellular components, and molecular functions, indicating that the identified targets participate in diverse regulatory and signaling pathways relevant to neuronal and inflammatory processes (Fig. 2). Key biological processes included “response to stimulus” (252 genes), “biological regulation” (234 genes), and “multicellular organismal process” (233 genes), highlighting roles in cellular responses and regulatory mechanisms. Enriched cellular components featured “membrane” (187 genes), “nucleus” (118 genes), and “endoplasmic reticulum” (114 genes), indicating prominence of membrane-bound structures and organelles. Molecular functions were dominated by “protein binding” (252 genes) and “molecular transducer activity” (210 genes), suggesting critical protein interaction networks. Notably, FDR-corrected terms (FDR <0.05) such as “regulation of inflammatory response” exhibited enrichment ratios exceeding 1.5, underscoring immune and homeostatic functions. Notably, several FDR-corrected terms (FDR <0.05), including regulation of inflammatory response, exhibited enrichment ratios exceeding 1.5, highlighting the potential involvement of these targets in immune regulation and neuronal homeostasis.

Compound-target network indicated distinct functional profiles between GPCR-associated and non-GPCR genes (Table 1). For GPCR genes in Fig. 3, biological processes were enriched in cell communication (48 genes), response to stimulus (47 genes), and biological regulation (47 genes), with cellular components dominated by membrane-associated structures (45 genes) and cell projections (29 genes). Molecular functions featured molecular transducer activity (48 genes) and protein binding (44 genes), consistent with signal transduction roles. In non-GPCR genes in Fig. 4, biological processes emphasized metabolic processes (204 genes) and cellular responses (195 genes), while cellular components highlighted membrane (142 genes), cytosol (109 genes), and nuclear localization (107 genes). Molecular functions prioritized protein binding (173 genes) and hydrolase activity (68 genes), indicating enzymatic roles. Network analysis demonstrated GPCR-centric pathway interconnectivity, whereas non-GPCR networks showed compound-target interactions (e.g., α-pinene →EGFR/MAPK14) involving metabolic and regulatory pathways.

3.7. Molecular dynamics simulations
Molecular dynamics simulations demonstrated distinct stabilization profiles for ligand-receptor complexes (Fig. 6). For CHRM2, Caryophyllene oxide exhibited superior structural stability compared to Nerol oxide, evidenced by reduced RMSD fluctuations (converging at ∼3.0 Å after 60 ns) and lower residue flexibility (residues 250–350). This enhanced stability correlated with a more compact conformation, reflected in decreased solvent accessibility (SASA: 270–280 Å2) and lower radius of gyration (Rg). Conversely, NR1H3 complexes demonstrated marked ligand-dependent behavior: α-Himachalene maintained exceptional conformational stability with lower RMSD (1.0–1.2 Å vs. α-Copaene's 1.6 Å), reduced N-terminal flexibility (residues 0–50/100–120), and significantly compact topology (Rg and SASA: Å2vs. 210–220 Å2). These metrics collectively identify Caryophyllene oxide and α-Himachalene as optimal stabilizers for CHRM2 and NR1H3, respectively, through distinct compaction mechanisms.

(A) Rg for Nerol Oxide and Caryophyllene Oxide with CHRM2 (B) RMSD for Nerol Oxide and Caryophyllene Oxide with CHRM2; (C) RMSF for for Nerol Oxide and Caryophyllene Oxide with CHRM2; (D) Rg for α-Copaene and α-Himachalene docked complex with NR1H3 (E) RMSD for α-Copaene and α-Himachalene docked complex with NR1H3; (F) RMSF for α-Copaene and α-Himachalene docked complex with NR1H3; (G) SASA for α-Copaene and α-Himachalene docked complex with NR1H3; (H) SASA for α-Copaene and α-Himachalene docked complex with NR1H3.

3.8. MM/PBSA free binding energy analysis
To validate docking predictions and assess complex stability, MM/PBSA binding free energy calculations were performed on α-Copaene-NR1H3, α-Himachalene-NR1H3, Caryophyllene oxide-CHRM2, and Nerol oxide-CHRM2 (Fig. 7). In the NR1H3 complexes, α-Himachalene exhibited markedly superior binding (ΔGbind = −168.21 kJ/mol) compared to α-Copaene (−149.00 kJ/mol), primarily driven by stronger van der Waals interactions (−221.56 kJ/mol vs. −198.47 kJ/mol), reflecting optimized hydrophobic packing within the ligand-binding pocket. Electrostatic contributions were modest for both ligands (−27.84 to −34.21 kJ/mol), consistent with the non-polar nature of the binding domain. Although the polar solvation penalty was higher for α-Himachalene (112.43 kJ/mol vs. 98.65 kJ/mol), this was compensated by enhanced non-polar contacts. Per-residue decomposition identified key hydrophobic residues, PHE-257, ILE-295, LEU-299, PHE-326, and TRP-443as major stabilizing contributors, forming a tightly packed core, while interactions in the α-Copaene complex were 15–20% weaker. For the CHRM2 complexes, Caryophyllene oxide displayed more favorable binding (−143.04 kJ/mol) than Nerol oxide (−115.98 kJ/mol), dominated by van der Waals interactions (−176.83 kJ/mol vs. −152.37 kJ/mol). Aromatic residues TRP-155, TYR-403, TYR-426, and TYR-430 formed an aromatic cage stabilizing Caryophyllene oxide, whereas Nerol oxide interactions were uniformly weaker (>30% reduction). Overall, hydrophobic and aromatic residues constitute the principal binding hotspots, and the enhanced affinities of α-Himachalene and Caryophyllene oxide arise from optimized packing and stronger van der Waals interactions, resulting in tighter complex stabilization.
