Longitudinal studies are needed to confirm its sensitivity to clinical trajectory and therapeutic response.

1. Introduction

Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is a rare, autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder caused by GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions in the FXN gene, resulting in reduced expression of the mitochondrial protein frataxin. Frataxin deficiency impairs mitochondrial function, disrupts iron-sulfur cluster biogenesis, and leads to oxidative stress and progressive neuronal degeneration. Clinically, FRDA is characterized by early-onset gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, loss of proprioception, and progressive cardiomyopathy, features that often emerge in childhood or adolescence and worsen over time. Despite advances in genetic characterization, there remains a critical need for non-invasive, in vivo biomarkers capable of tracking disease progression and evaluating therapeutic response.

Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) has been used in FRDA to detect neurochemical alterations in the central nervous system, including reduced N-acetylaspartate (NAA; neuronal marker) and elevated myo-inositol (mI; glial marker) in the cervical spinal cord and in the cerebellar vermis/hemispheres and pons. Prior work in the cerebellar hemispheres and pons using short-TE MRS at 4 T has reported alterations in NAA and mI, summarized as a reduced NAA/mI ratio, and has also suggested pontine GSH abnormalities, including an elevated GSH/tNAA ratio in FRDA. To our knowledge, the NAA/mI ratio in the primary motor cortex has not been reported in FRDA, particularly in pediatric cohorts. Beyond these conventional markers and their ratios, there is strong rationale to expand the neurochemical profile to include glutathione (GSH) and γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA): GSH is the brain’s primary antioxidant and an in vivo indicator of oxidative stress, central to FRDA pathogenesis, yet brain GSH by MRS has been examined only rarely in FRDA and, to our knowledge, has not been studied in the motor cortex in either adult or pediatric cohorts. GABA, the main inhibitory neurotransmitter critical for motor control, may reveal altered inhibitory tone with edited MRS. Together with established measures like NAA/mI, GSH and GABA could provide a more comprehensive view of FRDA pathophysiology and improve sensitivity for tracking progression and treatment response.

Hadamard Encoding and Reconstruction of MEGA-Edited Spectroscopy (HERMES) is an advanced edited MRS technique developed to enable simultaneous detection of multiple low-concentration metabolites, such as GABA and GSH, in a single scan. In the method described by Saleh et al., HERMES applies a Hadamard encoding scheme to interleave multiple MEGA editing pulses across four sub-experiments. The Hadamard combination of sub-spectra isolates the signals of interest, GABA and GSH. Although HERMES is designed primarily for edited detection of low-concentration metabolites like GABA and GSH, the acquisition also yields high-quality sum spectra that can be used to quantify conventional metabolites such as NAA and mI. Previous studies have demonstrated that reliable quantification of abundant metabolites such as NAA and mI is feasible from longer-TE summed spectra, particularly when LCModel is used in combination with simulated basis sets and optimized spectral modeling. In this study, we leveraged the sum spectra from HERMES to derive NAA and mI estimates, ensuring internal consistency across all acquisitions and subjects while enabling simultaneous examination of both canonical and edited metabolites within the same voxel.

Assessments of GSH and GABA in the cerebellum and motor areas of FRDA patients using in vivo MRS are notably absent from the current literature. While GSH is a key antioxidant involved in counteracting oxidative stress, a core feature of FRDA pathology, and GABA is central to inhibitory neurotransmission, in vivo measurements of these metabolites in FRDA have been limited, with prior GSH findings restricted primarily to brainstem regions and adult cohorts. In this study, we addressed this gap by using edited MRS to quantify GSH and GABA levels in the cerebellum, where pathology is well established, and in the primary motor cortex, which is increasingly recognized as a site of disease involvement. We hypothesized that in vivo levels of both GSH and GABA would be reduced in proportion to clinical severity.

2. Methods

2.1. Ethics

This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (IRB# 23-021822). All procedures conformed to the Declaration of Helsinki and HIPAA regulations. As participants were minors, written parental or guardian consent was obtained for all subjects and child assent was obtained when age-appropriate (≥7 years, per IRB policy). MRI/MRS procedures were noninvasive, and all data were de-identified prior to analysis.

2.2. Inclusion criteria

FRDA patients between the ages of 8 and 15 years were of specific interest for recruitment, as they were unexposed to omaveloxolone (FDA approved for individuals with FRDA > 16 years of age).

2.3. Data acquisition

MR imaging (MRI) and MRS experiments were conducted on a 3 T Siemens Prisma scanner using a 32-channel head coil. MRS was performed in three regions: cerebellum, where the voxel was placed to straddle the midline and thus capture both dentate nuclei, and the left motor cortex and right motor cortex with voxels centered on the precentral motor hand knob anatomical landmarks. Before every MRS acquisition, a high-resolution 1 mm3 whole-brain T1 structural image was acquired to aid with voxel placement. The MRS experiments involved using the Hadamard Encoding and Reconstruction of MEGA-Edited Spectroscopy (HERMES) sequence. The multi-vendor standardized HERMES sequence was designed with slice-selective and frequency-selective RF pulses for PRESS localization and editing. The duration of the slice-selective excitation and refocusing pulses were 7.2 ms and 7.0 ms, respectively. The HERMES editing scheme has four sub-experiments (A, B, C, and D) for the simultaneous detection of GABA at 3.0 ppm and GSH at 2.95 ppm. Hadamard combinations A + B - C - D yielded GABA-edited spectra, A - B + C - D yielded GSH-edited spectra, and A + B + C + D yielded the sum spectra. The GABA-edited spectrum detects the GABA + macromolecule signal at 3 ppm (GABA+ from here on).

HERMES data in the right and left motor cortices were acquired using the following parameters: 30 × 30 × 30 mm3 voxel size; TE/TR = 80/2000 ms; 20-ms editing pulse duration; 2048 data points; 2 kHz spectral width; 320 transients; and WET water suppression. For the cerebellar region, the same parameters were used except for 30 × 30 × 20 mm3 voxel size. Outer-volume suppression pulses were applied to saturate spins outside the volume of interest and reduce signals from outside the voxels. Finally, unsuppressed water acquisitions were performed using the above parameters, except that 16 transients were collected from every region. The total scan time per region was about 12 minutes.

2.4. Data processing

Data were processed in Osprey. The 3.02-ppm total creatine (tCr = creatine + phosphocreatine) signal was used to estimate magnetic field (B0) drift in the in vivo data before frequency- and phase-correction (FPC). Within every MRS dataset, any transients with a B0 drift exceeding 5 Hz were removed. Finally, FPC was performed on the remaining transients of every MRS dataset. The fully processed sub-spectra were combined to generate the GABA-edited, GSH-edited, and sum spectra. The residual water signal was removed using an HSVD filter.

2.5. Data modeling

The HERMES data were modeled using LCModel (Version 6.3-1R). Two-dimensional localized density-matrix simulations were performed using the HERMES parameters in MRSCloud to generate LCModel basis sets. The following metabolites were included in the generation of the basis sets: alanine, ascorbate, aspartate, creatine, phosphocreatine, GABA, glycerophosphocholine (GPC), GSH, glutamate (Glu), glutamine (Gln), glycine, myo-inositol (mI), lactate, N-acetyl aspartate (NAA), N-acetylaspartylglutamate (NAAG), phosphocholine (PCh), phosphocreatine (PCr), scyllo-inositol, and taurine.

The water-scaled GABA+ estimates were obtained from the GABA-edited spectra modeled between 0.5 and 4 ppm. The water-scaled GSH estimates were obtained from the GSH-edited spectra modeled between 2.2 ppm and 3.4 ppm. In order to enable water scaling in LCModel, a singlet at 3.3 ppm, devoid of any in vivo signal, was simulated using the HERMES parameters without the editing pulses and added to the basis functions to enable water scaling of the GSH-edited spectra. The water-scaled estimates of total NAA-acetyl compounds (NAA + NAAG, tNAA), total creatine, total choline (tCho), and glutamate came from the sum spectra modeled between 0.6 and 4 ppm.

2.6. Quality control (QC)

Every subject’s modeled edited and sum spectra were visually assessed, and those with spurious signals, baseline distortions, or the absence of poorly defined signal at expected resonance frequencies were removed from further analysis. The T1-weighted images were segmented to calculate gray matter (GM), white matter (WM), and CSF voxel tissue fractions. Water-scaled concentrations were corrected for partial volume and relaxation effects in each voxel. The values for T1/T2 of GABA were 1310/88.5 ms, GSH were 1265/116.75 ms, tNAA were 1337.5/225.9 ms, and mI were 1120/198.7 ms. The following tissue-specific relaxation times for water were used: T1/T2 of GM were 1331/110 ms, WM were 832/79.2 ms, and CSF were 3817/503 ms.

Data quality indices (LCModel SNR and spectral linewidth, FWHM) are summarized in Table 1. Cerebellar spectra showed lower SNR and broader linewidths relative to motor cortex; however, there were no significant group differences in SNR or FWHM within any ROI, indicating comparable spectral quality between FRDA and control participants.

3. Results

3.1. Participants

Our sample included 16 children with Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) and 15 age-matched typically developing controls. The mean age of the control group was 12.5 years (SD = 1.8, range = 9.9 to 16.0), while the FRDA group had a mean age of 11.9 years (SD = 1.8, range = 8.9 to 15.3). The sex distribution was similar across groups, with 7 females and 8 males in the control group and 7 females and 9 males in the FRDA group. The mean short-arm GAA repeat length in the FRDA group was 905 (range = 560-1210). The mean disease burden, defined as the product of age and GAA1 repeat length, was 10,800 (range = 5,850-18,600).

3.2. MRS results

For edited spectra, the number of transients retained after drift removal did not differ significantly between groups. Following visual quality assessment, the remaining datasets from right motor, left motor, and cerebellum that generated GABA-edited spectra were 15/14/13 for controls and 15/16/13 for FRDA; GSH-edited spectra were 15/15/13 for controls and 15/16/12 for FRDA; and sum spectra containing tNAA and mI were 15/15/13 for controls and 16/16/13 for FRDA.

A linear mixed model (LMM) was used to evaluate group and region (ROI) effects on tissue-corrected GSH, with subject as a random effect. The model revealed no significant effect of group (p = 0.93), indicating that overall GSH levels did not differ between the FRDA and control groups. In contrast, there was a highly significant main effect of ROI (p < 0.001), with GSH levels significantly lower in both motor cortices compared to the cerebellum, consistent with a regionally specific gradient in glutathione concentration.

A linear mixed model (LMM) was used to evaluate group and region (ROI) effects on tissue-corrected GABA concentrations, with subject as a random effect. The model revealed no significant main effect of group (p = 0.953), indicating no global difference in GABA levels between FRDA and control participants. In contrast, there was a highly significant main effect of ROI (p < 0.001), with GABA+ levels significantly lower in both motor cortices compared to the cerebellum, consistent with a strong regionally specific gradient.

An LMM revealed a significant main effect of group on the tissue-corrected tNAA/mI ratio (p < 0.001), with individuals with FRDA exhibiting reduced tNAA/mI levels relative to controls across brain regions. A strong main effect of ROI was also observed (p < 0.001), with tissue-corrected tNAA/mI ratios significantly higher in both motor cortices compared to the cerebellum. The omnibus Group × ROI interaction was not significant, indicating that the FRDA-related reduction in tNAA/mI did not differ across regions.

A linear mixed model conducted after excluding outliers revealed a significant main effect of group (p < 0.001), indicating a global reduction in tissue-corrected tNAA/mI among individuals with FRDA compared to controls. The group effect remained statistically significant when outliers were included (p = 0.009), confirming that the observed group difference was not driven by extreme values.

To determine whether the group-level reduction in the tNAA/mI ratio reflected neuronal loss (reduced tNAA), gliosis (elevated mI), or both, we conducted follow-up LMMs for each metabolite separately. These analyses revealed no significant group difference in tissue-corrected tNAA (p = 0.150), but a significant elevation in mI in the FRDA group (p < 0.001), indicating that the group effect on the tNAA/mI ratio was primarily driven by increased myo-inositol.

3.3. tNAA (motor cortex and cerebellum)

Although group differences in tNAA did not reach statistical significance in the primary linear mixed-effects model, inspection of the regional data suggested that tNAA values were numerically lower in FRDA, particularly in the motor cortices. ROI-specific Welch t-tests showed a trend toward reduced tNAA in the left motor cortex (p ≈ 0.08; Cohen’s d ≈ 0.67), with a smaller difference in the right motor cortex (p ≈ 0.27). In contrast, cerebellar tNAA values were nearly identical between groups. Taken together, these findings suggest that reductions in cortical tNAA may be present in FRDA, although the current study was likely underpowered to detect these effects with statistical confidence.

ROI-specific Welch’s independent-samples t-tests, Bonferroni-corrected across 3 ROIs, showed higher mI in FRDA in the left motor cortex (pcorr = 0.009) and right motor cortex (pcorr = 0.021); the cerebellum showed a non-significant trend (pcorr = 0.054), establishing that elevated mI is a regionally consistent contributor to the reduced tNAA/mI ratio in FRDA.

To assess whether increased mI was related to clinical severity, we fit linear mixed models with disease stage as a fixed effect, ROI as a covariate, and subject as a random intercept. Across ROIs, controlling for ROI, stage showed a positive but non-significant association with tissue-corrected mI (β = 0.19, p = 0.093). In ROI-specific LMMs, no association survived Bonferroni correction for three comparisons. Stage × ROI interactions were not significant.

4. Discussion

This study provides the first in vivo assessment of glutathione (GSH) and γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA+) in pediatric FRDA using multi-metabolite edited MRS. Across cerebellum and bilateral motor cortex, we identified a robust reduction in the tNAA/mI ratio driven by elevated myo-inositol. In contrast, tissue-corrected GSH and GABA+ did not differ between groups. The null GSH result should be interpreted cautiously: conventional edited MRS primarily quantifies reduced GSH, whereas disease-related oxidative stress may shift the redox balance toward oxidized GSH (GSSG), which is not detected. Region-specific preservation or developmental compensation in children may also contribute, and redox-sensitive methods and longitudinal designs are warranted. The absence of a corresponding GSH elevation in the present study may reflect differences in region of interest, participant age, or both. Collectively, these findings highlight mI as a practical in vivo marker of astrocytic activation and gliosis in pediatric FRDA.

The reduction in the tNAA/mI ratio, largely attributable to increased mI rather than significantly reduced tNAA, supports a model of reactive gliosis in response to progressive neurodegeneration. Myo-inositol is highly concentrated in astrocytes, and its elevation likely reflects astrocytic activation in the setting of neuronal stress, particularly within the motor cortex and cerebellum. These findings align with histopathological evidence of astrocytosis in FRDA and with the broader interpretation of mI as a marker of glial response to neurodegeneration. Importantly, the elevation of mI in motor regions occurred in the absence of significantly reduced tNAA, suggesting a temporal dissociation between early astrocytic responses and later neuronal loss. Nonetheless, numerical reductions in tNAA were observed in the motor cortices, raising the possibility that subtle cortical tNAA abnormalities may emerge with greater statistical power or larger samples.

Reactive gliosis, indexed by increased mI, is widely recognized as an early response to cellular dysfunction, whereas neuronal loss, reflected by reduced tNAA, may emerge only after prolonged progression. This temporal pattern is consistent with findings from other neurodegenerative conditions such as multiple sclerosis, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and Huntington’s disease, where elevated mI often precedes or occurs independently of reductions in NAA. Such cross-disease parallels reinforce the potential of mI as a sensitive, early biomarker of disease progression in FRDA.

We fit LMMs with disease stage as a fixed effect, ROI as a covariate, and subject as a random intercept. Across ROIs, controlling for ROI, stage showed a positive but non-significant association with mI (β = 0.19, p = 0.093). In ROI-specific LMMs, no association survived Bonferroni correction for three comparisons; the strongest nominal effect was in the cerebellum (β = 0.35, p = 0.042; pcorr = 0.126). Stage × ROI interactions were not significant. Overall, these analyses suggest insufficient power to detect region-specific stage effects at corrected thresholds. To ensure consistency across metabolites and account for regional differences in voxel composition, we applied tissue correction to all quantified metabolites, including edited GABA+ and GSH. This correction is particularly important in pediatric cohorts with potential structural variability and follows best practice recommendations for edited MRS.

Taken together, these data support myo-inositol as a practical, early in vivo biomarker of astrocytic activation in pediatric FRDA and a candidate marker for disease progression and treatment response. By demonstrating significant myo-inositol elevations and a reduced tNAA/mI ratio in the primary motor cortex, this study extends FRDA MRS findings beyond cerebellum and brainstem and provides the first motor-cortex in vivo biomarker evidence in pediatric FRDA.

4.1. Limitations

While our findings expand the neurochemical profile of FRDA beyond conventional neuronal and glial markers, several limitations warrant consideration. First, the sample size was modest, limiting power to detect subtle region-by-group interactions or metabolite-clinical associations, as well as possible group differences in tNAA. Second, analyses were restricted to three a priori regions of interest: cerebellum and bilateral motor cortices. Although chosen for their established neuropathological involvement in FRDA, the absence of a neutral control region limits assessment of regional specificity. Third, while CSF-based tissue correction reduces dilution effects, residual partial-volume variability likely remains due to differences in gray-white matter composition and local anatomical heterogeneity, which is especially pronounced in the cerebellum. Fourth, GSH detection with MRS is constrained to the reduced form, leaving potential oxidative imbalance through GSSG elevation undetected. Complementary methods are needed for a full redox profile. Fifth, while the tNAA/mI ratio was significantly reduced, this effect appeared to be driven primarily by elevated mI, with possible but nonsignificant contributions from lower tNAA. This may reflect the younger age and earlier disease stage of our cohort, in which gliosis is detectable but overt neuronal loss is not yet manifest at the voxel level. Further, since these data were collected at a relatively long TE, optimized for GABA+ and GSH editing, some loss of overall signal and precision is expected. Short-TE acquisitions would likely retain more signal and improve quantification of metabolites such as NAA and mI. Finally, the cross-sectional design limits conclusions regarding progression; longitudinal studies are needed to establish whether mI reliably tracks disease progression and treatment response.
Nerve Ultrasound in Patients With Friedreich Ataxia

ABSTRACT
Introduction/Aims
Nerve enlargement has been reported in patients with Friedreich ataxia (FRDA). The underlying cause remains unclear, and both inflammatory processes and dysmyelination have been suggested as potential mechanisms. This study was aimed at assessing nerve morphology with high-resolution ultrasound, to identify and describe patterns of nerve pathology.

Methods
Patients with genetically confirmed FRDA were included, clinically examined, and assessed with high-resolution ultrasound. Cross-sectional area measurements were compared with previously published normal values.

Results
Among 20 included patients, ultrasound abnormalities were found in 17 (85%). Nerve enlargement of the median and/or ulnar nerve in the proximal nerve segments was observed in 45% of patients and was statistically significant compared to published normal values. Lower extremity nerve enlargement was observed in 20% of patients. Eight patients did not show any nerve enlargement. Diminished cross-sectional area, indicative of nerve atrophy, was present, particularly in the distal segments of the ulnar nerve (in 25% of patients, p < 0.05) and the tibial nerve (popliteal fossa in 30% of patients, medial malleolus in 30% of patients, both p < 0.05). Nerve enlargement showed no significant correlations with disease severity or age of disease onset.

Discussion
Peripheral nerve morphology in FRDA is variable and includes not only nerve enlargement but also nerve atrophy, thus reflecting complex segmental pathology beyond axonal degeneration.

1 Introduction
Although most demyelinating diseases lead to increased cross-sectional area (CSA), as measured with high-resolution ultrasound (HRUS), CSA in axonal neuropathies is either normal or enlarged, depending on the cause of the neuropathy, such as vasculitis, sarcoidosis, or type 2 diabetes mellitus. In contrast, sensory neuronopathies typically result in diminished CSA, as seen in cerebellar ataxia, neuropathy, and vestibular areflexia syndrome.

In FRDA, a homozygous guanine-adenine-adenine (GAA) trinucleotide repeat expansion leads to a transcriptional defect in the FXN gene, thus resulting in a significant reduction of the mitochondrial protein frataxin. This genetic defect results in developmental rather than progressive neurodegeneration affecting the spinocerebellar pathways, dorsal root ganglia, posterior columns, corticospinal tracts, and sensory neuropathy.

Electrophysiological examinations in patients with FRDA have indicated sensory axonal neuropathy, whereas HRUS studies have described nerve enlargement, predominantly in proximal nerves of the upper extremity, such as the median nerve.

A missense mutation in FXN is known to cause dysmyelination, and consequently axonal atrophy as well as nerve hypertrophy, as seen in other peripheral neuropathies. In contrast, in vitro studies have identified a satellite cell disturbance associated with inflammatory-mediated destruction, primarily of dorsal root ganglia cells, as observed in neuronophagia. Therefore, the exact cause of this peripheral nerve pathology—inflammation or dysmyelination—remains unknown. From a clinical viewpoint, studies have suggested a correlation between nerve enlargement and the extent of clinical impairment.

Previous HRUS studies are limited by small sample sizes, which introduce uncertainty regarding the generalizability and reproducibility of the reported findings.

The aim of this study was to systematically evaluate peripheral nerve morphology with HRUS, with a focus on identifying patterns of nerve pathology.

2 Methods
2.1 Cohort
Between May 2015 and December 2017, patients with FRDA were evaluated in our specialized ataxia outpatient clinic. Clinical examination and additional electrophysiological assessments, including nerve conduction studies (NCS) and HRUS, were conducted and retrospectively analyzed. The study was approved by the local ethics committee of the University of Tübingen (702/2015BO2) and conformed to the World Medical Association's Declaration of Helsinki. All examinations were conducted after informed consent was provided by all participants.

This study excluded patients with a history of harmful alcohol consumption, severe vitamin deficiency (vitamin B1, B6, B9, B12), confirmed by abnormal laboratory blood test results, or toxin exposure.

2.2 Clinical Assessment and Electrophysiology
The clinical assessment involved a standardized neurological examination performed by a movement disorder specialist (ZF, SH, and LS) using the Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA).

Clinical signs of sensory neuropathy, assessed in all patients, included diminished or absent deep tendon reflexes, impaired proprioception, paresthesia, dysesthesia, and distal hypoesthesia.

Nerve conduction studies were performed in patients who provided informed consent, under standard conditions according to published data, with a Dantec Keypoint G4 workstation (Natus Medical Inc., Middleton, Wisconsin, USA). Motor nerve conduction studies included the distal motor latency, compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitude, and motor nerve conduction velocity (NCV) of the ulnar or median nerves in the upper extremity, and the tibial and fibular nerves in the lower extremity. F-wave latency was tested for the median or ulnar nerves in the upper extremity and the tibial nerve in the lower extremity. Sensory nerve action potentials were assessed for the sural and ulnar nerves, with amplitudes measured from baseline to peak.

In all patients, motor nerves were tested alternately on both sides; for example, the left side for the ulnar and tibial nerves, and the right side for the fibular nerve. Sensory nerves were tested on the right side.

Neuropathy was defined as demyelinating if the NCV was slower than 75% or the distal latency was longer than 130% of normal values, and was defined as axonal if the amplitudes decreased with only a mild decrease in NCV or a mild increase in distal latency, according to Preston and Shapiro(comparable to the guidelines of the European Federation of Neurological Societies and the Peripheral Nerve Society for chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy).

Additional demyelinating features included partial conduction blocks, characterized by a focal decrease in CMAP amplitude and in area by > 50% between distal and proximal stimulation sites, without temporal dispersion. Complete conduction blocks were identified according to the absence of a CMAP under proximal stimulation despite a normal distal response. Temporal dispersion was defined by a prolonged CMAP duration with diminished amplitude but preserved area. Published reference values were used.

2.3 High-Resolution Nerve Ultrasound
High-resolution B-mode ultrasound was performed according to a previously published protocolwith a high-resolution probe (range 12–18 MHz, linear transducer with 46 mm depth, Mindray T7, Ultrasound systems, Darmstadt, Germany). The “NERVE” preset was used for all participants, with consistent image amplification (80 G “Gain”). The preset corresponded to a maximum frequency of 18 Hz. Basic settings remained unchanged during the entire examination, except for focus adjustments.

The examination, conducted by experienced sonographers, assessed the CSA of peripheral nerves and the diameters of cervical roots. CSA and nerve diameter were compared with previously published normal values. High-resolution nerve ultrasound was performed on the right side, including the median, ulnar, radial, tibial, fibular, sural, and vagus nerves, as well as the C5 and C6 nerve roots. Each nerve was systematically evaluated along its entire course, and CSA measurements were obtained at predefined anatomical sites: the median nerve at the mid-forearm, cubital fossa, and mid-upper arm; the ulnar nerve at the mid-forearm and mid-upper arm; the superficial radial nerve proximal to the forearm deep fascia; the tibial nerve at the popliteal fossa and medial malleolus; the fibular nerve at the popliteal fossa and the superficial fibular nerve; the sural nerve adjacent to the Achilles tendon; and the vagus nerve at the carotid triangle. Additionally, a longitudinal assessment of the C5 and C6 nerve roots was conducted (Figure S1).

Nerve enlargement in anatomic nerve entrapment sites, such as the carpal tunnel or the cubital tunnel, was excluded.

Nerve echogenicity was assessed subjectively by the sonographer, through comparison of the nerve echogenicity with that in surrounding tissue, including vessels, muscle, and subcutaneous fat.

2.4 Statistical Analysis
All analyses were conducted in SPSS version 24 (IBM, Armonk, NY, USA). Mean ± standard deviation (SD) is reported for normally distributed results, whereas the interquartile range (IQR) is reported for results that were not normally distributed.

Statistical significance was assessed with the independent t-test for normally distributed results or the Mann–Whitney U-test for non-normally distributed data. The threshold for statistical significance was set to p ≤ 0.05. Pearson's test was used to determine correlations between variables for normally distributed data and Spearman correlation testing for non-normally distributed data.

3 Results
3.1 Cohort
Twenty patients with FRDA were included in this study (patient characteristics summarized in Table 1). The mean age was 41.6 years (IQR: 34–64), and the mean disease onset occurred at 17 years (IQR: 10.5–22). Three patients with diabetes mellitus were included in this study, and all other patients showed no abnormal oral glucose tolerance test findings and had normal HbA1c levels.

TABLE 1. Baseline characteristics.
3.2 Clinical Assessment and Electrophysiology
All 20 included patients showed clinical signs of sensory neuropathy with absent muscle stretch reflexes and impaired proprioception. Of these, 13 patients were investigated with NCS in our facility. Seven patients declined to consent to electrophysiological testing. Details of the electrophysiological measurements are summarized in Table 2.

TABLE 2. Nerve conduction study data.

Twelve patients demonstrated sensory neuropathy on NCS, and no abnormalities were detected in CMAP. One patient with late-onset FRDA demonstrated clinical signs of sensory neuropathy but showed no abnormalities on NCS. Two patients showed slightly prolonged F-wave latencies (< 130% the upper limit of normal) as well as mildly diminished NCV (< 75% of normal) in the upper and lower extremities (Table 2). In all other patients, the F-wave latencies were unremarkable. No patients showed any electrophysiological signs of demyelination.

No significant differences were observed between patients with or without diabetes mellitus, including clinical neurological presentation and NCS data. No abnormal CMAP amplitudes were detected.

3.3 High-Resolution Nerve Ultrasound
HRUS was performed in all 20 patients and ultrasound abnormalities were found in 17 (85%). Details of the sonographic findings are summarized in Table 3.

TABLE 3. High-resolution ultrasound results of Friedreich ataxia patients.

Nerve enlargement of the median and/or ulnar nerves in the upper arm was observed in 9 of 20 patients (45%), two (10%) of whom also exhibited nerve enlargement in the forearm and cubital fossa, which was not statistically significant. The remaining 11 patients (55%) had CSA values that were within upper normal limits.

Nerve enlargement in the lower extremities, including the tibial, fibular and sural nerves, was identified in 4 of 20 patients (20%) but was not statistically significant. Of these, two patients also demonstrated CSA enlargement of the median and/or ulnar nerve in the upper extremity, whereas the remaining two patients showed no CSA changes in the upper limb nerves. Overall, no correlation was found between disease duration or severity and the extent of nerve enlargement (r = 0.1).

Beyond nerve enlargement, diminished CSA indicative of atrophy was observed in several nerve segments, in which the nerve itself appeared hypoechoic (Figure 1). For the upper extremity, two patients showed diminished CSA in the proximal segments of the median and ulnar nerves. A statistically significant decrease in the CSA of the ulnar nerve in the forearm was found in five patients.


FIGURE 1
Comparison of high-resolution ultrasound of the median nerve in the upper arm between 3 patients.

The tibial nerve CSA was significantly below the lower limit of normal in 6 of 20 patients (30%) at the popliteal fossa and in 6 of 20 patients (30%) at the medial malleolus. In contrast, the fibular nerve at the popliteal fossa showed diminished CSA in only 2 of 20 patients (10%), and this finding did not reach statistical significance. No patients showed affected cervical nerve roots (C5 and C6) or vagus nerves.

Diminished CSA was identified in patients with or without previously described segmental nerve enlargement.

Both, nerve enlargement and nerve atrophy occurred in seven patients (35%); nerve atrophy alone occurred in 5 (25%) and nerve enlargement alone occurred in 5 (25%).

The diabetic patients, when compared with the non-diabetic cohort, showed neither significant differences in the nerve conduction study data nor greater CSA.

4 Discussion
Overall, our findings are consistent with the current literature regarding the distribution pattern of CSA enlargement in Friedreich ataxia patients.

Nerve enlargement was observed in both the upper and lower extremities, predominantly in the proximal segments of the upper limb nerves rather than their distal portions. Nerve enlargement in the lower limb was uncommon and non-significant. The rate of nerve enlargement abnormalities in our cohort was notably lower than observed in previous studiesand 40% of patients did not show any nerve enlargement at all. Given the larger sample size in our study, this discrepancy suggests that findings from smaller cohorts might not be directly generalizable to broader patient populations.

Beyond nerve enlargement, diminished CSA indicative of nerve atrophy was found to affect the nerves of the upper and lower extremities, preferentially affecting the tibial nerve and the distal segment of the ulnar nerve. This atrophic pattern was present in both subgroups, i.e., patients with or without segmental nerve enlargement. Nerve enlargement and atrophy were sometimes observed within the same nerve but in different anatomical segments, thus underscoring the heterogeneous nature of peripheral nerve involvement in FRDA.

We observed no differences in the age and sex distributions between our patient cohort and previously described FRDA cohorts. Our electrophysiological data are in line with findings from prior studies showing a sensory axonal neuropathy in 12 of 13 examined patients. In contrast to previously described FRDA cohorts, no correlation was found between disease duration or severity and the extent of nerve enlargement.

The underlying cause of this pleomorphic sonographic pattern remains unclear:

As previously described by Mulroy et al., a primary inflammatory process might potentially account for the observed nerve enlargement. Similar to other inflammatory neuropathies, such as Guillain-Barré syndrome or chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, the predominant involvement of proximal arm nerves might support this hypothesis. Cervical root involvement has been reported in more than 90% of immune-mediated neuropathiesbut was completely absent in our and previously described FRDA cohorts. This absence of cervical root enlargement alone should not be considered to exclude the possibility of an inflammatory component. Nerve enlargement preceding nerve atrophy, due to a disturbed blood-nerve barrier, may be considered, as has been observed in other neurodegenerative disorders, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

Alternatively, dysmyelination induced by the frataxin mutation might lead to compensatory remyelination and subsequent hypertrophic remodeling, as described in other neurodegenerative diseases. Evidence from murine models has demonstrated the presence of axonal vacuoles, which might serve as a compensatory mechanism in response to ongoing cycles of degeneration and regeneration.

Whether these processes occur simultaneously and continuously in every nerve fascicle and segment remains unclear. Our findings suggested an asynchronous degeneration–regeneration cycle across different nerve segments.

In cases of advanced axonal loss, hypertrophic remodeling might be limited to fascicular enlargement, as previously described by Pitarokoili et al.. However, whether a failed remyelination process ultimately leads to secondary inflammation or nerve atrophy remains uncertain.

In cases of significant nerve enlargement, further diagnostic steps—such as lumbar puncture, additional blood analysis, MR neurography, or, if possible, nerve biopsies to rule out any other treatable inflammatory processes indicated by albuminocytological dissociation, contrast agent uptake, or lymphocytic infiltration—might be warranted. Additionally, individual therapeutic approaches, including immunotherapy, could be considered.

Limitations of this study include the absence of electrophysiological data in seven patients and the lack of bilateral electrophysiological assessments. Lower boundary reference values for the HRUS data were obtained from literature. However, these values could only be applied to seven of our measurement sites, as the anatomical locations of the remaining nerve segments investigated differed from the reference papers. Additionally, detailed GAA repeat length data were missing in 8 of the 20 patients, and clinical severity was assessed solely using the SARA score.

5 Conclusion
The nerve morphology in FRDA showed variable nerve enlargement affecting nerves of the upper and lower extremities, and indicated a potential for nerve atrophy with or without prior nerve segment enlargement. No correlation was found between nerve enlargement and disease duration or severity. The cause of this sonographic pattern remains unclear. Further studies in larger patient cohorts are needed to reproduce our findings, clarify the underlying pathomechanism, and guide potential treatment.
Neuropathology of Friedreich ataxia and its links to metabolic pathways

ABSTRACT
Frataxin is an evolutionarily conserved mitochondrial protein essential for energy metabolism. Biallelic GAA repeat expansions in the FXN gene reduce frataxin expression, causing Friedreich’s ataxia. Frataxin deficiency impairs key mitochondrial metabolic enzymes, leading to widespread mitochondrial dysfunction with disrupted glucose and fatty acid oxidation. Although systemic mitochondrial dysfunction affects multiple organ systems, neurological deficits are the only feature uniformly observed in all FRDA patients. This review highlights recent insights into the neuropathology of FRDA, emphasizing the detailed developmental timing of neuroanatomical changes. It also focuses on selective mitochondrial metabolic pathways, including fatty acid metabolism, ceramide synthesis, and ketogenesis, which may underlie neuron-specific vulnerability and serve as potential targets for pharmacological or dietary intervention. The possibility of non-traditional interventions based on metabolic features of FRDA offers hope for ameliorating the severity of FRDA.

1. Introduction
Evolution has selectively preserved molecular components essential to life, with proteins as a prime example. Many of these conserved proteins function in iron and redox biology, where iron plays critical roles in cellular processes. These functions depend on evolutionarily conserved proteins such as frataxin, which has homologs in mammals, invertebrates, plants, and yeast. Interest in the protein grew in the late 1990s, following the discovery in 1996 that mutations in the frataxin gene (FXN) cause Friedreich’s ataxia (FRDA), which was first described in 1863 by German pathologist Nikolaus Friedreich. He provided a detailed account of six clinical cases (including two pairs of siblings), in which motor dysfunction emerged as the predominant symptom. Patients described lower limb weakness and fatigue as the earliest symptoms, which later developed into gait and postural impairments, upper limb incoordination, and dysarthria. Even after the patients were fully incapacitated and bedridden for years, the patients retained considerable voluntary movement (i.e., specific muscle contraction on command). Friedreich noted that the novel disease, rather than a matter of muscle strength, was a failure in the harmonious integration and coordination of group muscle activity. After the passing of four of the patients, his postmortem examinations showed degeneration of the posterior columns of the spinal cord. Friedreich’s early reports first connected hereditary ataxia with spinal cord degeneration, laying the foundation for the condition that now bears his name as the most common inherited ataxia.

2. Clinical features of FRDA
Although the primary clinical features of FRDA were described by Friedreich and others in the years after his initial report, the details of the clinical phenotype are much better understood today (Table 1). All patients develop neurological dysfunction characterized by a combination of ataxia, weakness, spasticity, somatosensory loss, dysarthria, and fatigue, with varying degrees of complex hearing loss, visual dysfunction, and cerebellar cognitive abnormalities (including attentional and emotional control issues). All of these reflect neuronal loss in the dorsal root ganglia, the dentate nucleus of the cerebellum, and the pyramidal neurons of the lower cortical layers in the motor cortex, accompanied by degeneration of the corticospinal tract. Neuronal loss may also involve cerebellar Purkinje cells, while the retinal ganglion cells, cochlear nucleus cells, and other scattered nuclei in the brain are affected less consistently. Along with the neurological dysfunction in FRDA are extra neuronal features including:

Cardiomyopathy, initially beginning as a hypertrophic phase, followed in the most affected patients by features of fibrosis and diastolic dysfunction, with systolic dysfunction prominent in advanced disease. This is the major cause of mortality, with arrhythmias and end-stage heart failure being the major causes of death.

Scoliosis occurring in approximately 75% of patients, with severity varying widely; many with early-onset disease require surgical correction during adolescence.

Myopathy, usually subclinical, reflecting both mitochondrial myopathy and decreased levels of muscle bulk in the context of small stature. This does not typically lead to weakness; most weakness is related to upper motor neuron issues in FRDA and occurs late in the disease.

Diabetes, reflecting both insulin loss from nonimmune Beta cell loss and increased muscle insulin resistance. FRDA diabetes is best classified as neither type 1 nor type 2

Decreased bone density. Patients have lower mean whole body areal bone mineral density than healthy controls.

Neuropsychiatric symptoms, including depression, decreased motivation, and emotional dysregulation, are highly prevalent.

Table 1. Clinical features of FRDA.

Download CSVDisplay Table
These anatomically diverse components generally give rise to an organ autonomous pathophysiology. Treatment of individual organs does not influence manifestations of the disease in other organ, best demonstrated by the effect of heart transplantation. Cardiac transplantation is curative for cardiac disease but has no effect on neurodegeneration. Similarly, the effects in different brain regions are largely viewed autonomously, though this may be an oversimplification. Thus, most treatments are directed to the pathophysiology shared by all organs (mitochondrial dysfunction, frataxin deficiency, intracellular metabolic dysfunction). Still, other less discuss features of the disease (diabetes, interorgan metabolic changes) could be targeted to lead to effects on multiple organs in theory.

Despite being described over 150 years ago and a causative mutation identified nearly three decades ago, Friedreich ataxia still has only one approved therapy – Omaveloxolone – restricted to individuals aged 16 years or older, in spite of many previous attempts. Such attempts consistently showed no neurological benefit but occasionally changed biomarkers of disease activity. Early attempts at treatment usually reflected the idea that ROS production is a major feature of FRDA in vitro and the idea that FRDA is similar phenotypically to ataxia with Vitamin E deficiency. However, over time, the role of ROS production has become less clearand the similarities of FRDA to AVED have been minimized, as AVED has a different neuroanatomy, cardiac physiology, and developmental course from FRDA. Current clinical trials primarily target two strategies: (1) improving mitochondrial function – by blocking/limiting ROS production (idebenone, vatiquinone, A0001, SS31/elamipretide, vitamin E/Coenzyme Q10), enhancing NRF2 activation, promoting mitochondrial biogenesis, or inhibiting ferroptosis; and (2) increasing frataxin levels through protein replacement (nomlabofusp), gene therapy (LX2006), or epigenetic reactivation (DT216). To date, none of these approaches have achieved complete success, and significant limitations remain. Here, we review the neuropathophysiological and pathobiology of the disorder to explain in detail where future advances may occur as well as to understand the ways in which previous trials may have failed to account for the complex systemic and developmental features of FRDA.

3. Genetic basis of FRDA
The genetic cause of Friedreich ataxia, biallelic GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions in the first intron of the FXN gene, are found on chromosome 9q21.113. Normal alleles contain under 33 GAA repeats, whereas pathogenic alleles typically have more than 66 and can range up to over 2000. As a recessive disorder, all FRDA patients carry mutations of both FXN alleles. Carriers of a single expanded allele have no pathologic features but may have altered insulin resistance. The majority have GAA repeat expansions on both alleles, while 4% are compound heterozygotes, carrying an expanded GAA repeat on one allele and a point mutation or deletion on the other. Expanded GAA repeats induce epigenetic modifications, including decreased acetylation of histones H3 and H4 and increased trimethylation of H3 lysine 9. These modifications promote heterochromatin formation, reducing DNA accessibility and hindering RNA polymerase II progression, which leads to transcriptional silencing and ultimately results in markedly reduced FXN mRNA and protein levels. Patients with FRDA usually have less than 20% of normal frataxin levels in unaffected tissue, though the amount is tissue specific.

4. The role of frataxin
Neurological manifestations are found in all patients with FRDA. Neurons rely almost exclusively on aerobic respiration to meet their energy demands; thus, mitochondrial impairment was anticipated to be involved in the underlying pathology. The full range of frataxin’s function remains incompletely understood, however, several of its roles are well defined. Frataxin participates in iron metabolism- specifically in iron-sulfur cluster biosynthesis. Iron-sulfur clusters (ISCs) are evolutionarily conserved prosthetic groups that are essential in many cellular reactions and processes such as mitochondrial energy metabolism, cellular iron homeostasis, and nuclear genome stability. Proteins throughout the cell use ISCs to mediate biological electron transport. Frataxin is a 210-amino acid protein, with an N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence comprising residues 1–80. Following proteolytic cleavage at two sites, the mature form (residues 81–210) localizes to the mitochondria matrix, where it binds and delivers iron to iron-sulfur cluster assembly enzyme (ISCU), the scaffold protein on which ISCs are assembled. It also accelerates the rate limiting step as an allosteric activator in sulfur transfer to ISCU.

ISCs are utilized by proteins across all cellular compartments; however, mitochondrial enzymes are particularly vulnerable. In FRDA, reduced activity has been observed in subunits of mitochondrial respiratory complexes I, II, and III, leading to impaired oxidative phosphorylation. Additionally, several key metabolic enzymes-such as aconitase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase, and citrate synthase-also show diminished activity, contributing to compromised cellular respiration.

5. Frataxin and mitochondrial dysfunction
Mitochondrial cellular respiration defects induced by frataxin deficiency include decreased ATP synthesis, decreased mitochondrial membrane potential, increased oxidative stress, and mitochondrial iron accumulation. These defects have profound consequences on multiple tissues and organ systems, particularly those which rely heavily on oxidative phosphorylation such as the nervous system and heart. Additionally, mitochondria in FRDA are prone to accumulation of ferrous iron (Fe2+), which produce further reactive oxygen species (ROS) that damage membrane integrity via lipid peroxidation. This lipid peroxidization is a mechanistic feature of ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death now being investigated as a potential therapeutic target in FRDA.

Since cells affected by FRDA are deficient in ATP production at baseline, intracellular signaling pathways will activate to stimulate ATP synthesis. Calcium flux into mitochondria enables these organelles to adjust metabolic activity and ATP production in accordance with cellular energetic demands, while also buffering cytosolic calcium. Mitochondrial matrix calcium stimulates components of the ETC and dehydrogenases of the Krebs cycle to stimulate ATP production. The loss of frataxin decreases the ATP supply and in turn leads to changes in mitochondrial calcium flux to compensate. However, these changes are ultimately maladaptive, as mitochondrial calcium overload triggers mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) opening and subsequent cell death. Mitochondrial matrix calcium levels are balanced by calcium uptake via the mitochondrial calcium uniporter complex (mtCU) and calcium efflux, most notably regulated through the mitochondrial sodium/calcium exchanger (NCLX). Changes in either of these nodes shape the tendency of mitochondria to drive energy production or execute cell death. Frataxin deficiency in patient lymphoblasts, cardiomyocytes, or DRGs leads to decreased NCLX protein and increased mPTP-medicated cell death. Downregulation of NCLX is likely a maladaptive strategy that increases mitochondrial calcium content to stimulate calcium-dependent enzymes and ETC subunits but ultimately exceeds the matrix calcium threshold that triggers cell death. While there is no direct data to demonstrate altered mtCU activity in Friedreich ataxia, samples from patient skeletal muscle indicate a decrease in mRNA and protein expression of MCU, the pore forming subunit of the mtCU, suggests that mitochondrial calcium uptake is decreased. Conversely, models of Complex I dysfunction and impaired mitochondrial biogenesis demonstrate increased mitochondrial calcium uptake and the levels of the mtCU, suggesting that increasing matrix calcium is a conserved response to impaired mitochondrial ATP production. Altogether, the mitochondria in Friedreich ataxia face numerous triggers for mPTP opening-mediated cell death: ROS production from dysfunctional ETC and from iron overload via the Fenton reaction, and matrix calcium overload. Further study is required to determine how FXN loss leads to the maladaptive response of increasing mitochondrial calcium content to stimulate ATP production, but trigger cell death.

6. Frataxin and metabolism
Frataxin deficiency alters the metabolic efficiency of mitochondria which inevitably alters the metabolic pathway flux and substrate utilization of the affected cell types. Frataxin deficiency disrupts many of these pathways, both at the intracellular and whole organism level. Glucose metabolism is disrupted at the whole-body level in FRDA, with patients developing insulin resistance and requiring greater secretion of endogenous insulin to achieve blood glucose reduction, with concomitant elevated blood lactate and decreased glucose-derived carbon entering the Krebs cycle (Figure 1(A)). This pattern suggests that frataxin deficiency limits mitochondrial glucose oxidation through the Krebs cycle, forcing cells to depend more on glycolysis to produce ATP. In addition, frataxin deficiency – associated metabolic alterations are supported by decreased expression of mitochondrial solute carrier transporters in patient skeletal muscle, likely impairing anaplerotic flux through the Krebs cycle. As a result, frataxin-deficient mitochondria are compromised in supplying metabolic intermediates (such as acetyl-CoA, alpha-ketoglutarate, and oxaloacetate) for lipid and amino acid synthesis. Impaired supply of these intermediates could also alter gene expression, as acetyl-CoA and alpha-ketoglutarate are required co-factors for histone acetylation and histone/DNA demethylation, respectively.

Figure 1. Diagram of Proposed and proven alterations in metabolism and fatty acid formation in FRDA. (A). Diagram of metabolic pathways responsible for lipid droplet accumulation and anaplerotic Krebs cycle input that are altered in FRDA. (B). Diagram of altered lipid synthesis pathways in FRDA. Red down arrowhead indicates decreased activity of enzyme or enzymatic process. Green up arrowheads indicate increased activity of enzyme or enzymatic process. LDH (lactate dehydrogenase); PHD (pyruvate dehydrogenase); CS (citrate synthase); IDH (isocitrate dehydrogenase); αKGDH (α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase); SCS (succinyl-CoA synthetase); SDH (succinate dehydrogenase); MDH (malate dehydrogenase); LCFA (long-chain fatty acid); BDH1 (β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase 1); OXCT1 (3-oxoacid CoA-transferase 1); ACAT1 (acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase 1); PCC (propionyl-CoA carboxylase); MCEE (methylmalonyl-CoA epimerase); MCM (methylmalonyl-CoA mutase).

Frataxin deficiency is associated with failure of glucose metabolism (reduced pyruvate oxidation and conversion to acetyl-CoA), but also fatty acid metabolism. Several fatty acid oxidation enzymes require ISCs, including ETF – ubiquinone oxidoreductase involved in fatty acid oxidation, as well as enzymes in lipoate and biotin biosynthesis such as lipoate synthase and biotin synthase, respectively. FRDA patient fibroblasts exhibit elevated levels of HMG-CoA (an intermediate generated during cholesterol synthesis), acyl-carnitine, and β-hydroxybutyryl-CoA. In addition, ceramide and other sphingolipid synthesis is disordered, with elevations in selected ceramides and decreases in others (Figure 1(B)). The accumulation of these metabolites as well as lipid droplet accumulationwhich are linked to neurodegeneration suggests aberrant β-oxidation, matching alterations in palmitoylation in FRDA fibroblasts. Frataxin deficiency also mediates abnormal disposition of products of β- oxidation as decreased levels of 3-oxoacid CoA-transferase 1 (OXCT1; the enzyme mediating ketone entry to the TCA cycle) leads to increased ketone bodies. During ketogenesis, β-hydroxybutyrate is converted to acetoacetate, which OXCT1 then converts to acetoacetyl-CoA, enabling further ATP production through its entry into the Krebs cycle. In FRDA, systemic fat metabolism is also disordered, as patients have lower serum levels of apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1) and lipoprotein lipase, thus potentially altering triglyceride and cholesterol supply to tissues (though serum levels are inconsistently elevated.

Neurons rely primarily on glucose metabolism. However, they can also store and metabolize fatty acids, demonstrating a metabolic flexibility that includes shifting to fatty acid utilization. Neuronal β-oxidation rate is lower than other tissues (i.e., liver and muscle), but it increases during metabolic stress or altered energy demands. While enhanced mitochondrial β-oxidation could, in principle, compensate for energy deficits in FRDA neurons, frataxin deficiency disrupts fatty acid metabolism; this adaptation – though aiding neuronal survival – is incomplete, ultimately potentially contributing to the selective vulnerability of neurons in FRDA. Interestingly, a polymorphism in SIRT6, the protein controlling the transition from glucose to fatty acid metabolism in some situations and acting as a master regulator of fatty acid metabolism, predicts the speed of neurological progression in FRDA, further suggesting a role of fatty acid metabolism in neurodegeneration of FRDA. No direct role of SIRT6 has yet been identified.

7. Neuropathology
Although frataxin is globally reduced in FRDA, clinical phenomena are largely restricted to specific tissues and cell types. This selective vulnerability may reflect distinct metabolic demands (such as the capacity to β-oxidize fatty acids) or inherent high frataxin expression in these cells, but no single explanation completely explains the tissue distribution of FRDA. Understanding the cause of such selectivity is crucial for designing cell-selective therapies. In addition, simply cataloging the detailed neuroanatomy and its temporal course is necessary for identifying the targets for frataxin replacement.

The exact cell-type specificity distinguishes FRDA from other hereditary ataxias. Within the nervous system, the most affected cell types classically include large dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons and their axons in the dorsal root and dorsal column; satellite glial cells of the DRG; Clarke’s column neurons; large glutamatergic neurons of the dentate nucleus (thought to be the primary site causing ataxia), corticospinal tract projection neurons of the motor cortex (including so-called Betz cells) and their axons; and possibly Purkinje cells (Figure 2). Some of these neurons undergo progressive degeneration, while others, particularly DRG neurons, exhibit signs of hypoplasia (including the failure of spinal development and developmental changes in sural nerves), indicating a developmental defect rather than acquired degeneration. Notably, the severity and onset of disease phenomena do not align with the extent of DRG atrophy, further emphasizing the importance of understanding the temporal progression of pathology in FRDA. Interestingly, the concept of a mixed developmental and degenerative pathology is not unique to FRDA, as such ideas have also been suggested for disorders such as schizophrenia and autistic spectrum disorders.

Figure 2. Neuroanatomical targets in Friedreich’s ataxia. Schematic representation of the principal neuronal populations affected in FRDA. In the visual system, retinal ganglion cells and optic nerve axons show axonal loss and thinning of the retinal nerve fiber layer. In the dorsal root ganglia, large principal sensory neurons undergo mitochondrial degeneration and axonal loss, accompanied by activation and hypertrophy of satellite glial cells. In the lower motor cortex (layer V), pyramidal neurons, including Betz cells, exhibit axonal degeneration and cortical thinning. In the cerebellum, large glutamatergic neurons of the dentate nucleus are markedly depleted, whereas Purkinje cells remain largely preserved but display synaptic and morphological alterations. Collectively, these selective neuronal vulnerabilities highlight the region-specific impact of frataxin deficiency underlying the neurological features of FRDA. Created in BioRender. MERCADO AYON, Y. (n.d.) https://BioRender.com/2baxrwc.

8. Spinal cord
In his original postmortem reports, Friedreich described a reduction in spinal cord surface area in individuals with FRDA, reflecting prominent spinal cord atrophy and selective pattern of structural and cellular degeneration that result in a markedly reduced overall volume. Affected regions include the dorsal column tracts (and their nuclei in the medulla), dorsal spinocerebellar tracts, and lateral corticospinal tracts. The nucleus dorsalis of Clarke (NDC) is absent or severely depleted, consistent with its role as the origin of the dorsal spinocerebellar tract. The dorsal columns exhibit marked absence of myelinated fibers, consistent with loss of the largest axons arising from DRG, and secondary demyelination. In FRDA, the spinal cord reaches a developmental plateau within the first decade of life, after which further maturation ceases. This plateau likely reflects residual effects of sensory and motor pathway damage that occurred earlier in development. Consistent with this, somatosensory evoked potentials, originating from the dorsal columns, and motor evoked potentials, originating from the corticospinal tracts, are already markedly reduced or absent at the time of presentation. Together, these selective patterns of neuronal and axonal degeneration characterize the motor and sensory deficits observed in FRDA.

In contrast, little change is seen in intrinsic spinal cells outside of the NDC. Anterior horn motor neurons are largely spared, and effects on propriospinal neurons are not commonly discussed. Spinal cord damage is thus limited to the longer projecting neurons, which presumptively have higher energy demands. Furthermore, much of the damage occurs early, as the spinal canal is small in patients with FRDA, and reduction in spinal cord size by MRI is found at presentation in many patients. This again identifies hypoplasia in addition to neurodegeneration as a component of the disease process in FRDA.

9. DRG
Dorsal root ganglia (DRG) pathology is one of the most consistent and earliest features of FRDA, with DRG neurons exhibit marked atrophy and loss, particularly affecting large proprioceptive neurons. Such degeneration contributes to the profound loss of proprioception seen in patients but has perhaps a lesser impact on conscious sensory deficits as large fiber proprioceptive nerve conduction fibers are undetectable at presentation when sensory loss is not an overt complaint. These neurons give rise to large, myelinated axons that form the dorsal roots, and their degeneration leads to a severe large fiber sensory neuropathy. Within the DRG, satellite glial cells proliferate, which may reflect both a reactive pro-inflammatory effect that potentially disrupts neuronal signaling and a compensatory (neuroprotective and supportive) response to neuronal degeneration. In addition, loss of sensory peripheral nerves may occur early in disease progression and may reflect a developmental defect (hypoplasia) rather than a purely degenerative process. Somatosensory potential reflecting proprioceptive input is largely absent at presentation, demonstrating that proprioceptive loss is largely developmental. The degree of loss correlates with GAA repeat length (and thus genetic severity) but not with disease duration, suggesting that it is largely static and genetically determined. Still, smaller nerve fibers die over the course of disease, consistent with a progression to complete anesthesia in some patients. Thus, while DRG represent a potential target in FRDA, much of the damage may be done early such that later treatment produces, at most, modest benefit.

10. Cerebellum
Neuronal atrophy in the cerebellum, another key site of FRDA pathology, corresponds with the progression of clinical loss of coordination. The progressive loss of dentate nucleus (DN) integrity correlates with ataxia severity and disease duration, reflecting the evolving and selective vulnerability of this cerebellar nucleus in FRDA. The DN exhibits spatially heterogeneous damage, with the gray matter in rostral-caudal regions showing the most pronounced degeneration, corresponding to the region where large glutamatergic neurons atrophy. The medial white matter displays comparatively milder damage, yet higher iron accumulation. In the white matter hilus, there is loss in oligodendrocytes; these iron-rich cells undergo degeneration, contributing to local iron accumulation. Oligodendroglia atrophy also disrupts Purkinje cell axonal myelin sheaths. Iron accumulation in FRDA occurs in distinct subregions of the DN, but as it reflects oligodendroglia loss, most iron accumulation in the DN is extracellular and a late biomarker of degeneration. The large glutamatergic DN neurons that atrophy receive glutamatergic afferents from the inferior olive, input from the spinocerebellar tracts, and synaptic input from Purkinje cells. While these populations appear intact early in the disease, they degenerate progressively, unlike small GABAergic neurons and glycinergic interneurons that remain unaffected.

The cerebellar cortex is largely preserved in FRDA, and Purkinje cell (PC) loss is limited and regionally variable, which is surprising given the high levels of frataxin in PCs. However, subtle yet significant signs of PC injury are present. Evidence of PC stress and compensatory responses includes a high incidence of binucleated PC somata and dendritic swelling. Importantly, climbing fiber (CF) synapses are not lost but instead undergo synaptic remodeling: rather than terminating on proximal PC dendrites, as in the healthy cerebellum, CFs are redistributed to more distal dendritic branches, indicating altered synaptic targeting and wiring specificity. In addition, PC axons projecting into the DN develop grumose degeneration and torpedoes. Such cerebellar cortical features suggest ongoing cellular stress and compensatory remodeling rather than widespread degeneration.

11. Cerebellar-cortical connections
The dentato-thalamo-cortical pathway is critical not only for motor coordination, but also for higher-order cognitive functions. This pathway begins with glutamatergic projection neurons of the DN synapsing onto thalamic neurons, which in turn transmit cerebellar output to motor and premotor cortical areas. Evidence of impaired cerebellar-cortico connectivity in FRDA suggests broader network dysfunction beyond motor control planning. Although mild, cognitive deficits in FRDA include reduced processing speed, poorer performance in language and visuospatial tasks, impaired executive functioning, and diminished ideational fluency. Some patients also show signs of progressive cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome (CCAS), characterized by impairments in conceptual thinking, verbal expression, and emotion recognition, which correlate with disease duration. Additionally, abnormalities in cortical glucose metabolism have been reported. Structural damage in the cerebello-cerebral pathway, as revealed by diffusion MRI, shows prominent microstructural abnormalities and demyelination, particularly in the dentato-thalamic cortical segments of the tracts, with the superior cerebellar peduncles being most affected.

12. Corticospinal tract
The corticospinal tract, also known as the pyramidal tract, originates in the primary motor and premotor cortices and projects directly to spinal motor neurons and interneurons, playing a critical role in voluntary motor control. Early pathological studies in FRDA patients demonstrated selective degeneration and demyelination of the longer axons in the caudal lateral corticospinal tract, while sparing the lateral corticospinal tract rostral to the medulla. This would suggest sparing of the shortest axons that innervate cranial nerve nuclei, and greater effects on axons directed to limb regions. Within the corticospinal tract, Betz cells – large glutamatergic pyramidal neurons located in the motor cortex – and other cortical pyramidal cells of layers 5 and 6 form direct synapses with lower motor neurons in the spinal cord. Their thick, heavily myelinated axons facilitate rapid signal conduction, enabling precise temporal coordination of motor output. In FRDA, axons from Betz cells and other cortical pyramidal neuron atrophy, leading to progressive demyelination, and eventual loss. In addition, motor evoked potentials arising from the motor cortex are decreased in size at presentation, suggesting that as in other pathways in FRDA, some of the abnormalities represent hypoplasia rather than degeneration.

13. Visual
FRDA affects both afferent (retinogeniculate) and efferent (oculomotor) visual pathways. Ocular motility disturbances – such as saccadic dysmetria and square-wave jerks – are frequently observed in FRDA, although the degree to which they lead to symptomatology is unclear. In most FRDA patients, retinal and optic nerve atrophy are present, accompanied by reduced low-contrast visual acuity; as the disease progresses, high-contrast visual acuity and central visual fields may also be affected, potentially culminating in clinical vision loss in severe cases. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) and MRI revealed that most patients exhibit progressive marked thinning of the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL), with severity increasing over the course of disease. The RNFL thickness correlates with frataxin levels and with the structural integrity of cortical visual processing areas. Notably, significant RNFL thinning occurs in children with early disease onset, suggesting potential developmental deficits, paralleling the hypoplasia reported in DRG and the spinal cord. In addition to RNFL thinning, patients show reduced ganglion cell complex (GCC) thickness – which includes the nerve fiber layer (NFL), ganglion cell layer (GCL), and inner plexiform layer (IPL) – reflecting loss or dysfunction of retinal ganglion cells and their axons, which may contribute to visual deficits in FRDA. Impaired color discrimination and contrast sensitivity have also been reported, as seen in other optic neuropathies.

14. Neuropathology in FRDA models
Although most of our understanding of FRDA clinical neuropathology derives from adult patients with long-standing disease, observations in children – often before overt symptoms – indicate that pathogenesis begins during development, a process that remains incompletely understood. Animal models, such as the KIKO mouse (GAA expansion knock-in and frataxin knockout) and the YG8R/YG8JR mouse (human frataxin with expanded GAA repeats), largely replicate key features of FRDA neuropathology and support the idea that developmental abnormalities precede neurodegeneration. For example, Complete absence of frataxin is developmentally lethal and KIKO mice have biochemical abnormalities before cerebellar development is complete. Notably, frataxin expression is developmentally regulated: in healthy mice, FXN mRNA becomes detectable around embryonic day 12 (E12), with highest levels observed in the DRG (particularly in large sensory neurons), as well as in the spinal cord, axial skeleton, and heart.

Certain features observed in FRDA mouse models are not recapitulated in patients. In the FRDA-knockdown (FRDAkd) model (doxycycline-inducible frataxin knockdown model), frataxin knockdown results in an almost complete loss of frataxin. The level of frataxin deficiency and the rate at which it is lost produces a phenotype more akin to a sub-acute frataxin knockout rather than the chronic and minimally progressive frataxin deficiency seen in patients, which may account for the extreme manifestations observed in this model. FRDAkd mice develop rapid and severe motor deficits, widespread neuronal loss, and early lethality – features that progress more slowly, or may be absent, in patients with the disease. The FRDAkd mouse should provide the most insight into the degenerative aspects of FRDA without capturing developmental components. In addition, the FRDAkd mouse might model events that occur with rapid onset of frataxin deficiency in patients, as might occur following withdrawal of an ongoing frataxin-restoring therapy.

In FRDA models, DRG pathology includes glial proliferation, sensory neuron hypoplasia, axonal demyelination, and reduced antioxidant defenses. DRG axons also exhibit impaired regeneration and guidance due to defective growth cones, which are essential for sensing environmental cues and guiding axonal extension during development and repair. These deficits may be compounded by the developmental abnormalities in the boundary cap cells, a transient population of neural crest derived cells critical for organizing the interface between the peripheral and central nervous systems. Boundary cap cells guide DRG axons into the spinal cord while preventing central nervous system (CNS) glial invasion into peripheral nerves. In FRDA patients, projections of CNS-resident astroglia into the dorsal roots suggest a disruption of this boundary, potentially contributing to the loss of myelinated axons. Moreover, human-derived sensory neurons and DRG organoids show impaired synaptic transmission and connectivity, activation of pro-inflammatory pathways, and gliosis.

FRDA mice also exhibit atrophy of major spinal tracts including the dorsal columns, Clarke’s column, and corticospinal tract. In YG8JR mice, corticospinal tract axons show mitochondrial displacement and swelling. In both KIKO and FRDAkd mouse models, as well as in derived neuronal cultures, cerebellar dysfunction is marked by PC hypoexcitability, occasional PC loss, mitochondrial morphological and bioenergetic abnormalities, oxidative stress, disrupted calcium and iron homeostasis, and altered cerebellar circuitry. These impairments are accompanied by compromised glutamatergic and GABAergic synaptic integrity within the cerebellar cortex.

Discrepancies in visual system pathology between FRDA mouse models and human patients highlight limitations in the translational relevance of mouse models. In the YG8R model, significant thinning of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) occurs, despite the RPE appearing functionally intact in patient-derived iPSC models, which show no abnormalities in RPE function or oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). Furthermore, retinal ganglion cells – the site of retinal dysfunction in FRDA patients—are not notably impacted in either the YG8R or YG22R models. These findings underscore a critical caveat: the cell types affected in these mouse models do not fully recapitulate human pathology. This divergence should be considered when interpreting visual system findings from these models and their relevance to patient outcomes.

15. Hypothesis: the biochemical cause of FRDA neuroanatomy
As a system, FRDA reveals a complex and profound disruption in the intersection of energy metabolism, development, and neural circuit integrity necessary for maintaining nervous system function. Frataxin deficiency perturbs mitochondrial homeostasis globally, yet the system-level consequences are highly localized and temporally structured. This suggests that the nervous system’s architecture – with its wide range of metabolic demands, developmental trajectories, and interdependent neuronal-glial networks – creates zones of vulnerability that are not evenly distributed. In this system, long-projecting, heavily myelinated neurons (e.g., DRG, Betz, and dentate nucleus neurons) represent points of high energy demand; they are structurally complex, developmentally active during early critical windows, and depend on glial support and intact myelination for function and survival. When frataxin is insufficient, these points in the system begin to fail, initially through failed maturation (e.g., DRG hypoplasia), and later via degenerative cascades (e.g., axonal atrophy). Such cell specific metabolic features could explain the neurons that are paradoxically preserved in FRDA such as spinal cord motor neurons. The degree to which individual systems fail may represent features not only of their bioenergetic demand but also features of particular neurons to utilize different fuels. For example, neurons have a limited capacity for β-oxidation, which likely contributes to the cell-type–specific vulnerability observed in FRDA. The role of fatty acid metabolism in specific neurons might also alter the susceptibility of individual neurons.

What emerges is a hierarchical systems failure: first in developmental wiring (especially proprioception and spinal growth), followed by failure of maintenance in high-demand adult circuits (proprioceptive, cerebellar, spinocerebellar, and visual systems) (Figure 3). The disease also exposes how tightly integrated neurons and glia are, and how damage in one component (like satellite cells and oligodendrocytes) propagates dysfunction throughout the circuit. Moreover, the combination of static and progressive elements suggests that some points of the system become permanently nonfunctional early (developmental effects), while others degrade gradually and may still be rescued.

Figure 3. Timing of neuronal decline and fundamental pathogenic mechanisms in Friedreich’s ataxia. GAA repeat expansions, reduced frataxin expression, and mitochondrial dysfunction are present from conception and remain constant throughout lifetime in all patients with FRDA. Large dorsal root ganglion neurons undergo developmental loss. Cerebellar dysfunction continuously declines. The corticospinal tracts are affected developmentally, followed by a rapid decline until approximately age five, and then continue to deteriorate progressively throughout life. Retinal ganglion cells are developmentally affected, remain stable through most of life, and decline later. DRG (dorsal root ganglion); A.U. (arbitrary units).

FRDA demonstrates how mitochondrial deficits destabilize not just individual cells, but the balance, adaptability, and resilience of entire neural networks. This systemic view emphasizes the need for integrative and multifaceted therapeutic approaches that go beyond gene replacement and address circuit-level plasticity, metabolic support, oxidative damage, and developmental timing.

16. Future perspective
This review has concentrated on the most recent details of the detailed components of FRDA, particularly neurological components as neurological dysfunction is the only features present in all patients with FRDA. Despite advancing knowledge on the pathophysiology of FRDA, treatment options include only omaveloxolone, an agent with modest but significant neurological benefits. The exact site of action of omaveloxolone remains unclear, demonstrating the relative lack of mechanistic and anatomical detail in understanding its action.
