Plasma biomarker evaluation: Cardiac troponin (cTnI) leak was identified in all Group II participants but not in any Ctl or Group I subject (Table 2 and Fig. S6). No subject in the Ctl cohort (mean of 0.014 ng/mL ± 0.0245 ng/mL) or Group II cohort (mean of 0.012 ng/mL ± 0.0020 ng/mL) had an elevated cTnI above 0.03 ng/mL. In contrast, all participants in Group II had levels of cTnI above the 99th percentile of 0.03 ng/mL and significantly higher than Ctl or Group I cohorts30. This group had a mean of 0.6617 ng/mL ± 0.5199 ng/mL with a range that was also quite broad at 3.21 ng/mL (0.04 ng/mL to 3.25 ng/mL). Thus, severe hypertrophy in this FRDA population was associated with cTnI leak and, in some cases, reached levels associated with acute injury.

Full size table
Table 2 also shows the biochemical assays for the 3 cohorts. Interestingly, plasma glucose, insulin, total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol, and triglyceride content were not different between the 3 cohorts, nor were 2 markers of fibrosis, soluble ST2 and Galectin-3. However, HDL cholesterol was significantly lower in the Group I cohort than in the Ctl group. The Cholesterol / HDL ratio was significantly higher in the Group I cohort (> 5 mg/dL) than in the Ctl group.

Gene expression in the FRDA mouse heart: To obtain a more mechanistic understanding of the cardiac fuel switch in FRDA patients, we turned to a murine model for molecular profiling of heart tissue. The Frdaf/f::MCK-Cre conditional ablation mouse (FXN MCK-KO) has a loss of FXN expression in the heart and skeletal muscle and develops HF, leading to death. The floxed Frdaf/f mouse has normal expression of FXN and no disease phenotype (Ctl)31,32. We performed bulk RNA sequencing on cardiac ventricular tissue from both models to identify changes in pathways associated with central energy metabolism. Table 3 presents those metabolic genes with significant differences, log2 fold change, and false discovery rate (FDR), and supplemental Table S3 contains the complete listing of these genes.

Table 3 Murine metabolic gene expression.
Male and female mice were analyzed separately to look for sex-dependent effects and mapped onto pathway diagrams in Fig. 4; Table 3. The glycolytic pathway (Fig. 4A) displays a mixture of genes upregulated in the Ctl or the FXN MCK-KO mice. The Slc2a1 gene, which codes for the Glut1 transporter, is upregulated in the male FXN MCK-KO heart, suggesting that insulin-independent glucose uptake is increased. The Slc2a4 gene, which codes for the Glut4, insulin-dependent transporter, is higher in male and female Ctl mice. This is consistent with the observation that the FRDA mice display signs of insulin resistance33,34. In the next step, hexokinase 1 (Hk1) expression is upregulated in the FXN MCK-KO mice, and hexokinase 2 (Hk2) is upregulated specifically in the female mice. This irreversible step suggests more glucose is being committed to the glycolytic pathway.

Fig. 4
Gene expression in FXN MCK-KO mouse relative to metabolism. (A) Gene expression by RNAseq for metabolic genes relative to glycolysis (cytosol). (B) Relative lactate levels (µM) in the heart by mass spectrometry. The box represents 25% and 75% values, the heavy line in the box is the median, and the whiskers are minimum/maximum. Significant differences are marked with the p-value. Each condition had 4 males and 4 females (n = 16 mice total). Ctl_f = control female, Ctl_m = male, KO_f = FXN MCK-KO female, KO_m = male. (C) Gene expression by RNAseq for metabolic genes in mitochondria relative to the Tricarboxylic Cycle (TCA). In Figures A and C, Blue = higher expression in Ctl mouse; Red = higher expression in FXN MCK-KO mouse. (f) and (m) = female and male sex.

The next several steps in the glycolytic pathway (Fig. 4A) show predominantly higher gene expression in the Ctl than in the FXN MCK-KO mice, consistent with an overall reduction in energy production in the KO mice. Expression of the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase, Pdk2 isoform, is upregulated in the Ctl females, whereas the Pdk4 isoform is upregulated in both sexes of the FXN MCK-KO mouse. This kinase blocks the action of pyruvate dehydrogenase (Pdh), which is responsible for transforming pyruvate into acetyl-CoA. When the levels of Pdk are elevated, it inhibits Pdh, which leads to the conversion of pyruvate to lactate via lactate dehydrogenase (Ldh). We measured lactate in these hearts by mass spectrometry, revealing a significant increase in the lactate levels of both sexes in the FXN MCK-KO mice (Fig. 4B). This suggests that the Pdk4 perturbation may be dominant, which further supports the glycolytic phenotype in the FXN MCK-KO heart.

The gene expression changes within the TCA cycle are mapped to the pathway in Fig. 4C. Nearly all the genes displayed higher expression in the Ctl mice, which predicts lower overall energy production in the FXN MCK-KO mice. The one exception is the expression of mitochondrial phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 2 (Pck2). This isoform is the only one that bridges the TCA cycle and glycolysis. Table 3 shows that the change in Pck2 represents the most significant gene upregulation in the FXN MCK-KO mice. Figure 4C also shows that Pck2 transforms oxaloacetate (OAA) into phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP). This can be transported into the cytosol using the citrate-isocitrate transporter. PEP then moves back up the glycolytic pathway to feed biosynthetic pathways such as serine biosynthesis or glyceroneogenesis. Thus, the RNA data from the FRDA cardiac model confirms a shift towards glycolysis and reduced energy production.

Discussion
This study is the first to investigate fuel substrate utilization in the human FRDA heart. This novel approach is crucial because metabolic flexibility is a key finding in healthy myocardium; loss of this flexibility is associated with failure and death35. Fatty acids are the preferred fuel in the heart, but in pathologic conditions, such as HF or ischemia, the heart can shift fuel utilization to glucose, which is more efficient and requires less oxygen but generates less energy36.

The primary finding of this study is that fuel substrate utilization by the heart in a subset of FRDA patients is altered to emphasize glucose uptake over fatty acid oxidation. All of the Group II participants had a rate of FDG uptake and an FDG/PAL ratio significantly above the 95% for the Ctl. This would suggest that these hearts rely more on glycolysis as a source of ATP generation than those in which the FDG / PAL ratio was not different from Ctl participants. In addition, 2 participants from Group I also had significantly increased FDG/PAL ratios with increased rates of FDG uptake, suggesting that there are intermediate phenotypes, i.e., these hearts may be progressing in their cardiomyopathy. Previous studies looking at FDG and PAL uptake in dilated cardiomyopathies showed a similar increase in myocardial glucose uptake but differed by a decrease in fatty acid metabolism37. In this study, we found that the primary driver of the FDG/PAL ratio is the increased rate of FDG uptake and not a decrease in the rate of fatty acid uptake. This is important because positron emission tomography with FDG uptake is readily available in most major medical centers as a clinical tool, e.g., for evaluation and detection of cancer. FDG PET has also been widely used to evaluate coronary artery disease, myocardial viability, and HF14. Radiolabeled PAL, however, is typically available only in a research setting. Thus, the rate of FDG uptake is informative when quantified in the heart and would predict an alteration of substrate utilization in the FRDA heart when compared with Ctl.

The mechanism(s) of increased reliance on glucose metabolism in the hypertrophic human FRDA heart is informed by the changes in gene expression in the conditional mouse heart. Here, genes associated with insulin-independent glucose uptake and favoring glycolysis are upregulated in the FXN MCK-KO mouse. In contrast, genes associated with fatty acid oxidation decreased in the FXN MCK-KO state, and gene expression supporting the TCA cycle generally decreased. This emphasizes the diminished role of the TCA cycle in energy generation in FRDA. Additionally, the phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (Pck1 and Pck2) is the rate-limiting enzyme of gluconeogenesis. The increased expression of Pck2 strongly favors the export of a valuable fuel substrate from mitochondria back to the cytosol, where it participates in other biosynthetic pathways38. In addition, mitochondrial Pck2 is a direct binding target of Lin28a in cardiomyocytes, which increases the expression level of Pck2 and promotes hypertrophic growth39.

Multiple authors have reported that the mean LV ejection fraction was not different between controls and FRDA participants, as we found in this study3,40. However, tissue Doppler interrogation in this study demonstrated clear differences in systolic and diastolic parameters compared with Ctl41. Those participants in Group II had evidence of significantly worse systolic and diastolic function, and this correlated strongly with the increased rate of FDG uptake. In contrast, those participants in Group I had diastolic and systolic indices that were not different from Ctl. The clinical implication of these findings is that under stressful conditions like major surgeries or illnesses, the FRDA heart with hypertrophy may face a higher risk due to mitochondrial dysfunction.

In this study we also found that severe hypertrophy in FRDA was associated with cTnI leak. None of the participants with an LVMi < 51 g/m2.7 (Group I) had evidence of troponin leak in this study, whereas all of Group II participants had evidence of cTnI leak at the time of study. Although the presence of troponin in blood is typically associated with coronary insufficiency, such as acute coronary syndrome, there are multiple etiologies of cTnI leak that predict poor outcomes30,42.

Study strengths and limitations: This study has two main strengths. First, FRDA is a rare disease that makes enrolling large cohorts for studies challenging. Nonetheless, the current study shows that cardiac metabolism is significantly affected in a subset of FRDA patients with severe LVH. Gene expression changes in the cardiac conditional murine model of FXN ablation support a potential mechanism for this metabolic shift. This study also suggests that a single tracer PET scan using FDG can identify these patients without the need for assessment of fatty-acid oxidation. Thus, PET scan may be useful for evaluating the FRDA heart prior to stressful events. Second, there is a strong correlation between LVMi and cTnI release with the finding of higher metabolic ratios of glucose uptake to fatty acid utilization in the heart. Thus, these may be predictive biomarkers for FRDA patients who are at risk of HF during stress, such as scoliosis surgery, which has been reported to have a higher risk of perioperative complications and death12,43,44.

There are several limitations to this study. First, as a rare disease the cohort size of the FRDA participants is small. Although no attempt was made to select specific participants, and statistical significance was high for the primary results, it is possible that enrollment of greater numbers of participants with FRDA would reveal intermediate phenotypes. This is suggested by Fig. 3A and B, where 2 of the participants in the Group I cohort have an FDG / PAL ratio that is as high as the Group II cohort, although their LVMi is normal. It is also possible that these participants may be progressing in their cardiac disease state. Second, investigational PET scans of participants are expensive and not widely available. Whereas FDG is commonly used in clinical practice, PAL use is restricted to institutions with a cyclotron. Additionally, the estimation of rates of metabolic substrate utilization from the kinetics of PET radiotracers has inherent limitations associated with tracer kinetic model assumptions, limitations associated with the use of venous blood samples to infer arterial blood metabolite levels45, limitations imposed by patient motion (cardiac cycle, repiratory cycle, and gross movement), and the spatial resolution and sensitivity of PET scanners. Collectively these limitations lead to bias and variance in PET estimates of metabolic substrate utilization. Third, FRDA is a progressive disease affecting multiple organs. This study provides only one snapshot of its progression and cannot show how metabolism changes over time. Fourth, although a diagnosis of diabetes was an exclusion criterion, FRDA patients can still have abnormalities in glucose utilization. Additionally, certain medications, such as β-blockers can affect serum glucose levels: 40% of Group I and 67.7% of Group II were on β-blockade. Although the glucose and serum insulin levels were not significantly different between groups, these factors could potentially affect uptake of FDG by heart and can be explored in future studies. Finally, exercise testing was not possible due to advanced neuromuscular disability. This would provide correlation between cardiopulmonary function relative to the PET scans.

Conclusions
In this cohort of FRDA patients, a PET scan identified two metabolically distinct subclasses of FRDA cardiomyopathy. FRDA patients with severe LVH had greater FDG uptake relative to palmitate utilization than FRDA patients without severe LVH. FRDA patients with severe LVH have systolic and diastolic dysfunction, as well as ongoing cardiac damage as indicated by cTnI leak. These findings suggest that FRDA patients with significant LVH may be at increased risk of complications from surgery or major illness.
Real-world evidence supporting orphan drugs approvals for rare neuromuscular disorders in the European Union and the United States: Review of public assessment reports (2015–2025)

Real-world data (RWD) and real-world evidence (RWE) are becoming essential complements to conventional clinical trials for drug assessment, particularly for rare neuromuscular disorders where small patient populations heighten outcome uncertainty. Robust RWE could reduce that uncertainty and inform regulatory decisions on orphan drugs (ODs). To review how the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) have incorporated RWE into OD approvals for neuromuscular diseases from January 2015 to January 2025. We reviewed all publicly available EMA European Public Assessment Reports and FDA review packages for ODs targeting neuromuscular indications. Each document was screened for mention of RWD sources and by the regulatory weight assigned to the resulting RWE. We identified 14 OD approvals by the EMA and 13 by the FDA, with greater use of RWE by the FDA. Indications comprised spinal muscular atrophy (3/3 EMA/FDA), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (1/3), amyloid neuropathies (2/2), Friedreich ataxia (1/1), Lambert–Eaton syndrome (1/1), myasthenia gravis (2/2), myotonic disorders (1/0), and Duchenne muscular dystrophy (2/1). Among 18 evaluable dossiers, clinical outcome assessments (COA) were reported as follows: patient-reported outcomes - 39.1%, clinician-reported outcomes - 34.7%, observer-reported outcomes - 13.1 %, and performance outcomes - 13.1%. Only tofersen incorporated all COA types. The use of RWE for the evaluation of ODs is increasing for both the FDA and the EMA, more so for the former than for the latter. Harmonized methodological standards and transparent reporting frameworks are urgently needed to generate quality evidence that benefits stakeholders.

Introduction
The possibility of generating and storing clinical data electronically is making significant progress in the study of orphan drugs (ODs). Nevertheless, to help advance progress, regulatory agencies should consider implementing innovative trial designs, developing flexible policies, and incorporating real-world data (RWD) to evaluate clinical outcomes. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) definition of RWD is data relating to patient health status and/or the delivery of health care routinely collected from a variety of sources such as electronic health records or disease registries. Real-world evidence (RWE) is clinical evidence on the use and potential benefits or risks of a medical product derived from the RWD analysis. It can inform therapeutic development, research on health care systems, quality improvement, safety surveillance, and well-controlled effectiveness studies. Caution should be exercised when relying on the analysis of existing data and the evidence presented in the reports as it can lead to erroneous conclusions. This concern is particularly relevant in precision molecular medicine for rare diseases. For these reasons, an important aspect to consider is how RWE should be used and reported. A group of Canadian researchers published a guide with recommendations for reporting RWE in May 2023.
There are different types of RWE, such as those obtained by collecting and using patient-reported outcomes (PROs), which can provide valuable information on the effectiveness, safety, and tolerability of health interventions from the patient’s perspective. The European Medicines Agency (EMA) currently uses RWE for safety monitoring and recently announced that the use of RWE will be established across its spectrum of regulatory use cases by 2025. The 21st Century Cures Act, signed into law in December 2016, was designed to help accelerate medical product development and bring innovations to patients who need them in the US. The regulation builds on the FDA's work to incorporate patient perspectives into the development of drugs, biologics, and devices. It enhances the ability to improve clinical trial designs, including the use of RWE and clinical outcome assessments (COA), which is expected to accelerate the development and review of new medical products. COA describes feelings or functions and can be reported by a health care provider, patient, or caregivers. There are four types: patient-reported outcomes (PROs), clinician-reported outcomes (ClinROs), observer-reported outcomes (ObsROs), and performance outcomes (PerfOs). The difference between them is the perspective on a patient's health status. PROs are direct patient feedback through questionnaires or numerical rating scales. ClinROs are information coming from a trained health-care professional regarding their interpretation of signs or behaviors that can be observed related to a patient's disease. ObsROs are assessments of observable signs related to a patient's health condition as reported by caregivers. PerfOS are measurements collected when a patient is asked to complete a well-defined, repeatable, and standardized task, such as the word recovery test.
Both agencies release comprehensive assessment dossiers for every marketing-authorization application—whether approved or refused. The EMA issues a European Public Assessment Report (EPAR), while the U.S. FDA provides a Drug Approval Package (DAP).
The aim of this study was to analyze how the EMA and the FDA have incorporated RWD and RWE into orphan drug approvals for neuromuscular diseases between January 2015 and January 2025.
Methods
We reviewed orphan drugs for neuromuscular diseases that were authorized or denied by the EMA and the FDA from 1st January 2015 to 1st January 2025. Veterinary drugs, withdrawn drugs, and drugs that did not meet the temporary criteria were excluded.
The EMA strategy for the search was an advanced search on March 5, 2025, with the inclusion criteria being the human category, medicine name and active substance/international non-proprietary name (INN)/common name with ‘show all’ selection, medicines and orphan designations, authorized or refused medicine status, therapeutic area (neuromuscular diseases, neurodegenerative diseases, and spinal diseases), and first published from 01/January/2015 to 01/January/2025. After that, we applied the filter for orphan medicine.
Also, we searched on Drugs@FDA: FDA-Approved Drugs, all Approvals and Tentative Approvals by Month with the time criteria described above. Results were organized and summarized using Excel and Visio Microsoft 365®.
One point to consider at the methodological level is that both the EMA and the FDA, through their accelerated approval programs, can provisionally approve drugs for serious diseases with unmet medical needs based on a surrogate endpoint. Pharmaceutical companies are still required to conduct studies to confirm the anticipated clinical benefit. If the drug is shown to provide a clinical benefit, the regulatory agency grants traditional approval for the drug. If the confirmatory trial does not show that the drug provides a clinical benefit, the FDA has regulatory procedures in place that could result in the drug being withdrawn from the market.
Initially, we collected data on medicine characteristics such as trade name, active substance, neuromuscular diseases, orphan drug, accelerated assessment or priority, date of authorization or provisional authorization, last updated, and state.
For each drug, we searched for the corresponding EPAR and DAP, focusing particularly on COA. These documents were downloaded for review from their respective official websites. They was identified by searching the documents using a list of keywords including “patient experience data”, “patient reported outcome”, “PRO”, ‘observer reported outcome’, “ObsRO”, “clinician reported outcome”, “ClinRO”, “performance outcome”, ‘PerfO’, “clinical outcome assessment”, “COA”. We systematically recorded the use of COA for each drug. If information was missing, we concluded that the documents did not report any evidence in this regard. The information available in EPAR and DAP was analyzed by two reviewers independently (BGP and JMG). A third reviewer resolved any disagreement between the two reviewers (MP or PM).
Finally, quantitative descriptive research methods were used based on data obtained from documentary sources. The results were analyzed to describe the characteristics of the different COAs used in EPAR and/or DAP over time and across neuromuscular diseases. The occurrence and type of COA were analyzed using descriptive statistics (absolute frequency and percentage).
Results
We retrieved 110 results from the EMA website by applying the inclusion criteria previously described. Then, we selected the “orphan medicine” filter on the EMA search and only 17 results remained. When reviewing them, two orphan drugs were excluded because they are used to treat non-neuromuscular diseases. Finally, 15 orphan medicines from the EMA were included.
On the other hand, the FDA search was conducted with a temporal filter, and drug approval reports by month with all approvals and provisional approvals for selected drugs were downloaded. We found 53.823 results (Table 1) and we had to review month by month in search of orphan drugs for neuromuscular diseases. At the beginning, we got 14 results, but finally, 13 were included because Relyvrio® (sodium phenylbutyrate and taurursodiol) for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis treatment was withdrawn from the market by the manufacturer. A flowchart with all steps summarizing the review process is available in Figure 1.
Table 1. Summary FDA search.

Figure 1. Flowchart.

Neuromuscular diseases with orphan drugs authorized in this time period (EMA/FDA) were spinal muscular atrophy (3/3), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (1/3), familial amyloid neuropathies (2/2), Friederich ataxia (1/1), Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (1/1), myasthenia gravis (2/2), myotonic disorders (1/-) and Duchenne muscular dystrophy (2/1). Specific information on the authorization conditions of these medicines was summarized in Table 2.
Table 2. Orphan drugs and neuromuscular diseases.

We reviewed the presence of COAs in the available approval documents of these medicines. A total of 18 orphan drugs were included, comprising authorized (15), refused (2) or discontinued (1).
When analyzing the EPAR documents, PROs were identified in 3 ODs (tofersen, rozanolixizumab, and mexiletine). However, DAP documents provided more information on these orphan drugs. PRO data were described in 9 ODs (risdiplam, tofersen, acoramidis, vutrisiran, omaveloxolone, amifampridine, efgartigimod alfa, rozanolixizumab, and mexiletine), ClinRO in 8 ODs (risdiplam, tofersen, vutrisiran, omaveloxolone, amifampridine, efgartigimod alfa, rozanolixizumab, and vamolorone), ObsRO in 3 ODs (risdiplam, tofersen, and vamolorone) and PerfO in 3 ODs (tofersen, vutrisiran, and vamolorone). These results are summarized in Table 3 and also took into account information that was unavailable or whose application had been withdrawn.
Table 3. Orphan neuromuscular drugs and COA.
A descriptive statistical analysis (absolute frequency and percentage) of the occurrence and type of COAs by OD was performed. The absolute frequency and percentage per COAs are as follows: PRO (9; 39.1%), ClinRO (8; 34.7%), ObsRO (3; 13.1%), and PerfO (3; 13.1%). Only one OD, tofersen, had the four COAs under consideration within the available documents.
Discussion
This study has limitations regarding the inference of the weight of RWD and RWE in decision-making. This is because the identification of RWE in the documents was based on explicit mentions and contextual use, which inherently reflects the reporting practices of the EMA and the FDA. However, the extent to which RWE influenced the final regulatory decision cannot be objectively quantified from these documents alone as neither the EPAR nor the DAP explicitly assign relative weights to different types of evidence. Therefore, although the inclusion of RWE in these reports was considered an indicator that it had been taken into account during the evaluation process, the precise magnitude of its contribution to the decision-making process remains an assumption that cannot be empirically established from publicly available information.
The increasing accessibility of RWD and the fast development of artificial intelligence, together with rising costs and recognized limitations of traditional trials, has spurred great interest in the use of RWD to enhance the efficacy of research and clinical finding. However, an important point to consider is the sources and methodology used to analyze RWD. In addition to the harmonization of methodology, it is needed to implement initiatives such as the one described by the FDA, committed to developing robust policies under the proposed Prescription Drug User Fee Act VI reauthorization for drugs and biologics. This includes public workshops with research stakeholders–from patients to providers to sponsors–to gather feedback on the use of RWE in regulatory decision-making. With this information, the agency would launch activities to manage key concerns and publish draft guidance on how this evidence can be used to assess safety and efficacy in pre- and post-marketing regulatory requirements.
An interesting study on PROs in medicines for neurological diseases approved by the EMA between 2017 and 2022 concludes that neurology is one area in which the use of this type of COA evidence is an inherent part of the clinical evaluation and for which core outcome sets exist. Nevertheless, they also show that better harmonization of the tools recommended for use would facilitate their consideration at all stages of the drug development process.
COAs are especially valuable in the regulatory evaluation of orphan drugs like antisense oligonucleotides. A case in point is tofersen, an anti-sense therapy for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Because many endpoints for such agents involve subjective or patient-centered variables, incorporating COAs helps anchor and enrich the evidence base, enhancing the consistency and interpretability of trial results for regulators.
The main limitation of our study was to identify the causes of the unavailable information in EPAR and/or DAP because sometimes it could be due to confidential information or the non-inclusion of COAs in the documents. Although RWD/RWE formed part of the core dossier submitted to the EMA—according to the Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use assessment report for the Marketing Authorization Application (MAA)—subsequent literature review confirmed that COAs were absent from both the core and supplementary studies. In addition, the edaravone MAA was withdrawn for the EMA, where its dossier had included RWD only as supportive evidence.
The European Medicines Regulatory Network (EMRN) launched a European Union (EU)-wide distributed RWD network called Data Analytics and Real World Interrogation Network (DARWIN EU) in 2021, with the objective of generating high-quality evidence to support regulatory decisions. At this time, DARWIN EU® has been playing a pivotal role in advancing the EU regulators' vision to enable the use of RWE and establish its value for regulatory decision-making in Europe. There are European Commission research calls that explicitly recognize the link of RWE in general and DARWIN EU in particular to regulatory decision-making.
In addition, the FDA also wants to optimize the utility of RWD and RWE to support regulatory decision-making. Historically, it has used RWD in its assessment of safety, most notably in the post-marketing phase. Only in limited circumstances has RWD been used to inform efficacy decisions, such as for rare disease treatments. In these cases, conducting traditional Phase III randomized clinical trials is usually not feasible. For this reason, the FDA published a document in 2019 ‘Rare Diseases: Natural History Studies for Drug Development Guidance for Industry’ to help inform the design and implementation of natural history studies that can be used to support the development of safe and effective drugs and biologics for rare diseases.
Articles on the efficacy and safety of approved orphan drugs in relation to RWE are gradually being published. In this regard, it is worth noting a letter published by a French research group in May 2025. They comment that the article ‘Efficacy and safety of onasemnogene abeparvovec gene therapy in children with spinal muscular atrophy in the D-A-CH region: a population-based observational study’ generates real-world evidence and highlights the importance of rapid access to disease-modifying therapy in newly diagnosed patients. However, they recommend confirmatory studies to better understand the impact of treatment sequences, especially in the presence of prior exposure to other drugs, given that spinal muscular atrophy has a heterogeneous population and currently has three orphan drugs available for its treatment.
Conclusion
This review shows a clear and growing integration of RWE into the regulatory assessment of ODs for neuromuscular disorders. Across 2015–2025 approvals, the FDA cited RWE in a higher proportion of dossiers and employed a broader range of data sources than the EMA. Reliance on RWE for OD assessment is accelerating, with the FDA outpacing the EMA in both frequency and depth of use. Harmonized methodological standards and transparent reporting frameworks are urgently needed to generate quality evidence benefiting regulators, health-care systems, and patients.
Safety and efficacy of individualised exercise and NAD+ precursor supplementation in patients with Friedreich's ataxia in the USA: a single-centre, 2 × 2 factorial, randomised controlled trial

Summary
Background
Friedreich's ataxia is a rare, chronic, progressive, neurodegenerative condition affecting multiple organ systems, including neurological, musculoskeletal, cardiac, and endocrine systems, and is marked by low cardiopulmonary fitness. We tested the effect of exercise and NAD+ precursor supplementation with nicotinamide riboside, which have each shown benefits in animal and early clinical studies, on cardiopulmonary fitness in individuals with Friedreich's ataxia.
Methods
This 12-week, outpatient, phase 2, single-site (Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, Philadelphia, PA, USA), randomised, 2 × 2 factorial clinical trial recruited individuals aged 10–40 years with an ejection fraction of 45% or greater who were able to exercise. A computer-generated randomisation sequence was developed by the trial statistician. Random allocation was age-stratified (<18 years vs ≥18 years) to one of four groups: placebo and no exercise with attention control (weekly phone calls; henceforth placebo only), nicotinamide riboside and no exercise with attention control (henceforth nicotinamide riboside only), placebo and exercise (exercise only), and nicotinamide riboside and exercise (combination therapy). Individualised exercise plans were developed by the exercise physiologist (three aerobic and two resistance training sessions weekly), performed at the individual's home, and overseen remotely (telephone check-ins by the physiologist). Weight-based dosing of nicotinamide riboside or placebo was 300 mg (1 capsule) for weights of 24 kg up to 48 kg, 600 mg (2 capsules) for weight 48 kg up to 72 kg, and 900 mg (3 capsules) for weights of over 72 kg. The primary outcome was change in peak VO2 (L/min) during cardiopulmonary exercise testing at 12 weeks versus baseline, and the effect of treatment group was assessed in a statistical model accounting for age (stratification variable), sex, and baseline peak VO2. Stage 1 analysis tested the difference between each active treatment versus the control group, and stage 2 analysis (if combination therapy was effective) tested the difference between combination treatment and exercise alone; family-wise type 1 error was maintained <0·05. Analyses were by intention-to-treat. Adverse events were recorded systematically. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04192136) and is complete.
Findings
Between Sept 3, 2020, and April 23, 2025, we enrolled 74 individuals, of whom 66 met the eligibility criteria and were randomly allocated to the four study groups. All participants completed the study. 33 (50%) were children (aged 10–17 years) and 33 (50%) were adults (aged ≥18 years); 37 (56%) were male and 29 (44%) were female. Least mean squares for the change in peak VO2 in L/min were –0·05 (95% CI –0·16 to 0·06) for the 17 participants in the control group; 0·06 (–0·05 to 0·17) for the 17 participants in the nicotinamide riboside and no exercise group; 0·11 (0·00 to 0·22) for the 16 participants in the placebo and exercise group; and 0·16 (0·05 to 0·27) for the 16 participants in the nicotinamide riboside and exercise group. Differences between active treatment and the control group were 0·10 (95% CI –0·05 to 0·26; padjusted=0·188) for nicotinamide riboside and no exercise; 0·16 (0·00 to 0·31; padjusted=0·103) for placebo and exercise; and 0·21 (0·05 to 0·36; padjusted=0·0299) for nicotinamide riboside and exercise in combination. Combination therapy was not statistically different from exercise alone (difference –0·05 (; p=0·49). Adverse events were all mild or moderate, and included gastrointestinal symptoms, falls, upper respiratory infections, and skin rashes. At least one moderate adverse event of interest in these categories was reported by seven (41%) participants in the control group; six (35%) in the nicotinamide riboside and no exercise group; three (19%) in the placebo and exercise group; and four (25%) in the nicotinamide plus exercise group.
Interpretation
The combination of nicotinamide riboside plus exercise for 12 weeks was safe and increased cardiopulmonary fitness in children and adults with Friedreich's ataxia. Longer studies are needed to establish whether adding nicotinamide riboside to exercise could be considered as part of a long-term, comprehensive treatment approach.
Introduction
Friedreich's ataxia is a rare, chronic, progressive multisystemic condition.1 For most individuals, GAA triplet repeat expansions on both alleles of the FXN gene lead to gene silencing through epigenetic and chromatin-mediated mechanisms.2 Friedreich's ataxia manifestations are the result of tissue-specific frataxin deficiency and include ataxia, cardiomyopathy, fatigue, scoliosis, diabetes, and vision and hearing problems, with cardiac complications representing the leading cause of premature mortality.3, 4 There is only one US Federal Drug Administration (FDA)-approved therapy, omaveloxolone, an Nrf2 activator, which has demonstrated the ability to slow neurological progression.5
Individuals living with Friedreich's ataxia have substantial limitations in cardiopulmonary fitness that are associated with worse disease severity and impaired day-to-day function.6, 7, 8 Although current guidelines recommend that individuals engage in regular exercise, the evidence base in humans with Friedreich's ataxia is scant.9 Animal models demonstrate benefits of regular exercise, with long-term voluntary running preventing the onset of symptoms without restoring frataxin levels.10 Barriers to exercise include safety concerns (primarily the fear of falls), as well as limited energy and time.7 Exercise in individuals with multiple comorbidities, including mobility impairment, requires substantial investment of time and resources, and insights regarding the safest and most effective individualised prescriptions are needed.
Research in context
Evidence before this study
Friedreich's ataxia is a rare, multisystem neurodegenerative disorder that also affects cardiac and skeletal muscle. Low cardiopulmonary fitness is common and associated with both disease severity and impaired function. Only one drug, omaveloxolone, has been approved specifically for the treatment of individuals with Friedreich's ataxia based on its ability to slow neurological disease progression. We searched PubMed from database inception between April 23, 2025, and Oct 1, 2025, for Articles available in English using search terms, “Friedreich's Ataxia,” “exercise,” “NAD+ precursor,” AND “muscle”, yielding several studies suggesting a benefit of NAD+ precursor supplementation either alone or in combination with exercise in this and other neurodegenerative conditions. One NAD+ precursor, nicotinamide, was initially tested in an 8-week open-label, dose-escalation study in humans with Friedreich's ataxia, as nicotinamide seemed to relieve heterochromatin-induced FXN gene silencing in animal studies, ostensibly by acting as a class III histone deacetylase inhibitor. Participants receiving the highest nicotinamide doses had increased concentrations of circulating mature mitochondrial frataxin, towards levels observed in those who carry mutations for Friedreich's ataxia but are not affected, although they also developed gastrointestinal symptoms including nausea. Studies in animal models of Friedreich's ataxia and in humans with related conditions such as mitochondrial myopathy indicate that NAD+ precursor supplementation might also decrease oxidative stress and increase mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation capacity. NAD+ precursor supplementation has been pursued as a therapeutic strategy for neurogenerative diseases including Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease because of promising findings from animal and early, open-label clinical studies, and is currently being studied in longer and larger randomised controlled trials, and is correlated with functional status and habitual exercise in older adults. Aerobic exercise training has been shown to increase endurance in animal models of Friedreich's ataxia but has not been tested specifically in humans with the condition, in whom the benefits of physical therapy, aerobic and resistance exercise, and balance training have been suggested by small studies.
Added value of this study
In this randomised controlled trial in individuals with Friedreich's ataxia aged 10–40 years, an ejection fraction of 45% or greater, and the ability to exercise, the combination of NAD+ precursor supplementation with nicotinamide riboside and in-home aerobic and resistance training for 12 weeks produced a clinically relevant increase in cardiopulmonary fitness. Overall, these interventions, alone and in combination, were safe and well-tolerated.
Implications of all the available evidence
Our trial results indicate that exercise training in combination with nicotinamide riboside supplementation is a safe and effective approach to address low cardiopulmonary fitness in individuals with Friedreich's ataxia. Although we were not able to fully parse the effects of exercise or nicotinamide riboside in isolation, our findings suggest potential therapeutic mechanisms that did not depend on increases in circulating frataxin. Adding nicotinamide riboside to exercise could be considered as part of investigations supporting a long-term comprehensive treatment approach for individuals with Friedreich's ataxia. Our findings also highlight the value of testing mechanistically complementary interventions in complex disorders, and adds to the growing body of evidence testing NAD+ precursor supplementation in a variety of neurodegenerative, neuromuscular, and metabolic disorders.
One of the physiological adaptations to exercise in healthy individuals is an increase in skeletal muscle NAD+ concentrations, which ostensibly supports ongoing energy production in exercising muscle. Moreover, skeletal muscle NAD+ concentrations are correlated with functional status in older adults,11 and supplemental NAD+ precursors have shown clinical benefit in measures of function in patients with mitochondrial myopathy12 and peripheral arterial disease,13 raising the possibility that increasing NAD+ might complement or enhance the benefits of exercise alone. Although it is not clear whether systemic NAD+ deficiency is present in Friedreich's ataxia, several studies have suggested a survival benefit from NAD+ precursor supplementation in animal models of the disease.14, 15 In humans with Friedreich's ataxia, an exploratory, open-label, dose-escalation study of an NAD+ precursor (high-dose nicotinamide) was pursued based on the action of nicotinamide as a class III histone deacetylase (sirtuin) inhibitor.16 Increases in circulating frataxin were noted with 8 weeks of nicotinamide administration. However, detailed, placebo-controlled follow-up studies of NAD+ precursor supplementation in humans with Friedreich's ataxia had not been undertaken until the current trial. Additionally, the possibility that NAD+ precursor supplementation could increase the capacity of individuals with Friedrich's ataxia to engage in exercise training by directly supporting metabolic reactions that drive skeletal muscle energy production had not been tested.
To address these unmet needs, we pursued a mechanistic clinical trial, with a 2 × 2 factorial design, to test the effects of exercise (aerobic and resistance) training and supplementation with an NAD+ precursor, nicotinamide riboside, both alone and together, on cardiopulmonary fitness (primary outcome, aim 1) and glucose homeostasis (aim 2) in children and adults with Friedreich's ataxia. This Article reports findings related to aim 1, and the findings related to aim 2 will be published in a separate paper.
Methods
Study design and participants
This study was a randomised, placebo-controlled trial with a 2 × 2 factorial design. Participants were assigned to one of four groups: placebo plus no exercise with attention control (hereafter referred to as placebo only, the control group), nicotinamide riboside plus no exercise with attention control (nicotinamide riboside only), placebo plus exercise (exercise only), and nicotinamide riboside plus exercise (the combination group). All procedures occurred at our single site in Philadelphia, which included outpatient centres of the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) and the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA.
Ethics approval was obtained by the CHOP Institutional Review Board (FWA00000459) on Nov 19, 2019. The Friedreich Ataxia Research Alliance patient advocacy organisation and the RideATAXIA organisation that supports adaptive cycling were involved in trial design and recruitment.
Children and adults aged 10–40 years with genetically confirmed Friedreich's ataxia were recruited from clinical practices, from website postings, and through a natural history study (UNIFAI; NCT06016946). Participants were eligible if they did not have clinically significant uncontrolled and persistent arrhythmia, had a left ventricular ejection fraction of 45% or greater, and were able to complete an incremental cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET) in a cycle ergometry chair. Individuals already meeting age-appropriate US public health physical activity guidelines were excluded. Full inclusion and exclusion criteria are presented in the appendix (p 86). Written informed consent, and assent for those younger than 18 years, were obtained before enrolment. The trial is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04192136) and is currently closed to new participants.
Randomisation and masking
The statistician transferred a computer-generated randomisation sequence to a secure REDCap database, ensuring allocation concealment. Participants were allocated in a 1:1:1:1 ratio with randomly permutated block sizes of four and eight. Randomisation was stratified by age (age ≥18 yearsand age <18 years). Trial participants, care providers, data collectors, and outcome assessors were masked to participant allocation to nicotinamide riboside versus placebo. Nicotinamide riboside and placebo were dispensed in identical capsules. The trial was masked for exercise versus attention control for the outcome assessors.
Procedures
Total trial duration for each participant was 12 weeks and included a baseline visit (week 0), a 12-week intervention, and a follow-up visit (week 12). Each 2-day study visit (at week 0 and week 12) included the same procedures: medical history review, anthropometric measurements, Tanner staging (at baseline for childrenonly), Friedreich's Ataxia Rating Scale (FARS) examination,17 laboratory assessments, patient-reported outcomes, dual energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA), dynamometry, MRI, and a CPET.
Whole blood NAD+ measurements were obtained after an overnight fast as previously described.18 Mitochondrial frataxin isoform (FXN-M)19 and erythrocyte frataxin isoform (FXN-E)20 were measured in blood. Creatine chemical exchange transfer (CrCEST) MRI scans were performed on a 3-Tesla whole body scanner (Siemens Medical Systems, Erlangen, Germany) to generate an index of skeletal muscle mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation capacity (post-exercise CrCEST recovery, in ms).21
All participants completed an incremental symptom-limited CPET on a recumbent leg cycle ergometer (Lode Corival Recumbent Ergometer, Model Number #929900, Groningen, Netherlands).8 Respiratory gas exchange measurements were obtained breath-by-breath using a commercially available system (Vmax 29Cuntil March 2023; then Vyntus CPXafter March 2023). Peak oxygen uptake (VO2) was recorded as the mean value of VO2 during the last 20 s of the test. O2 pulse was oxygen uptake divided by heart rate. Methods for assessing body composition via DXA, grip strength via dynamometry, fatigue, and physical function are described in the appendix (p 86).
During the intervention, participants took the nicotinamide riboside supplement or placebo by mouth daily, typically in the morning with food. Weight-based dosing was 300 mg (1 capsule) for weights of 24 kg up to 48 kg, 600 mg (2 capsules) for weight 48 kg up to 72 kg, and 900 mg (3 capsules) for weights of over 72 kg. Nicotinamide riboside was provided as a commercial formulation (300 mg capsules, ChromaDex, Irvine, CA, USA). Matching placebo was backfilled with microcrystalline cellulose (national formulary, Spectrum Chemical MGF Corp, Gardena, CA, USA). Remaining unused nicotinamide riboside and placebo capsules were collected at the 12-week visit for calculating adherence.
Participants assigned to exercise were provided with a recumbent tricycle (Catrike Pocket or Catrike Villager) and supplies (indoor trainer, wheel lifts, clip-in pedals, cycling shoes, resistance bands, and a FitBit watch). The 12-week programme consisted of at-home sessions with individualised recommendations by the study exercise physiologist: three aerobic sessions per week on the in-home trike trainer (pedalling at 60–80% of maximal heart rate from baseline CPET for 20–25 min), and two resistance exercise sessions per week targeting the whole body using resistance bands; aerobic and resistance training occurred on separate days. Exercise prescriptions were provided through MyHeart CHOP, a mobile health app which was loaded with an individualised calendar, target heart rate zones, and prerecorded video refreshers on how to perform the exercises. Participants not randomly allocated to the exercise groups were in the attention control groups and received weekly telephone calls. No limitations were placed on self-selected physical activity or exercise for any participant; patient-reported time in physical activity or exercise was measured by questionnaire. To encourage retention, participants not initially randomly allocated to the exercise intervention could elect to receive training (up to 12 weeks) at the end of the study.
Outcomes
The primary outcome was the within-participant change in peak VO2, the highest oxygen uptake achieved on CPET, from baseline to 12 weeks, with peak VO2 expressed in L/min. Key secondary outcomes (change from baseline to 12 weeks) included other CPET outcomes (maximum workload in Watts, maximum O2 pulse in mL per beat, anaerobic threshold, and resting heart rate), grip strength via dynamometry, fatigue via the Modified Fatigue Impact Scale, and physical activity via the Physical Activity and Disability Survey-Revised (PADS-R) questionnaire (for the full list of secondary outcomes see the appendix p 101). Exploratory outcomes included body composition (change in visceral fat, fat mass index, lean mass index, and appendicular lean mass) and HbA1c.
All randomly allocated participants were included in the safety analysis. A safety monitoring uniform report form was used to assess potential adverse events systematically and was administered at each in-person visit. Adverse events were classified according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 5.0. Additional information on the assessment of adverse events can be found in the appendix (p 86).
Statistical analysis
Efficacy analyses included all participants who were randomly allocated. For the primary outcome (peak VO2) and key secondary outcomes, we fitted a linear model for change in outcome from baseline using treatment group as the exposure, with adjustment for baseline peak VO2, random allocation stratum (child vs adult), and sex. Using a previously described non-factorial approach to the analysis,22 stage 1 tested if mean peak VO2 in any of the three active treatment groups differed from the control group. In stage 2, if combination therapy differed from the control group, we compared combination therapy to exercise only to determine whether nicotinamide riboside increases mean peak VO2 beyond the effect of exercise alone. The family-wise type I error rate was maintained at 5% by using a Holm–Bonferroni correction in stage 1, and a single prespecified contrast in stage 2.22 Recognising the need to balance control of family-wise type I error rate with good statistical power, we prespecified a limited number of contrasts. We thus prioritised each of the three contrasts that were of clinical interest along with the contrast of particular mechanistic importance (combination therapy vs exercise only). The same approach was used for primary and secondary outcomes. Only the primary outcome had family-wise error control. Analyses of secondary outcomes are exploratory with nominal p values not adjusted for multiple testing.
The four prespecified subgroups were: age (child vs adult), sex (male vs female), CPET performance (a respiratory exchange ratioachieved during CPET ≥1 vs <1), and omaveloxolone status (prescribed or not, restricted to participants aged 16 years and older for whom the drug is approved in the USA). For the primary outcome the analysis included a hypothesis test of the interaction between the subgroups and study group. These exploratory analyses were not adjusted for multiple comparisons. The frequencies of adverse events by type and severity were summarised by study group; adverse events and their relationship to nicotinamide riboside, placebo, and exercise were summarised by group.
The sample size was 64 individuals (eight children and eight adults per treatment group). We previously found that the mean peak VO2 in 19 individuals with Friedreich's ataxia undergoing cycle ergometry was 20·2 mL/kg per min, decreasing by 0·5 mL/kg per min after 1 year (SD 2·4 mL/kg for the difference).8 By simulating normally distributed data for the analytic plan described above22 and assuming an SD of 2·5 mL/kg per min, this study had at least 80% power to detect the following improvement or improvements: in the stage 1 analysis, 3·0 mL/kg per min if exactly one group improved versus control (equivalent to approximately 13% of the previous mean of 20·2 mL/kg per min), or 3·1 mL/kg per min if all three groups improved; and in the stage 2 analysis, 2·6 mL/kg per min for combination therapy versus nicotinamide riboside alone (appendix p 97). Allowing for 12% attrition, we aimed to enrol 72 individuals.
Analyses were implemented in R version 2024.04.0 + 735. The appendix includes the statistical analysis plan, which was finalised before the investigators were unmasked.
Role of the funding source
The funders of the study had no role in study design, data collection, data analysis, data interpretation, or writing of the report. Nicotinamide riboside was donated by ChromaDex, representatives of which were able to review the manuscript before submission to ensure no proprietary information was disclosed.
Results
Between Sept 3, 2020, and April 23, 2025, we enrolled 74 individuals after a pre-screening, of whom 66 met the eligibility criteria and were randomly allocated to the four study groups. All participants completed the study (figure 1). Baseline characteristics are given in table 1; the appendix (p 106) gives the characteristics stratified by age. 33 (50%) were children (aged 10–17 years) and 33 (50%) were adults (aged ≥18 years); 29 (44%) participants were female and 37 (56%) participants were male; and the mean age was 20·3 years (SD 7·7). 62of 66 participants were homozygous for GAA triplet expansions in the FXN gene. Nine (27%) of 33 adults and three (9%) of 33 children were taking omaveloxolone; proportions were similar across treatment groups. Appendicular lean mass index Z-score, a proxy for skeletal muscle mass, was lower than the population reference means in both adults and children, whereas fat mass index Z-scores were near or slightly higher than population reference values for both adults and children (appendix p 106). 45 (68%) of participants achieved measurable anaerobic threshold on their CPET.

Median adherence ranged from 90% to 98% across treatment groups for pill counts for placebo or nicotinamide riboside. Over the entire cohort, median adherence for pill counts was 97% (IQR 93–99). Median adherence for exercise ranged from 82% to 97% of prescribed sessions. Of the individuals prescribed exercise, median adherence was 94% (IQR 84–97; appendix p 107). Whole blood NAD+ measurements demonstrated increased whole blood NAD+ concentrations in those taking nicotinamide riboside compared with placebo (appendix pp 120–21). The dose of nicotinamide riboside per kg of body weight was nominally, but not significantly, higher in children than in adults (median 9·60for adults vs 10·88for children; p=0·0539; appendix p 122); whole blood NAD+ concentrations were not different between children and adults, and we did not detect an association with nicotinamide riboside dose achieved per kg of body weight (appendix p 121).

Differences between active treatment and the control group were 0·10 (95% CI –0·05 to 0·26; padjusted=0·188) for nicotinamide riboside only group; 0·16 (0·00 to 0·31; padjusted=0·103) for exercise only group; and 0·21 (0·05 to 0·36; padjusted=0·0299) for the combination group. The percentage change in each group was calculated as the least mean squares change divided by the baseline mean peak VO2 (L/min) for each treatment group: control –0·05/1·29 (–3·9%), nicotinamide riboside only 0·06/1·21 (5·0%), exercise only 0·11/1·16 (9·5%), and combination 0·16/1·21 (13·2%).

In the stage 2 analysis, testing exercise only versus nicotinamide riboside and exercise in combination, combination therapy was not statistically different from exercise only (β coefficient 0·05; p=0·49). Results for prespecified analyses for primary and secondary outcomes are shown in table 2. Absolute changes in study outcomes are shown in the appendix (pp 108–113).
With respect to other prespecified CPET outcomes, maximal workload was increased by combination therapy relative to the control group, and O2 pulse was increased similarly by both combination therapy and exercise only (appendix p 124) relative to the control group. For those who met the anaerobic threshold, the threshold and resting heart rate were not changed. Boxplots with changes in CPET outcomes are shown in the appendix (pp 125–26).
The PADS-R exercise and leisure activity subscore increased in response to combination therapy versus control (0·80; unadjusted p=0·0197). Fatigue, measured by the Modified Fatigue Impact Scale, and muscle strength, measured via dynamometry, were not changed regardless of intervention (table 2). Boxplots for non-CPET outcomes are shown in the appendix (pp 127–29).
In unadjusted analyses, several suggestive changes in exploratory outcomes were noted outside primary endpoint family-wide error control (appendix pp 114–116, 127–129). The nicotinamide riboside only group had decreases in body fat, whether expressed as visceral fat (–0·08 kg) versus the control group. Lower extremity lean mass was positively associated with peak VO2 before and after the intervention in all treatment groups (appendix p 130). Of the 66 individuals who were randomly allocated, only 40 had useable MRI scans. No changes in CrCEST parameters from interventions were detected. Both starting HbA1c and final HbA1c were within the reference range for all treatment groups—baseline HbA1c for the combination therapy group was 5·1% (IQR 4·8–5·1); combination therapy resulted in a –0·15% decrease in HbA1c within the normal range versus control (95% CI –0·29 to –0·01; appendix p 116).
No changes in circulating FXN-M, FXN-E, or total modified FARS (mFARS) or FARS upright stability were detected. Forest plots for total mFARS and FARS upright stability, which are used as registration outcomes in Friedreich's ataxia, are shown in the appendix (pp 127, 131). For the prespecified exploratory subgroup analyses, the effect of treatment differed between children and adults (unadjusted pinteraction=0·011), with children demonstrating response to nicotinamide riboside alone but not exercise alone, and adults demonstrating response to exercise with or without nicotinamide riboside. No effect of omaveloxolone was detected (appendix p 132).
There were no serious adverse events. Only grade 1 (mild) or 2 (moderate) adverse events occurred. These are summarised in table 3 and were similar across groups. Moderate adverse events of special interest were reported in seven (41%) in the control group; six (35%) in the nicotinamide riboside and no exercise group; three (19%) in the placebo and exercise group; and four (25%) in the nicotinamide plus exercise group. Commonly reported adverse events included gastrointestinal symptoms (30of 66 participants, including dyspepsia, nausea and vomiting, and diarrhoea), falls (13of 66), upper respiratory infections (23of 66), and skin problems (35of 66, mostly rashes). Cumulative time-to-event plots suggest nominally fewer grade 1 and 2 adverse events in those allocated to exercise (appendix p 133).
Table 3. Adverse events by treatment group
Adverse events were tracked systematically and reported according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0. Grade refers to the clinical severity of the adverse event (grades 1–5, where 1 is mild requiring only observation, 2 is moderate with only local or non-invasive intervention, 3 is severe or medically significant but not immediately life-threatening, 4 is life-threatening, and 5 is death). Only grade 1 and 2 adverse events occurred. Adverse events of interest were summarised, including with input from the Data and Safety Monitoring Board as the study proceeded. Adverse events of interest included: those expected to occur commonly (in between one in ten and one in 100 individuals) related to nicotinamide riboside: gastrointestinal disorders (nausea or vomiting, heartburn, diarrhoea, constipation, and bloating); skin and subcutaneous disorders (rash or pruritus); flushing, a potential effect of a different NAD+ precursor, niacin; falls, an important safety event in Friedreich's ataxia, and a theoretical risk of exercise; and upper respiratory infections, which occurred frequently in the cohort. We did not include here adverse events that were clearly related to study procedures eg, rash from electrocardiogram leads or reactive hypoglycemia following oral glucose tolerance testing.
Discussion
This randomised controlled trial tested the effects of 12 weeks of exercise training and an NAD+ precursor, nicotinamide riboside, alone and in combination, on cardiopulmonary fitness in children and adults with Friedreich's ataxia. Consistent with our previous work,8 exercise testing, modified to address mobility limitations, was both feasible and reflective of low fitness before the intervention. Compared with the control group, individuals receiving combination therapy improved on several indices of cardiopulmonary fitness, including the primary outcome, peak VO2, and related outcomes including oxygen pulse (a surrogate marker reflecting a combination of stroke volume and peripheral oxygen extraction during exercise). This trial yields several important findings. First, exercise training is safe and well tolerated by people with Friedreich's ataxia. Second, combination therapy produced a clinically relevant improvement in cardiopulmonary fitness in individuals with Friedreich's ataxia. Finally, although we did not demonstrate significant effects of exercise or nicotinamide riboside in isolation, our findings suggest potential therapeutic mechanisms that do not require increases in circulating frataxin. NAD+ precursor supplementation as a therapeutic strategy for neurogenerative diseases including Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease has been suggested by findings from animal and early, open-label clinical studies, and is currently being studied in longer and larger randomised controlled clinical trials.23 Our randomised controlled trial in this rare neurodegenerative disorder, enrolling equal numbers of children and adults, adds to this important and growing body of evidence. Skeletal muscle effects of NAD+ precursors could plausibly be enhanced by concurrent exercise training, a strategy that we are also pursuing in people who are in recovery from cancer.24
Multiple previous studies have identified low cardiopulmonary fitness as a substantial problem in individuals with Friedreich's ataxia.6, 7, 8 Notably, these cross-sectional studies also found that low fitness was associated with both more severe Friedreich's ataxia and adverse functional outcomes. Despite this problem, there is currently no evidence from randomised controlled trials demonstrating effective strategies to address low cardiopulmonary fitness specifically in Friedreich's ataxia. In our study, fitness—as reflected by peak VO2—increased 12·7% with combination therapy and decreased 2·4% in the control group. This increase would be considered effective in most patient populations, perhaps even more so in a condition such as Friedreich's ataxia, where even those without overt heart failure have markedly lower functional capacity than healthy reference cohorts.25 Even smaller changes are clinically relevant in patients with related conditions such as adult heart failure, where a 6% increase in peak VO2 is associated with an 8% lower risk of cardiovascular mortality and hospitalisation.26 A previous cross-sectional study in Friedreich's ataxia found that a 7% difference in peak VO2 was correlated to approximately 3 points of difference in FARS (around 1 year of disease progression)27 and a 15% difference in timed 25-foot walk performance.28
Notably, the interventions in the present study were safe and well-tolerated, with no serious adverse events. Overall, mild and moderate adverse events were commonly reported, and similar across treatment groups. Since fear of falling is a patient-reported barrier to exercise in Friedreich's ataxia,7 we specifically tracked falls and observed similar rates across interventions. We did not detect any excess rate of cardiac or other adverse events in the individuals assigned to exercise.
Our findings are consistent with a recent 12-month randomised controlled trial including 62 individuals with various cerebellar ataxias that tested aerobic exercise versus balance training (6 months supervised, 12 months in total) and noted improvements in both ataxia symptoms and fitness with aerobic exercise.29 Aligned with a recent meta-analysis,30 continued adherence was predictive of sustained benefits.29 Unlike many other forms of cerebellar ataxia, Friedreich's ataxia has skeletal muscle as well as cardiac involvement,21, 31 which represents additional potential barriers to exercise; many individuals with Friedreich's ataxia have historically been advised to avoid exercise based on theoretical safety concerns. Fortunately, in our short-term study, adherence to prescribed exercise was high and exercise was safe. In prespecified subgroup analyses, age appeared to affect response to treatment, with adults responding to exercise with or without nicotinamide riboside, and children responding to nicotinamide riboside alone. Pre-intervention fitness was nominally lower in adults across treatment groups, which might have led to a more demonstrable response to exercise training in adults (appendix p 106). Physical therapy, particularly goal-directed rehabilitation, is another form of physical activity with demonstrated functional benefits in individuals with ataxia.32 Taken together, the evidence supports continued exercise prescriptions for individuals with cerebellar ataxias, although to achieve larger and more sustained effects, complementary strategies might be valuable.
Our finding that combination therapy increases cardiopulmonary fitness in individuals with Friedreich's ataxia suggests exciting potential benefits of combining exercise with complementary interventions. Although differences between exercise only and combination therapy were not statistically significant, possibly due to sample size and power considerations, our findings suggest several potential mechanisms of effect. Previous studies have indicated that NAD+ precursor therapy might work by increasing frataxin concentrations.16 However, circulating frataxin restoration is probably not required to achieve the improvements in fitness we report in this trial. Circulating FXN-M concentrations did not change significantly in response to any of the interventions tested. Similarly, in animal models of Friedreich's ataxia, long-term voluntary running prevents the onset of symptoms without restoring frataxin levels.10 It is possible that frataxin concentrations might have increased within tissues (eg, skeletal muscle) but not in peripheral blood. The previous early phase human study testing 2–8 g daily of oral nicotinamide found increased circulating frataxin at the highest doses;16 a planned follow-up study did not proceed for logistical reasons.33 The dose of NAD+ precursor was lower in the present study to avoid dose-related risks of gastrointestinal symptoms, and the frataxin assays differed—two potential additional reasons for the differences in study findings with respect to effects on frataxin. Notably, increasing NAD+ was beneficial in an animal model created by deletion of the frataxin gene, indicating at least one mechanism independent of restoring expression.14
An alternative potential mechanism of benefit of NAD+ precursor supplementation is repletion of tissue-specific deficiencies in NAD+, especially in individuals with underlying vulnerability to metabolic stress. In humans with systemic NAD+ deficiency, as in adult-onset mitochondrial myopathy, NAD+ precursor treatment with niacin for 10 months restored muscle NAD+, and increased muscle strength and mitochondrial biogenesis.12 Unlike mitochondrial myopathy, however, there is not clear evidence of tissue compartment-specific NAD+ deficiency in Friedreich's ataxia,15 although we speculate that exercise training could increase the demand for skeletal muscle NAD+ and thus account for the additional benefit of NAD+ precursor supplementation in this context.
Other studies have found possible benefits for NAD+ precursor supplementation in humans.13, 34 In the present study, nicotinamide riboside dose selection might have contributed to the response. Children, who received a marginally higher dose of nicotinamide riboside per body weight, had an increase in fitness in response to nicotinamide riboside alone, whereas adults did not. Using the bodyweight-based dosing strategy, adults at bodyweights of 72 kg or more received a maximum of 900 mg of nicotinamide riboside daily. We speculate that individuals with bodyweights much higher than 72 kg might have benefited from higher doses of nicotinamide riboside to achieve a bodyweight-based dose similar to the rest of the cohort. Also, participants receiving combination therapy reported spending more time in discretionary exercise and physical activity, so they might have felt that they had more energy to participate meaningfully in exercise training, despite no change in self-reported fatigue.
Body composition changes could also contribute to the benefits observed.35 We did not detect changes in appendicular lean muscle mass, reflecting mostly skeletal muscle, from any intervention. However, changes might have been too small to be reliably detected using DXA over only 12 weeks, and could be discernible over longer interventions. As in our previous studies,36, 37 mean appendicular lean mass index, an index of skeletal muscle mass, was well below population reference values for age and sex. As expected, lean mass was also related to exercise capacity in Friedreich's ataxia. In exploratory analyses, nicotinamide riboside alone led to a decrease in both visceral fat and fat mass index, similar to effects observed for both nicotinamide riboside and niacin in previous studies and to the decrease in liver fat observed in adults with mitochondrial myopathy taking niacin.12 Thus, nicotinamide riboside could improve skeletal muscle quality indirectly by decreasing muscle fat infiltration, a possibility not directly assessed.
In mouse models of Friedreich's ataxia, treatment with either nicotinamide riboside or nicotinamide mononucleotide prolongs survival and improves cardiac phenotypes.15 Increased glutathione, suggestive of increased antioxidant capacity, was identified as one possible mechanism of benefit from NAD+ precursors.15 Although not assayed here, increased antioxidant capacity might also explain the benefits reported in the current trial. Interestingly, omaveloxolone, the Nrf2 activator FDA-approved for use in humans with Friedreich's ataxia, might also act by decreasing excess oxidant burden.38
Our study has several limitations. First, since Friedreich's ataxia is a rare disorder, our sample was not sufficiently large to permit well-powered subgroup analyses. Larger treatment groups might have been better able to detect differences between the effects of interventions. Also, to minimise duration and participant burden, our study design did not attempt to maximise NAD+ precursor dose. An individualised dose escalation phase, as has been proposed previously,33 might have permitted the use of higher doses and appreciation of even larger independent effects. We elected to use a dose low enough to avoid gastrointestinal effects in most participants and were successful in achieving excellent adherence and tolerability. Recumbent CPET was selected as a clinically relevant, reproducible outcome that would be sensitive to interventions.8 However, many individuals with more advanced Friedreich's ataxia do not have sufficient coordination to perform this testing, or the intervention, and thus results might not be generalisable across the range of disease severity. Future longer-term trials and specific data on NAD+ precursor supplementation use, exercise habits, and fitness from ongoing natural history studies will be needed to discern the persistence of any disease-modifying effects of these interventions.
In summary, in this randomised controlled trial in individuals with Friedreich's ataxia aged 10 to 40 years, the combination of NAD+ precursor supplementation and exercise training for 12 weeks produced a clinically relevant increase in cardiopulmonary fitness and led to other potential benefits on related measures. Overall, these interventions, alone and in combination, were safe and well-tolerated, and add to the growing body of evidence testing these innovative metabolic interventions in neurodegenerative and other conditions. Our trial results support the consideration of including exercise plus NAD+ precursor supplementation in investigations supporting a long-term, comprehensive approach to clinical management of individuals with Friedreich's ataxia.
