Survival in Brazilian Patients with Friedreich´s Ataxia

Abstract
Friedreich’s Ataxia (FRDA) is a progressive condition leading to reduced life expectancy in European/North American cohorts, but little is known about Latin American cohorts. Herein, we assessed FRDA survival data from a large Brazilian reference center (UNICAMP). We conducted a retrospective study including patients with FRDA followed at UNICAMP between 1998 and 2025. For those patients who died, we recorded age at death. For those alive or lost to follow-up, we considered the age at last visit. Potential prognostic markers (sex, age at onset, presence of cardiomyopathy and diabetes) were explored. Statistics was carried out using Kaplan-Meier curves and log-rank tests. We gathered information on 151 patients, 24 of which died (15.9%), 125 were still alive (82.7%) and 2 were lost to follow-up (1.3%). For those who died, the mean age at death was 33 ± 10.7 years. The cause of death was known for 12 out of the 24 patients: cardiac in 7, pulmonary in 3, diabetic ketoacidosis in 1 and sepsis in 1. Shorter life expectancy was found: in men relative to women (Mean age: 54.0 yo vs. 56.8 yo, p = 0.03), in patients with classical relative to late-onset (Mean age: 52.2 yo vs. 71.0 yo, p < 0.01) and in patients with cardiomyopathy relative to those without it (Mean age: 50.8 yo vs. 65.0 yo, p < 0.01). FRDA impacts life expectancy and death is primarily from cardiac and pulmonary causes. Male sex, early onset and presence of cardiomyopathy are negative survival prognostic markers.

Introduction
Friedreich’s ataxia (FRDA) is the leading cause of autosomal recessive ataxia worldwide. The estimated prevalence of the disease varies from 0.36 to 5 per 100,000 in different populations. It is caused by biallelic GAA repeat expansions in the first intron of the FXN gene, which leads to reduced expression of the Frataxin protein. Mitochondrial dysfunction then ensues causing cell death in multiple tissues, including the central as well as the peripheral nervous system, heart, and pancreas.

Disease manifestations may begin either in childhood or adolescence (age at onset < 25 years of age, in 80–85% of the patients, known as classical FRDA) or in adulthood (age at onset >25 years of age, in 15–20% of the patients, known as late onset FRDA – LOFA). Patients with FRDA present primarily neurological features which manifest through a mixed sensory and cerebellar ataxia, loss of proprioception, areflexia, dysarthria, abnormal saccadic eye movements and pyramidal signs. However, systemic features such as diabetes mellitus and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are frequent along the course of the disease, and both can lead to serious complications that might directly impact patients´ survival.

Previous European studies have indeed reported shortened life expectancy in patients with FRDA, with death typically occurring during the 3rd or 4th decades of life. Earlier age at onset and presence of cardiomyopathy were recognized as negative survival predictors in some of these reports. These data emphasize the huge impact that the disease poses to affected individuals, but they were essentially obtained in European and/or North American cohorts. To this date, little is known about FRDA-related survival in Latin America, a region where genetic background as well as medical care for ataxic individuals are strikingly different. So, we attempted to address this knowledge gap in the current study. Our primary goals were to estimate the survival rate in a cohort of Brazilian patients with long-term follow up and to assess the impact of potential prognostic factors.

Methods
Subjects’ Selection and Data Collection
This observational and retrospective study gathered all patients who had confirmed molecular diagnosis of FRDA and were followed at UNICAMP neurogenetics outpatient clinics from January 1998 to February 2025. The study was approved by our institution Research Ethics Committee under registration number CAAE 86939625.2.0000.5404. For those patients who were alive at the time of data collection, all data reported were collected after obtaining informed consent from patients and/or legal guardians. For those who had died, medical data retrieval was granted after an authorization was obtained from the Hospital Chief Medical Officer.

We systematically collected clinical and demographic data from the medical records of each enrolled patient, including sex assigned at birth. The primary outcome of interest was age at death. For those patients still alive or who were lost to follow-up, data were censored: we took into account the age in February 2025 or the age at the last visit, respectively. Survival was computed considering the time from disease onset and life expectancy was computed considering the time from birth (i.e., age). Cardiomyopathy and diabetes mellitus were explored as potential survival predictors. FRDA-related cardiomyopathy was defined as the presence of left ventricle hypertrophy and/or systolic dysfunction as seen in echocardiograms or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. Diabetes was defined according to the American Diabetes Association standard criteria: fasting glucose plasma levels ≥ 126 mg/dL, oral glucose tolerance test with glucose levels ≥ 200 mg/dL and glycated hemoglobin ≥ 6.5%. henever available, we also recorded information on the cause of death.

Statistical Analysis
Results were expressed with descriptive statistics: means, proportions and Standard Deviation (SD) for quantitative and categorical variables. We estimated survival/life expectancy and compared these parameters in the entire cohort and subgroups (with and without comorbidities, with and without diabetes, with and without cardiomyopathy, female vs. male, classical vs. LOFA) using the Kaplan–Meier method and log-rank statistics. We ran these statistical analyses in the software SYSTAT v13.0. Restricted mean survival analyses were later computed using the MedCalc software v.23.2.0 taking into account times from disease onset and the time point set at 25 years. For all comparisons, P-values < 0.05 were considered significant.

Results
From January 1998 to February 2025, we gathered information on 151 patients with FRDA regularly followed at UNICAMP (126 with classical onset and 25 with LOFA). Mean follow-up for this cohort was 9.6 ± 7.4 years. From those, 24 died in this period (15.9%), 125 were still alive (82.7%) and 2 were lost to follow-up (1.3%). More demographic and clinical details on the cohorts of patients who died and who were alive are provided in Table 1.

Table 1 Demographic and clinical data of enrolled patients stratified according to living status

For those 24 who died, the mean age at death was 33 ± 10.7 years. Considering decades of life, four died (16.6%) in the first decade, 6 (25%) in the second, 9 (37.5%) in the third, 2 (8.3%) in the fourth and 3 (12.5%) in the fifth decade or later. The cause of death was known for 12 out of the 24 patients: cardiac in 7, pulmonary in 3, diabetic ketoacidosis in 1 and sepsis in 1.

Survival results are shown in Fig. 1. Table 2 presents restricted mean survival analyses considering the time point of 25 years of disease duration. Considering the entire cohort, the overall cumulative 10-year survival rate was 97%. When we split patients into subgroups according to potential prognostic markers, distinct estimates were found. Indeed, shorter life expectancy was found: in men relative to women (Mean age: 54.0 yo vs. 56.8 yo, p = 0.03), in patients with classical relative to patients with LOFA FRDA (Mean age: 52.2 yo vs. 71.0 yo, p < 0.01) and in patients with cardiomyopathy relative to those without it (Mean age: 50.8 yo vs. 65.0 yo, p < 0.01). Although the presence of diabetes presented a statistically significant difference on life expectancy while compared with patients without it (Mean age: 49.7 yo vs. 64.1 yo, p = 0.02), it did not influence survival in this cohort when we looked at time from disease onset: (Mean duration: 36.3 y vs. 36.7 y, p = 0.43).

Discussion
This is the first study assessing survival in Brazilian patients with FRDA. Our neurogenetics center, established in 1998, was the first one to provide genetic testing for the disease in Brazil. So, it turned out to be a major reference center for FRDA in the country with many patients followed since then. Hence, the combination of a large cohort and a long-term follow-up put the neurogenetics center at UNICAMP in a favorable position to collect FRDA-related survival data. The mean age at death in our cohort was 33 years, which was slightly lower than that published in a recent multicentric European survey (39 years). Even though both cohorts had different sample sizes, the mean age at onset and the proportion of patients with classical/LOFA phenotypes were similar. So, it is rather unlikely that a selection bias could account for such survival difference. One potential explanation might be related either to environmental and/or genetic factors present in Brazilian patients that could potentially modulate the phenotype and aggravate disease progression. Alternatively, one may attribute reduced survival in Brazilian patients to the limited access to multidisciplinary care. For many years, only neurologists and clinical geneticists ran UNICAMP neurogenetics clinic. Cardiological and pulmonological appointments were carried out in our institution for some patients, but outside of it for others (those living far away from the center). In the end, the standards of care were rather different from patient to patient. This may have impacted survival because cardiac and pulmonary issues are the main causes of death in this population.

Cardiomyopathy was the main cause of death among our patients, accounting for almost 60% of those with known cause of death. This agrees with the reports from Indelicato et al. and Pousset et al.. These authors identified cardiac causes in 30% and 50% of deceased patients followed by them. Such data highlight the importance of timely detection and proper management of FRDA-related heart damage in these individuals. Pulmonary complications – including but not limited to aspiration pneumonia - come next as the 2nd cause of death not only in our survey, but also in the European publications (10,11). The proportion of pulmonary-related deaths in FRDA was slightly higher in our cohort (25%) compared to the European cohorts (6–11%). Such disproportion may be related to the pandemic, which took place between 2020 and 2023. Our data collection encompassed this period, whereas the European studies did not.

In our cohort, early onset and presence of cardiomyopathy were found to impact survival, which is in line with the results from the European survival study led by Indelicato et al.. Age at onset is a known marker of disease severity in FRDA and related to the extent of frataxin reduction. Cardiomyopathy may cause heart failure and/or the appearance of ‘malignant’ ventricular arrythmias, both of which may lead to death. Nevertheless, some of our results on survival prognostic markers contrast with those found in the European survey. Indeed, diabetes mellitus was found to be an independent survival predictor by Indelicato et al., but not in our study. We speculate that our study may have been underpowered to detect this association. Other discrepant result is sex, which we found to influence survival (meaning that women live longer than men with FRDA). Such association was not reported by the 3 large studies that investigated survival in European patients with FRDA. This seemingly specific Brazilian phenomenon admits at least 2 possible explanations. First, it is possible that local patients have specific genetic and/or environmental underpinnings, which may affect men disproportionately more than women with FXN expansions. An alternative reason is that such sex-related survival difference merely reflects the widely recognized survival advantage of women over men in the Brazilian population.

Some limitations of this study should be acknowledged. This is a survey whose data rely upon a large, but single center. Furthermore, data collection was retrospective, and some important data were missing for a reasonable proportion of patients (such as the GAA repeat length quantifications and the cause of death for those who died outside UNICAMP). So, we envisage the need for additional longitudinal and ideally multicentric initiatives to gather more accurate and current data on life expectancy in Brazilian individuals with FRDA. These new data become now increasingly critical as disease-modifying therapies are emerging for this degenerative condition.

In summary, we have shown that FRDA impacts life expectancy of affected Brazilian patients. On average, our patients died at an earlier age in comparison to European patients, but the reasons for such difference are not yet clear and deserve further investigation. These subjects die primarily of cardiac and pulmonary causes. Male sex, early onset and presence of cardiomyopathy are negative survival prognostic markers.
Targeting frataxin deficiency in DRG neurons and fibroblasts: omaveloxolone restores metabolic and iron balance to reduce ferroptosis

Abstract
Friedreich ataxia (FA) is a rare, multisystemic neurodegenerative disorder caused by a deficiency of the mitochondrial protein frataxin. It is characterized by degeneration of the large sensory neurons in the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) and spinocerebellar tracts, leading to progressive neurodegeneration and muscle weakness. Frataxin deficiency induces iron dyshomeostasis, defective energy production, and oxidative stress, all regulated by NRF2. Omaveloxolone, an NRF2 activator, is currently the only approved therapy for FA; however, its effects on DRG neurons remain unknown. Here we used frataxin-deficient DRG neurons to better understand the drug’s role in these sensory neurons. Omaveloxolone improved most of the analyzed parameters, including frataxin levels, cell survival, mitochondrial respiratory activity, iron homeostasis, oxidative stress, transferrin receptor 1 and glutathione peroxidase 4 levels, as well as the GSH/GSSG ratio. Moreover, lipid peroxidation, a key marker of ferroptosis that was increased in frataxin-deficient neurons, was almost completely rescued by omaveloxolone. Both total and nuclear NRF2 levels were decreased in frataxin-deficient neurons, and omaveloxolone treatment fully prevented this alteration. In addition, most of these results were validated in fibroblasts from FA patients. We also evaluated a combinatorial treatment using low doses of omaveloxolone together with honokiol, a SIRT3 activator with known neuroprotective properties. This combination enhanced cell survival and produced a synergistic effect increasing mitochondrial respiration in frataxin-deficient DRG neurons. In summary, these findings demonstrate the beneficial effects of omaveloxolone and further suggest that combination therapy with honokiol may provide an effective strategy for the treatment of FA, potentially mitigating adverse effects.

Keywords
Friedreich ataxiaomaveloxolonedorsal root gangliafibroblastsferroptosishonokiol
1. Introduction
Friedreich Ataxia (FA) is a rare (prevalence 1:25:000–1:50,000), inherited recessive disease first described by Nikolaus Friedreich in 1863. The clinical presentation is characterized as a progressive sensory neuropathy caused by dorsal root ganglionopathy which manifest as limb and gait ataxia. Additional features may include scoliosis, diabetes, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the latter being the main cause of death in FA patients. The disease is caused by mutations in FXN gene on chromosome 9, that results in decreased frataxin content or expression. In most patients, frataxin deficiency is caused by the homozygous GAA triplet expansion in the first intron of the FXN gene. Around 4 % of patients are compound heterozygotes for a GAA expansion and a FXN point/insertion/deletion mutation. Decreased expression of frataxin (remaining levels are 10–30 %) primarily affects the dorsal root ganglia (DRG), cerebellum, and heart. Frataxin is widely accepted to play a central role in the biosynthesis of iron–sulfur (Fe–S) clusters. However, it has also been involved in heme maturation, iron storage or detoxification and modulation of iron regulatory protein-1 activation (reviewed by Montfort el al.). Iron deposits or accumulation have been reported in the DRG,and in the myocardium,of FA mouse models. According to Koeppen, in patients with FA, total iron does not accumulate in any of the affected tissues. However, an apparent translocation of ferritin and ferroportin to perineuronal satellite cells in the DRG suggests iron dysmetabolism at the cellular level. In addition, cardiomyocytes from FA patients display characteristic Fe‑reactive inclusions. Indeed, frataxin deficiency causes mitochondrial iron dyshomeostasis, decreased content and/or function of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) components and oxidative stress, denoted by uncontrolled production of reactive oxygen species (ROS),,,,.
The transcription factor nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) controls the response of cells to oxidative injury by binding to antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoter of genes involved in the antioxidant defense, thereby increasing their transcription. Under most conditions, the ubiquitin-proteasome system degrades NRF2 through the E3 ligase Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1), but oxidative stress dissociates NRF2 from KEAP1, allowing NRF2 to enter the nucleus and activate the transcription of genes that encode proteins involved in the antioxidant response. Although oxidative stress induced by frataxin deficiency should activate NRF2, in most of the FA models, NRF2 activity is impaired,,,,. Such deficiency leads to decreased levels of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), which is regulated by NRF2. GPX4 plays a key role in reducing lipid peroxides in a glutathione-dependent manner and its impairment increased lipid peroxidation in FA,. All these alterations are hallmarks of ferroptosis, a regulated form of cell death triggered by the accumulation of lipid peroxidation products in membranes and determined by an iron-dependent ROS overload.
The NRF2 stabilizer called omaveloxolone (also known as RTA-408) is the first medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) to treat FA patients aged 16 years and older. This improves mitochondrial function, prevents lipid peroxidation, and ameliorates some clinical features of the disease,,,. However, its role in DRG sensory neurons, the cells that are affected the most and the earliest, is largely unknown. In addition, omaveloxolone treatment is not curative, and some adverse effects have been described,,.
Honokiol is a small-molecule polyphenol isolated from different species of the Magnolia genus. It exhibits anti-inflammatory, anti-tumor, anti-oxidative, and neuroprotective properties,,. Honokiol plays a key role in tissues like brain,and it has garnered attention in the prevention of multiple diseases, including neurodegenerative and cardiovascular diseases,,,. Although it probably might have multiple mechanisms of action, it is a well-known activator and inducer of SIRT3, a mitochondrial NAD-dependent protein deacetylase. SIRT3 targets include mitochondrial proteins involved in antioxidant activity, energy metabolism and mitochondrial dynamics. Increased acetylation in mitochondrial proteins has been described in a model of FA cardiomyopathy, and was associated with impaired mitochondrial fitness, altered lipid metabolism, and a decline in heart function as well as the development of steatosis and cardiac fibrosis.
In this study, we analyzed the effect of omaveloxolone in primary cultures of frataxin-deficient DRG sensory neurons, as well as fibroblasts from FA patients. Cell survival and parameters related to mitochondrial function and oxidative stress, including mitochondrial respiration, iron dyshomeostasis, several markers of ferroptosis, NRF2 levels and activation were analyzed. In addition, we evaluated the effect of combining lower doses of omaveloxolone with honokiol.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Animals
Female and male Sprague Dawley rats (RRID:RGD_70508) were maintained in a constant temperature of 20 °C, with food and water available ad libitum and with a 12-h photoperiod. Only neonatal rats were used and all experiments were performed according to the National Guidelines for the regulation of the use of experimental laboratory animals issued by the Generalitat de Catalunya and the Government of Spain (article 33.a 214/1997), which comply with the ARRIVE guidelines. All experimental protocols were approved by the Experimental Animal Ethical Committee of the University of Lleida (CEEA 02–01/24).
2.2. Cultures of primary neonatal rat DRG neurons, treatments and viability
Primary DRG neuronal cultures were established from P3–P4 neonatal Sprague Dawley rats following the purification protocol described by Sanz-Alcázar et al.. The ganglia (without the nerve roots) were dissociated by incubation in 0.025 % trypsin without EDTA in GHEBS (137 mM NaCl, 2.6 mM KCl, 25 mM glucose, 25 mM HEPES, 100 μg/mL penicillin/streptomycin) for 30 min. Ganglia were then gently disrupted using a pipette to obtain a single cell suspension in Neurobasal culture media (GIBCO, Cat# 21103049) enriched with 2 % horse serum (GIBCO, Cat# 16050–122), 2 % B27 Supplement (ThermoFisher Scientific, Cat#17504–044), 0.5 mM L-glutamine, 100 U/mL penicillin plus 100 ng/mL Streptomycin. Aphidicolin (Sigma–Aldrich, Cat# A0781) was added at a final concentration of 3.4 mg/mL to prevent the growth of non-neuronal cells and supplemented with 50 ng/mL murine β-nerve growth factor (PeproTech, Cat# 450–34) with 3 mg/mL DNAse I grade II (Roche, Cat# 104159). The cell suspension was centrifuged at 1300 rpm for 5 min with 7.5 % BSA solution (Sigma, Cat# A8412) to separate neurons from smaller non-neuronal cells. After 1 h of pre-plating in a p60 tissue dish at 37°C/5 %CO2, the cells were then plated in tissue dishes pre-treated with 0.1 mg/mL of collagen (Sigma, Cat# C7661–25) at a cell density of 14,000 cells/well. After 1–2 days, lentivirus transduction was performed with shRNA sequences targeting frataxin mRNA. The shRNA lentiviral plasmids (pLKO.1-puro) for human/mouse/rat frataxin were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. The RefSeq used was NM-008044, which corresponds to mouse frataxin. The clones used were TRCN0000197534 and TRCN0000006137 (here referred to as FXN1, FXN2). FXN1: 5′-CCGGCAAACTGGACTTGTCTTCATTCTCGAGAATGAAGACAAGTCCAGTTTGTTTTTTG-3’; FXN2: 5′-CCGGGCAGACGCCAAACAAGCAAATCTCGAGATTTGCTTGTTTGGCGTCTGCTTTTT-3’. The vector SHC002, a non-targeted scrambled sequence (Scr), served as a control. Scr: 5′-CCGGCAACAAGATGAAGAGCACCAACTCGAGTTGGTGCTCTTCATCTTGTTGTTTTT-3’. Lentivirus particles (20 ng/1000 cells) were added and replaced 6 h later with new medium containing dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, vehicle) or 50 nM omaveloxolone. Concentration of omaveloxolone was selected based on values previously reported to be effective in in vitro models of FA,,. In combinatorial treatments, omaveloxolone and honokiol were used at the indicated concentrations. All experiments were conducted 5 days after lentivirus transduction.
Neuronal survival was measured with a 16 × objective lens and cross-marked wells as described previously,and expressed as the percentage of neurons counted after 5 days with respect to the initial value (100 %). Cellular viability was also measured by the 3-(4, 5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2, 5-diphenyltetrazoliumbromide (MTT) assay (ref. M5655, Sigma-Aldrich,) as described.
2.3. Cultures of human fibroblasts and treatments
Human skin fibroblasts were obtained from both Dr. Marek Napierala (Department of Neurology, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center), and Innoprot (Parque Tecnológico Bizkaia, Spain). They were from 3 controls and 3 FA patients. Controls: i) 45-years-old male (ref. 6718); ii) 22-years-old female (ref. 6719); iii) 22-years-old female (ref. 231218). Patients: i) 35-years-old male, age of onset 8 years old, and GAA repeats 622/738 (ref. 21); ii) 21-years-old female, age of onset 7 years old, GAA repeats 570/1200 (ref. 40); iii) 21-years-old female, age of onset 14, and GAA repeats 581/1069 (ref. 4758). They were cultured in a 5 % CO2 atmosphere at 37°C, with Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) (GIBCO, ref. 11965–092) supplemented with 10 % fetal bovine serum (GIBCO, ref. A5256701), 1 % non-essential amino acids (GIBCO, ref. 11140–050) and 1 % penicillin/streptomycin (GIBCO, ref. P4458). Cells were treated with either DMSO (vehicle) or 50 nM omaveloxolone for 24 h, except in experiments measuring mitochondrial respiration, which were conducted 5 days post-treatment.
2.4. Mitochondrial respiration
The oxygen consumption rate (OCR) of cell cultures was measured using the Seahorse XFp Cell Mito Stress Test Kit (ref. 103010–100, Agilent) using the Seahorse XFp Analyzer (Agilent) following the manufacturer’s protocol, with some modifications. DRG neurons were plated at 14,000 cells/well, while fibroblasts were plated at 40,000 cells/well. The next day, vehicle or omaveloxolone was added, and the OCR measured after 5 days. One hour before the assay, the culture medium was changed to DMEM, pH 7.4 with 2 mM glutamine, 1 mM pyruvate, and 10 mM glucose. The plates were placed in a 37°C non-CO2 incubator, and the OCR were measured. Mitochondrial function was assessed using a sequential injection of oligomycin (1.5 μM), FCCP (3.0 μM for DRG neurons and 2.0 µM for fibroblasts), and rotenone-antimycin A (0.5 μM).
2.5. Western blotting
To perform western blot analysis, homogenates from either fibroblasts or primary neuronal cultures were obtained. After drug treatment, cells were lysed with 2 % sodium dodecyl sulphate (SDS), 125 mM Tris-HCl pH 6.8 and protease (Roche, ref. 04 693 159 001) and phosphatase (Roche, ref. 04 906 837 011) inhibitor cocktails. Then, the samples were treated with high-frequency sound waves generated by an ultrasonic bath and incubated at 95°C for 5 min. The protein concentration was quantified by Micro-BCA Protein Assay Kit (ref. 23235, Thermo Scientific) for DRG samples, and the Pierce BSA Protein Assay Kit for fibroblasts samples (ref.23227, Thermo Scientific). The samples (7–10 μg of protein) were subjected to SDS–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, then transferred to polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes and incubated with I-Block (ref. T2015, Thermo Scientific) to block nonspecific protein binding. Nitrocellulose membranes were used to detect frataxin. The following primary antibodies were used: frataxin (1:500; ref. Ab219414, Abcam), OXPHOS (1:20,000 to detect complexes III, IV, and V, and 1:4000 to detect complexes I and II; ref. 458,099, Invitrogen), GPX4 (1:500; ref. sc-166570, Santa Cruz), NRF2 (1:1000; ref. ab62352, Abcam). After blotting, the membranes were stained with Coomassie brilliant blue (CBB). The total protein stained was quantified with the Image Lab software (Bio-Rad) and used as loading control for normalization of the target proteins.
2.6. Oxidative stress analysis: Mitochondrial superoxide, mitochondrial iron, and lipid peroxidation
In both fibroblasts and DRG neuronal cultures, mitochondrial superoxide levels and mitochondrial ferrous ion (Fe2 +) content were quantified with the fluorescent probes MitoSOX Red (ThermoFisher, M36008) and Mito-FerroGreen (Dojindo, M489–10), respectively. To quantify lipid peroxidation in DRG neurons, BODIPY™ 581/591 C11 (D3861, Thermo Scientific) was used. All probes were used according to the manufacturers’ instructions. Human-derived fibroblasts were seeded onto an M6 plate and after 24 h of treatment, the cells were washed 3 times with PBS, trypsinized and collected in Hank’s buffered saline solution (HBSS) with 10 mM HEPES medium. Cells were then incubated at 37ºC with 10 μM Mito-Ferro Green (30 min) or 10 μM MitoSOX Red (15 min) and analysed by flow cytometry. Rat DRG neurons were plated in ibiTreat 4-well m-slides (ref. 80426, Ibidi) pre-treated with 0.1 mg/mL of collagen. Five days after lentiviral transduction and treatment, DRG neurons were washed once with Hank’s balanced salt solution (HBSS) with 10 mM HEPES, incubated at 37ºC either with 2.5 μM Mito-Ferro Green (30 min), 5 μM MitoSOX Red (15 min), or 10 µM BODIPY™ C11 581/591 (30 min). Following incubation, the neurons were washed, and images were captured with a confocal microscope (FV1000, Olympus) with a 60 × objective and using the Z stack configuration. For each probe, all images were acquired with the same laser intensity. The images were analyzed with the FIJI analysis software and fluorescence quantification was performed as described below (Section 2.7). In fibroblasts, lipid peroxidation was analyzed by measuring malondialdehyde (MDA), a compound derived from the peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids. To do that, the MDA Assay Kit (Assay Genie, ref. MAES0041) was used. Cells were seeded onto M6 plate, and the manufacturer’s protocol was followed. The results were obtained using a microplate reader.
2.7. Immunofluorescence, image acquisition, and analysis
For both fibroblasts and DRG neurons, the cells were initially plated on glass coverslips (ref. CB00120RA020MNZ0, Epredia) coated with collagen and subsequently seeded in 4-well-plates with the appropriate culture medium. After drug treatment, the cells were fixed with a 4 % paraformaldehyde (PFA) and cold methanol. A 0.5 % Triton X-100 solution in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) was used to permeabilize the cells then were incubated with a blocking buffer containing 5 % bovine serum albumin (BSA) and 0.5 % Triton X-100 in PBS. The cells were incubated with the primary antibodies —TFR1 (1:100, Invitrogen, ref. 13–6800) and NRF2 (1:100, AbCam, ref. ab62352)— overnight at 4°C. After, the cells were incubated with the secondary antibody—goat anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 594 (1:400; ref. A11012, Invitrogen) or goat anti-mouse Alexa Fluor 488 (1:400; ref. A11017, Invitrogen) for 1 h at room temperature in the dark. Nuclear localization was visualized using Hoechst stain (1:400). Olympus FV1000 laser-scanning confocal microscope was used with a 60 × objective for DRG neurons and with a 20 × objective for fibroblasts, using the Z stack configuration. Fluorescence intensity was quantified using FIJI analysis software.
For DRG, analyses were performed on 3 independent cultures. For each culture, 4–8 images from different areas were taken, and each image contained between 5 and 15 DRG neurons. Thus, 30–150 cells were analyzed per culture, resulting in a total of 90–300 cells per condition. For each experiment, all images were acquired using the same laser intensity. Background fluorescence was subtracted for each image. Fluorescence intensity was quantified by delineating the entire neuron, and a mean value per independent culture was obtained. The average of the three mean values from the Scr cultures (treated with vehicle) was normalized to 1, and values for all other conditions and treatments were adjusted accordingly. When nuclear–cytosolic separation was performed, the nuclear area was delineated to obtain nuclear intensity; cytosolic intensity was calculated by subtracting the nuclear area from the total cellular area. For fibroblasts, 4 independent cultures were analyzed to quantify TFR1, with 30–40 cells examined per experiment, totaling 120–160 cells per condition. Normalization was performed as described above for DRG.
2.8. Determination of reduced glutathione (GSH) and oxidized glutathione (GSSG)
To quantify GSH, GSSG, and the GSH/GSSG ratio, the GSH/GSSG-Glo™ Assay (ref. V6612, Promega) was used. Cells were were seeded in a 96-well white plate (ref. 33696, SPL) pre-treated with 0.1 mg/mL of collagen, and the assay was performed following the manufacturer’s instructions. For each experimental condition, two wells were used: one for total gluthathione (GSx) and another for GSSG. A standard curve was constructed to determine the GSH concentration in each sample. The plate was read using the ChemiDoc instrument to detect chemiluminescence. The data were normalized based on the protein concentration.
2.9. Statistical analysis
All data are expressed as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Data normality was evaluated using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Comparisons between two groups were performed using Student’s t-test for normally distributed data, while one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was applied for comparisons among multiple groups. For data not conforming to a normal distribution, the Kruskal–Wallis test followed by Dunn’s multiple comparison test was employed. Representative images presented in the figures were selected to reflect the average values observed within each group. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. All analyses and graphical representations were generated using GraphPad Prism version 9.0 (GraphPad Software, Inc., La Jolla, CA, USA).
3. Results
3.1. Omaveloxolone enhances frataxin expression and mitochondrial respiration and reduces frataxin depletion-induced cell death
To evaluate how omaveloxolone treatment improves cellular alterations caused by frataxin deficiency, we used two cellular models: (i) primary cultures of frataxin-deficient DRG neurons and, (ii) human fibroblasts from FA patients. Since one of the earliest targets in FA are the DRG sensory neurons, we analyzed the effects of 50 nM omaveloxolone on neonatal rat DRG neurons transduced with lentiviral vectors carrying frataxin-interfering shRNA (FXN1 or FXN2) or a non-interfering shRNA (Scr) as a control,. Using this model, as previously shown,,,, frataxin levels began to decline at 24 h after transduction. Using the cross-marked well methodology, we found that, at the end of the experiment (5 days after transduction), the mean frataxin level in FXN1 and FXN2 was 50 % and 20 %, respectively (Fig. 1A and B). Omaveloxolone treatment almost fully prevented the reduction in frataxin levels in FXN1 neurons, and there was a tendency for frataxin levels to increase in FXN2 neurons (Fig. 1A and B). Omaveloxolone concentration was chosen at 50 nM because it is within the range of concentrations reported to be effective in cellular models,,,. Cell viability was analyzed 5 days after lentivirus transduction in Scr and frataxin-deficient FXN1 and FXN2 cells and the effect of drug treatment (Fig. 1 C). As shown in Fig. 1D, frataxin-deﬁcient neurons showed, as expected, a signiﬁcant decrease in viability compared with control neurons (48 % and 39 % cell survival in FXN1 and FXN2 cells, respectively). Omaveloxolone increased FXN1 neuronal survival to 74 %. However, the increase in FXN2 was not statistically significant, but it showed a tendency, consistent with its effect on frataxin levels. Cell viability was also assessed by the MTT assay and, in agreement with the cross-marked well methodology, FXN1 neurons showed decreased viability which was rescued by omaveloxolone (Fig. 1E).
Fig. 1. Omaveloxolone recovers frataxin deficiency, cell viability and mitochondrial respiration in frataxin-deficient DRG neurons. Scr, FXN1, and FXN2 cells were treated with DMSO (vehicle, V), or omaveloxolone (OMAV, O). (A and B) Western blotting was used to analyze frataxin levels. Representative images are shown; CBB staining was used as a loading control. The histogram presents the mean ± SEM from n = 4–5 independent cultures. (C and D) Representative images obtained by inverted microscopy of the same microscopy ﬁelds at 0 and 5 days after lentivirus transduction are shown (C). Scale bar: 10 µm. The data are presented as the mean ± SEM from n = 2–4 independent isolations. Between 3 and 4 fields were analyzed in each condition and experiment. Each biological replicate is color coded (day to day variability), small symbols represent experimental replicates the big symbols are the mean of each culture. (E) MTT assay was used to determine viability of Scr and FXN1 cells. The data are presented as the mean ± SEM from n = 6 independent isolations. (F and G) Mitochondrial respiration (OCR) analysis of Scr versus FXN1 neurons (F), and Scr versus FXN2 neurons (G). Significant differences are indicated: FXN1 or FXN2 vehicle versus Scr vehicle (*); FXN1 OMAV versus FXN1 vehicle ($); (H-J) Basal respiration, ATP-linked respiration production, maximal respiration, and spare capacity were obtained from F and G for Scr (H), FXN1 (I), and FXN2 (J) cells. The data are presented as the mean ± SEM from n = 3–4 independent cultures. Significant differences between conditions are indicated (p values < 0.05(*), 0.01(**), or 0.001(***)).

It is well described that mitochondrial respiration is impaired in FA, either in cellular and animal models of FA, as well as in tissues from patients with FA,,,,. In frataxin-deficient DRG neurons, we previously described a reduction in ATP-linked respiration, maximal respiration, and spare capacity compared with non-interfering shRNA (Scr),. To study how efficiently omaveloxolone could recover such mitochondrial alterations, the Oxygen Consumption Rate (OCR) was analyzed in FXN1 and FXN2 neurons after omaveloxolone treatment and compared it in Scr neurons (Fig. 1 F and G). While no significant differences were observed in Scr cells by omaveloxolone treatment (Fig. 1 H), in FXN1 neurons, the drug increased the basal, maximal and spare capacity to the levels found in Scr cells (Fig. 1I). In FXN2 cells, omaveloxolone increased these parameters, but the results were statistically significant only in the ATP-linked respiration (Fig. 1 J).
To analyze whether such deficiencies in their activities can be totally or partially attributed to decreased protein levels, selected proteins from each mitochondrial complex were analyzed in untreated versus treated cells. NDUFB8 (complex I) and SDHB (complex II) were decreased in frataxin-deficient neurons compared with their controls, while there were no differences in UQCR2 (complex III), MTCO1 (complex IV), and ATP5A (complex V), consistent with our previous findings,. Omaveloxolone treatment resulted in increased levels of NDUFB8 and SDHB; however, these changes did not reach statistical significance. Notably, ATP5A expression was significantly elevated by omaveloxolone (Supplementary Fig. S1). Collectively, these findings indicate that the drug enhances mitochondrial respiration, most likely through a combination of increasing the protein abundance of existing complexes and improving their activity and efficiency.
To validate such results in human cells, fibroblasts from FA patients were cultured and compared with healthy controls. We first checked the frataxin levels in human fibroblasts by western blotting. Although frataxin levels showed some variability within individuals (Supplementary Fig. S2), in average, fibroblasts from FA patients had 10 % of control frataxin levels (Fig. 2A and B). As shown in Fig. 2B no significant differences were observed in frataxin levels after omaveloxolone treatment, neither in control nor in patient’ fibroblasts. It has been published that mitochondrial respiration is decreased in FA fibroblasts,. Thus, we studied cellular respiration and the effect of the drug in our patient-derived fibroblasts using Seahorse technology (Fig. 2 C to G). Using these data, basal respiration, ATP-linked respiration, maximal respiration and spare capacity, all decreased in FA fibroblasts compared to control fibroblasts, although only maximal respiration and spare capacity were statistically significant (Fig. 2D). Omaveloxolone treatment did not affected OCR from control fibroblasts (Fig. 2E and F), while in patients’ fibroblasts, maximal respiration was increased compared with vehicle-treated fibroblasts (Fig. 2E and G).
Fig. 2. Omaveloxolone recovers mitochondrial respiration in fibroblasts from FA patients but does not increase frataxin levels. Fibroblast cultures from healthy individuals and FA patients were treated with DMSO (vehicle, V), or omaveloxolone (OMAV, O). Western blotting was used to analyze the indicated proteins. Representative images are shown; CBB protein staining was used as a loading control. (A and B) Western blotting for mature frataxin from two control and two FA patients. The histogram presents the mean ± SEM of n = 10–12 independent cultures. (C and D) Mitochondrial stress analysis of control and patient’s fibroblasts (C). Basal respiration, ATP production, maximal respiration rate, and spare capacity from n = 7 independent cultures (D). (E to G) Mitochondrial stress analysis after drug treatment of control and patient’s fibroblasts (E). Basal respiration, ATP production, maximal respiration rate, and spare capacity were obtained from n = 4–5 independent cultures of control (F) and FA patients (G). (H to J) Indicated proteins of the mitochondrial OXPHOS system were analyzed by western blotting (H). Histograms represent the mean ± SEM between control and patient’s fibroblasts from n = 3–6 independent experiments (I). Histograms represent the mean ± SEM between fibroblast cultures treated with drugs from n = 5–7 independent experiments (J). Significant differences between control and patient’s fibroblasts are indicated (p values < 0.05(*), 0.01(**), or 0.001(***)).

Proteins from each mitochondrial complex were analyzed by western blotting in fibroblasts from patients and controls (Fig. 2 H). Cell extracts of FA-derived fibroblasts showed a 34 % reduction in NDUFB8 (complex I) and 25 % reduction in both SDHB (complex II) and MTCO1 (complex IV) protein levels compared to control cells (Fig. 2I). Treatment with omaveloxolone was able to completely prevent the decrease in SDHB (complex II). A 10 % increase in MTCO1 (complex IV) was observed in omaveloxolone-treated fibroblasts from FA patients, but no changes were observed in NDUFB8 (complex I). Interestingly, a 22 % increase in ATP5A (complex V) were found after omaveloxolone addition (Fig. 2 J). No significant differences were observed in control fibroblasts treated with omaveloxolone (Supplementary Fig. S3).
3.2. Omaveloxolone alleviates disturbances in iron homeostasis and reduces oxidative stress in frataxin-deficient cells
One of the main and well-known biomarkers in FA is iron dysregulation. To explore whether omaveloxolone could ameliorate these alterations, we quantify intramitochondrial Fe2+ with confocal microscopy after labelling frataxin-deficient DRG sensory neurons with Mito-Ferro Green (Fig. 3A). In agreement with our previous results, quantification of green fluorescence showed 2.2 and 2.4-fold ferrous accumulation in FXN1 and FXN2 cells, respectively, compared to Scr cells (Fig. 3B). Omaveloxolone treatment restored mitochondrial Fe2+ in both FXN1 and FXN2 close to the normal levels found in vehicle-treated Scr cultures (Fig. 3B). Such increase in ferrous iron inside the mitochondria in frataxin-deficient cells can promote superoxide generation and oxidative stress in this organelle. Using the fluorescent probe MitoSox Red, increased mitochondrial superoxide levels were observed in FXN1 and FXN2 neurons (Fig. 3 C). Quantification of red fluorescence showed a 2.3 and 2.4-fold increase in mitochondrial superoxide anion in FXN1 and FXN2 cells compared to Scr cells (Fig. 3D). Omaveloxolone was able to fully prevent superoxide levels accumulation in FXN1 neurons and partially in FXN2 neurons (Fig. 3D).
Fig. 3. Omaveloxolone reduced oxidative stress and iron alterations in frataxin-deficient primary DRG neurons. Scr, FXN1, and FXN2 cells were treated with DMSO (vehicle) or omaveloxolone (OMAV). Representative Z-stack images obtained with confocal microscopy are shown. (A and B) Mitochondrial Fe2 + staining with MitoFerro Green probe. Scale bar: 10 μm. The data are presented as the mean ± SEM from n = 3 independent isolations. Between 90 and 180 cells were analyzed in each condition. (C and D) Mitochondrial superoxide levels were analyzed using MitoSox Red. Scale bar: 10 µm. The data are presented as the mean ± SEM from n = 3 independent isolations. Between 90 and 180 cells were analyzed in each condition. (E and F) TFR1 was analyzed by immunofluorescence staining. Scale bar: 10 μm. The data are presented as the mean ± SEM from n = 3 independent isolations. Between 90 and 180 cells were analyzed in each condition. In B, D, and F, each biological replicate is color coded (day to day variability), small symbols represent experimental replicates, and the big symbols are the mean of each culture. Significant differences between conditions are indicated (p values < 0.05(*), 0.01(**), or 0.001(***)).

This increase in iron can be attributed to several factors. The upregulation of the TFR1, the main protein involved in cellular iron uptake has been described in cellular and animal models of FAas well as in human FA fibroblasts. Because TFR1 upregulation may explain iron accumulation, this receptor was analyzed by immunohistochemistry in Scr, FXN1 and FXN2 neurons (Fig. 3E). Quantification revealed that TFR1 levels increased by 2.2-fold in FXN1 neurons and by 2.6-fold in FXN2 neurons, relative to Scr controls (Fig. 3 F). Omaveloxolone was able to fully prevent TFR1 increase in FXN1 and FXN2 neurons (Fig. 3 F).
In cultured fibroblasts, intramitochondrial Fe2+ was quantified by flow cytometry using the fluorescent probe Mito-Ferro Green. The results showed a 1.45-fold increase in FA fibroblasts compared to controls (Fig. 4A), in accordance with published results. Omaveloxolone treatment decreased mitochondrial Fe2+ in patients’ fibroblasts by 25 % but the difference was not statistically significant (Fig. 4A). Mitochondrial iron reduction upon omaveloxolone treatment was also observed by confocal microscopy after cell labelling with Mito-Ferro Green (Fig. 4B). Excess of ferrous iron can promote oxidative stress inside the mitochondria of FA fibroblasts. Using the fluorescent dye MitoSox Red, we measured, by flow cytometry, mitochondrial superoxide levels (Fig. 4 C). As shown, fibroblasts from patients exhibited elevated mitochondrial superoxide levels compared with control fibroblasts. However, omaveloxolone treatment did not result in significant differences. We analyzed the levels of TFR1 in control and FA fibroblasts, as well as the effects of drug treatment, using immunohistochemistry (Fig. 4D). Quantification revealed a 1.45-fold increase in TFR1 in FA-derived fibroblasts compared to controls. Treatment with omaveloxolone reduced TFR1 to control levels in FA fibroblasts, while no significant effect was observed in control fibroblasts (Fig. 4E). Collectively, these findings indicate that alterations in iron metabolism are more pronounced in DRG neurons than in fibroblasts, potentially contributing to the heightened vulnerability of frataxin-deficient neurons. In this context, omaveloxolone may exert a neuroprotective effect.
Fig. 4. Omaveloxolone reduced iron alterations in fibroblasts from FA patients. Fibroblast cultures from healthy individuals and FA patients were treated with DMSO (vehicle), or omaveloxolone (OMAV). (A) Mitochondrial Fe2 + content was analyzed by flow cytometry with the MitoFerro Green probe. Data are mean ± SEM obtained from n = 7 independent cultures. (B) Representative Z-stack images from fibroblasts, obtained by confocal microscopy after mitochondrial Fe2 + staining with Mito-FerroGreen. Scale bar: 10 μm. (C) Mitochondrial superoxide content was analyzed by flow cytometry with the MitoSox Red probe. Data are mean ± SEM obtained from n = 6 independent cultures. (D and E) TFR1 was analyzed by immunofluorescence staining of fibroblast cultures. Scale bar: 10 μm. The data are presented as the mean ± SEM of n = 4 independent cultures. In E, each biological replicate is color-coded (day to day variability), small symbols represent experimental replicates, and the big symbols are the mean of each culture. Between 30 and 40 cells were analyzed in each experiment. Significant differences between control and patient’s fibroblasts are indicated (p values < 0.05(*), 0.01(**), or 0.001(***)).

3.3. Omaveloxolone reduces ferroptotic markers in frataxin-deficient cells
Ferroptosis has been proposed to play a role in several models of FA,,,, including fibroblasts obtained from patients,. Lipid peroxidation plays a pivotal role in mediating ferroptotic cell death and arises from iron-induced oxidative stress combined with dysfunction of the GSH–GPX4 antioxidant system. GSH is essential for GPX4 activity, which catalyzes the reduction of lipid peroxides to their corresponding lipid alcohols.
To assess to what extent omaveloxolone could rescue the changes observed by frataxin deficiency in primary cultures of DRG neurons, first, GPX4 levels were analyzed by western blotting (Fig. 5A). The quantification showed decreased GPX4 levels in frataxin-deficient neurons compared to Scr neurons in agreement with published results. Treatment with omaveloxolone fully prevented this reduction (Fig. 5B). The analysis of the redox state showed decreased levels of reduced GSH in FXN1 and FXN2 cells compared with Scr cells; however, the drug was not able to reverse such decrease (Fig. 5 C). Compared to Scr cells, GSSG was slightly increased in FXN1 and reduced in FXN2 cells. Omaveloxolone treatment significantly reduced GSSG in Scr neurons, but the decrease in FXN1 and FXN2 neurons did not reach a statistically significant effect (Fig. 5D). More important, the GSH/GSSG ratio decreased by approximately 40 % and 55 % in FXN1 and FXN2 cells, respectively, compared with Scr cells. Treatment with omaveloxolone fully restored such ratio to the control levels in both FXN1 and FXN2 cells (Fig. 5E). GSx in FXN1 and FXN2 neurons was lower compared to Scr neurons; however, the drug could not restore this alteration (Supplementary Fig. S4). This indicates that the positive effect of the treatment on the GSH/GSSG ratio is probably due to the decrease in oxidative stress, which would reduce GSSG levels.
Fig. 5. Omaveloxolone prevents the increase in ferroptotic markers in frataxin-deficient primary DRG neurons. Scr, FXN1, and FXN2 cells were treated with DMSO (vehicle, V) or omaveloxolone (OMAV, O). (A and B) GPX4 levels were analyzed by western blotting. Representative images are shown; CBB protein staining was used as a loading control. The histogram presents the mean ± SEM of n = 5–6 independent cultures. (C, D and E) GSH, GSSG, and the GSH/GSSG ratio were measured. The histograms present the mean ± SEM of n = 3–4 independent cultures. (F and G) Lipid peroxidation was analyzed with BODIPY™ C11 581/591. Green shows oxidized BODIPY C11 and red shows reduced BODIPY C11. Scale bar: 10 µm. The data are presented as the mean ± SEM of n = 3 independent isolations. Between 60 and 80 cells were analyzed for each culture. Each biological replicate is color coded (day to day variability), small symbols represent individual neurons that were analyzed, and the big symbols are the mean of each culture. Significant differences between conditions are indicated (p values < 0.05(*), 0.01(**), or 0.001(***)).

Because of the reduction in both GPX4 levels and GSH/GSSG ratio, we assessed cellular lipid oxidation in the DRG neurons by using BODIPY C11 581/591 (Fig. 5 F). Frataxin-deficient neurons showed increased green fluorescence indicative of lipid peroxidation. Based on quantification, the ratio of oxidized to reduced Bodipy C11 was increased by 2.2- and 3.4-fold in FXN1 and FXN2 cells, respectively, compared with Scr cells (Fig. 5 G). Lipid peroxidation was partially reduced after treatment with omaveloxolone, with a decrease of 40 % and 60 % in FXN1 and FXN2 neurons, respectively, compared with their controls (Fig. 5 G). Taken together, these data clearly indicate that, in our model, omaveloxolone rescued the analyzed ferroptosis markers.
In FA fibroblasts, GPX4 levels were found decreased compared to control fibroblasts (Fig. 6A and B). When treated with omaveloxolone, fibroblasts from patients increased GPX4 levels with respect to vehicle-treated fibroblasts, although the results did not reach statistical significance (Fig. 6B). We then measured GSH, GSSG and the ratio GSH/GSSG in FA fibroblasts (vehicle or omaveloxolone treated) and compared them to their respective controls (Fig. 6C-E). No significant differences were found in GSH levels among cultures (Fig. 6 C); however, GSSG levels were increased in FA fibroblasts, probably due to the oxidative stress situation. Treatment with omaveloxolone normalized GSSG to control levels (Fig. 6D). In accordance, the cellular redox state, measured by the ratio GSH/GSSG was decreased in patients’ fibroblasts and such reduction was reversed after drug treatment (Fig. 6E). GSx showed no differences between control and patients’ fibroblasts, and no effect was observed after omaveloxolone treatment (Supplementary Fig. S5). We analyzed lipid peroxidation by measuring malondialdehyde (MDA), a compound derived from the peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids. As shown in Fig. 6 F, MDA levels showed a 1.9-fold increase in FA fibroblasts compared to controls. FA cells treated with omaveloxolone showed reduced MDA levels, comparable to those observed in control cells.
Fig. 6. Effect of omaveloxolone in ferroptotic markers in fibroblasts from FA patients. Fibroblast cultures from healthy individuals and FA patients were analyzed. Cells were treated with DMSO (vehicle, V) or omaveloxolone (OMAV, O). (A and B) Western blotting for GPX4. Representative images are shown; CBB protein staining was used as a loading control. The histogram presents the mean ± SEM of n = 6–12 independent cultures. (C, D and E) GSH, GSSG and the GSH/GSSG ratio were measured; the histograms present the mean ± SEM of n = 6–12 independent cultures. (F) Lipid peroxidation was analyzed as MDA content. Data are mean ± SEM obtained from n = 3–5 independent cultures. Significant differences between different conditions are indicated (p values <0.05(*), 0.01(**) or 0.001(***)).

3.4. Omaveloxolone prevents NRF2 impairment in frataxin-deficient cells
NRF2 is the main transcription factor that regulates cytoprotective responses to ferroptotic damage as well as oxidative stress and its response has been impaired in several models of FA,,,,. First, we measured total NRF2 levels in cultured DRG neurons by the western blot. The results showed that total NRF2 amount was decreased, with a 50 % and 80 % reduction in FXN1 and FXN2 cells, respectively (Fig. 7A and B), in agreement with our previous publications,. Omaveloxolone was able to fully prevent the decay of NRF2 in FXN1 neurons, and a tendency to increase was observed in FXN2 neurons (Fig. 7B). Because NRF2 is regulated by nuclear/cytosolic localization, we analyze it by confocal microscopy (Fig. 7 C). Consistent with the western blotting results, we found a decrease in total NRF2 in FXN1 and FXN2 cells compared to Scr cells (Fig. 7D). These results are in agreement our previous findings,and those from DRG isolated from the YG8R mouse model. Omaveloxolone treatment did significantly increase total NRF2 levels in Scr, FXN1, and FXN2 neurons in a similar manner (Fig. 7D). There were similar results regarding cytosolic NRF2 (Fig. 7E). Active nuclear NRF2 decreased by 50 % and 55 % in FXN1 and FXN2 cells, respectively, compared with Scr cells. The drug increased nuclear NRF2 to levels above the vehicle-treated Scr (Fig. 7 F). Because both nuclear and cytosolic NRF2 showed similar patterns, there were no differences in the nuclear-to-cytosolic ratio (Supplementary Fig. S6).

Fig. 7. Role of omaveloxolone in NRF2 dysregulation in frataxin-deficient cells. (A-F) Scr, FXN1, and FXN2 cells were treated with DMSO (vehicle, V) or omaveloxolone (OMAV, O). (A and B) Western blotting for NRF2. Representative images are shown; CBB protein staining was used as a loading control. The histogram presents the mean ± SEM of n = 4–6 independent cultures. Each biological replicate is color coded (day to day variability), small symbols represent individual neurons that were analyzed and the big symbols are the mean of each culture.
